descs.en: He forgot to thank her. She sat on his desk until he looked up. Ten minutes, every night at nine, until Lima needed her more.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Inspector Song Wei Long is collecting an extradited fraudster at the airport when the paperwork collapses, in a language nobody at the custody desk speaks. A Canadian consular officer in a soaked coat fixes it in three languages in eleven minutes. He says Correct, and forgets to thank her. She leaves a card under his windscreen wiper to tell him so.

A week later she’s sitting on his desk at nine at night, on top of his files, telling him the world can wait ten minutes. It does. Then a body comes out of the harbour, he fires his gun in a stairwell, and Isla is offered the posting she has wanted for years: three years in Lima, thirteen hours away.

The man who has never asked anyone for anything has to learn to say go, and mean it. And then, when the ground moves, to get on a plane.

She sits on his desk · Stoic hero · Long distance · Complete in four volumes, plus ten side stories

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Wei Long has been at the edge of every Lin book: the inspector at the door, the one who already knows. I wanted to know who he went home to. The answer was nobody, and then a woman who sat on his desk.

This isn’t a slow burn. The ice goes in a week. What’s hard is everything after: a shooting he has to answer for, a posting on the other side of the world, an earthquake, and a man learning to ask the woman he loves what she wants.

The police work and the consular work are as real as I could make them. The ten minutes are true.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers.

Dry, funny and warm, with real police cases shown plainly. It includes:

• Love scenes on the page throughout, from the first week

• A woman strangled and found in the harbour, and her post-mortem

• A stalker

• A police shooting, on the page, and the review that follows

• A death in police custody abroad

• A major earthquake: the dead, the missing, an aftershock

• Fear and grief during a long silence

chapters.title: Three Languages in a Wet Terminal
chapters.desc: An extradited fraudster arrives on the wrong form, in a language nobody at the custody desk speaks, and a consular officer in a soaked coat fixes it in eleven minutes in English, French and Chinese. Inspector Song watches her the whole time and forgets to thank her. Cold, clipped, funny; no heat yet but the look.
chapters.epigraph: “You forgot thank you.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Inspector Song Wei Long noticed about the woman was that she was losing an argument with a printer.

She wasn’t shouting at it. She stood in front of the machine at the end of the custody counter with a phone wedged between her shoulder and her ear, a wet folder pinned to her hip, and the face of someone who had tried every polite option and was now thinking about violence against office equipment.

“That’s so helpful. No, I understand what the system says. I’m asking what the system intends to do about it,” she said into the phone.

The printer made a grinding noise.

“Wonderful. Then perhaps the system would like to explain that to the receiving officer in French.”

Wei Long looked away. It was eleven forty-seven on a Monday night in March, and the rain had been coming down on the terminal roof since lunchtime like gravel on a tin tray. He had been up since five. He had sat through two briefings, signed a search warrant, reviewed an interview tape and spent the last three hours arranging the handover of an extradited fraudster whose lawyers treated international cooperation as a personal insult. He had no interest in printers, and less in women arguing with them.

“Inspector Song?”

Sergeant Liu came across the hall with a plastic wallet of papers and the careful expression he wore when he was about to say something Wei Long wouldn’t like.

“The flight’s down. They’re bringing him through the restricted corridor.”

“Documents?”

“Received. There’s a problem with them.”

“What problem?”

Liu said, “The name. The French certificate has one spelling, the extradition order has another, and the arrival manifest has a third. They all mean the same man.”

Wei Long held out his hand for the wallet. “Then we have three spellings and one criminal.”

“Yes, sir.”

At the end of the counter the printer surrendered a sheet of paper. The woman examined it, looked up at the ceiling, and said to nobody, “Eleven minutes.”

The prisoner came through just before twelve between two escorting officers from the French side, a narrow man in a grey jacket with the exhausted face of someone who had spent four months learning that treaties were less flexible than his lawyers had promised.

“Name?” said Wei Long.

The man answered in French. Liu looked at Wei Long. Wei Long looked at the paperwork. The man said it again, louder, as if volume were a kind of translation.

“Does he speak English?”

“No,” said a woman’s voice behind them. “But he speaks the northern language. He spent nine years defrauding people in it.”

She had abandoned the printer. Up close she was younger than he’d expected anyone at an extradition handover to be: a navy coat soaked dark at the shoulders, hair coming loose from whatever she’d done with it before the rain got to it, three documents and a small black notebook held against her chest. She put the documents down on the counter and her card on top of them.

“Good evening. Isla Ren, consular officer. Mr. Xiong is one of ours.”

Wei Long looked at the card. “You’re with the consulate.”

“That’s generally what the card means.”

He looked up. She smiled at him, and didn’t apologise for it.

“Inspector Song, I assume. I’ve been looking for you, because everybody else in this airport has decided a man can have three legal identities depending on which printer he came out of.”

She turned to the prisoner before he could answer and spoke French to him, quick and level. Wei Long caught the shape of it and not much else: her name, her office, his rights. The man’s face changed. He began to talk with both hands, and she let him, nodding once, and then switched to the northern language without a pause.

“Your French certificate uses the spelling in your old passport, Hsiung. The extradition order uses your current one, Xiong. The airline put your given name where your family name should be. Nobody here is confused about who you are. They’re confused about the paper.”

“That’s what I’ve been telling them,” said the prisoner.

“I know.”

“Nobody here speaks French.”

She glanced at Wei Long. “One of them does a little.”

“Enough,” said Wei Long.

“That’s more than the printer,” she said, and opened her notebook.

She asked for the original order. He gave it to her. She read it, then the manifest, then the French certificate, with two lines between her eyebrows. “Who prepared this?”

Liu raised a hand halfway. “Not us.”

“Good. I was about to be disappointed. There’s no question about identity. It’s a transliteration problem with a data-entry reversal on top. The custody record needs an explanatory note before the handover’s signed, with the old spelling recorded as an alias. I can certify the translation of our consular correspondence. The extradition papers have to stay with their own authenticated copies.” She uncapped a pen.

“Can we accept the handover?” said Wei Long.

“Once the note’s on the record and your escorts have checked him against the travel document.”

He looked at her. She looked back. Then he stepped aside.

“Proceed.”

It took her seven more minutes. Wei Long watched her the whole time and told himself he was watching the documents. She spoke French to the escorts, the northern language to the prisoner and English to the custody sergeant, and never once raised her voice. When someone made her explain a thing twice she gave them a particular look, patient and amazed, that suggested the conversation was continuing only out of courtesy. He knew the look. He used it himself.

“Here. Originals intact. Certified translation of the consular notification attached, signed statement on the name, current spelling on the receiving record, former spelling noted as an alias.” She slid the corrected note across the counter.

He read it. The wording was exact and the references were right. He checked the passport number against the order, then the date of birth, then the photograph. Everything matched.

“Correct,” he said.

She blinked. “That’s it?”

“What else is there?”

“I’ve just spent eleven minutes negotiating with a printer, three departments and a man who thinks his surname is a matter of international importance.”

“It is his legal identity.”

“Yes. I’m aware.” She stared at him. Something moved at the corner of her mouth, and then she laughed, surprised and warm, completely wrong for a custody hall that smelled of wet coats under fluorescent light. “Do you ever say anything else, Inspector?”

“Yes.”

“When?”

“When necessary.”

She laughed again. Wei Long wasn’t used to being laughed at. People didn’t avoid it because they were afraid of him, although some were. He didn’t give them much to work with. Old Superintendent Pun had once told him his face had been assembled without the instructions for smiling, and Wei Long had considered that unnecessarily personal. This woman seemed to find it entertaining.

“I’ll leave you to the real police work.”

She handed the translations to Liu. “Please make sure the consular notification is on the record before he’s moved into holding, and his passport goes with his property, not inside the extradition packet,” she said.

“Understood,” said Liu, who had never said understood to a civilian in four years.

“Good night, Inspector.”

“Good night.”

She went two steps, stopped, and turned round. “Actually. You should say thank you.”

He looked at her. Nothing came out.

“Good night,” she said, and smiled, and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

The handover was complete just after twelve. The prisoner’s property was inventoried, photographed, sealed and signed for. Wei Long checked every entry himself, corrected one time, sent Liu for a missing signature, and walked out into the rain at 12:46.

His car was in the staff bays under a security light that couldn’t decide whether to stay on. There was something under his windscreen wiper. A white card, soft at the edges from the wet.

ISLA REN. Consular Officer. A number. On the back, in blue ink that had just started to run:

You forgot thank you.

He stood in the rain and read it twice. Then he got into the car, put the card in the compartment under the dashboard and sat without starting the engine. She was twenty-five, according to the identification he had looked at for slightly longer than he needed to. Three languages. Eleven minutes. Entirely too comfortable telling a police inspector what he’d forgotten.

He took out his phone, opened a new contact and typed her name. Then he deleted it and typed THANK YOU (OWED), and saved the number under that, and didn’t send anything, because there was no reason to.

His phone rang before he’d reached the airport road. It was Liu.

“Sir. Prisoner’s in holding. Everything’s in order. The consular officer left before I could thank her.”

Wei Long looked at the dashboard compartment.

“She knows,” he said, and hung up.

✦ ✦ ✦

Across the city, Isla Ren was in the back of a taxi with her shoes in her lap, trying to pry a paper clip out of the lining of her coat pocket. Her phone lit up.

Hao (Loud): Home?

Isla: Taxi.

Hao (Loud): Why are you still working?

Isla: International cooperation. A man had three spellings of his name.

Hao (Loud): Date someone with one spelling.

Isla: Good night, Hao.

Hao (Loud): Love you!!

She put the phone away and watched the airport lights slide off behind the rain. She thought about the inspector, which was annoying, because she’d met a lot of policemen and hadn’t thought about any of them in a taxi.

Song Wei Long. Tall, with black hair that fell over his forehead whether he liked it or not, and a stern mouth, and a stillness that made the room arrange itself round him. He had the face of a man who had never been late, never lost a document, and never had a feeling he couldn’t file. He was also unreasonably handsome, in a way she found inconvenient. He’d watched her for the whole eleven minutes. Not rudely. Every time she looked up, his eyes were already there.

“Oh, no,” she said out loud.

The driver looked at her in the mirror. “Everything all right?”

“I left my umbrella at the custody desk.”

“Want me to go back?”

She looked at the rain. “No. It’s fine.”

Somewhere behind her a man with a glacier for a face was driving home, probably without an umbrella either. She hoped he’d remember to say thank you next time.

✦ ✦ ✦

He got in at 1:17, hung his coat by the door, washed his hands and put his keys in the dish. The phone lay on the kitchen counter. He looked at it twice. THANK YOU (OWED). There was no reason to ring a consular officer at one in the morning, so he turned off the light and went to bed.

For three days he would tell himself he’d kept the card because it was a useful professional contact. On the fourth he would still have it. On the fifth he would realise he knew the number by heart. And on the sixth, when Liu asked, in a voice that was trying hard to be casual, whether the consular officer had been helpful, Wei Long would say, “She was competent.”

“And polite, sir?”

He would think about it for a second longer than he meant to.

“Debatable,” he’d say, and keep the card.

chapters.title: She Calls the Station
chapters.desc: She rings the station to check the prisoner arrived. He answers his own desk phone, which nobody in the squad room has ever seen. She asks him to dinner; he writes Friday on his hand.
chapters.epigraph: “Do you always sound like a glacier?”
chapters.content:
The first time Isla Ren rang the station on Tuesday morning, Inspector Song was in the middle of an argument about a missing surveillance recording. The second time, twenty minutes later, he was in the middle of the same argument. The difference was that the second time he picked up the phone on his desk himself, and the squad room, which had never once seen him answer his own extension, went quiet in a ring round him like water round a dropped stone.

“Song.”

“Good morning, Inspector Glacier.”

He looked at the receiver. Then at the clock, which said 10:16. Then at the receiver again.

“Who is this?”

“Oh, that’s disappointing. I thought I’d made an impression.” She sounded delighted.

The airport. The rain. The printer. He knew the voice before she’d finished the sentence and resented that slightly.

“Miss Ren.”

“Isla.”

“Miss Ren.”

“Fine. We’re making progress. You remembered my name. I’m calling to confirm Mr. Xiong arrived safely in holding.” He heard a cup go down on a saucer.

“He did. Custody’s complete. His property’s recorded and secured, and his passport is with the property file.”

“Not in the extradition packet?”

“No.”

“Excellent. His lawyer rang our office three times before nine. He’s requested a consular visit and he seems to believe the entire police force is conspiring to stop him making a phone call.” She meant it, he could hear.

“He’s not.”

“I assumed. Has anyone actually told him the visit’s being arranged?”

“The custody team will.”

“Would you mind checking that someone has? I’d like him to stop ringing me before lunch.”

Wei Long wrote Xiong, lawyer, consular visit on his pad and underlined it. “He’ll be contacted today.”

“Thank you. You sound exactly the same as last night.”

He stopped writing. “What’s wrong with it?”

“Nothing. It’s consistent. Do you always sound like a glacier?”

Across the room Sergeant Liu’s head came up from his screen. Wei Long turned his chair a few degrees towards the window.

“Yes.”

She laughed, properly this time, and he found he was listening to it with the same attention he gave a recording he’d been told contained something.

“At least you’re honest. I’ll let you get back to your recording, Inspector. Goodbye, Glacier.”

He put the phone down. Liu was standing beside his desk before the receiver had settled.

“Who was that, sir?”

“Consular office.”

“Ah.” Liu didn’t move. Wei Long turned a page. Liu still didn’t move.

“Something else?”

“Was that the woman from last night? The one who fixed the paperwork?”

“She had a question about custody arrangements.”

“How thorough of her,” said Liu.

Wei Long looked at him.

Liu said he’d get back to work, and made it four steps before turning round. “Sir? Did you thank her this time?”

Wei Long looked at him until he went away.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before eleven, eleven floors up in the consulate, Isla stood at her office window with a coffee and watched the rain stop being interesting.

“Was that the police?” said Margaret from the next desk, without looking up from a stack of passport renewals.

“Inspector Song.”

“The one from last night? How was he?” Margaret looked up.

Isla thought about it. “Extremely polite.”

“Really?”

“No. He’s interesting. He’s like a locked filing cabinet.” Margaret laughed, and Isla put her cup down.

“That sounds dreadful.”

“Not if you like puzzles.”

“Is he handsome?”

Isla picked her cup up again. “Unfortunately.”

Margaret laughed so loudly that someone in the next office looked through the glass. “Unfortunately?”

“He speaks in complete sentences with no adjectives. It’s distracting.”

“You’re interested.”

“I’m curious.”

“That’s what interested people say when they want to sound respectable,” said Margaret, and went back to her passports.

Isla sat down and read her notes from the call. The prisoner was safe. The lawyer would be told. Everything was in order and she had no further reason to speak to Inspector Song. The station’s switchboard had given her his direct line, and the number sat on her pad in her own handwriting. It was ten forty-five. She smiled, and decided that a reason could probably be found.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after twelve Wei Long’s phone buzzed on the briefing-room table, between a witness statement and Liu’s elbow.

Thank You (Owed): For the record, I don’t think you’re actually a glacier.

Thank You (Owed): Glaciers move. Slowly, but they do move.

He looked at it for long enough that Liu’s elbow went still. Then he typed with one thumb.

Wei Long: Who is this?

Thank You (Owed): I’m wounded. Isla. The woman who fixed your paperwork.

Wei Long: I know.

Thank You (Owed): Then why ask?

Wei Long: Verification.

Three dots came and went and came back.

Thank You (Owed): You’re quite difficult to flirt with, aren’t you?

He considered whether she was, in fact, flirting. He decided she was. He decided it was simplest to ask.

Wei Long: Are you flirting with me?

The reply took twelve seconds. He knew because he watched them go.

Thank You (Owed): I was considering it. You’re handsome. And you still haven’t thanked me.

He had questioned armed men in locked rooms and lawyers who treated every safeguard as an invitation. None of them had been as persistent as this, in so few words. He put the phone face down. He turned it over again.

Wei Long: Thank you for your assistance last night.

Thank You (Owed): You’re welcome. See? That wasn’t difficult.

He opened her contact, deleted OWED, typed PAID, and saved it. Liu watched him do it, and said nothing, with enormous effort.

Thank You (Paid): Have you eaten?

Wei Long: Yes.

Thank You (Paid): Liar. You answered too fast.

Wei Long: I’m working.

Thank You (Paid): That’s not an answer. That’s an explanation.

He put the phone in his pocket and kept it there.

At three he went down to the custody suite himself, which he didn’t need to do, and asked the custody sergeant whether Mr. Xiong’s lawyer had been told about the consular visit.

“Rang him at eleven, sir. Twice, because he didn’t believe me the first time.”

“Note it.”

“It’s noted. Anything else?” The sergeant looked at him over his glasses.

Wei Long looked down the corridor of cells. Xiong was sitting on his bench in the third one with his hands between his knees, and when he saw who was at the hatch he stood up.

“The consular woman,” he said in the northern language. “She’s coming on Thursday?”

“Thursday morning.”

“She’s the only one in this building who listened to me.”

“She isn’t in this building,” said Wei Long, and Xiong sat down again with the air of a man who had expected nothing better and was still disappointed.

On the stairs back up Wei Long thought about that. She’d listened to the man for eleven minutes and he’d remembered it for two days, a fraudster who had lied to hundreds of people in two languages and knew exactly what it was worth when someone didn’t. Wei Long had interviewed him for twenty minutes on Monday night and couldn’t have said what colour his eyes were. He could have said what colour hers were. He went back to the recording argument and won it in four sentences, and Sham said afterwards that he’d never seen the inspector so short with anyone, and Liu said he’d never seen him so cheerful, and neither of them was wrong.

✦ ✦ ✦

Around half past one Liu put a paper bag on his desk.

“Lunch, sir. The canteen had a spare.”

Wei Long opened it. Rice, chicken, greens, a small tub of soup. He looked up. “Why?”

“Because you haven’t eaten.”

“Who told you that?”

“Nobody. It’s nothing complicated,” said Liu, with the innocence of a man who’d been reading over a shoulder.

“Thank you. Sergeant. Did you give my number to anyone?” Liu nodded and turned.

“No, sir.”

“You’re certain.”

“Yes, sir. Is this about the consular officer?” Liu’s eyes went to the phone and came back.

“Go back to work.”

Liu went back to work grinning, which wasn’t the same thing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before seven Isla was finishing a report when her brother rang, and she answered without taking her eyes off the screen.

“You’re alive,” said Ren Hao.

“Unfortunately.”

“That’s a terrible attitude to your only brother. Dinner tonight?”

“I’ve got work.”

“You always have work.”

“So do you.”

“Yes, but I’m important. Tomorrow I’m in Vancouver for two days. Friday?” She could hear his office round him, thirty-two floors of people being shouted at affectionately.

“Friday I’m free after six,” said Isla, and as she said it she looked at the calendar on her screen. Friday the seventh. Clear after six.

“I’ll book somewhere nice. And don’t bring a date.”

“Why would I bring a date?”

“Because you’re twenty-five and beautiful and you can’t spend an evening without working, and one day you’ll bring one just to prove me wrong. Love you.”

“Love you too.”

She put the phone down and looked at the pad with the inspector’s number on it. She hadn’t saved it. She opened her contacts, typed Song Wei Long, deleted it, and typed Inspector Glacier, and smiled at it more than was reasonable for a contact. Then she texted her brother.

Isla: Actually Friday’s bad. Saturday?

Hao (Loud): WHY

She didn’t answer that.

✦ ✦ ✦

At five to eight the consulate was down to the night duty officer and the cleaners. Isla sat at her desk with her coat on and her bag on her knee and didn’t go home. She had rung the lawyer herself at seven, to be sure, and he had thanked her as if she’d personally opened the cell door. That was the reason. It was a perfectly good reason. She could ring the station, pass on the lawyer’s thanks, and put the phone down.

She practised it once in her head and didn’t like how it sounded, so she practised it out loud.

“Good evening, Inspector. I’m calling because...”

The cleaner emptying her bin looked at her.

“Work,” said Isla.

“At eight o’clock,” said the cleaner, who had worked in that building for fourteen years and had seen the inside of a great many careers, “it’s never work.”

Isla laughed, and the cleaner went on to the next desk, and Isla picked up the phone before she could practise again.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 8:17 the squad room had emptied to the night desks and the sound of the heating. Wei Long was reading the last case notes of the day when his phone rang. He knew the number.

“Song.”

“Good evening, Inspector. Are you still at work?”

“Yes.”

“Do you ever go home?”

“When the work’s finished.”

“That’s a depressing answer.”

“It’s an accurate one.”

He heard her settle somewhere, a chair taking her weight. “The consular visit’s arranged for Thursday morning. The lawyer has been told, by a real person, and he thanked me. So I’m ringing to pass on the thank you. You can have it. You need the practice.”

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome. I have another question.”

“What is it?”

“Are you free on Friday?”

He looked at the report under his hand. “Why?”

“Because I’d like to take you to dinner.”

His pen stopped. On the other end of the line Isla waited. She wasn’t nervous. She’d asked men out before, and she had no intention of turning a dinner invitation into a treaty negotiation. She did, however, badly want to see his face, and couldn’t, and was imagining it instead.

“Inspector?”

“I’m here.”

“Good. I was starting to think the glacier had frozen.”

“What time?”

She blinked. “Eight?”

“Where?”

“I’ll send you the address.”

“All right.”

“All right? You’re agreeing?” She sat up.

“You asked me to dinner.”

“Correct.”

“Then yes.”

“Well, that was almost enthusiastic. I was hoping for something like, ‘I’d love to, Isla, I’ve been waiting all day.’” said Isla.

“I haven’t.”

She burst out laughing. “You’re terrible.”

“I’ve been told.”

“Friday at eight. And Inspector? Don’t bring your police face. The one from the airport that makes everyone think they’ve committed a crime.”

“Some of them have.”

“Not me.”

He considered it. “I’ll try.”

“Good night, Wei Long,” she said, and hung up before he could answer.

He sat with the phone in his hand. She’d said his name. Not Inspector, not Glacier. He didn’t know why he’d noticed, and he noticed that too.

There was a black biro beside the report. He picked it up, turned his left hand over and wrote on his palm, in neat capitals, FRIDAY 8.

“Sir?”

Liu was at the end of the desk with the vehicle log under his arm. Wei Long closed his hand. Liu looked at the pen, then at the fist, then at Wei Long’s face.

“Do you need the vehicle log, sir?”

“No.”

“Right. Friday?” Liu walked away, stopped, and turned round.

Wei Long stared at him.

“I didn’t see anything,” said Liu.

“Go home, Sergeant.”

“Immediately.”

When the door had closed behind him, Wei Long opened his hand. FRIDAY 8. He capped the pen. He had accepted dinner with a professional contact who’d been helpful and had asked, and there was no reasonable objection, and it was an entirely ordinary arrangement. He had no reason to smile, and didn’t, in any way anyone could have proved.

He left just before nine and checked his phone twice before he reached the car.

Thank You (Paid): Friday. Eight. Don’t be late, Inspector.

Wei Long: I won’t.

Thank You (Paid): I’ll try not to miss you too much till then.

Wei Long: It’s three days.

Thank You (Paid): I know. I’m being brave about it.

He stood by the car in the empty staff bays with the writing on his palm going pale in the cold, and the corner of his mouth moved. Then he got in and drove home, and Friday seemed further away than three days had any right to be.

chapters.title: The Inspector Who Forgot Dinner
chapters.desc: He forgets: a stabbing at the fish market keeps him till ten. At eleven she walks into the squad room with two boxes of noodles, sits on his desk on top of his files and kisses him first. A first kiss that is hers entirely; mouths, his hands not knowing where to go, six detectives pretending to read.
chapters.epigraph: “The world can wait ten minutes”
chapters.content:
Just before eight on Friday evening, Song Wei Long was supposed to be getting into a car to go to dinner. Just before eight he was standing in the wet market by the fish piers with blood on his shoes. By quarter past eight he had forgotten that dinner existed.

A market supervisor in his late forties had been found behind a seafood stall with one stab wound to the abdomen, conscious when the ambulance came and much less so by the time it reached the hospital. The stall assistant who had done it, a twenty-six-year-old with a cut thumb and a story about self-defence, was caught two streets away running in rubber boots. The market’s cameras had stopped recording eleven minutes before it happened. Three witnesses had given four different versions.

By half past nine Wei Long was in Interview One under the white light, reading the assistant’s statement back to him.

“What time did you leave the stall?”

“About seven.”

“Your first statement says quarter past.”

“I don’t remember.”

“You remembered an hour ago.”

“I was nervous.”

“Understandable. Then let’s try again,” said Wei Long, and turned a page.

There was no anger in it. There wasn’t anything in it at all for the young man to push against, and after twenty minutes he stopped pushing. Behind the glass, Sergeant Liu checked his watch.

“He’s going to be in there all night,” said Detective Sham, eating crackers over a file.

“He’s already missed dinner.”

“With who?”

Liu gave him a look, and Sham understood, and put a cracker down. “The consular officer?”

“Don’t.”

“I’m only saying. Poor woman.”

“Don’t say anything.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He came out just after ten. The assistant was in a cell, the recording was sealed, the bloody apron had gone to the lab and somebody had been sent back to the market with a warrant for the camera system’s hard drive. He took his watch off at the sink, washed his hands, and checked his phone because he always checked his phone at the end of an interview, and stood still.

Three missed calls. Three messages.

Thank You (Paid): I’m here. The restaurant is lovely. You’d hate the music.

Thank You (Paid): I hope you’re all right.

Thank You (Paid): I’m starting to suspect you’ve been murdered by your own paperwork.

The first was just before eight. The last was just after nine. His face changed by a degree that nobody in the room would have noticed, except that there was nobody in the room, and he noticed it himself. He typed, deleted it, and typed again.

Wei Long: I’m sorry. There was a stabbing. I’m still at the station.

The answer came at once.

Thank You (Paid): Are you hurt?

Wei Long: No.

Thank You (Paid): Is everyone else all right?

Wei Long: The victim’s in hospital. The suspect’s in custody.

Thank You (Paid): All right. When did you last sit down?

He looked at the clock. 10:09.

Wei Long: Not since this morning.

Thank You (Paid): Of course not. I’ll come by.

Wei Long: You don’t need to. It’s late. You should go home.

Thank You (Paid): I’m aware of the time, Inspector. Do you like noodles?

He had no idea how to answer that in a way that would stop her.

Wei Long: Yes.

Thank You (Paid): Excellent. See you soon.

He put the phone away and remembered, properly this time, that he’d been supposed to meet someone, and that she’d sat in a restaurant for an hour and a quarter listening to music he’d have hated.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before eleven the front desk got a visitor with two paper bags.

She was wearing a cream blouse under her dark coat, with her hair down over her shoulders and her make-up still neat, and a small line between her eyebrows that said the evening hadn’t gone the way she’d planned.

“I’m looking for Inspector Song.”

Constable Choy looked at the bags. “Is it about a case?”

“Dinner.”

Choy looked at the bags again. Then at her. “Sorry?”

“Tell him Isla’s here.”

Choy rang upstairs. He put the phone down and said, “Second floor, end of the corridor,” and watched her walk to the lift, and then picked the phone up again and said, low, “Sergeant Liu?”

✦ ✦ ✦

The squad room was quieter than a Friday had any right to be. Six detectives sat at six desks: one reading statements, one checking the assistant’s record, two going through photographs of the fish stall, two arguing about whether a witness had said navy or black. Wei Long was at his desk with his jacket off, his sleeves rolled to the elbow and his tie loose, reading the first medical report. He had pushed a hand through his hair so many times it had given up and fallen over his forehead.

“Sir. There’s someone here for you,” said Liu.

“Who?”

“Your dinner.”

“Good evening,” said a voice behind him, and he turned round.

She stood in the doorway with the bags. He only looked at her, and she let him, and then she smiled.

“Hello, Wei Long.”

“Isla. You didn’t have to come.” He stood up.

“You’ve mentioned that.”

“It’s late.”

“It is. I was home. Then I realised my dinner had been kidnapped by a fish market.”

Somebody behind him made a small choking noise. Wei Long didn’t turn round. “You’re in a police station. People are working.”

She looked round the room. Six heads went down to six documents in one movement. “Oh, I think they’re managing.”

Liu coughed into his fist. Wei Long looked at him, and Liu became fascinated by a statement.

“Where would you like these?” said Isla, and before he could answer she walked to his desk and set both bags down on the only clear surface, which was his files.

“Those are case documents.”

“I noticed.”

“You’re on them.”

“Then you’ll have to move them. Please.” She waited.

He seemed to consider whether refusing was possible. Then he lifted the files out from under the bags and stacked them on the cabinet. She unpacked: two boxes of noodles, beef and chicken, a tub of dumplings, two cans of tea. Steam came off them into the cold room.

“You brought too much,” he said.

“You’re welcome.”

“I haven’t said thank you.”

“I know. I’m giving you the opportunity.”

“Have you eaten?”

“Yes. At the restaurant. I ordered, I ate, I paid.”

He looked at her. “You waited.”

“Not all evening. Just most of it.” She smiled, and something under the smile was tired.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

She blinked. He’d said it with nothing on either side of it. No case, no stabbing, no explanation. She’d been ready for all three.

“I should have called.”

“Yes.”

“I didn’t.”

“No. Fortunately I’m forgiving.” She opened a box and held out a pair of chopsticks.

“Are you?”

“Not usually. But I like you.” She snapped the chopsticks apart for him because he hadn’t moved.

The room went silent in a new way. A detective turned a page of his file, upside down. Isla saw it, and her mouth twitched, and Wei Long saw her see it and shut his eyes for a second.

“Ignore them.”

“I’m trying. Eat.”

He ate. She sat in the visitor’s chair beside his desk and told him about her day: a meeting that had run two hours over, a detained citizen whose passport had turned up in the luggage of a family who’d never met him, a colleague who’d sent a confidential email to the whole building. He listened. He asked one question about the passport. Mostly he ate, and she found it strangely satisfying to watch a man who looked as if he could silence a courtroom sitting at his desk eating the noodles he’d been told to eat.

“What did you have? At the restaurant,” he said, when the box was half empty. He meant it. She could tell.

“Sea bass.”

“Good?”

“Lovely.”

“Then we’ll go there another time,” he said, and picked up his tea, in the voice of a man reporting tomorrow’s weather.

She stopped. “You want to take me there?”

“You said the food was good.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

He looked at her, and held it, and answered without looking away. “Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after eleven he closed the empty box. She stood up and started gathering the containers, and he reached for them.

“I’ll take those.”

“No. You’ve been working for six hours. Sit down.”

She came round the desk with the bags, and turned, and stopped, because he was looking at her. Not at the food or the files. At her. The fluorescent lights hummed. A printer started somewhere near the windows, which felt like the city making a joke.

“What?” she said.

“Nothing.”

“You’re staring.”

He didn’t deny it. She put the bags down, and then, before he could ask what she was doing, she sat on the edge of his desk, in the space where his files had been.

“Isla. You’re sitting on my desk.”

“Excellent observation.”

“My files were there.”

“Your files are on the cabinet. Your files are safe.”

“That’s not the point.”

She leaned towards him. “Then what is?”

He was close enough now to see that her eyes were brown with flecks of gold in them, and to smell her perfume, something clean with a faint flower in it that he had smelled at the airport and not let himself think about.

“You’re distracting me,” he said.

“Good. Can I ask you something? Did you forget about me?” She reached for his loose tie and held it.

“Yes.”

Her fingers paused. “I dressed up.”

“I noticed.”

“I booked.”

“I know.”

“I waited. I know work comes first sometimes. I do. I was looking forward to tonight.” She smiled, and the tiredness under it showed for a second.

“So was I. I wanted to see you,” he said, lower.

It was a plain sentence. It went through her like heat.

“Then you should have come.”

“I should have.”

“Or called.”

“Yes.”

“You’re impossible to stay angry with,” she said.

“I didn’t know you were angry.”

“See? Being a glacier again,” she said, laughing.

“I have work,” he said, and glanced at the medical report on the edge of the desk, and she caught his tie a little tighter.

“The world can wait ten minutes,” said Isla, and kissed him.

He didn’t understand it was happening until it had happened. One moment she was sitting on his desk holding his tie, and the next her hand was on his cheek and her mouth was on his, warm and certain, more certain than anything in his head. He went completely still. She kissed him once, drew back far enough to look, and found his eyes open and his face unreadable.

“Hello,” she said.

“Hello.”

She laughed under her breath and kissed him again, and this time she stayed. Her hand slid from his cheek to the back of his neck, into his hair. His own hands hung at his sides. A man who always knew where everything belonged had no idea where to put either of them. She felt it and drew back.

“You’re thinking.”

“Yes.”

“About what?”

He looked at her mouth, and then her eyes, with the gravity of a man answering under caution. “Where to put my hands.”

She stared at him and burst out laughing. “Oh, Wei Long. Here. And here.” She took one of his hands and laid it on her waist. She took the other and put it flat on her back.

“Is this acceptable?”

“Yes,” she said, and kissed him.

This time he didn’t stay still. His hand settled on her waist. The other spread across her back and drew her in. He was careful about it, almost cautious, until she tilted her head and opened her mouth against his, and then his fingers tightened and he kissed her back properly, slow and thorough.

When she pulled away she was smiling. She touched his lower lip with her thumb. “You’re a good kisser.”

“You’ve kissed me twice.”

“Three times.”

He considered it. “All right.”

She kissed the corner of his mouth to make it four, and then he remembered, belatedly, that they weren’t alone. Six detectives were reading. One had been on the same paragraph for four minutes. One held a pen over a blank page. One still had his file upside down. Liu was staring at his monitor with the intensity of a man memorising the criminal code. Nobody had seen anything, and everybody had seen everything.

Isla looked over his shoulder. “Oh.”

“Sergeant Liu,” said Wei Long. “Is there a problem?”

“No, sir.”

“Then why is everybody reading so hard?”

“Because we’re working, sir. Diligently.”

Isla pressed her lips together. Her shoulders shook. Somebody dropped a pen, and six heads looked down at it.

“Oh, darling,” she said, helpless, and then heard herself. “Sorry. Too soon?”

He studied her. “No.”

“No?”

“No,” he said, and she kissed his cheek, and behind them Liu made a noise like a cough with a laugh inside it.

“Sergeant. Go home.”

“All of us, sir?”

“Would you prefer individual instructions?”

Within thirty seconds the squad room was full of people leaving at speed. Someone knocked over a stack of folders. Someone else said he’d forgotten his umbrella and went back for it twice.

“You’re terrible at romance,” said Isla, when the door had stopped swinging.

“Is that what this is?”

She went still for half a second, and then smiled, and touched his tie. “I certainly hope so.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Around half past eleven he turned off his computer and opened the bottom drawer of his desk and took out a folded black umbrella.

She looked at it. “That’s mine.”

“You left it at the custody desk.”

“On Monday.”

“Yes.”

“You’ve had my umbrella in your drawer for four days?”

“It was lost property. I knew the owner,” he said.

She took it from him. He walked her down to the taxi rank with the rubbish in one hand and her hand in the other. It was the first time she’d held it, and his fingers closed round hers and stayed. The rain had thinned to a fine fall that made the pavement shine. He opened her umbrella and held it so that nearly all of it was over her.

“You’ll get wet,” she said.

“It’s fine.”

“You’re standing in the gutter.”

He moved the umbrella an inch. “Better?”

“Much.”

At the rank a taxi pulled in. He opened the back door, and she didn’t get in.

“Thank you for walking me down.”

“You brought dinner.”

“Then thank me for that.”

“Thank you for bringing it,” he said, and she went up on her toes and kissed him, brief and soft, and when she drew back he followed by half an inch before he stopped himself. She saw it.

“Good night, Wei Long. Don’t work too late.”

“I won’t.”

“You’re lying.”

“Probably.”

She laughed and got in, and he closed the door and gave her the umbrella through the window, and the taxi pulled away with its tail lights smeared red down the wet road. He stood there in his shirt sleeves until it had turned the corner. Then he walked back into the station, and up the stairs, and into the squad room, where Liu was finishing a report at his desk.

Liu looked up. Then at the wet shirt. “Sir. Your coat.”

Wei Long looked down at himself. His coat was where it had been all evening, over the back of his chair. He’d walked her out and stood in the rain without it and not noticed.

“Don’t say anything,” he said.

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You were.”

“Yes, sir.”

His phone buzzed while he was putting the coat on.

Thank You (Paid): Home. Thank you for tonight. Even though you forgot the first half.

Wei Long: I’ll make it up to you.

Thank You (Paid): Are you asking me out again?

Wei Long: Yes.

Thank You (Paid): Good. And Wei Long? I liked kissing you.

He read it twice. He typed, stopped, and deleted the first attempt.

Wei Long: I liked kissing you too.

Thank You (Paid): You could have said that earlier.

Wei Long: You didn’t ask.

Thank You (Paid): I’m going to have to teach you everything, aren’t I.

Wei Long: Apparently.

He switched off the lights. The case was still open, there would be a new version of the story by morning, and none of his work had got any easier. There was a trace of her lipstick on the side of his thumb. When he thought about going home, for the first time in years he caught himself wishing someone would be there when he did.

chapters.title: A Second Case, a Second Language
chapters.desc: He asks for her by name on a case with a French-speaking witness, a frightened au pair who saw a beating. In Stairwell B afterwards he tells her he’s going to kiss her, and does, against the rail, deep and unhurried. He admits he’s read her consular file.
chapters.epigraph: “Isla. I’m going to kiss you now.”
chapters.content:
The second time Song Wei Long asked for Isla Ren, he did it in front of six people. He didn’t think it was significant. Sergeant Liu did.

“The witness from the apartment block is in Interview Two, sir. The au pair. She won’t give a statement.”

Wei Long looked up from the report. “Why not?”

“She says she doesn’t understand us. Her English isn’t good enough for a formal statement, and she’s French-speaking. Canadian. The interpreter service says forty minutes.”

“How long has she been waiting?”

“Nearly an hour. She keeps asking whether he knows she’s here.”

“Does he?”

“We don’t know.”

Wei Long stood up. “Keep her away from anyone connected to the household. Don’t promise her anything about her visa or her job. Whatever she says before the interpreter comes is an informal account, not an interview.” He took out his phone, scrolled to THANK YOU (PAID), and pressed it, and Liu’s eyebrows went up and stayed there.

She answered on the second ring. “Good morning, Inspector Glacier.”

“Good morning. I have a witness who speaks French. She’s one of your citizens. She saw an assault and she’s frightened, and she won’t talk to us.” He felt Liu not looking at him.

The lightness went out of Isla’s voice at once. “Is she hurt?”

“No. She saw it. She wasn’t touched.”

“Which station? I’ll come. Are you asking me because I’m consular or because I speak French?” He told her.

“Both.”

“That’s a sensible answer. Twenty minutes.”

He put the phone in his pocket. Liu was looking at the ceiling.

“Should we put Miss Ren on the rota, sir?”

“No. Forty minutes for the interpreter. Get the room ready.”

“Yes, sir,” said Liu, and walking away, not quite under his breath, “Twenty, apparently.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Camille Moreau was twenty-three, from Montreal, eight months into an au pair job she’d found through an agency, living in with a family in a tower block near the commercial district. Three nights ago she’d stood in the hallway of that flat and watched her employer hit his wife in the kitchen, again and again, and heard something break, and heard the wife crying on the floor. When he saw Camille in the doorway he’d told her that if she spoke to anybody she’d be on a plane home without her wages. In the morning she packed a bag and left. She’d been on a friend’s sofa since. When the police found her she agreed to come in, and that was all she’d agreed to.

She sat in Interview Two with her coat buttoned to the neck in a warm room and her foot going under the table.

“Has she eaten?” said Wei Long at the glass.

“She said no to breakfast.”

“Find out whether the agency arranged her accommodation and whether anyone’s contacted her since she left. Nobody rings the employer without the team.”

Isla came down the corridor just after ten in a pale blue blouse and a long camel coat, with a leather folder under her arm and her hair tied at the nape of her neck. She looked a great deal more awake than she had at the airport, and Wei Long had been thinking about the last time he’d seen her more than he meant to, especially the part where she’d kissed him in front of six detectives and taken his rubbish home.

“Have you slept?” she said.

“Yes.”

“How much?”

“Enough.”

“That’s not a number.”

“Six hours.”

“Better. You look serious today. I was hoping the kissing might have helped.” She looked at his face and her mouth curved.

“It hasn’t.”

“Tragic. Tell me.” Then she looked through the glass at the girl in the coat, and her whole face changed.

He told her: the beating, the threat, the bag, the friend’s sofa. She asked whether the wife was safe. He said she’d been treated and had given a first account. Isla nodded.

“I’ll go in first and introduce myself. Don’t come in until I ask. And please don’t stand behind the glass looking as if you’re about to sentence someone.”

“I wasn’t.”

“Your face was,” she said, and went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Bonjour, Camille. Je m’appelle Isla Ren. Je travaille au consulat.”

Camille’s shoulders came down an inch. “Vous êtes du Québec?”

“Non. De Vancouver. Mais je parle français.”

Isla sat opposite her and put the folder on the table and didn’t open it. Through the glass Wei Long watched her talk, slowly, not in the loud careful way people speak to foreigners, just clearly, each sentence finished before the next began. He could follow perhaps a third of it. She told the girl who she was and what she could do. She told her she wasn’t a police officer and couldn’t make her give evidence. She told her, and he understood this part from Camille’s face, that if Camille said something that meant someone was in danger, she couldn’t keep it secret.

Camille asked a question. Isla answered. Camille twisted her fingers together and said, fast, “Il sait où j’habite. Il connaît l’adresse de mon amie. Il a appelé hier soir.”

He knows where I am. He rang last night.

Isla leaned forward. “Qu’est-ce qu’il a dit?”

“He said he would find me,” said Camille, in English, as if the words were too heavy to carry in her own language.

“Est-ce qu’il vous a déjà touchée?”

Camille shook her head, then stopped, and her eyes filled. “Il m’a attrapée par le bras. Il a dit que personne ne me croirait.”

Isla reached across the table and stopped her hand an inch short of the girl’s. “Je vous crois.”

It came out of Camille in a rush after that: the argument, the glass, the wife against the counter, his hand in her hair, the money he owed for three months, and the passport he’d kept in a locked drawer “for safety” since the first week. Isla didn’t interrupt. When it was over she let the room be quiet, and then she turned to the glass and nodded once.

Wei Long went in with Liu. Camille stiffened at the sight of them. Isla said something to her and then, to him, “She wants you to explain how this works. She can ask me about anything.”

He sat down, put the recorder on the table and didn’t switch it on yet. “You’re not under arrest. You’re not accused of anything. You’re here because we think you saw a serious assault. You don’t have to answer anything you don’t understand. If you need to stop, say so. If you want to talk to Miss Ren alone, you can.”

Isla translated every sentence. Camille asked whether her employer would be told she was there.

“We won’t give him her location,” said Wei Long.

Whether he’d be arrested.

“I can’t promise that. It depends on the evidence.”

Isla translated it exactly, and Wei Long watched her not soften it. Then he asked whether Camille had her passport, and the answer was no, and he said, “We’ll find out how he came to have it and what can be done to get it back. We won’t send her back into that flat to fetch it.”

For the first time Camille looked at him instead of Isla. He met her eyes and waited, without any impatience at all, until she nodded.

“Sergeant, I want the safeguarding officer and somewhere she can stay that isn’t on his list. And the agency, and what personal details he has. Can you stay for the statement?” He looked at Isla.

“Yes.”

“Thank you,” he said, and she looked at him.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took two hours. There was nothing dramatic about it. Where had she been standing. What had she heard. Which hand. How many times. Had she touched anything. Who else was there. When Camille remembered something late she went back, and he let her. When she contradicted herself he asked her to explain and didn’t assume she was lying. When she didn’t know the time he wrote down that she didn’t know.

At a break Isla leaned on the corridor wall with her phone and he came and leaned beside her.

“She wouldn’t have talked without you.”

“She would have. Not today. She’s been threatened by someone who controls her job, her bed and her passport. She needs to see that she isn’t a problem being processed.” Isla put the phone away.

“I know.”

“Do you?”

“Yes.”

She studied him, and something in her face eased. “All right.”

He told her the employer had a lawyer, who had already rung to ask why the police were interested in his staff, and that the lawyer could put his request in writing like everyone else. She asked how he could be so calm. He said the lawyer wasn’t relevant to the evidence.

“That’s such an Inspector Song answer.”

“It’s a police answer.”

She pushed off the wall. “I’ve got a report to write. Are you going to kiss me goodbye?”

Two officers were coming along the corridor towards the stairs. He looked at them, and then at her. “Not here.”

“Shy?”

“No.”

“Then where?”

He thought about it. “Somewhere private.”

Her eyebrows went up. “Inspector. You’re becoming interesting.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By ten to five Camille had a copy of her statement, a room in a hostel the safeguarding officer trusted, and a telephone number to ring. The technical team had found that the tower block’s camera hadn’t failed; somebody had unplugged it and taken the hard drive out, and the case had become a different, harder kind of case.

“Miss Ren’s still downstairs, sir. She says she has something to discuss with you,” said Liu.

“About the witness?”

“I don’t think so. She’s in Stairwell B. Sir? Stairwell B?”

Wei Long looked at him, and Liu held up both hands and went.

Stairwell B ran from the second floor to the car park and nobody used it unless they were avoiding somebody. The lights were dimmer. The rail was cold. She was on the landing between floors with her coat over her arm, looking at her phone, and when the door shut behind him she put the phone away.

“How’s the case?”

“Continuing.”

“Any progress?”

“The camera was disconnected deliberately. Someone took the drive.”

“Good. I mean, bad. Good that you know. Are you going to kiss me?” She tilted her head.

He came up one step, then another. “Yes.”

“That’s a promising answer.”

He stopped in front of her and looked at her. There was a small crease by her left eyebrow that came when she was tired. Her lipstick had worn off in the middle. A strand of hair lay against her cheek. He lifted his hand, and paused.

“Isla. I’m going to kiss you now.”

Her face went soft. “All right.”

He put his hand along her jaw, his thumb under her cheekbone, and kissed her. Slowly, and so deliberately that she could have stepped away at any point. She didn’t. Her hand found the front of his shirt and held it, and his other hand settled at her waist, and when he tilted his head she pulled him down by the collar and followed. Her back met the rail. She’d expected him to be restrained, and he was, but she was starting to understand that restraint wasn’t the absence of feeling. He felt all of it and showed only what he’d decided to. His thumb moved once along her cheek. His hand at her waist went firm. When she opened her mouth he followed with a patience that made her forget, for the length of it, that she was standing in a police stairwell.

She broke away to breathe. He didn’t move back. His forehead almost touched hers.

“Hello,” she said.

“Hello.”

“You’re getting better at this.”

“Am I?”

“Much. You still look as if you’re concentrating.” She touched his collar.

“I am.”

“On what?”

“You,” he said, and kissed her again before she could answer, and this time she smiled into it.

They stayed on the landing a while, her against the rail, his hand flat on the metal beside her shoulder.

“Why did you ask for me today? The real answer,” she said.

“I could have waited forty minutes for an interpreter. I rang you because I wanted to see you.”

“That’s almost romantic.”

“Almost?”

“There’s room for improvement.”

He nodded, taking it as useful feedback. “You’re beautiful. I like your voice and the way you speak to people. I like that you don’t seem worried about what I think of you. You probably should be.” He considered it.

She laughed. “Why?”

“Because I’m not easy to deal with.” He was looking at her, and there was something in the look she’d noticed all day and couldn’t place. Not interest. Familiarity. As if he knew things she hadn’t told him.

She let go of his collar. “How much do you know about me?”

He went still. Only slightly, but she saw it, and she saw his hand come off the rail.

“Wei Long.”

He said, “I’ve read your file. Last winter there was an inquiry into a risk consultancy. Every firm in that business was checked. Your brother’s was one of them, and it came back clean. You’re on his record as next of kin, and that took me to the accreditation file your consulate lodges with the government. Your address. Your postings. Your family. Your emergency contacts. Your medical declaration.”

The stairwell got colder.

“All of it?”

“Everything I could open.”

She folded her arms. “And you thought that was acceptable?”

“No,” he said, and that stopped her, because she’d been ready for a justification and there wasn’t one.

“Then why?”

“Because it was there. And because when I read it you were a name in a list, and when I met you at the airport I remembered the name.”

“So you’ve been carrying round things about me I never chose to tell you, while I sat on your desk telling you about my day.”

“Yes.”

“Before or after you kissed me were you planning to mention it?”

“I should have said before.”

“That would have been useful. It isn’t that you know things. It’s that I didn’t know you knew.” She looked away.

“I know.”

“Have you looked at it since?”

“No.”

“Kept a copy?”

“No.”

“Can you prove that?”

He said, “I’ll ask for the access log to be reviewed through the proper channel. What I opened, when, and on what authority. If any of it was outside the scope of that inquiry I’ll report it myself.”

She studied him. It undid nothing, and it was a great deal better than pretending.

“I need to go. Don’t use anything you read in there to pretend you know me,” she said, and picked up her coat, and at the door she turned.

“I won’t.”

“I like you, Wei Long. I don’t like being investigated while I’m dating someone.”

“Understood,” he said, and she went.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 6:18 he sat at his desk and opened the access log and read every line of it. Then he rang the inspector who handled internal reviews and asked for a formal review of his own access to the accreditation file of Ren Isla, and wrote down the purpose of the original search, and the date he had met her, and the date he had kissed her, and didn’t delete anything.

Wei Long: I’ve asked for a formal review of my access to your file. I’ll tell you the result. I won’t open it again.

At 9:41 Isla was on her sofa with a book she’d been failing to finish for a fortnight when her phone lit up.

Inspector Glacier: I’m sorry I didn’t tell you sooner. You were right to ask.

She didn’t want to decide anything while she was still upset. She liked him; that was the inconvenient part. She liked how he’d looked at a frightened girl from Montreal without treating her fear as a nuisance. She liked that he’d told her he was going to kiss her and then waited for her to say yes.

Isla: Thank you for telling me. I need a little time.

Inspector Glacier: Take all the time you need.

At 10:16 he was getting his coat on when it buzzed again.

Thank You (Paid): One question. Did you notice me before you read the file?

Wei Long: Yes. At the airport.

Thank You (Paid): You didn’t even say thank you.

Wei Long: I was distracted.

Thank You (Paid): By the paperwork?

Wei Long: No.

Thank You (Paid): Oh. That’s actually quite sweet. For the record I liked the kiss today. We’ll see whether you’re still a good kisser when I’m not being nice to you.

Wei Long: I suppose we’ll find out.

Outside the rain had started again. He drove home in it, and somewhere across the city Isla turned her book face down on her chest and began to suspect that the hard part of Song Wei Long wouldn’t be getting him to open up. It would be deciding what to do with what she found when he did.

chapters.title: Ten Minutes on His Desk
chapters.desc: It becomes a rule. Nine o’clock, she sits on his desk, the world waits ten minutes, blinds down. The squad starts timing it. Kisses grow longer and hungrier: her fingers in his collar, his hands on her thighs over her skirt, both stopping at the ten-minute mark because he’s literal.
chapters.epigraph: “Fortunately, I like you too.”
chapters.content:
The review came back on Friday the twenty-first. His access to her file had been inside the authority of the inquiry, logged and lawful, and the reviewing inspector had added a line saying that the officer’s decision to refer himself was noted. Wei Long told Isla on the phone that night, all of it, including the line. She was quiet for a while. Then she said, “Monday. Nine o’clock. Your office,” and rang off, and that was how the rule began.

At three minutes to nine on Monday she stood in his doorway with two coffees. The door was open, the blinds were open, and he was reading a report.

“You’re early,” he said.

“Three minutes. I know. Busy?” She put one coffee on his desk and looked at the report.

“Yes.”

“Available?”

“No.”

“Wrong answer. You owe me ten minutes from Friday the seventh. The world can wait ten minutes, remember? I’m collecting.” She put her bag on the visitor’s chair.

“I need to finish this report.”

“How long?”

“Ten minutes.”

She patted the empty corner of his desk where the files were. “That’s unfortunate. I was going to sit here.”

He looked at the corner. “Those are case files.”

“Move them.”

“Isla.”

“Or I could sit in your chair,” she offered.

He put the files in the cabinet. She watched him do it.

“You’re cooperative.”

“You’re persistent.”

“Thank you.”

“It wasn’t a compliment.”

“I’ve decided it was. Starting now.” At nine exactly she sat on the desk, and crossed her ankles, and smiled at him.

He looked at the clock on the wall. “All right.”

“You’re taking this seriously.”

“I thought that was the point,” he said, and she caught his tie between two fingers and pulled.

He stood. She stayed sitting, so that when he came round the desk her knees brushed his hips. This close, under the office light, his eyes were darker than she’d thought, and he’d undone the top button of his shirt, and he looked the way he always looked at nine at night, a little tired and entirely awake.

“Bad day?”

“Not particularly.”

“Did you eat?”

“Seven. Rice.”

“That isn’t what I meant.” She kissed him.

He took it with the stillness that had once made her wonder whether she was kissing a man or an unusually handsome statue. He’d improved. His hand found her waist and the other her back, and he let her set the pace until she caught his collar and drew him down, and then he answered her. Her fingers slid under the edge of his collar to the warm skin at the back of his neck. She smiled against his mouth. She’d meant to tease him for the whole ten minutes and found she’d forgotten what she’d been going to say, which was becoming a habit.

His phone buzzed on the desk. He ignored it. It buzzed again.

“Shouldn’t you answer that?”

“No.”

“Who is it?”

“Work. Not important enough. For another six minutes.” He glanced at the clock.

She laughed into his shoulder. At 9:10 he straightened.

“Time.”

“Already? One more.” She didn’t move.

“That’s not the agreement.”

“Thirty seconds.”

He looked at her. She kissed him. He let her, and when she drew back he said, “Time,” and she laughed so hard she had to put a hand on his shoulder.

“You really are literal.”

“You asked for ten minutes.”

“You’re supposed to be a little flexible.”

“Not with time. Thank you. It’s good.” He picked up the coffee she’d brought.

She slid off the desk and picked up her bag. “I know. Tomorrow?” she said at the door.

“Nine,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

By Tuesday the squad had noticed. Not because anyone was watching, which was the official position, but because Inspector Song, who had always treated his office door as an architectural feature, now closed it every night at nine and lowered the blinds, and at ten past opened both again.

“Interesting,” said Liu, just before nine.

“What is?” said Detective Sham, without looking up.

“Nothing. I think we should keep records.” Just before nine the inspector put his phone down. At 9:00 the door closed. The blinds came down. Liu leaned back.

“Of what?”

“Human behaviour.”

Sham looked at him and went back to his screen. “I don’t want to know.”

Inside, Isla was already on the desk with a bag of pastries. Wei Long took his watch off and put it by the keyboard.

“Why are you taking that off?”

“So it doesn’t catch on anything.”

“How thoughtful. I’m here to see my boyfriend.” She held out a pastry. He didn’t take it.

He stopped. She’d never used the word. She watched him take it in, and tilted her head.

“Something wrong?”

“I wasn’t expecting it.”

“Would you prefer another word?”

He thought about it properly, which was the thing about him. “No.”

“Good.”

He put one hand on the desk beside her. “Then it’s fine.”

“You’re supposed to say something romantic.”

“I thought I had,” he said, and she stared at him, and pulled him in by the shirt.

It was becoming a pattern. The first kiss was usually hers. The second, more and more, was his. By the third she generally forgot she’d meant to tease him. Tonight she started with his tie and loosened it and slid her fingers inside his collar, and he set his hand on her thigh, over the wool of her skirt, deliberately, and looked at her.

“Is that all right?”

“Yes,” she said, and he drew her an inch closer to the edge of the desk and kissed her with enough intent that both her hands went to his shoulders. When she could, she told him someone had been practising.

“I haven’t.”

“Natural talent?”

“Possibly,” he said, and at 9:10 exactly he called time.

She put her forehead on his shoulder. “You’re ruining romance.”

“I’m keeping our agreement.”

“Same thing,” she said, and he rested his chin on her hair for a second and said, “Come tomorrow,” as if it were a concession.

✦ ✦ ✦

The betting sheet turned up on Wednesday because Sham was careless. Wei Long came back from a meeting and found a folded sheet beside his keyboard, and opened it.

THE TEN-MINUTE OBSERVATION PROJECT, it said across the top, and underneath, in five different hands:

Liu: 10 minutes exactly.

Sham: 12.

Choy: 15.

Sin: 10, plus 2 minutes negotiation.

Tak: 11. Inspector forgets the time.

Monday: 10. Tuesday: 10. Conclusion: subject alarmingly punctual.

On the back someone had written Don’t let Inspector find this.

He folded it in half and called Liu in.

Liu looked at the sheet, and at him, and at the sheet. “That’s not mine, sir.”

“I didn’t ask.”

“Collective research?”

Wei Long waited. Liu sighed. “Sham started it.”

“I did not. I drew the table. I didn’t start the project,” said Sham from across the room.

“Is this how you spend your working hours?”

“No, sir.”

Wei Long put the sheet in his drawer. Liu watched it go. “You’re keeping it, sir?”

“As evidence. Nobody places bets on duty. And stop calling it a project.” He went back to his screen.

Liu’s mouth twitched. “Yes, sir.”

Just before nine Isla arrived with a small box of chocolates, and saw the folded sheet on his desk before he could move it, and held out her hand. He gave it to her because there was no point pretending. She read the title and covered her mouth. By the bottom of the page she had to sit down in the visitor’s chair.

“Alarmingly punctual.”

“Accurate,” he said.

“You’re not even offended? Your whole team is timing our kisses!”

“They’re timing the ten minutes.”

She looked at him and laughed again, helplessly. Then she stood up. “Well. We can’t disappoint them. Blinds.”

He lowered the blinds.

“Door.”

He closed it.

When he turned round she was on the desk. She kissed him before he could say anything, her arms round his neck, and he put his palms on her waist and she drew him in between her knees. It was longer than Monday’s and easier than Tuesday’s. There was less hesitation between them now. She knew he tilted his head when she touched his cheek. He knew she liked being drawn in rather than having to lean across the gap. She kissed his jaw and the corner of his mouth and his mouth, and he watched her between kisses.

“What?” she whispered.

“You’re here.”

“That’s a terrible answer.”

“It’s the truth,” he said, and laid his hand on her thigh again and left it there, and she settled forward with her knees either side of his hips while he kissed her so patiently that she lost track of the clock completely and was only reminded of it by his voice.

“Isla. Time.”

“You’re joking. One more.”

“We’ve had more than one.”

“One more,” she said, and he kissed her, thoroughly, and then let her go, and opened the blinds on six detectives who were all fascinated by their monitors.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday the phone rang just before nine while she was taking her coat off. He answered it standing up.

“Song.”

A man’s voice, fast, in English with a French accent. Wei Long listened, and his face set.

“Repeat that. Where? How long ago? Keep the line open. Don’t negotiate.”

He put it down. “A ransom call. A businessman’s daughter was taken outside her school this afternoon. She’s eleven. The family’s had two calls. The second was in French.”

Isla had already put her coat back on the chair. “Whose citizen is he?”

“Yours. Montreal. He’s been here six years. Our interpreter’s on the other side of the city. The evidential translation will be done again by a court interpreter. Tonight I need it now.” He looked at her.

“Play it.”

The voice on the recording was distorted, low and slow. She listened all the way through without moving, then asked for the last thirty seconds again, and leaned on the desk beside him.

“He’s not asking them to pay tonight. He’s telling them to confirm they’ve understood before the next call. It’s a deadline to answer, not a deadline to pay. And he says the next instruction comes before midnight. Not at midnight. Before. Write that down.” She listened again.

“Is the difference important?”

“It’s two hours of your timeline. There’s something else. He tells them not to bring anybody outside the family into it, but he says it the way people say it at home in Quebec, not the way they’d say it in Paris. And his pronoun changes halfway. He starts with vous, formally, and then he says tu.” She held up a hand.

Wei Long looked at her. “Why?”

“Either he wants to frighten them, or he knows the father. I won’t write that as a conclusion. I’ll write exactly what he said and what it could mean.” She shook her head.

“Every word. Including the odd ones,” said Wei Long.

The third call came just after nine. She sat in his chair with his headphones on and translated it as it came, phrase by phrase, while he stood behind her and passed it to the operations room. The caller asked whether the father had been to the bank. He said the amount hadn’t changed. He asked whether the father’s business account was still active, which made Wei Long’s head come up. He said not to use a third party. He said the next call would come from a different number.

“Preserve the call data. Originals, metadata. Nobody rings that number on their own initiative,” Wei Long said into the operations line.

When a phrase could mean two things she gave him both. When the caller used an idiom she gave him the words and what they meant underneath. She didn’t guess. At some point she pulled one headphone off and said without turning round, “You’re standing close.”

“Do you want me to move?”

“No,” she said, and put the headphone back on.

Just before ten the team had a car. Just before ten he had his coat on.

“Stay with the translation team till Liu tells you the transport’s arranged.”

“Are you giving me instructions?”

“I’m asking you to be available.”

“Better. Go.” She didn’t look up from the screen.

“Thank you,” he said, and she looked up then, and he was gone.

He came back around half past ten to find her still at his desk with a cup of tea Liu had made her, reading through her own translation with a pen. He took his coat off.

“You’re still here.”

“Obviously. The caller used one more phrase on the last call. It sounds like he knows the family, or wants them to think he does. Is there news?” She capped the pen.

“Not yet.”

He looked at the clock. 10:34. “We missed our ten minutes,” he said.

She stared at him. Then she laughed, tired and surprised. “We did.”

“Do you want them now?”

“Are you asking me to sit on your desk?”

“Yes.”

“That’s a first,” said Isla, and he moved her translation to one side, and she sat, and he stood in front of her, and for ten minutes nothing in the room belonged to the police. She held his tie and called his timekeeping a disgrace. He kissed her, and rested his forehead on hers, and said, “Thank you for staying,” and just before eleven exactly he stepped back and picked up the papers.

“You’re hopeless,” she said.

“Apparently.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday morning the girl was found in a flat on the far side of the commercial district after a joint operation. She was alive and frightened and asked for her mother before anything else. A man who had once been her father’s business partner was arrested in the stairwell, and the father, when they told him, said in French and then in English that he’d known that voice since he was twenty-five.

Just before nine that night Isla didn’t knock. She came in and shut the door behind her and put her bag down.

“How was your day?”

“Long.”

“Did you eat?”

“Rice.”

“We’re going to have to work on your vocabulary. Do you know your detectives have stopped pretending not to notice?” She looked at him.

“I know.”

“I think they’re timing us.”

“I know. Since Wednesday.”

“And you didn’t tell me?”

“Would it have changed anything?”

She considered it. “No.”

“Good,” he said, and closed the blinds.

She sat on the desk and he stood between her knees, and she no longer had to show him where his hands went. He knew she liked his palm flat on the small of her back. He knew she liked to stop in the middle of a kiss to say something unnecessary. He knew she’d catch his lower lip between hers and smile when he followed, and tonight she did exactly that. He kissed her forehead, which surprised her into silence.

“That was sweet. Do it again,” she said.

He did. She kissed him, and this time he was the one who didn’t seem interested in stopping. His hand was on her thigh and his thumb moved slowly over the wool. Her fingers were in his hair. His phone buzzed and he let it.

From the other side of the door a muffled voice said, “Two minutes.”

Another voice said, “Shut up.”

Isla froze. Then she put her face in his shoulder and laughed until she shook. “Are they actually timing us through the door?”

“Apparently. Two minutes.” He looked at the clock.

“You’re not seriously going to stop now. Song Wei Long. You’re going to kiss me.” She took hold of his collar.

He considered that. “All right,” he said, and did, until 9:10, and then stepped back and straightened her collar.

“You’re supposed to be irresponsible sometimes.”

“I have other responsibilities.”

“Unfortunately,” said Isla, “I like you.”

He put his hand on her cheek. “Fortunately, I like you too.”

She went still. He hadn’t said it that plainly before, and he seemed to hear it only after it was out. He didn’t take it back.

Just after nine he opened the door. Six detectives were at their desks. Liu was holding a file upside down. He turned it round.

“Good evening, sir.”

Wei Long walked to his desk, took the betting sheet out of the drawer and unfolded it.

“Sergeant. Your prediction was ten minutes exactly.”

“Yes, sir.”

“Congratulations. You owe Sham lunch.” He folded it again.

Liu’s mouth fell open. Across the room Sham started laughing. In the doorway, with her bag on her arm, Isla had both hands over her mouth and the most delighted face he’d seen all week.

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside the rain had stopped and the pavement was still wet. At the taxi rank she told him Hao had rung three times that afternoon to complain about a business partner and once to tell her about a restaurant, and he listened and asked which restaurant. When a car pulled in she caught his hand.

“Ten minutes every evening?”

“If I’m available.”

“Even with a bad case?”

“If I’m available.”

“Even when I’m annoying?”

“You’re frequently annoying,” he said.

She gasped. “Excuse me?”

“It isn’t a problem.”

“You’re lucky you’re handsome.”

“I know.”

She stared at him and laughed and kissed him, slow, and when she pulled away he was looking at her with the expression she was starting to recognise, the one that made her want to kiss him twice more.

“Nine tomorrow?” she said through the window.

“Nine.”

The taxi pulled out. He looked at his watch. 11:29. He had ten minutes tomorrow, and the day after, and he found that the best part of his evening was the easiest thing in it to schedule.

chapters.title: Twelve More Pages of Testimony
chapters.desc: He has to sign twelve pages she translated and can’t get past the first because she’s kissing his neck. She takes the pen out of his hand and takes him home. First night, fully on the page: she undresses him, tells him exactly what she wants, and for once he says nothing at all.
chapters.epigraph: “I have twelve more pages of testimony to sign.”
chapters.content:
The trouble with a girlfriend who spoke three languages was that she could make twelve pages of translated testimony read better than they had any right to. The trouble with a girlfriend who knew exactly how much he liked being kissed was that he could no longer finish reading them.

Wei Long had been on page two for twenty-three minutes. He knew, because he’d checked his watch twice.

The statement was French, from a witness to a hit-and-run outside a hotel, and Isla had done the English and attached translator’s notes where the woman had used a phrase with no clean equivalent. It was thorough and exact and had to be signed tonight, and it was currently impossible to read, because Isla was standing behind his chair kissing the side of his neck.

“Page two,” he said.

She kissed the place under his ear. “Mm?”

“I haven’t finished page two.”

“That’s unfortunate.”

He looked down at the paper. The last paragraph blurred as her mouth moved along his skin. The witness stated that she saw... Isla kissed his neck again, lower, where his collar was open, and he shut his eyes and put down the pen.

“I have twelve more pages of testimony to sign,” he said, without turning round, “but if you don’t stop kissing my neck, neither of us is leaving this room tonight.”

She laughed against his skin. “Is that a threat or a promise, Inspector?”

“It’s an accurate forecast.”

She came round the desk and sat in the visitor’s chair and folded her hands, and for twelve seconds behaved. Then she leaned over, took the pen out of his fingers, and laid it on the desk.

“What are you doing?”

“Taking you home.”

“I haven’t finished.”

“You’ve read the same paragraph four times.”

“Three.”

“Four. I counted. There’s a discrepancy on page seven, you’ll say. It’ll keep till tomorrow. The file will survive till tomorrow. Come home with me.” She reached across and loosened his tie.

The words were light. Her eyes weren’t. He looked at her and understood what she was asking, and asked it back.

“Are you sure?”

“Yes. And I know there are things we haven’t finished with. The file. I’m not pretending that didn’t happen, and I still need you to understand why it mattered.” She touched his cheek.

“I do.”

“I want to believe that. But tonight I want you to come home with me. Those are two separate things.”

He held her gaze. Then he put the twelve pages in the locked drawer and switched off the lamp. At the door she caught his hand.

“Bring the tie.”

“Why?”

“I haven’t finished with it.”

He stared at her. Slowly, slightly, the corner of his mouth moved.

“Understood.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her flat was quiet. A lamp by the sofa, books on the coffee table, a cardigan over the arm of a chair, a neat pile of unopened post by the kitchen. He’d been there before, for tea, for twenty minutes, for a goodnight at the door. He knew where she kept the cups. He’d never been asked to stay.

He took his shoes off and put them beside hers. She put her bag down. Neither of them moved.

“You’re thinking,” she said.

“Yes.”

“About work?”

“No. That I’m here.”

“Yes,” said Isla, and came and stood in front of him, and drew the tie out of his collar. She didn’t look at the clock and neither did he.
