She folded the tie and put it on the little table by the door, and unbuttoned his jacket and eased it off his shoulders and hung it on a chair, and took his watch off his wrist and laid it beside the tie.

He looked at the small arrangement. “You’re undressing me one item at a time.”

“That’s generally how it works.”

“I see.”

“You’re allowed to help. Not yet. Tonight I want to do this,” she said, and when he lifted his hands she caught one and kissed the knuckles.

He went still, and nodded. She opened his shirt one button at a time, watching his face between them the way he’d once watched hers in a stairwell, giving him every chance to stop her. He didn’t look away once. When the last button was undone she slid her palms flat onto his chest and felt how his breathing had changed, and smiled, because she’d done that.

“You’re quiet.”

“I’m listening.”

“To what?”

“You.”

She pulled his head down and kissed him. He answered carefully, one hand finding her waist, and she drew back an inch.

“Can I tell you what I want?”

“Yes.”

“I want you to kiss me. Not so carefully.”

His hand tightened. He kissed her again, and it wasn’t careful, and she made a small pleased sound into his mouth and took his other hand and moved it down her back, and lower, and pressed it there. “Here. And you don’t have to ask me whether every touch is correct. I’ll tell you. I want you to touch me because you want to, not because you’re trying to get it right,” she said.

“I don’t know what you like.”

“Then I’ll tell you. You’re allowed to enjoy yourself, Wei Long.” She kissed the line between his eyebrows.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bedroom was dim, the curtains drawn, a glass of water on the bedside table and her book face down beside it. She pushed the shirt off his shoulders and kissed the creases his collar had left in his skin, and then the hollow of his throat, and then she put her hands on his belt and looked up at him, and he said nothing at all. He’d said nothing since the doorway. He just looked at her with that complete attention and let her do it.

She undressed him slowly. When he was naked she stepped back to look at him, and he stood under it the way he stood under everything, still, except that his hands had closed at his sides and his breathing wasn’t steady any more.

“Your turn. Zip,” she said, and turned round and lifted her hair.

He drew it down the length of her back. His knuckles touched her spine all the way, and she shivered. The dress fell. She stepped out of it in her slip and turned, and took his hands and put them on her.

“Here. Now take it off,” she said, at her breasts, through the thin silk, and he learned the weight of them in his palms, and the sound she made when his thumbs found the points of them.

He did. He looked at her for long enough that she felt the heat climb into her face, and then she sat on the edge of the bed and drew him down by the wrist, and lay back, and pulled him over her.

“Your mouth. Here,” she said.

He kissed her throat, her collarbone, the curve of her breast, and when she pushed her fingers into his hair and held him there he closed his lips round her nipple and she arched off the bed. She talked. She couldn’t help it. She told him slower, and he went slower; harder, and he did that; there, and he stayed. She talked in English and then in French when she lost the English, and he couldn’t understand half of it and obeyed all of it, by the sound of her voice. When she pressed on his shoulders he understood that too, and went down the bed, kissing the soft skin under her ribs and the dip of her navel and the inside of each thigh, and she opened her knees for him and caught her breath when his mouth found her.

He was the most attentive man she had ever let near her. He did what she told him, exactly, and then he learned what she didn’t have to tell him: that she liked his tongue slow and flat, that when her hips came up she wanted him to hold them down, that she wanted his fingers too, one, then two, curled. She came with her hand twisted in his hair and his name broken in the middle, shaking against his mouth, and he didn’t stop until she pushed him away, laughing and gasping, and pulled him back up.

“Come here. Come here, come here,” she said.

She rolled him onto his back and reached into the drawer of the bedside table for a condom, and opened it with her teeth, and rolled it down him while he watched her hands with an expression she would remember for the rest of her life. Then she straddled his hips. He put his hands on her thighs and she held them there and lowered herself onto him, slowly, all the way, and they both went still.

“Look at me,” she said.

He was already looking.

She rode him slowly at first, her palms flat on his chest, finding the angle, and then less slowly. He moved under her the way she showed him, rising to meet her, his hands on her hips learning her rhythm and then keeping it for her when her own began to go. She talked to him the whole time. She told him how he felt inside her, what she wanted, that he was beautiful, that he should stop being so quiet, and he wasn’t quiet exactly, his breath came hard and rough, but he didn’t say a single word. His eyes didn’t leave her face. When she reached down between them and touched herself he groaned, low, the first real sound he’d made, and his fingers dug into her hips.

“Not yet,” she said, and he obeyed that too, his jaw set, holding on, until she came a second time, tight round him, her head thrown back, and only then did he let go. He pulled her down onto his chest and drove up into her once, twice, and came with his face in her hair, and the only word he said all night was her name.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay on him with her cheek on his shoulder and her fingers drawing idle shapes on his collarbone. The room smelled of her perfume and of them. He’d dealt with the condom and come straight back, and gathered her up again as if it were obvious.

“Are you all right?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“You didn’t say anything.”

“You said enough for both of us.”

She laughed into his skin. “Was that a complaint?”

“No. Isla.” He was quiet.

Only her name, the way he’d said it at the end, and she lifted her head to look at him. He drew her back down. The phone in his jacket on the chair in the other room didn’t ring, and he didn’t think about the twelve pages in the drawer, or the clock, and when the room went quiet around them neither of them needed to fill it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke before the alarm on Saturday and didn’t recognise the ceiling. Then he felt the warmth beside him. She was asleep on her side with one hand under her cheek and her hair across her mouth. He moved the hair. She didn’t wake. It was 7:16. He wanted to stay, and the thought of her waking to an empty kitchen got him out of bed.

The kitchen required investigation. Plates in one cupboard, bowls in another, a third full of small appliances he couldn’t identify. He found a frying pan, and eggs, and on the side of the egg box, instructions. He read them twice. They said cook until the whites are set, and didn’t say whether the heat should be low or medium, and he stood in front of the stove considering the omission, and chose medium. Some shell went into the pan with the first egg. He removed it. The second went better. He waited for the whites to set and they took longer than he’d been led to believe.

He made toast. He found the butter. He discovered she kept honey in a cupboard rather than on the counter, which seemed to him a decision with consequences. The coffee machine took him six minutes and the manual.

Just before eight she came to the kitchen doorway in his shirt, with the sleeves over her hands, and looked at the table, and at him.

“You made breakfast?”

“Yes.”

“Did you follow a recipe?”

“The instructions were on the box.”

She stared at him, and began to laugh, and had to hold on to the door frame. “You followed the instructions on the egg box?”

“They were clear.”

“Oh, Wei Long. They’re good.” She sat down and tasted the eggs and pointed her fork at him.

He looked relieved, as far as he ever looked anything. “Good.”

“You’re awfully domestic for a man who arrests people for a living.”

“I do arrest people for a living.”

“I know,” she said, and then, lower, over her coffee, “I liked waking up with you here.”

“I liked it too.”

“Then stay for breakfast next time.”

“I will.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She found the notebook at nine looking for a phone charger. It was on the side table under yesterday’s paper, the plain black one he took out at the station when he didn’t want to forget something. She picked it up only to move it away from the edge, and a loose slip of paper fell out of the back. She caught it. Three lines, in his small, upright hand.

Isla Ren.

Takes her coffee without sugar. Laughs before she finishes a joke.

The weather was clear today.

The last line was so completely unnecessary that she started smiling and couldn’t stop. She shouldn’t have opened the book. She opened it anyway. Dates, reminders, a case number. Then:

24 March. Nine o’clock. She brought coffee.

27 March. She stayed to translate.

11 April. Twelve pages. Couldn’t finish page two.

12 April. Breakfast: eggs, toast, coffee. Followed instructions.

She laughed out loud, and he appeared in the doorway with a tea towel and stopped when he saw what she was holding.

“Isla.”

She held up the slip. “What’s this?”

“Notes.”

“About me?”

“Some of them.”

“Don’t take it,” she said, and held the notebook against her chest.

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You’re looking at it as if you’re about to confiscate evidence.”

“It’s my notebook. You can read it. You’ve read it.” He came into the room.

“Why is the weather in here?”

“It was clear.”

“Did you think it was important?”

“No.”

“Then why is it there?”

He thought about it. “I was writing things down.”

She looked at him, and the laughter went out of her face and something else came into it. “Can I keep this?”

He took the slip from her and folded it once and put it in her palm. “All right.”

“You know most people write something romantic.”

“I did,” he said, and took the notebook from her, and opened it to page seven, and held it out.

She talks when she’s nervous.

She talks when she’s happy.

She talks when she’s angry.

I hope she keeps talking.

Isla went still. She read it twice and looked up at him. “You’re terrible at this.”

“At what?”

“Romance.”

“I thought you liked it.”

“I do. Especially the last line,” she said, and put her arms round his waist and her cheek against his chest, and he put his chin on her hair.

“Even when you interrupt my work.”

“Frequently,” she said, before he could, and pinched his side, and he looked down at her with what anyone else would have called a smile.

“Can I have the notebook?”

“No.”

“It has me in it.”

“That doesn’t make it yours.”

“Fine. I’ll write my own. Song Wei Long. Makes eggs by following the box. Handsome. Terrible at flirting.”

“I made breakfast.”

“That isn’t flirting.”

“Then what is?”

She reached up and kissed him. “That,” she said, and he kissed her back with his hand at her waist, and when she laughed against his mouth he didn’t need to write it down.

chapters.title: The Inspector Smiles, Allegedly
chapters.desc: Three officers claim to have seen him smile at a text during a briefing. Nobody can prove it; he denies everything. A pickpocket ring at the cruise terminal; a quick, greedy kiss in the car park because she can’t wait for nine.
chapters.epigraph: “Because I wanted to kiss you now.”
chapters.content:
The allegation was first made at 9:17 on the last Tuesday in April, by Sergeant Liu, who had worked for Inspector Song for four years and therefore knew exactly which things were dangerous to say in front of him. He said it anyway, at the end of the morning briefing, with the plans for the cruise terminal still on the screen.

“Sir. Did you get a message just now?”

Wei Long didn’t look up from the briefing sheet. “Yes.”

Liu waited. Wei Long turned a page. “Is there a question?”

“No, sir.”

“Then why are you standing there?”

Liu sat down. Detective Sham became interested in his notebook. Constable Choy, who had been brought up from the front desk for the day, stopped drinking his coffee. The briefing went on for six more minutes without incident, and then Sham, who had apparently decided his life was worth less than the chance to be irritating, raised his hand.

“Sir. May I clarify something?”

“About the operation?”

“Not exactly.”

“Then no.”

Sham lowered his hand. Liu looked at the ceiling. Wei Long put down his pen. “What?”

“Three officers believe they saw you smile, sir. At 9:17. At your phone,” said Liu, in the voice of a man reading a charge.

The room was silent.

“No,” said Wei Long.

“That’s what I said, sir. Unfortunately they insist.”

“Who?”

Liu looked at Sham. Sham looked at Choy. Choy looked at the coffee machine.

“You saw me smile, Detective?”

“Yes, sir.”

“I haven’t smiled.”

“That’s what we were discussing, sir.”

“Describe it.”

Sham thought about it. “Your mouth moved.”

“That isn’t a description.”

“Upwards, sir.”

Wei Long turned to Choy, who considered his answer with the care of a man deciding whether to jump from a moving vehicle.

“Yes, sir. After your phone lit up. It was an expression.”

“What kind?”

“A happy one,” said Sham, before Choy could save himself.

Wei Long closed his folder. The sound was small. It had roughly the effect of a gun being put on a table.

“The terminal operation is at eleven. I want the camera review finished before then. Sham, you have the plain-clothes teams. Choy, statements. Sergeant, the property trail and the timeline. Are we finished?”

“Yes, sir,” said Liu.

Three notebooks opened. The allegation was suspended. It wasn’t withdrawn.

✦ ✦ ✦

The message in question had come in at 9:17.

Thank You (Paid): Question. If I come at nine tonight, will you have finished your paperwork?

Wei Long: Yes. Before nine.

Thank You (Paid): I’m not asking you to work harder.

Wei Long: Then what are you asking?

Thank You (Paid): Whether I can have you without competing with twelve pages of testimony.

He had looked at the screen, and, apparently, smiled. He had typed Yes, put the phone away, and gone on with the briefing, and hadn’t thought the matter worth further discussion. Three of his officers had.

✦ ✦ ✦

The pickpockets were sisters, sixty-three and sixty-seven, and they had been working the cruise terminal for at least fourteen months.

The younger, Ngok Mei-lan, wore a pale blue cardigan and carried a handbag with a broken clasp. The older, Ngok Mei-ying, liked floral scarves and glasses she pushed up her nose with one finger. Neither looked like anything, which was the point. When the big ships came in and the tour groups bunched by the baggage belts, one sister made a small trouble, a dropped map, a question about the toilets, and the other went into a jacket. Two younger men took the wallets and phones and passports out of the building within minutes, and a fifth person in a hi-vis vest watched the security staff and sent a text when a uniform came near. The first report had looked like nothing: a tourist’s wallet, thick with cash, lost somewhere between the gangway and the taxi rank. Then there was another, and another, and when someone ran the terminal footage side by side, the same two women were in the background of every one of them, close enough to matter, never close enough to notice.

In the operations room Wei Long stood in front of the screen. “Stop.”

The image froze. A family by the belts, a man in a white shirt looking down at his phone. The younger sister behind him with a folded map. The older one three metres away, adjusting her scarf.

“Run it.”

The map dropped. The man turned to pick it up for her. The older sister stepped in, and her hand went behind his jacket and came out empty-looking.

“Stop. Who has the wallet?”

“The younger one, sir. The older one’s the distraction,” said Sham.

“Then why is the older one looking at the camera?”

Sham leaned in. “She’s checking the angle.”

“She’s the organiser. They know where the cameras are, which officers work the terminal and how long a report takes to reach the control room. Don’t mistake their age for incompetence.”

He turned to the room. “We have the method. I want the two men before we touch the women. Follow the property, not the cardigans. Nobody moves until I say,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ship had come in at ten and the arrivals hall was full of it: tour guides holding up coloured paddles, families with trolleys, porters threading between them, the roar of a thousand suitcase wheels on polished stone. Wei Long stood at the rail on the upper level with one hand on the metal. The younger sister was by the information desk. The older stood by a vending machine reading a brochure about the harbour.

“Primary’s moving,” said Sham in his ear.

The younger sister had found a couple with two big cases and was pointing at the exit for them. The woman turned to look.

“Wait,” said Wei Long. His eyes were on the older one. She’d stopped reading. She was looking at a man in a dark jacket by the baggage carousel, and when he walked, she folded her brochure and followed him.

“Teams hold.”

The man stopped to answer his phone. She came closer. A child ran past and bumped her shoulder, and she looked down and smiled at the child and stepped aside, and her hand was already in the man’s coat.

“Now.”

It took under a minute. Two plain-clothes officers came up either side of the older sister, a third took the younger at the information desk, and neither of them struggled. The younger looked offended. The older looked disappointed.

“Officer,” she said, straightening her scarf, “you’ve made a mistake.”

Wei Long came down the stairs. “Ngok Mei-ying. I’m Inspector Song. You’re under arrest on suspicion of theft and conspiracy to steal.”

She looked at her sister, who had begun to talk fast, and told her not to answer questions. Then she turned to him. “Young man, I’m old enough to be your mother.”

“That doesn’t change the procedure.”

For the first time she looked genuinely annoyed. As they walked her to the van she looked back over her shoulder.

“You should be careful, Inspector.”

“About what?”

She gave him a small, kind smile. “Women.”

The officer beside her nearly tripped. Wei Long’s face didn’t change.

“I’ll bear it in mind.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The search of the sisters’ bags turned up eleven wallets, six phones, four passports and a small notebook of initials and dates in a neat old-fashioned hand. The two young men were picked up that afternoon at a storage unit the property trail led to. By six the operation was over, and there was a long evening of statements, exhibits and inventory still ahead of it.

“The older one wants to talk to you, sir,” said Sham, by the van.

“About what?”

“She won’t say.”

“Then she can say it to her lawyer. You’re looking at my phone.” Wei Long noticed where Sham’s eyes had gone.

“No, sir.”

“You are.”

“I was wondering whether you’d had any messages, sir. Relating to the operation.” Sham’s face was perfectly straight.

“If you have time to investigate my phone, you have time to finish the inventory.”

“Yes, sir.”

When Sham had gone he took the phone out.

Thank You (Paid): How many people have you arrested today?

Wei Long: Four.

Thank You (Paid): And how many have you smiled at?

He put it back in his pocket without answering, which was its own kind of answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

The inventory was finished around half past seven. The statements were checked around half past seven. Around half past seven he was writing the operation report when the phone buzzed again.

Thank You (Paid): I’m nearby.

Wei Long: Where?

Thank You (Paid): Outside.

He looked out of the window. The station car park was mostly hidden by a concrete pillar. He stood up and took his jacket off the chair.

“Sir?” said Liu.

“I’m leaving.”

Liu looked at the clock, which said 7:37, and visibly decided not to mention that the inspector had never left before nine in four years. “Good evening, sir.”

The door closed behind him. Sham leaned across two desks.

“He smiled again.”

“Did you see it?”

“No.”

“Then stop saying it.”

“I saw his face.”

“You saw the back of his head.”

“His shoulders were different,” said Sham.

Choy put his pen down. “You’re both going to be transferred.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She was leaning on his car with one hand in her coat pocket and her phone in the other, in a dark skirt and a cream blouse, her hair down. She looked up when she heard his steps.

“You’re early,” she said.

“Seven minutes.”

“Did you finish your work?”

“All of it.”

“Look at you. A man of his word. Something happened.” She studied his face, and her eyes narrowed.

“No.”

“You’re doing the thing where you’ve already decided not to tell me something.”

He considered her. “Three officers believe I smiled during a briefing.”

She opened her mouth, and nothing came out, and then she laughed until she had to turn away and put a hand on the roof of the car.

“Three? Three officers? And you deny it?” she said.

“I didn’t smile.”

“Of course you didn’t. Who?”

“Liu, Sham and Choy. They said my mouth moved upwards.”

She covered her face. “Oh, I know exactly what happened. You read my message.”

“Yes.”

“And smiled.”

“Three unreliable witnesses.”

She stepped closer and laid her hand on the front of his coat. “Perhaps they saw something rare. An inspector being happy.”

He looked down at her hand. “Is that what you think?”

“I think you were reading something you liked. Was it my message?”

“Yes.”

Her face went soft. Then she looked past him at the station windows. A shape moved behind one of them and vanished.

“Are they watching?”

“No.”

“You’re a terrible liar,” she said.

She caught his lapels and pulled him down. The first kiss was quick, a hello. The second wasn’t. He put one hand flat on the car door beside her head and leaned in, and she smiled against his mouth.

“You’re late.”

“I’m seven minutes early.”

“Not for this,” said Isla, and kissed him again, and slid her hand inside his open coat and laid it flat on his waist through his shirt. The air was cool and the space between them wasn’t. He drew back far enough to look at her.

“You could have waited till nine.”

“I could have.”

“Why didn’t you?”

She looked at him as if the answer were obvious. “Because I wanted to kiss you now.”

His hand settled at her waist. “All right.”

“That’s your answer?”

“Yes,” he said, and kissed her with a good deal less restraint. She’d meant to give him one kiss, perhaps two. She hadn’t meant to forget where they were. But his mouth was warm and he held her with the last few hours finally out of the way, and her fingers curled into his shirt under the coat.

“Do you know what I like? That you never pretend you don’t want me,” she said, when she could.

“I don’t.”

“I know.” She kissed the corner of his mouth, and his cheek, and the other corner, and he caught her hand before she could go on.

“Isla. We’re in the station car park.”

“Yes.”

“There are people here.”

“Are you asking me to stop?”

“No.”

“Then I don’t see the problem.”

He looked at her for a second longer. Then he opened the passenger door.

“What are you doing?”

“Getting you out of the car park.”

She laughed all the way into her seat. “How romantic,” she said, when he’d got in on his side, and then, “Inspector? I think you smiled.”

He started the engine. “No.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They hadn’t decided where to eat. She scrolled through her phone and he turned down each place for a practical reason.

“Too far.”

“It’s fifteen minutes.”

“Traffic.”

“This one.”

“It closes at nine.”

“We’d be there before nine.”

“Not with traffic.”

“You really are difficult.”

“I thought you knew.”

“I did. I keep hoping you’ll improve. Do you want to know something? I was going to wait till nine. Then I sat in my meeting thinking about you, and I thought, why should I wait? You’re ten minutes away.” She put the phone down.

“Seven.”

“Seven minutes away. Besides, I wanted to see whether the rumours were true. That the inspector smiles when he gets a message from a certain woman.” She put her hand on his arm.

He glanced at her. “Allegedly.”

At the next red light he looked down at her hand on his sleeve, and turned his own hand over on the gear stick, palm up, and she put her fingers into it. The light changed. He drove on one-handed. Back at the station three officers were still arguing about whether the inspector had smiled. None of them had proof, and all three were certain.

chapters.title: The First Dinner He Remembers
chapters.desc: He arrives early with flowers he doesn’t know the name of. Over dinner he tells her one true thing: his grandfather, Old Song, walked the Walled City beat for thirty years and he did his homework at the station desk. At his flat the scanner on the bedside table is ignored. Explicit, slower than the first: he takes his time and narrates nothing.
chapters.epigraph: “He used to say that if you walked the same streets long enough, people stopped seeing the uniform.”
chapters.content:
Wei Long arrived twenty-three minutes early. He had checked the address twice, confirmed the booking the afternoon before, and left the station with time for traffic. He hadn’t allowed time for the flowers.

They lay on the passenger seat in brown paper and a narrow ribbon. He’d stood in front of the florist’s window near the restaurant for some minutes trying to decide what was appropriate, and then gone in, and the woman behind the counter had asked if they were for a birthday.

“No.”

“An anniversary?”

“No.”

She’d waited. He had eventually said, “Dinner,” and she’d smiled at him in a way he found unhelpful, and picked out a bunch of pale things somewhere between cream and butter yellow, with more petals than seemed necessary, packed in tight like paper roses. He’d asked what they were called. She had told him. He’d forgotten by the time he reached the car.

Just after seven he got out and stood by the restaurant door with one hand in his coat pocket and the flowers in the other, and felt, for the first time in some years, conspicuous.

Isla saw him before he saw her. She slowed on the pavement. He was standing exactly as he stood at a crime scene, upright and watchful and entirely still, holding a bouquet as if it might go off. She smiled, and he looked up, and for a second neither of them moved.

“Hello,” she said.

“Hello.”

“Are those for me?”

“Yes.”

She took them carefully and put her face into them. “Oh. Ranunculus.”

He looked at the flowers. “What?”

“They’re ranunculus. You didn’t know.” She looked up at him over the paper, and saw his face, and started to laugh.

“The florist told me.”

“And you forgot.”

“Between the shop and the car.”

“That’s sweet,” she said, and kissed his cheek. “How long have you been standing here?”

“Not long.”

She looked at the clock over the door. “Twenty minutes.”

He said nothing.

“Did you miss me?”

“Yes.”

Her smile went smaller and warmer. “You could have said that first,” she said, and put her arm through his, and he opened the door for her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The restaurant was quiet enough to talk in. She laid the flowers on the chair beside her. He’d read the menu on the way in and decided. She took her time, and ordered something with prawns, and he ordered beef and a pot of tea.

“So,” she said. “How was your week?”

“Busy.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It was a busy week. We charged the sisters from the terminal. The younger one cried. The older one asked her lawyer whether she could keep her scarf in the cell.” She gave him a look, and he tried.

“Did she say anything else to you about women?”

“She said I was the first policeman in forty years who’d had the decency to arrest her himself.”

Isla laughed. “That’s practically a compliment.”

“I haven’t decided.”

“You could ask about my week too, you know.”

“How was your week?”

“Lovely. That was a terrible question.” She waited. He waited.

“You told me to ask it.”

“I told you to sound interested.”

“I am interested.”

She studied him and saw that he was. “All right. I had a detained citizen on Wednesday with no family here and a lawyer who kept insisting our office could make the court change its mind.”

“Could you?”

“No.”

“Did you tell him?”

“Eventually.”

“Good,” said Wei Long.

“You’re so supportive.”

“What should I have said?”

“That I’m brilliant and the lawyer was an idiot.”

“Was he?”

“Yes.”

“Then he was an idiot,” he said, and she looked so pleased that he had to look at his tea.

The food came. She told him about a colleague who’d sent a message meant for one person to the whole consulate, including its unfortunate last sentence, which she repeated in a whisper, and he laughed. Once, under his breath. She put her fork down.

“There.”

“What?”

“You laughed. At my story. I like that.” She picked her fork up again.

A little later she asked, carefully, whether he ever talked about his family.

“Sometimes. With Yu Chen.”

“Your cousin. The medical student?”

“Final year. He has exams in June and he’s pretending he isn’t worried.”

“Does he live with you?”

“No. He’s in the old Song house. It’s beside the Lin estate. You’ve seen the name in my cases.”

She had, once or twice, in the way you see the name of a weather system. “Is that where you grew up?”

“Yes.”

She waited. He poured himself more tea, and then.

“Do you want to hear about it?”

“Yes.”

He looked at her, deciding where to begin.

“My grandfather was a police sergeant. Old Song. He walked the Walled City beat for thirty years. He knew everybody. Shopkeepers, families, the ones who’d been in trouble more than once. Which staircases flooded in the rain. Which doors you didn’t knock on after midnight. He used to say that if you walked the same streets long enough, people stopped seeing the uniform.” His voice was level, but something in it had shifted, the way a room sounds different with a door opened.

“What did they see instead?”

“Someone who’d remember them. I didn’t understand that when he said it. I understand it better now.” He turned his cup a quarter turn.

“Is he the reason you joined?”

“Partly. School finished at four and his shift finished at ten. I did my homework at the station desk.”

She smiled. “I can see that. A small boy at a desk that’s much too big for him, doing sums while everyone talks over his head.”

“That’s accurate.”

“Did the officers help you?”

“Some tried. He checked my work. If it was wrong, I did it again.”

“That sounds familiar.”

“Why?”

“You do that now. Make people do it again.”

“That’s not the same.”

“Isn’t it?”

He didn’t argue, which meant he’d lost. “There’s a photograph of him inside the front door of the Song house. In uniform, outside the old station, after his last shift on the beat. He has one hand on his belt. He isn’t smiling.”

“Like you.”

“Perhaps.”

“Was he handsome?”

“I don’t know. I never asked.”

“That’s such a man answer,” said Isla, and reached across the table and put her fingers over his. “Do you miss him?”

“Yes.”

He said it plainly, without anything to make it easier. She rubbed her thumb over his knuckles and didn’t ask anything else, and he was grateful.

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside she asked whether she could see his flat. He said yes. She asked whether tonight. He said, “If you want,” and she said, “I do,” and got into the car with the ranunculus in her lap.

It was exactly what she’d expected, which made her want to laugh. Clean, quiet, everything with a place. Nothing on the walls. A dark jacket by the door. A stack of files squared at the far end of the dining table. She told him the flowers needed water, and he found a glass vase that had plainly never been used and arranged them in it, stem by stem, with the concentration of a man fitting a firearm back together.

“You still don’t know what they’re called,” she said, from the doorway.

“Ranunculus.”

She turned. “You remembered.”

“Yes.”

“How?”

He held up his left hand. On the palm, in neat biro capitals that had smudged a little at the edges, was RANUNCULUS.

She stared at it, and then at him. “When did you do that?”

“In the restaurant. When you went to the bathroom.”

She was laughing too much and had to sit down on the arm of his sofa. Then she got up, and came to him, and took the hand and kissed the middle of the palm, over the ink.

“Do you know what I want?” she said.

“What?”

“To kiss you.”

“All right.”

“You’re always so accommodating.”

“You asked,” he said, and she kissed him, and this time he didn’t need convincing.

He drew her in by the waist. She slid her arms round his neck. When she pulled back she said, “Can I stay?”

“Yes.”

“Until morning?”

“Yes. I have an early start.”

“And?”

“I still want you to stay,” he said, and she stopped smiling because she didn’t need to any more.

✦ ✦ ✦

His bedroom was as orderly as the rest of it. A lamp, a glass of water, and on the bedside table a small black radio scanner with its display glowing blue and its volume turned low, a murmur of call signs and addresses underneath the silence.

“Is that yours?”

“Yes.”

“Does it stay on all night?”

“Not usually.” He took his watch off and put it beside the lamp.

“Do you ever switch off?”

“Yes.”

“When?”

He looked at her. “Now.”

She reached for his shirt buttons, and he caught her hands, gently, and held them.

“Let me,” he said.

She’d done all the work on that first night at her flat, and she’d loved it, and she found that she wanted this more. She let her hands fall. He undid the buttons of her blouse with the same patience he’d given the flowers, and slid it off her shoulders, and then didn’t do anything at all except look at her, so long and so seriously that she felt the colour come up into her face.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re looking.”

“Yes.”

She laughed. He touched her cheek, and kissed her, and then he kissed her jaw, and the side of her throat, and the hollow above her collarbone, and he didn’t hurry any of it. He didn’t speak either. He reached behind her and opened her bra and drew it down her arms, and bent his head and took her nipple into his mouth, and her laugh broke in the middle and turned into a breath. She put her hands in his hair. He unzipped her skirt and pushed it and everything under it down over her hips, kneeling to do it, and she stepped out of them and stood naked in his lamplight while he knelt in front of her with his shirt still on, and he looked up at her once, and then he put his mouth on her.

She stopped laughing altogether.

He was slow. He was so slow that she started to shake before he’d done anything that should have made her shake, his hands spread on the backs of her thighs, holding her up when her knees began to go. She said his name. She said, “Bed,” and he stood and lifted her onto it, and pulled his shirt over his head without unbuttoning it, and got rid of the rest, and came down over her, and for a while nobody narrated anything. He kissed his way down her body again and she let her thighs fall open and held the sheet in both fists while his tongue moved on her and his fingers pressed into her, steady, patient. When she came she said something in French that she would later decline to translate.

The scanner crackled. A burst of traffic came through it, a voice reading an address. Neither of them moved. It crackled again, louder.

Wei Long lifted his head. Isla was looking at him with one eyebrow up, flushed and breathing hard.

“Are you going to answer that?”

“No.”

“Are you sure?”

The scanner squawked a third time. He reached across without getting off her, turned it off, and set it back exactly where it had been.

“Good,” said Isla.

He reached into the drawer under it for a condom. She took it out of his hand and put it on him herself, slowly, because he’d made her wait, and watched his jaw tighten. Then she lay back and drew him down by the shoulders, and he came into her in one long slow push that made both of them stop breathing. He held still. His forehead came down to hers.

“Where were we?” he said, into her mouth.

“Here,” said Isla, and moved under him, and he moved with her.

He made love the way he did everything: completely, without wasted motion, paying attention. He watched her face to see what each change did. When she tilted her hips he followed the angle and kept it. When she dug her heels into the backs of his thighs he went deeper and slower, and when she pulled at him he gave her what she pulled for. He could set his restraint down now when she asked, and she asked, with her nails in his back, and he set it down, and moved hard enough to push her up the bed, one hand braced on the headboard. She came again with her mouth open on his shoulder. He followed with her name said once against her ear, low.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after one she was lying on his chest in the dark. A thin line of streetlight came under the curtains. His hand was spread on her back, and his breathing had slowed under her cheek.

“Uncomfortable?” he said.

“No. I was thinking about your grandfather. I want to see the photograph.”

“The one inside the door?”

“Yes. Not tomorrow. I don’t want to turn our first dinner into a family inspection.”

“Our first dinner?”

“Yes, the one you remembered,” she said.

He was quiet. Then, “All right.”

“I like your flat. I like your flowers. I like that you came early,” she said.

“And?”

She lifted her head. “I like you.”

He brushed her hair back off her face. “I know.”

“That’s not romantic.”

“I like you too,” he said, and she settled down again, satisfied. A few minutes passed.

“You know you can just ask me what flowers I like next time.”

“I can.”

“But I liked these,” she said, and he felt her smile against his skin.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 7:02 his phone buzzed on the bedside table. He reached for it without waking her. A message from Sham about one discrepancy in the terminal property inventory, sent with an apology for its being Sunday. He turned the phone off.

“Work?” she said into the pillow.

“Yes. It isn’t urgent.”

“Then ignore it. Are you staying?” She hadn’t opened her eyes.

“Yes.”

She reached for him under the blanket. “Then come here.”

He did. The phone stayed where it was. For once the first thing he remembered about the morning was her, ahead of any case or report or name to be entered into a system, and after her the flowers on the dining table in the next room. He had written their name in his notebook before bed. Ranunculus. He hadn’t written anything else, because he hadn’t needed to.

chapters.title: Her Brother Storms the Station
chapters.desc: Ren Hao finds out from someone else’s photo and comes to the front desk at volume. Wei Long takes him into an interview room and reads him his rights as a joke nobody laughs at. Isla takes both their phones away and makes them shake hands.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not going anywhere because someone is loud.”
chapters.content:
The first sign that something was wrong was the noise. The station always had noise: phones, printers, someone asking whether the coffee machine had been mended. This was a man’s voice at a volume that suggested he believed the building had been put up so that he could be heard in it.

“I’M NOT LEAVING UNTIL SOMEONE TELLS ME WHERE HE IS.”

At the front desk Constable Choy looked up. The man opposite him was tall and well dressed, with a heavy watch, a leather briefcase and the confidence of somebody used to walking into rooms without waiting.

“Sir, as I’ve explained, you can’t just walk into the station and...”

“Then call him. Inspector Song. Song. Wei. Long.”

“Do you have an appointment?”

The man stared at him. “Do I look like someone who makes appointments?”

Choy decided that wasn’t a question he had to answer. “Your name, sir?”

“Ren Hao.”

Choy wrote it down in careful capitals, because a man that loud was going to end up in somebody’s notebook today whatever else happened. “And your relationship to Inspector Song?”

“None. I’m here about his relationship with my sister. Isla Ren.” He leaned on the counter.

Choy put his pen down. That explained the noise.

✦ ✦ ✦

Wei Long was reading a case file when Detective Sham appeared in his doorway just after ten.

“Sir. There’s a visitor at the front desk. Ren Hao.”

He turned a page, and stopped. “What does he want?”

Sham looked at the ceiling. “Your relationship with his sister, apparently.”

Wei Long had met Ren Hao twice, both times through Isla’s phone: a video call that had lasted four minutes, and once when he’d picked up her phone by mistake and been greeted with enormous warmth by a man who hadn’t yet been told who he was talking to. He hadn’t expected him in person.

“Is he waiting?”

“Not in silence, sir.”

Wei Long stood. “Put him in Interview Two.”

Sham blinked. “Interview Two?”

“It has a door. Don’t let him touch the equipment.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao was standing by the table when Wei Long came in, and turned round with his chin up. He had his sister’s eyes and none of her patience.

“So you’re Song Wei Long.”

“Yes.”

Ren Hao looked him up and down. “You’re younger than I expected.”

“Would you prefer me older?”

Ren Hao opened his mouth and shut it. Wei Long closed the door, sat down, put his notebook on the table and opened it.

“Please sit.”

“I’m not here to sit.”

“Then stand.”

Ren Hao pulled out the chair and sat in it like a man insulted by furniture. “Don’t use that voice.”

“What voice?”

“The police voice.”

“I’m a police officer.”

“I know what you are. How long have you been seeing my sister?”

“Since March.”

“March? This year? And nobody thought to tell me?”

“Your sister may have her own reasons for deciding when to tell you.”

“You’re awfully calm,” said Ren Hao, and then, when that had no effect, he chose volume. “DO YOU UNDERSTAND THAT SHE’S MY SISTER?”

Wei Long waited until the walls had stopped ringing.

“Yes. And I understand you’re here because someone sent you a photograph of us at a restaurant on Saturday and you weren’t pleased to find out that way.”

Ren Hao’s face changed. “How do you know about the photograph?”

“Your sister told me. Last night.”

“She knew I knew? And she didn’t ring me? Unbelievable.” He looked at the ceiling.

“Yes,” said Wei Long, which didn’t help.

“What are your intentions?”

“To go on seeing her.”

“That’s it?”

“That’s what you asked.”

“You’re not going to tell me you love her?”

Wei Long considered that with the seriousness he gave everything. “I don’t think I should say that to her brother before I’ve said it to her.”

For the first time since he’d walked in, Ren Hao had nothing to say. Wei Long turned a page.

“Are you serious about her?”

“Yes.”

“How serious?”

“Serious enough that I don’t intend to waste her time.”

Ren Hao studied him. That answer seemed to irritate him less than the others. He was still chewing on it when Wei Long looked up from his notebook.

“Would you like me to read you your rights?”

“What?”

“You’ve entered a police station, raised your voice at the front desk, and declined to leave an interview room.”

“You’re joking.”

“Yes,” said Wei Long, with his face exactly as it had been.

Nobody laughed. Not even the officer behind the glass, who was Sham, and who later swore he had wanted to. Ren Hao looked at the mirrored window.

“Is someone watching?”

“Probably.”

“Wonderful. I’m going to find my sister.” He stood up.

“She isn’t here.”

“I know that.”

“Then sit down. I haven’t finished my questions.”

Ren Hao stared at him, and sat. Wei Long wrote something.

“What are you writing?”

“That you sat down.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Isla arrived twelve minutes later. She had been in a meeting when the front desk rang her: Miss Ren, your brother is here, then he’s asking for Inspector Song, then he’s been taken into Interview Two. She rang the desk back from the taxi.

“Is he still shouting?”

Choy considered. “Not at present.”

“That’s encouraging.”

“Miss Ren? Perhaps you should come quickly.”

She opened the door of Interview Two without knocking. Both men stood up.

“Why are you here?” she said to her brother.

“That’s what I’d like to know.”

“You came to a police station to shout at my boyfriend.”

Ren Hao turned on Wei Long. “Boyfriend?”

“He read me my rights,” Ren Hao said, pointing.

Isla turned slowly. “Was that necessary?”

“No,” said Wei Long.

She closed her eyes. Then she held out her hand to her brother. “Phone.”

“What? Why?”

“Because you’re going to stop ringing people and messaging people and asking strangers whether I’ve been seen in public with my own boyfriend.”

“I didn’t ask strangers.”

“You asked the person who sent you the photograph.”

“That’s not a stranger, that’s Theo from the gym.”

“Phone.”

He looked at Wei Long for support and got none, and put his phone in her palm with a sigh that could have filled a stadium. She put it in her bag and turned.

“Yours too.”

Wei Long looked at her. “Why?”

“Because I know you.”

He gave it to her. She put it beside her brother’s.

“Now. You’re both going to behave. Shake hands.”

Neither moved. She raised her eyebrows. Ren Hao put out his hand with the expression of a man consenting to a medical procedure, and Wei Long took it, and the handshake was brief and firm and entirely professional.

“That’s not enough. Hug him,” said Isla.

They said “No” at the same moment.

“Yes.”

“Isla, I’m not hugging him. I don’t know him.”

“That’s the point. Both of you.”

The silence went on long enough for Sham, behind the glass, to stop breathing. Then Ren Hao stepped forward, threw both arms round the inspector and crushed him.

Wei Long went completely still. His hands stayed at his sides for one full second. Then, with the precision of a man completing an unfamiliar procedure, he laid one hand flat on Ren Hao’s back. Ren Hao squeezed harder. Over his shoulder Wei Long looked at Isla with an expression that said, plainly, that this would be remembered. She smiled at him.

Ren Hao let go, straightened his jacket and cleared his throat. “Fine.”

“You’re stiff,” he said to Wei Long.

“I’ve been told.”

“Good, now we’re leaving. Lunch. Both of you. And I’m keeping the phones,” said Isla.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao walked ahead of them down the street, still talking. He had expected someone taller. He had expected someone friendlier. He had expected to be offered tea.

“He’s always like this. He’s worse when he’s nervous,” Isla said to Wei Long, with her arm through his.

“I’M NOT NERVOUS,” said her brother, from ten metres ahead.

“Nobody asked you.”

“I heard that.”

“Good. Did he offend you?” She looked up at Wei Long.

“No.”

“Did you enjoy being hugged?”

“No.”

“You’re not convincing.”

He looked at the back of Ren Hao’s head. “He’s protective.”

“He’s intrusive.”

“Both can be true. He came because he cares about you.”

She looked at him and her face softened. “I know. You’ll get your phones back after lunch. I want to eat with both of you without anyone checking messages.” She patted her bag.

“I’m on duty.”

“You have a lunch break.”

“I can be called.”

“Not for forty minutes. Please.” She squeezed his arm.

He thought about it, and said all right, and she pressed her cheek to his shoulder for a second as they walked.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao ordered enough for five people.

“Why so much?” said Isla.

“I don’t know what he eats.”

“Anything,” said Wei Long.

“That’s not an answer.”

“It is.”

“He’s not difficult about food. He’s difficult about everything else,” said Isla.

“That isn’t accurate,” said Wei Long.

Ren Hao pointed his chopsticks at him. “See? Disagreeing already.”

They ate. For the first few minutes Ren Hao asked about the job: the hours, what they did to him, whether he ever had time off. Wei Long answered what he could. Ren Hao asked whether he travelled, and Isla said, “He’s asking because he runs a risk firm and thinks everyone should be travelling,” and Ren Hao leaned back with the air of a man finally on his own ground.

“Global risk. Thirty-second floor, best view in the district. People think it’s security. It isn’t. It’s logistics, insurance, crisis response, intelligence, people. Sometimes it’s getting somebody home before something bad gets worse.”

“That sounds like your sister’s work,” said Wei Long.

Ren Hao glanced at her. “Yes. She gets the hard calls. She doesn’t always tell anyone when something’s difficult.”

“I know,” said Wei Long.

He said it without looking up and went on eating, and Ren Hao looked at him before he nodded.

“Good.”

“Are you two getting along?” said Isla.

“No,” said Ren Hao.

“Yes,” said Wei Long, at the same time, and she laughed.

“Don’t get comfortable. She’s my little sister. She was difficult as a child. She locked me out of the flat once because I wouldn’t lend her my laptop,” said Ren Hao, and pointed at him again with the chopsticks, in case it hadn’t been clear.

“You deleted my essay.”

“Because you hadn’t saved it.”

“Because you were using my computer!”

“She stole my clothes, too.”

“They were better than mine.”

“They were mine.”

“She still does that,” said Wei Long, and took a sip of tea.

Isla turned. “Excuse me?”

He looked at her. “Your cardigan.”

She looked down. The grey cardigan she had on over her blouse was his. She’d taken it off the back of his chair on Sunday and forgotten. Ren Hao looked from one of them to the other and burst out laughing, loud enough that the next table turned round.

“Already?”

“Can we talk about something else?” said Isla, and Wei Long’s mouth moved, and Ren Hao jabbed his chopsticks across the table.

“That. I saw that. You smiled.”

“No,” said Wei Long.

Ren Hao sat back. “All right. I see what we’re dealing with.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside on the pavement Isla gave them back their phones. Ren Hao had a meeting, and on Monday he was flying to Vancouver for a client, and he said so twice so that his sister would ring their parents before he got there.

“Don’t do this again. Don’t walk into someone’s workplace and shout,” she told him, fixing his collar.

“I didn’t shout.”

She looked at him.

“Fine. I promise.”

She hugged him, and he wrapped both arms round her, and for a second the noise went out of him altogether. He held her a little tighter than a lunch required.

“Call me. Properly. Not just messages,” he said, low.

“I will.”

He kissed the top of her head and let go, and turned to Wei Long, and after a pause held out his hand. Wei Long shook it.

“Take care of her,” said Ren Hao.

“She takes care of herself. But I’ll be there.” A second.

Ren Hao looked at him, and something in the answer satisfied him, and he nodded. “Isla? Love you.”

“Love you too.”

He got into a taxi. She watched it go, then turned to find Wei Long looking at her.

“What?”

“He hugged me.”

“Yes.”

“That was unexpected.”

She laughed and slipped her hand into his. “Thank you for being patient with him.”

He looked down at their hands. “He’s important to you. That makes him important enough for me to make an effort.”

She didn’t tease him. She stood on the pavement holding his hand. Then she tugged him down and kissed his cheek.

“You’re a good man, Inspector.”

“Don’t tell your brother,” he said, and she laughed out loud, and this time when his mouth curved he didn’t bother to deny it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao had been gone eight minutes when Wei Long’s phone buzzed with an unknown number.

Unknown: This is Ren Hao. I got your number from Isla. Don’t make me regret being civil.

Wei Long: Understood.

Unknown: Also she steals clothes. Don’t let her tell you otherwise.

Wei Long: I know.

He saved the number as REN HAO (CIVIL). Isla held out her hand for the phone, read it, and laughed.

“He’s making friends.”

“He gave me a warning.”

“That’s how he tells people he likes them. He’s never liked anyone I’ve dated before.” She put her arm through his again.

“Why not?”

“He didn’t know them.”

“Does he know me?”

“Not yet.”

He considered that. “Then he can take his time.”

“You’re not worried?”

“No. I’m not going anywhere because someone is loud.” He looked down the street, where the taxi had gone.

chapters.title: Headphones Over the Scanner
chapters.desc: Her one rule at his place: no police radio in bed. He breaks it once, goes out at three for a missing child on the harbour front, and comes back at six with the child found. She takes his boots off. Dawn love scene, slow, explicit, his head on her stomach afterwards.
chapters.epigraph: “But when you come back you take your boots off at the door, you put the radio away, and you come to bed.”
chapters.content:
Isla had one rule at Wei Long’s flat. No police radio in bed.

She’d made it three weeks earlier, after an evening spent listening to a disembodied voice read out vehicle registrations while he read a case file beside her. She had endured it for eleven minutes. Then she’d picked the scanner off his bedside table, switched it off and carried it to the far side of the room.

“That’s equipment,” he’d said.

“It’s a radio. It isn’t invited into bed.”

He had looked at her, and then got up and moved it to the living room, and she had kissed him for it, and the rule had held ever since. Just before three on Saturday morning it broke.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke because the room had changed. The scanner wasn’t loud; he’d brought it back to the bedroom at midnight, turned down to a murmur, because he was the duty inspector for the district until eight and the station had his phone as well. What woke her was his breathing. She’d learned what it did when he heard something that mattered.

He was sitting on the end of the bed in the dark, the little blue display lighting one side of his face.

“What’s happened?” she said.

“Go back to sleep.”

It wasn’t an answer, and they both knew it.

The radio crackled. Missing child, harbour front ferry terminal, male, seven years, last seen approximately one-forty... He was already reaching for his trousers.

The family had been coming home on the last ferry from a wedding banquet on one of the outlying islands, the boy asleep on his grandmother’s shoulder for most of the crossing. At the pier the terminal had been full of banquet guests and tired children and the grandmother had put him down to find her purse, and his mother had thought he was with his grandmother, and his grandmother had thought he was with his mother. By the time they understood, the hall was emptying. They’d searched, asked the staff, and rung the police at half past two. Blue jacket. Grey trousers. Red trainers. A small blue backpack shaped like a whale.

“Have they done the waiting areas? All of them? The ferry side too? No. Not all of them,” Wei Long said into the phone, buttoning his shirt with one hand. He listened.

Isla sat up. “How far?”

“Twenty minutes.”

“Then why are you still standing here?” She was already holding out his jacket. He took it from her.

“Stay.”

“I wasn’t going to follow you. You’re breaking the rule, though. At least put it somewhere I can’t hear it. Put the headphones over it or something.” She looked at the scanner.

He picked up the scanner, carried it into the living room, set it on the table and laid her big over-ear headphones on top of it so that they covered the speaker. The radio went on receiving. The bedroom went quiet. He came back for his belt and his warrant card, and fastened the holster, and she watched him do it.

“Call me when you know something.”

“I will.”

She caught his hand as he passed. “How frightened is the family?”

He thought about how to answer and gave up thinking. “Terribly.”

“Find him,” she said, and pulled him down and kissed him, and he stayed with his forehead almost against hers for a second before he left.

✦ ✦ ✦

The harbour was colder than the streets behind it. Wind came off the water carrying salt and diesel, and the lights along the promenade lay in long broken stripes on the black water. Two patrol teams were already working. A constable came to meet him at the terminal doors.

“Mother and grandmother are in the terminal office, sir. Last seen by the public seating. They don’t know whether he went towards the ferry gates or out to the promenade.”

“Cameras?”

“Staff are pulling them. We’ve asked for everything to be preserved.”

“Nothing gets overwritten. Has anyone suggested he went near the edge?”

“Nothing confirmed.”

“Then don’t assume he did. Walk every route he could have taken from the seats. Toilets, waiting areas, ticket desks, stairwells, under things. Ask the staff when they last saw a child on his own, not just whether they did.”

The mother stood up the moment he came into the office. Her hair had come down and she was holding her son’s school cap in both hands, the only thing of his she’d found, under a seat.

“Have you found him?”

“Not yet. I’m Inspector Song. We’re searching the whole terminal.”

“He’s never done this. He was right beside me. I turned away for one moment.”

He didn’t tell her that a moment was all it ever took. He wasn’t going to make her feel any worse than she already did.

“Show me exactly where you last saw him.”

She pointed at the floor plan on the desk. The grandmother spoke from the corner, low, without looking at anyone. “He likes the boats. He always wants to see where they go.”

“Does he know this terminal?”

“We come every month. He doesn’t know the back,” said the mother.

He took a recent photograph from her phone and his full name and the colour of his shoelaces, and stepped outside and rang Sham, who had been woken and was on his way.

“I want the last confirmed sighting from the cameras. Every exit, every waiting area on the ferry side. Don’t narrow it to the water. Talk to the boat crews. If a child got on anything, I want to know.”

Just after four the cameras gave them something: a small figure in a blue jacket walking away from the main seating a few minutes after the family lost him, then gone behind a knot of guests in banquet clothes. Grainy. Could be him.

“He’s heading for the ferry side,” said Sham.

“Then search it again.”

Around half past four the mother looked at the footage and said yes, that was the whale. Wei Long walked the route himself. Ticket windows, side doors, the covered walkway to the gates. Most of the night staff hadn’t seen a child. One woman in a cleaner’s tabard remembered a little boy asking her where the boats went.

“Was he frightened?”

“No. Quiet. About an hour ago.”

“Which way?”

She pointed at the outer waiting area, where the benches ran under the big windows. Some were empty. Some had passengers waiting for the first boat at six. He checked behind the vending machines and the far end of the rows, and found nothing, and was turning away when something moved at the edge of his vision.

There was a bench against the wall, half hidden by a tall lit advertisement for an island resort. A blue sleeve showed under it. He walked closer and crouched, not touching anything.

The boy was curled on his side under the bench with his red trainers sticking out and the whale backpack under his head, asleep. Wei Long looked at him for a second longer than he needed to.

“Hello,” he said, low.

The boy stirred and opened his eyes and looked confused, and then frightened. Wei Long held up one open hand.

“It’s all right. I’m a policeman. Are you lost?”

A small nod.

“Your mother’s looking for you.”

The boy’s lip began to go. “Is she angry?”

“No.”

“Did I do something wrong?”

“No,” said Wei Long. “Can you come out? Are you hurt?”

A shake of the head. “Cold.”

Wei Long took his jacket off and wrapped the boy in it to the chin. A small hand came out of the sleeve and took hold of two of his fingers, and he looked down at it, and closed his hand round it.

“Come on. Let’s go and find her.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The mother saw the blue jacket first, under the black one, and then her son, and made a sound that wasn’t a word, and went down on her knees on the office floor and pulled him in.

“I’m sorry,” the boy said, and began to cry.

“Don’t. Don’t say that. You’re all right.”

The grandmother was crying in her corner. Wei Long stepped back to the door and let them have it. A paramedic checked the boy and found nothing wrong but cold, and they kept him to be sure. He’d followed the lights to see the boats, he told the constable, and got tired, and gone under the bench because it was quiet, and fallen asleep.

Just after five Sham said, “Found at five, sir, family reunited, no injuries. Do I stand the search down?”

“When the rest of the building’s been checked. Keep the footage. Write it up.”

The mother came across the room to him. “Inspector. Thank you.”

He nodded. “He’s safe.”

She seemed to want to say more. She took his hand in both of hers for a second instead, and he let her, and then she went back to her son, who was sitting on his grandmother’s lap in Wei Long’s jacket drinking warm water out of a paper cup. Wei Long left the jacket with him. Outside, the sky over the harbour was starting to turn.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 6:03 Isla was on his sofa with a blanket round her shoulders and a book open on her knees and the scanner still muffled on the table. She looked up when the door opened.

He came in without a sound, in his shirt sleeves, with his hair pushed every way and a line on his forehead where he’d pressed his hand. He looked tired all the way through.

“Found him?”

“Yes. Asleep under a bench in the ferry waiting area.”

“Hurt?”

“No.”

She shut her eyes. “Oh, thank God. Where’s your jacket?”

“He was cold.”

She looked at him, and put the book down. “Sit.”

“I’m fine.”

“Sit down,” said Isla, and he sat on the edge of the sofa, and she knelt on the floor in front of him and untied his boots. He looked down at her hair.

“Isla.”

“Don’t,” she said, and pulled the first boot off, and the second. His socks were damp from the pier. She looked up. “Did you eat?”

“No.”

“Of course you didn’t. Can I?” She put her hands on his belt.

He nodded. She unbuckled it and drew it off with the holster still on it, and held it out to him without touching the gun, and he took it and locked it in the steel box in the wardrobe where it lived, and came back. She was standing now. She put her hand on his cheek.

“You’re home.”

“Yes.”

He sat down again and put his elbows on his knees. She stepped between them and laid her hands on his shoulders.

“How was the mother?”

“She thought she’d lost him.”

“She didn’t.”

“He asked whether she’d be angry,” Wei Long said, to the floor.

Isla’s hands moved over his shoulders and the back of his neck, slow. He leaned forward and rested his forehead against her stomach, and she held his head there with her fingers in his hair, and didn’t say anything at all for a while.

“Come back to bed,” she said.

“I should shower.”

“Later. You’re cold. I’ll warm you up. Unless you’d rather sleep.” She felt him smile against her through the cotton, or she thought she did.

“No,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She pulled the curtains almost closed and left the room in the grey of early morning. He stood by the bed in his shirt.

“Take it off. Slowly,” she said, and he did, and she kissed him, and felt the night still in him: the cold, the walking, the hours of listening. She drew back.

“All right.”

There was nothing to fill the room with and neither of them tried. She lay back and drew him down over her, his skin cool from the harbour against her warm skin, and he shivered once, and she wrapped her arms and her legs round him until he stopped. He kissed her mouth until she was warm all through. Then her cheek, her jaw, the side of her neck. When his mouth found her breast she held his head there and arched up into it, and he took his time with her, his tongue slow and his hand flat on her ribs, as if he were learning something by heart.

“You’re home,” she whispered.

“Yes.”

“You’re not at the terminal.”

“No.”

“You’re not listening to the radio.”

“No,” he said, against her skin, and she reached down between them and found him hard, and guided him, and he pushed into her slowly, all the way, and let out a breath he seemed to have been holding since three in the morning.

They hardly moved at first. He stayed deep inside her and rocked, barely, and kissed her, and she held him with her heels pressed into the small of his back, keeping him there, close and slow. The light grew round the curtain. Somewhere a bus went past. She told him nothing and he didn’t need telling; he felt her tighten and followed it, and when she began to come, with hardly a sound, her mouth open against his shoulder, he held still and let her, and only then began to move, long slow strokes that pulled the end of it out of her, until he shuddered and came with his face in her neck and her name said into it so low she felt it more than heard it.

Afterwards he lay with his head on her stomach. Her fingers went on moving through his hair. His eyes were closed, his arm across her waist, and his breathing had finally settled.

“Are you asleep?”

“No. I’m resting.”

“Of course. Did you know I was awake the whole time?” She traced his temple.

“Yes. You turned a page.”

“That was hours ago.”

“You were waiting,” he said, and opened his eyes and looked up at her along her body.

“Of course I was.”

He shut his eyes again. A few minutes later his arm went heavy across her, and he was asleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 8:06 his phone buzzed and he reached for it without lifting his head. She caught his wrist. He looked up.

“Work?”

“Sham. Search closed. The boy’s home.” He put the phone down. She stroked his hair.

“I have news too. Hao has a date.”

He lifted his head. “With whom?”

“Xu Song-Zhu. She’s a crash investigator. Black boxes, accident reconstruction, brilliant at explaining complicated things to people who don’t want to hear them. I introduced them last night at dinner and left early.”

“Without telling him?”

“He knows now. He rang me at eleven, at full volume, asking why I thought he needed help finding someone.”

“Does he?”

“Yes. I told him so. She’s intelligent and patient and she has a sense of humour, which he’ll need. I warned her that he says ‘I love you’ like other people say hello, talks too much when he’s nervous and thinks he’s always right.” She grinned.

“Accurate.”

“Maybe they’ll get married.”

“That’s a large conclusion from one dinner.”

“Let me dream,” said Isla, and he put his head back down on her stomach and let her.

At nine she slipped out of bed and went to the living room and lifted her headphones off the scanner. Its little display had gone dark. She left them on the table and went back to bed, and he woke as she settled.

“Where did you go?”

“To check your terrible radio was behaving.”

“Was it?”

“Silent. You broke my one rule.” She tucked herself against him.

“I’m sorry,” he said, entirely serious.

“Unless someone needs you. Then you go. Obviously. But when you come back you take your boots off at the door, you put the radio away, and you come to bed. And you let me look after you,” she said, and touched his cheek.

He was quiet a while. “All right.”

“Good,” said Isla, and he drew the blanket over her shoulder, and nothing came through the radio that morning that needed Inspector Song to get out of bed.

chapters.title: A Video Call With Two Professors
chapters.desc: Her parents in Vancouver, both academics, interview him on video like a dissertation committee. He prepared a written statement. After the call she climbs into his lap; heat, kissing, stopping only because her laptop is still on.
chapters.epigraph: “I would like her to keep choosing me.”
chapters.content:
At 8:17 on Sunday morning, Inspector Song Wei Long was reviewing a document he had written himself. It was titled STATEMENT REGARDING MY INTENTIONS TOWARDS ISLA REN.

Isla found it on the dining table. She’d come out of the bedroom in one of his shirts with her hair every way, meaning to steal his coffee, and stopped. He was sitting opposite it in a clean white shirt buttoned to the cuffs, hair combed, laptop open, a cup of tea at his elbow and her coffee already poured at her place. He looked ready to give evidence.

She picked the page up. “What’s this?”

“A written statement.”

“I can see that. Your intentions towards me?”

“Yes.”

“We’ve been seeing each other for four months.”

“Four months and two days.”

“Thank you. I was worried we’d lost count.”

He glanced at the laptop. “Your parents are on in twenty minutes. Your mother teaches political science. Your father teaches literature. They’ve both published books. I’ve read two.”

She lowered the page. “You’ve read my parents’ books?”

“Your father’s on modern fiction. Your mother’s on diplomatic institutions and regional security.”

“When?”

“Last month.”

“Without telling me?”

“I didn’t think it was necessary. I thought it would help to understand them.”

Something in her face went soft and she looked back down at the statement before he could see it. “Did you also prepare answers to questions they haven’t asked yet?”

“Some.”

“How many?”

“Eleven. I considered more. I rejected seven.”

She put her face in her hands and laughed into them. “You’re going to make me fall in love with you all over again before breakfast.”

He considered that with total seriousness. “That would be acceptable.”

She reached across the table and took his hand. “Wei Long. You don’t need a statement.”

“I know. I want them to know I’m serious about you.” He turned his hand over under hers.

She had no joke for that. She squeezed his fingers and leaned over the table and kissed him.

“Just don’t read it as if you’re giving evidence.”

“I wasn’t planning to read it. Unless they ask.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She propped the laptop up on a stack of his files, moved the coffee out of shot and checked the light. He sat beside her, not too close and not too far.

“You’re sitting as if you’re waiting to be questioned.”

“I am.”

“You’re meeting my parents.”

“Those aren’t mutually exclusive.”

“Please try to look less like you’ve come to arrest someone,” said Isla, and he relaxed his shoulders by roughly a centimetre, and the call connected.

Her mother appeared first, against a wall of bookshelves in the house in Vancouver where it was still Saturday evening. She had Isla’s eyes and a voice made for lecture halls that never needed raising.

“Isla! Your father’s looking for his glasses.”

“I can hear you. And this must be Inspector Song,” said her father from somewhere off screen, and then arrived in a cardigan with a mug of tea, and put the glasses on, and looked at Wei Long.

“Good evening, Professor Ren.”

“Please don’t call me sir.”

“I didn’t.”

“You were about to. It makes me feel older than I am.” Her father smiled.

“Hello, Wei Long. It’s lovely to finally meet you. We’ve been hearing about you for months,” said her mother.

Isla turned. “Have you?”

“Isla. You told us.”

“I didn’t tell you everything.”

“That’s clear. You’re so handsome,” said her mother, and looked back at the screen.

Wei Long paused. “Thank you.”

Isla covered her mouth.

“Composed, too,” said her father.

“He’s always like this. I’ve been trying to make him laugh for four months,” said Isla.

“You’ve succeeded,” said Wei Long.

She turned to him. “When?”

“Several times.”

Her father watched this with interest. “Well. That’s promising. Shall we begin?”

“Of course,” said Wei Long, and Isla whispered, “Please don’t say that,” and her father laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother went first.

“Isla says you’re an inspector. How long have you been in the police?”

“Eleven years. I joined at nineteen.”

“Do you enjoy it?”

He thought about it. “Most days. The work is necessary. Not all of it is enjoyable.”

“I appreciate the distinction,” said her father.

“I won’t ask about anything confidential,” said her mother, and glanced down at something on her desk that might have been notes. “But may I ask about your clearance rate?”

“Mum. You’ve known him for three minutes,” said Isla.

“I’m curious about his work.”

“I can talk about general performance. I can’t give internal figures. And a clearance rate depends on how you define cleared. An arrest isn’t a conviction, and a case can stay open after you’ve identified the suspect. I wouldn’t want to give you a number without saying what it measures,” said Wei Long, before Isla could rescue him.

Her mother looked at him with genuine interest for the first time. “That’s a useful distinction.”

“He’s like this ordering lunch. He once asked whether the soup stock had shellfish in it before ordering a vegetable dish,” said Isla.

“It wasn’t specified.”

“Exactly.”

“Is there anything else you’d like to know?” said Wei Long to the screen, and her father put his mug down.

“You’re making it remarkably easy to interview you.”

“Is that a problem?”

“Not at all. I’m deciding whether to continue.”

“Don’t frighten him,” said her mother.

“I’m not frightened,” said Wei Long, and Isla shut her eyes, and her father laughed properly.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then it was her father’s turn, and he adjusted his glasses, and Isla tensed, because this was the question she’d been dreading. Her father had once spent an entire family dinner explaining why the last chapter of a famous novel was structurally dishonest. He wouldn’t accept the news as an answer.

“What do you read?”

“History. Urban and social, sometimes military. Novels from home. Some European ones in translation. Crime fiction.”

“Crime fiction? For pleasure, or to criticise the police work?”

“Both.”

Her father looked delighted. “Anyone in particular?”

Wei Long named three. Then, after a pause, “I’ve read your book on modern fiction.”

Isla knew that look on her father’s face. He’d been complimented on his work by a great many people who hadn’t read it.

“Have you? What did you think?”

Wei Long paused. She knew that pause too: he was working out how to be honest without being rude.

“I thought the fourth chapter was the most useful. Your argument that a narrator who seems detached can be participating, not absent. That the way someone tells a story doesn’t tell you how much it cost them. I’ve found that true of witnesses after a traumatic event.”

Her father lowered his mug and looked at the screen differently. “Did you agree with the argument?”

“Mostly.”

“Mostly?”

“I thought you were too generous to one of the authors.”

Isla turned to stare at him. He had just criticised her father’s book, on their first call, with a straight face. Her mother laughed. Her father was leaning towards the camera.

“Which one?”

Wei Long told him. For the next nine minutes Isla watched her boyfriend and her father argue about a novelist who’d been dead for forty years, and watched her father lean further and further into the camera, and watched Wei Long answer in exactly the voice he used at work, except that something in him had loosened. He didn’t interrupt. He didn’t pretend to agree. When he didn’t know something he said so. When her father asked whether he’d read a particular novel he said no.

“Would you?”

“Yes. You recommended it.”

Her father looked enormously pleased.

✦ ✦ ✦

“May I ask something more personal? How did you two meet?” said her mother, folding her hands.

“He was rude,” said Isla at once.

“I wasn’t.”

“You forgot to thank me.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“To me it was.”

“It was an extradition handover. The paperwork was wrong and nobody at the desk could talk to the man. I fixed it,” said Isla.

“She also corrected the custody record,” said Wei Long.

“And he watched me the whole time without saying anything.”

“I was observing.”

“You were staring.”

“I was looking at the documents.”

“And what did you think of her?” said her father.

Wei Long didn’t answer at once. Isla turned. “Careful.”

He looked back at the screen. “She was competent.”

“Only competent?” said her mother.

“Extremely competent. She understood the problem quickly, saw what needed correcting and explained it clearly to everyone in the room. She didn’t make the situation any harder than it already was. She also left a note on my car.”

Her mother brightened. “What did it say?”

“’You forgot thank you.’”

Her mother burst out laughing. “Oh, Isla. You couldn’t even wait till the next day?”

“He was right there.”

“She was correct,” said Wei Long, and Isla said, “Thank you,” and he said, “You’re welcome.”

“And when did you realise you liked her?” said her father.

“Shortly after.”

“After what?” said Isla.

“Meeting her,” said Wei Long, and she forgot how to sit in a chair. Her mother saw, and her smile went soft.

“And what do you like about her?”

He answered without looking away from the camera. “She pays attention. She notices when someone’s uncomfortable even when they don’t say so. She asks when she doesn’t understand something. She doesn’t pretend to know everything. She talks a lot.”

Isla’s head came round. “Excuse me?”

“That isn’t a criticism. She fills silence without making it uncomfortable. And when she wants something she tells me. Usually.” He looked at her.

“Usually,” Isla agreed.

“And you like that?” said her mother.

“Yes. A great deal,” said Wei Long, and Isla looked down into her coffee, and could hear her father trying not to laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

“We’ve taken up a great deal of your Sunday,” said her mother at last. “What’s that paper by your hand, Wei Long?”

Isla froze. He looked down and picked it up.

“A written statement. Regarding my intentions towards Isla.”

Her father slowly took off his glasses. Her mother pressed a hand flat on her chest.

“Did you write that yourself?”

“Yes.”

Her father put his glasses back on. “Then I’d like to hear it.”

“Don’t you dare,” said Isla.

“They asked,” said Wei Long.

“That doesn’t mean you have to.”

He considered this, and looked at the screen. “Would you like me to read it?”

“Please,” said her father, and Isla dropped her forehead onto Wei Long’s shoulder and left it there.

He read it in his ordinary voice.

“I have been seeing Isla since March this year. I understand that a relationship with me may involve irregular hours, changed plans, and periods when I cannot discuss my work. I don’t consider those things hers to manage. I will tell her when my work affects our arrangements, and I will not expect her to wait without explanation.”

Isla lifted her head off his shoulder.

“I understand that her career may take her abroad. I will not ask her to make professional decisions to suit my circumstances. If she is posted elsewhere, I intend to discuss what that means for us, rather than assume that distance decides it. I can’t promise that my work will become less demanding. I can promise to be honest about it, and that I will not treat her time as less valuable than mine. I am not seeing her casually, and I don’t intend to waste her time. I care for her. I would like to build a life with her, if she goes on wanting the same thing.” He turned the page. He came to the last line.

He put the page down. Nobody on either side of the world said anything. Her mother’s hand had gone up to her cheek and stayed there.

“That is a thorough statement,” said her father at last.

“I thought it was important to be clear.”

Her mother said, “I appreciate what you said about her career. Do you understand she may be away for years at a time? That she’ll travel at a day’s notice, deal with emergencies, spend weeks with people who are frightened or grieving?”

“Yes. I don’t expect her to leave that part of herself at work.”

Her mother looked down, and up again. “Good.”

“And do you understand that she can be rather stubborn? Particular. Inclined to decide things before telling anybody. Difficult to persuade,” said her father.

“Yes,” said Wei Long, to each of them.

“Are we still discussing me?” said Isla.

“Yes, sweetheart.”

“I don’t consider those things problems,” said Wei Long.

“Not even the stubbornness?”

“No. She knows what she wants.”

Her father looked at him and then nodded once, the way he nodded at the end of a good viva. “All right. I think we’ve asked enough questions.”

✦ ✦ ✦
