Her mother made them promise to call again. Her father told Wei Long to read the novel and report back. Her mother told him to make sure they both ate properly, because Isla forgot meals when she was busy and she suspected Isla would encourage him to do the same, and her father told him not to let Isla win every argument.

“I’ll consider it,” said Wei Long.

“Don’t encourage him,” said Isla, and the screen went dark.

She turned on him. “That went well?”

“Yes.”

“You read a relationship proposal to my parents.”

“It was a statement.”

“It had a title. And eleven prepared questions.”

“Twelve, originally. I removed one.”

She laughed, but something else was under it now. She took the page from him and read the last paragraph again, and then she saw that at the bottom, under the typed lines, he had written one more in pen.

I would like her to keep choosing me.

She looked up. “Did you mean all of it?”

“Yes.”

“Closer,” said Isla.

He moved his chair a little. She shook her head and climbed into his lap instead, and his hands came up to her waist on their own to steady her. She put her arms round his neck.

“That was for the statement,” she said, and kissed him.

It was meant to be quick. It wasn’t. His hands settled on her and she kissed him again, smiling against his mouth, and he answered with that quietness that made her want to stay far longer than she’d planned.

“And that was for reading it,” she said.

“You’re welcome.”

She laughed and kissed him harder. He met her halfway this time, one hand moving to the small of her back and the other to her cheek, and she felt the carefulness in him give, not vanish, just stop being the only thing he let himself have. She shifted closer in his lap and pushed her fingers into his hair. He made a low sound into her mouth, and his hand slid from her back down to her hip and held her there against him.

“Found you,” she whispered.

“I’ve been here the whole time.”

The laptop chimed. Neither of them looked at it. It chimed again, and his hand stopped on her hip.

“Isla. The camera.”

She looked round. The call had ended, but the little green light beside the lens was still on.

“Oh, of course,” she said.

“Do you want me to turn it off?”

“Yes.”

He reached past her and closed the laptop. The light went out.

“Now,” said Isla.

“Now?”

“Now you can kiss me properly,” she said, and he did, with nobody in Vancouver watching, until her coffee had gone stone cold on the table.

chapters.title: The Man Who Trained Him
chapters.desc: Retired Superintendent Pun, the closest thing he has to a father, wants to meet the woman who sits on his desk, and interrogates her over tea. She interrogates him back and wins.
chapters.epigraph: “Somebody has to know what’s happening.”
chapters.content:
Retired Superintendent Pun had been asking to meet Isla Ren for six weeks, and Wei Long had been avoiding it for five of them. Not deliberately, he would have said. There had been a case, then a review, then a weekend she worked, then a weekend Pun had a hospital appointment, then a lunch Pun cancelled because he’d decided he didn’t like the restaurant. The truth was that Wei Long knew exactly what would happen. Pun would ask questions in that mild voice of his, with a cup of tea in his hand and the patience of a man who had spent forty years getting people to say things they hadn’t meant to. And Isla, who had never met a question she couldn’t improve on, would answer every one of them, possibly with questions of her own.

Just after ten on Saturday she stood in his living room holding up two scarves.

“Which one?”

“The blue. It goes with your dress. The grey one’s warmer.” He fastened his watch.

“Are you worried about the weather? It’s thirty-one degrees.”

“Mr. Pun keeps his air conditioning at eighteen.”

She smiled. “You were there recently?”

“Last week.”

“And you didn’t think to mention it?”

“I thought you’d prefer the blue one.”

She put the blue one on. He picked up the box of tea she’d bought the day before. “Pu’er. He likes this one. I’ve brought it before.”

“Good. We’ve established you can buy tea for your former superintendent. You’re nervous.” At the door she looked at him.

“Don’t be too comfortable. He’ll ask questions.”

“Wei Long. I spend whole afternoons being questioned by frightened parents, furious lawyers and men who think shouting will change an immigration decision.”

“Mr. Pun’s different.”

“How?”

“He doesn’t raise his voice.”

She thought about that, and her smile got wider. “Oh. I see.”

He went out into the corridor and heard her laugh behind him, and didn’t feel reassured.

✦ ✦ ✦

Pun was seventy-three according to the last birthday card Wei Long had sent him, and young enough, according to Pun, to know when someone was being a fool. He opened the door before the second knock.

“You’re late.”

“Three minutes.”

“Late is late.”

Then his eyes went past Wei Long to Isla, and his face did something that wasn’t a smile but was interested.

“So. You’re Isla. The woman who sits on his desk.”

Wei Long closed his eyes.

“I see the news has travelled, Mr. Pun,” said Isla.

“Come in. I want to see what kind of woman makes this man forget his manners.”

“I haven’t forgotten my manners,” said Wei Long, taking his shoes off.

“You didn’t thank her the first time you met her.”

Isla turned to Wei Long. “How does he know that?”

“He told me. Pu’er. Good,” said Pun, pleased, and took the tea out of Wei Long’s hands.

The living room was orderly without being formal. Old photographs on the shelves; framed commendations that looked as though they’d been hung under protest; a big wooden cabinet of books and files Wei Long had known since he was nineteen. A photograph of a much younger Pun stood beside one of Wei Long’s own passing-out portraits. Isla saw it and looked from one to the other.

“Sit,” said Pun, pointing her to the sofa, and when Wei Long went to the chair opposite he said, “Not you. Bring the water.”

“I made the tea.”

“Then bring the water anyway.”

Wei Long went. As he passed Isla she looked up at him with a face that said she had no intention whatsoever of not encouraging this. He heard the kettle start, and in the room behind him, Pun’s voice drop into its interviewing register.

“How long?”

“Since March.”

“Serious?”

“Serious enough,” said Isla, “that he prepared a written statement for my parents.”

There was a silence and then a laugh, low and surprised, the kind Wei Long had heard out of Pun perhaps five times in eleven years.

“He did what?”

“A statement of his intentions towards me. He read it to them on video. He covered what he’d do if I were posted abroad.”

The laughter stopped. “Did he? And what did he say?”

“That he wouldn’t ask me to make decisions about my career to suit his. That he’d tell me when work changed our plans. That he’d like to build a life with me, if I wanted the same.”

There was another silence, a longer one, and when Pun spoke again his voice had changed. “That sounds like a man who’s thought about it. What do you see in him?”

“Do you want the short answer or the long one?”

“The honest one.”

Isla said, “He’s dependable. He’s careful with people even when he doesn’t look it. He listens properly. He doesn’t promise things to make someone feel better. If he says he’ll be somewhere, he comes. He’s hard to read. Not because he’s hiding everything. I don’t think he knows how much he leaves out.”

“Does that bother you?”

“Sometimes. I ask.”

“And if he doesn’t answer?”

“I ask again.”

“Does he get angry with you?”

“Now and then. I let him finish. Then I tell him why I think he’s wrong.”

“You haven’t seen him when he’s decided he’s right.”

“I have. He’s still wrong sometimes,” said Isla.

In the kitchen the kettle clicked off. Wei Long had no idea what had just been said. He had a strong suspicion it hadn’t helped him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came back with the water. Pun poured himself a cup and nodded at Isla.

“She says you can be difficult. She says she has to ask you things more than once.”

“That’s possible.”

“Are we discussing me?” said Wei Long.

“Yes.”

“I thought I’d come to introduce her.”

“You did. I’ve met her.” Pun turned back to Isla. “What’s the worst thing about going out with a policeman?”

“Plans. Sometimes he has to leave and doesn’t know when he’ll be back. Sometimes he comes home and doesn’t want to talk. Sometimes I can tell something happened and he can’t tell me what. I don’t need every case. I need to know when he won’t be reachable, when he’s coming home, and whether he’s safe,” said Isla, at once. She shrugged.

“Does he tell you?”

“He’s getting better. He once told me he’d be late.”

“I was late,” said Wei Long.

“You were three hours late.”

“I didn’t know it would be three hours.”

“You could have sent another message.”

“I couldn’t use my phone.”

“Then tell her that, when you can,” said Pun, without looking at him, and Wei Long, who had once watched this man end a hostage negotiation with four sentences, understood why he’d put the visit off.

Pun asked what a consular officer did. Isla told him: detentions, deaths, hospital beds, missing citizens, families at the far end of a phone line who needed to hear something they didn’t want to. Pun asked whether she liked it. She said she didn’t like the circumstances, but she liked being useful to someone who was frightened and didn’t know what to do. Pun asked whether the work came home with her, and whether Wei Long asked, and whether he listened.

“Carefully. Like a man taking a statement,” said Isla.

“Does she tell you everything?” Pun asked Wei Long.

“No.”

“Does that bother you?”

“No. She has a right to her privacy.”

Pun looked at him, and then back at Isla. “Good answer. If you were posted abroad tomorrow, what would you do?”

“Go.”

“Without hesitating?”

“I’d have to think about the practical things. I wouldn’t turn a posting down because I was in a relationship.”

“Would you want him to follow?”

She paused. “Perhaps, one day. Not by throwing his life away without thinking about it. We’d talk. We’d work out what we could manage. If it didn’t work, we’d face that honestly too.”

She hadn’t looked at Wei Long once while she said it. She hadn’t softened it so that he could hear it more easily. Pun saw that, and approved of it.

“Most people tell me what they think I want to hear,” he said.

“I don’t think you’d respect that.”

“No, I wouldn’t,” said Pun, and laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

“May I ask you something?” said Isla, and put her cup down, and Wei Long saw the interview turn round like a car in a narrow street.

“Of course.”

“How long did you train him?”

“From nineteen. He was quiet and observant and convinced that if he worked hard enough nobody would ever have to worry about him. He was good. He had a habit of carrying things that weren’t his to carry.”

“Does he still?”

“You’re sitting beside him. You tell me.”

“Yes,” said Isla. “Did you ever tell him he didn’t have to do it all himself?”

Pun was quiet. The question hadn’t been sharp. That was what made it hard.

He said, “Not often enough. Don’t interrupt. I taught him how to do the work. How to keep his head. How to tell what he knew from what he suspected. I thought that was enough. It wasn’t. He’ll stay till the last report’s done and then go home and start on the next one.” Wei Long started to speak and Pun held up a hand.

“I take his files away,” said Isla.

“You move them,” said Wei Long.

“That’s a technical distinction. Sometimes I tell him to come to bed. Sometimes I make him eat. Sometimes I sit on his desk until he looks at me.”

“The famous desk,” said Pun, delighted. “Does she really?”

“Yes.”

“And you let her?”

“Yes.”

Pun shook his head. “Eleven years I couldn’t get you away from a desk, and she makes you look forward to one. Go on. You have another.” Then he looked at Isla, because she was already leaning forward.

“Who looks after you?”

Pun blinked. It was the first time that morning he’d had nothing ready.

“I’m retired.”

“That wasn’t the question.”

“I manage.”

“Do you have someone who checks whether you’ve eaten? Who notices when you’ve been sitting on your own too long? Someone who asks whether you need anything?” She said it gently.

“At my age people tend to leave me alone.”

“That isn’t the same as being looked after.”

He looked at her a long while. “You’re direct. Is this what you do at work? Interrogate people?”

“Not quite. I ask questions until I understand what they need.”

“Well. You’ve understood enough to be dangerous.” He looked down into his tea and up again.

Wei Long watched the two of them and saw what she’d seen while he was in the kitchen: that Pun had poured tea for everybody and not for himself until he was reminded, that the television was off and had been off for months by the dust on it, that the old man’s eyes kept going to the shelves whenever Wei Long’s grandfather came up. She hadn’t been studying a retired superintendent all morning. She’d been looking at a man.

“She’s better than you at this,” said Pun.

“Yes,” said Wei Long, without a pause.

“At what?” said Isla.

“Getting people to answer.”

“Don’t encourage her. She’ll start asking me more,” said Pun.

“I have several,” said Isla, and Pun laughed until he had to put his cup down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lunch was steamed fish, greens and rice. Wei Long was sent for another pair of chopsticks, and while he was in the kitchen Pun put the fish in the middle of the table and said, “His grandfather used to bring him to the station.”

“Old Song. He told me. The homework at the desk.”

“Did he tell you about the night he slept through a shift change? He was eleven. He’d lined up his books and sharpened his pencils like the station was a classroom, and he wouldn’t let anyone help him with his sums, and his grandfather’s shift ran on, and when the night relief came in at eleven he was asleep with his face on his arithmetic. Old Song carried him home. Four streets. The only complaint I ever heard him make about it was that the boy was getting heavy.” Pun served her a piece of the fish.

Isla looked towards the kitchen.

Pun said, “I asked him once what he wanted to be. He said an inspector. I asked him why. He said, ‘Somebody has to know what’s happening.’. Nine years old, in a room full of men twice his size.” He picked up his chopsticks.

Wei Long came back with the chopsticks. “What?”

“Nothing,” said Pun.

“You were talking about the station.”

“The night you slept through the shift change.”

Wei Long sat down. “I had school.”

“You were eleven,” said Pun.

Isla reached under the table and touched his hand. He turned it over and her fingers went into his. She could see it now: a boy at a desk too big for him, pencil going, the radio murmuring, a cup of tea going cold by a stack of reports, his grandfather finishing his shift. And even then, wanting to know what was happening.

✦ ✦ ✦

After lunch Pun brought out a plate of lychees and asked after the boy.

“He graduated. Thursday the tenth of July.”

“Medicine. Good. Working?”

“City Hospital in August. Junior doctor.”

“Your grandfather would have been proud. Still in the old house?”

“Yes.”

“Good. It’s a family house. Better than empty. Does he look after himself? Does he eat? Has he got someone?”

Wei Long was quiet. “He’s seeing someone. Eliana Lin.”

Pun put his lychee down. “The Lin girl? The youngest? Since when?”

“2021. It’s been public since the graduation. She graduated the same day.”

“And you knew?”

“Since July 2023.”

Pun looked at him. “You have an interesting family.”

“Yes.”

“Does she treat him properly?”

“Yes.”

Pun nodded. “And you? Do you still think you’re responsible for everyone? You took that boy on when you were fifteen. You did what needed doing. Nobody’s arguing with that. He’s grown. He’s a doctor. Let him have his life. And while you’re at it, remember you’ve got one too.” Wei Long didn’t answer, and Pun held his eyes. He picked up the lychee again.

“I know.”

“Do you?”

Under the table Isla’s thumb moved over his knuckles. Wei Long breathed out. “Yes.”

At the door, while Wei Long was putting his shoes on, Pun stopped her in the hall.

“He won’t always tell you when something’s wrong. He’ll tell you he’s fine.”

“I know.”

“You’re learning. He’s worth being patient with.” Pun’s mouth moved.

Isla said, “Can I tell you something? He talks about you carefully. When he quotes something you taught him, he remembers the exact words. He doesn’t have to call you family for you to be family to him.”

For once in his life the old superintendent had no reply. Then he opened the door. “Come again. Bring less tea. I have enough.”

“I’ll bring something else.”

“Song. Don’t make her do all the work.” Wei Long looked up.

“I won’t.”

Pun didn’t look convinced. He reached out and gave Wei Long’s shoulder one hard pat. “Go home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’re pleased with yourself,” said Wei Long at the car.

“You enjoyed watching me interrogate him.”

“He liked you. He’s proud of you, by the way. He says things by doing them. Like you.”

He looked back at the house. Pun had already gone in. “He taught me most of the job.”

Isla said, “Your grandfather taught you how to look at people, and he taught you what to do with what you saw. That’s a good pair. Tell me you’re glad I came.” She put her hand on his cheek.

“I’m glad you came.”

He kissed her by the car in the heat, one hand at the back of her neck. When he drove off she reached over the gearstick and put her hand on his thigh, and he put his hand over hers and left it there.

“Did you ever think you’d bring someone to meet him?” she said, a few streets on.

“No.”

“Why not?”

He was quiet till the next light. “I didn’t have anyone I wanted him to meet.”

She looked out of the window. Then back. “Well. Now you do.”

“Yes,” he said, and at the next corner, “You won.”

“The interrogation? You admit it?”

“Yes.”

She leaned over and kissed his cheek, and the corner of his mouth moved, and after four months she knew exactly what that meant.

chapters.title: The House Next Door Gets Quiet
chapters.desc: Eliana Lin moves into the old Song house next door to her father’s, the house Wei Long left to Yu Chen in summer 2024. Wei Long goes round to sign the last papers and finds he has no home of his own, only a flat he sleeps in. Isla gives him a key to hers, labelled HOME, PROVISIONAL.
chapters.epigraph: “I live here now.”
chapters.content:
The last document needed three signatures. Wei Long knew because he’d counted them twice. He’d given Yu Chen the old Song house in the summer of 2024 with a key and a list of everything that needed doing, but he had kept the household insurance and the utility accounts in his own name for another sixteen months, because nobody had asked him to change them and because, if he was honest, which he generally was, he hadn’t wanted to. Now Eliana Lin was moving in, and the insurer needed to know who lived there. Yu Chen would sign as owner, Eliana as resident, and Wei Long last, to say he had no further interest in the place.

It was an administrative formality. He told himself so on the drive over on Saturday morning, and again when he parked outside the gate.

There were two suitcases by the front steps, a box marked BOOKS, and a pair of white trainers that weren’t Yu Chen’s. Auntie Tsoi stood in the doorway with a tea towel over her shoulder and frowned at him.

“You’re late.”

He looked at his watch. “I’m on time.”

“Then the clock’s wrong.”

He looked at the clock inside the door. It wasn’t wrong. She flapped the tea towel at him. “Come in. They’re upstairs.”

The house smelled of ginger and soy and steamed fish. There were shoes he didn’t know by the door and a new umbrella stand. The old wooden cabinet was where it had always been, and so was the photograph: his grandfather in uniform outside the old station after his last shift on the beat, one hand on his belt, not smiling.

“I dusted it yesterday. Don’t thank me. Your grandfather would have complained if I hadn’t,” said Auntie Tsoi.

“Ge!”

Yu Chen came down the stairs in hospital trousers and a T-shirt, his hair wet from the shower and his eyes tired in a way Wei Long knew from the inside.

“You’re here,” said Yu Chen.

“You finished a night?”

“Two hours ago.”

“Have you eaten?”

“Hello to you too. Auntie Tsoi made me. Is that the papers? Eliana’s signed. I’ve signed. You’re last.” Yu Chen grinned. He took the folder.

From upstairs came the sound of a keyboard, a rhythm Wei Long recognised from a dozen interviews with people who typed faster than they talked.

“How much equipment did she bring?”

“Ge.”

“Understood.”

Yu Chen looked round the hall. “I’ll look after it, Ge. The photograph stays where it is. You can come whenever you like. Even when she’s taken over the living room.”

“That’s a lie,” said a voice from the landing, and Eliana Lin leaned over the banister in a black jumper with her hair clipped up and her glasses pushed into it. Behind her, through an open door, Wei Long could see two monitors on a desk and a third on the wall.

“Inspector Song. You’re early.”

“According to Auntie Tsoi I’m late. You’re here for the papers. They’re signed. Then you’re free.” She came down the stairs.

She said it lightly, and he heard the other meaning in it. Free to go.

“Do you need anything?”

She tilted her head. “Do you always ask people that when you’re leaving?”

He didn’t answer, and she smiled, not unkindly.

“Yu Chen’s asked me three times. We’re covered.”

“I was being polite,” said Yu Chen.

“You were hovering,” said Eliana, and from the kitchen Auntie Tsoi called that if they’d all finished talking the fish was getting cold.

✦ ✦ ✦

She fed him as if he hadn’t eaten in a week: fish, greens, soup, and a plate of cut fruit that appeared after everybody had started.

“You’re thin,” she said.

“I’m the same weight.”

“Then you’ve been thin too long.”

Auntie Tsoi complained about the price of vegetables. Eliana asked for one shelf in the kitchen, and Auntie Tsoi said she could have one if she stopped ordering deliveries to the house, and Eliana looked at Yu Chen, and Yu Chen looked at his rice and said, “Don’t involve me.”

Wei Long ate and listened. At one point Auntie Tsoi put another piece of fish in his bowl without asking.

“Thank you.”

“You’re going back to that flat after this?”

“Yes.”

“That place is too quiet. Here there’s always someone. When you worked late I could leave you food. There you come home to nothing.”

Yu Chen stopped eating. Eliana glanced at Wei Long.

“I’m used to it,” he said.

“Being used to a thing doesn’t make it good,” said Auntie Tsoi, and went back to the kitchen, and the conversation started again, but something had shifted under it. He looked at the table. At the spare chopsticks. At Eliana’s hand moving Yu Chen’s phone out of the soup without either of them noticing she’d done it. At the bowl Auntie Tsoi had put in front of him. He had eaten at this table after night shifts and bad cases and evenings when the station had been too busy for dinner, for most of his life. He’d never once thought the house was quiet. He hadn’t thought anything about it, until it wasn’t his to come back to.

✦ ✦ ✦

They signed in the living room. Yu Chen first, Eliana checking the dates, Wei Long last. He read the pages again although he knew them by heart. The policy, the accounts, the line that said he had no further interest. He put the pen down.

“That’s everything.”

Eliana squared the papers. “I’ll keep these.”

“Store them securely.”

She looked at him over her glasses. “Inspector Song. I’m the person who handed you the Magpie crew and Calder Risk Partners.”

“That doesn’t mean you can’t lose paperwork.”

Yu Chen made a noise that was nearly a laugh. Eliana stared at Wei Long and then smiled and turned her phone round. His number was in her contacts under NO FILES.

“Still that?” he said.

“Of course.”

Yu Chen leaned over. “NO FILES? Ge, what did you do?”

“Nothing.”

“He knows what he did,” said Eliana, and turned the phone away.

At the door she said, “You can visit. Even without a reason. I mean it,” and he nodded and thanked her and went out. Behind him the house filled up with voices again, Eliana saying something about the desk, Yu Chen answering, Auntie Tsoi calling them both back to the kitchen. The door shut. The house next door to the Lins got quiet, from the outside.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was at the car when he realised he still had the old key in his pocket. He looked at it. Then he went back.

The front door was open. Yu Chen was in the kitchen with Auntie Tsoi. Wei Long climbed the stairs without calling out and stopped in the doorway of his old room.

It was Eliana’s workroom now. The monitors sat on a new desk under the window. A small server hummed on the shelf where his schoolbooks had gone. Cables ran in a neat loom along the skirting. There was a daybed with a folded blanket where his bed had been, a plant on the sill, and the old wardrobe, the same one, with her dark coat hanging off its door. On a shelf stood a photograph from the tenth of July: Yu Chen in his graduation gown, Eliana beside him in hers, both trying hard not to look too happy in front of everybody. Wei Long had been there. He’d watched Yu Chen cross the stage and seen her waiting for him afterwards.

He looked at the corner where his desk had been. He could remember the weight of his school bag against his leg, his grandfather moving about downstairs, the radio, the smell of dinner. He could remember being fifteen with an eight-year-old asleep in his bed and a house full of adults telling him what had to be done, and listening, because somebody had to. He had studied here, decided things here, kept this house fed and paid and in order, and believed that if he kept doing it, it would be enough. It had been enough, right up until Yu Chen no longer needed him to do any of it.

There was no anger in him and no regret. He’d given Yu Chen the house because it was right, and he’d do it again. It came to him plainly. He didn’t have a home. He had a flat. He knew which light switch stuck and how long the hot water took and what the pipes did when the man upstairs showered, and he had never once called it anything but the flat.

“Inspector Song? Sorry. I didn’t know you were still here.” Eliana was at the end of the corridor.

He held up the key. “I forgot this.”

“Do you want to keep it?”

“No.”

She came and stood in the doorway beside him and looked at the room with him. “Yu Chen says you used to study in here. He says you were strict about the desk. He says you once made him rewrite a whole page because he used the wrong kind of pen.”

“He was eight.”

“Exactly.”

“He had to learn.”

“You’re lucky I wasn’t here.”

“You’d have argued.”

“Probably.”

“Then it would have taken longer,” he said, and she laughed.

“You can come back whenever you want. I don’t mean for him. I mean you,” said Eliana.

He put the key in his pocket. “Thank you, Eliana,” he said, and went, and didn’t look back.

✦ ✦ ✦

He sat in the car for some minutes before he started the engine. His phone buzzed.

Yu Chen (Eaten?): Ge you left your umbrella

Wei Long: Keep it.

Yu Chen (Eaten?): Eliana says dinner next week. No paperwork.

Wei Long: Tell her I’ll come.

Yu Chen (Eaten?): Tell her yourself

He didn’t know what to say to that, so he drove.

✦ ✦ ✦

Isla opened her door at five past two with one of his shirts over her arm. “You’re back early. Did it go well?”

“Yes.”

“Did you eat?”

“Auntie Tsoi.”

“Then I believe you. What?” She went back to the laundry on the sofa, humming, sorting it into two piles. He stood just inside the door. She looked up.

“Are those mine?”

“Some of them. You leave them here.”

His shirt. A pair of trousers. A dark jumper. The spare T-shirt she’d started keeping for him. She folded the jumper. “Do you want me to pack them so you can take them back?”

He looked towards the bedroom, and back. “Do you have room?”

She stopped folding. “In the wardrobe?”

“Yes. I don’t want to take them back.”

She put the jumper down. “Did something happen at the house?”

“I signed the last papers. Yu Chen has the house. Eliana’s moved in. I went into my old room. It was full of her things. She’s made it hers. I wanted him to have somewhere that belonged to him. I didn’t notice that I don’t have anywhere that belongs to me. I have a flat. I can sleep there and change there and leave for work from there. It isn’t a home.” He looked at the floor.

Isla’s hand came to his wrist. “All right. Come with me,” she said.

She led him into the bedroom and opened the wardrobe. Her clothes hung on the left. On the right were empty hangers, more than a few, waiting. She pulled out the bottom drawer, and then the one above it. Both were empty.

“When?” he said.

“A while ago. I didn’t want to assume. I thought you might.” She looked up at him.

He looked at the empty space, and then at her. “I do.”

“You’re allowed somewhere to come back to, Wei Long. You don’t have to earn it by being useful. You can just come home.”

He put his forehead down against hers. “I don’t know how to do that.”

“That’s all right.”

“I’ve always had somewhere to go. I don’t think I ever thought about somewhere to stay.”

“Then we’ll start there,” said Isla, and held him, and then said, “Wait,” and went out, and he heard a drawer in the living room. She came back with a plain silver key on a ring. There was a white tag on it, in her neat handwriting.

HOME, PROVISIONAL. He looked at it and didn’t take it.

“I thought the wording was right,” she said.

“Provisional?”

“Until you decide whether you want it permanent.”

“How long does that take?”

“As long as you need.”

He took the key and turned it over once. “Is it mine?”

“It’s yours. That’s generally what keys are for.”

He closed his hand on it. “I live here now.”

“Do you?”

“Yes.”

“Then I’d better make room,” said Isla.

“You already have,” he said, and looked at the wardrobe, and then at her.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went back to the flat at seven for what he needed. A suitcase. Work clothes, a few books, his shaving kit, the framed copy of his grandfather’s photograph that stood on the shelf by his bed. He stood in the living room with the case in his hand. He’d lived there for more than a year and never brought anybody into it, never put a picture on the wall, never bought anything that wasn’t for use. He hadn’t noticed how little of himself was in the place. He locked the door and put the key in his pocket beside the new one.

She opened her door before he could use it.

“You’re back. Is that everything?”

“Enough for now.”

They unpacked together. His clothes went into the empty drawers. His books went on her shelf, beside hers, spines mixed. His razor went into the bathroom cabinet. He put the photograph of his grandfather on the bedside table on his side and stood looking at it, and she came and stood beside him and leaned her head on his shoulder.

“Was he happy, that day?”

“I think so.”

“Good,” said Isla.

At a quarter past nine she was brushing her teeth when he came and stood in the bedroom doorway in a dark T-shirt, looking at her in the mirror with an expression she couldn’t quite read.

“What is it?”

“Nothing.”

“That’s not convincing,” she said, rinsing her mouth, and came to him, and he caught her hand and held it against his chest, and she could feel the shape of the key in his pocket.

“You’re really here,” he said.

“Where else would I be?” She put her hand on his cheek.

She kissed him there in the doorway, gently at first, the kind of kiss that belongs at the end of a long day, her hands on his chest and his on her waist. Then she drew back and took hold of the hem of his T-shirt.

“Off.”

He lifted his arms and she pulled it over his head and dropped it on the floor of her bedroom. She kissed his collarbone. She ran her palms down his chest and over his stomach and opened his trousers, standing in the doorway, and pushed them down, and he stepped out of them, and she looked at him with frank pleasure and put her hand round him, and he caught his breath.

“Slowly. You’re home. There’s no hurry,” she said.

She stroked him until his eyes closed, and then she led him backwards to the bed by that hand, and he laughed, once, low and unsteady, the sound startled out of him. She pushed him down to sit on the edge and stood between his knees and pulled her nightdress off over her head. He put his face against her stomach and his hands on her hips and breathed her in. She pushed him back onto the bed and climbed over him.

There was no radio and no phone and no case on the table, and she took her time with him, and he let her, and when he reached for her she drew him in with a word and the press of her hand and he followed. He was different tonight. Less guarded. Less like a man waiting to be told what had to be done next. He rolled her under him and pushed inside her, slow and deep, and stayed there, his weight on his forearms, looking down at her, and she wrapped her legs round him and held him, and they moved together without any hurry at all. She told him what she wanted in a whisper against his mouth and he gave it to her. She tightened round him and came, gasping his name, her nails in his shoulders, and he kept moving through it until his own breath broke, and he pressed his face into her neck and came with a long shudder.

“I live here now,” he said, into her neck.

“Yes, you do,” said Isla, and held his head there.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past eleven he came back from the bathroom and turned off the light and got in beside her, and she lifted the blanket for him and settled against his chest. After a while she felt him reach for the bedside table. He picked up the key and turned it over in his fingers, and the little white tag caught the streetlight.

“Still thinking about it?”

“Yes. I’ve never had one like this.”

“A house key?”

“A key that means I can come back.”

She touched his cheek. “You could always come back.”

He put the key down beside his grandfather’s photograph. “I want to hear you say it.”

She kissed him once, and again. “You’re home.”

His arm tightened round her.

“You’re home, Wei Long,” said Isla, and that time, for the first time in a long while, he let himself believe it.

chapters.title: Growing Up Beside the Walled City
chapters.desc: At two in the morning he tells her what it was to grow up beside the Walled City as a policeman’s grandson, never allowed through the Lins’ red door, and to take on an eight-year-old cousin at fifteen. She kisses the scar on his hand she never asked about.
chapters.epigraph: “He was there. And I was there.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Isla noticed was that he’d stopped sleeping. He was often awake at strange hours; his job had taught him to tell night from morning by the colour of the sky, and he could sleep through a neighbour’s drill and wake at a change in the note of his phone. This was different. He had been lying on his back with one arm under his head for nearly twenty minutes, looking at the ceiling. She knew because she’d counted.

At first she’d thought it was the case. Elara Wang had been knifed in the alley behind the Lin estate on Sunday the thirtieth of November, two weeks ago, and he was running it, and he’d brought it home in the quiet ways he brought everything home: a little less talk at dinner, a little longer at the sink washing his hands, his phone always where he could reach it without looking. He couldn’t discuss it and she didn’t ask. But tonight he’d come to bed without reaching for her. He’d checked the lock, and stood at the window, and then lain down and gone somewhere she couldn’t follow.

She turned on her side. “Wei Long. Is it the case?”

“No. Not directly.”

“That’s a precise answer.”

He went on looking at the ceiling. Then he said, “Have you ever wondered what it was like? Growing up there?”

She lifted her head. “Beside the Walled City?”

“I don’t think I’ve ever told you properly.”

“No. You haven’t.”

“It’s long.”

“It’s two in the morning. I’ve got nowhere to be until Monday. I’m practically unemployed. Tell me.” She put her hand on his jaw.

He looked at her, and then at the window, and began.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You know my grandfather walked the beat for thirty years. He knew the streets better than anyone, not the names, the streets. Which staircases flooded. Which shops opened before it was light. Which family had someone ill upstairs, which children should have been at school and weren’t. If I was waiting for him at the end of a shift, we walked home through it together. I was six. Seven. He told me not to touch anything.”

“And you did as you were told.”

“Usually. You could hear it from our house before you saw it. Hawkers. Arguments. Radios out of windows. Someone mending something at every hour. At night the lights from the upper floors made the alleys narrower, and you could hear people moving over your head, and water in the pipes, and someone shouting for a neighbour. He said you had to look up as well as ahead. People forget a street has more than one floor.” She laughed into his shoulder. He spoke as if he could still walk it with his eyes shut.

“He taught you to watch people.”

“He taught me to notice when they were trying not to be seen.”

He turned on his side to face her. “The Song house is right against the Lin estate. The walls nearly touch. There was a red door in theirs. I wasn’t allowed through it.”

“Why not?”

“Grandfather said I had no reason to be there.”

“That’s an answer designed to end a conversation.”

“It did.”

“Did you obey him?”

“Yes. Even when I was older. He didn’t dislike them. Careful is the word. He knew who went in and out. He knew which visitors were business and which ones wanted something, and who belonged to the family and who worked for it. He didn’t want me any part of it.” There was no resentment in it, only a fact that had stayed a fact.

“What did you imagine was in there? When you were small?”

“A courtyard.”

“That’s so ordinary.”

“I was a child. A room where people played mahjong. A kitchen. Stairs.”

“How disappointing.”

“I wasn’t expecting a palace,” he said, and she laughed again, and then saw his face change, not much, just enough.

“Was it hard? Being the policeman’s grandson there?”

He was quiet. “People knew who I was before they knew me. If something happened in the Walled City, they thought I knew about it. If he arrested someone, their family looked at me differently the next morning. Some people were kind. Some weren’t. A few told me to tell my grandfather something, usually something they wanted him to hear without having to say it themselves.”

“Did you?”

“Sometimes. He said I wasn’t a messenger. I used to think the red door was the line between two lives. The people inside it and the people outside.” He turned his palm up on the sheet and she laid her fingers in it.

“And now?”

“Now I think there were more than two. People were complicated on both sides of it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her thumb moved over the back of his hand. “What happened in 2010?”

She knew the outline. Yu Chen’s parents had died. Yu Chen was eight. Wei Long was fifteen, and had taken him on. She had the dates and the ages and had never asked him what any of it felt like.

He said, “It happened fast. There were arrangements to make. Relatives to ring. Documents. People asking where he’d stay. I remember someone asking him whether he understood what was happening.”

“Did he?”

“No. He knew they weren’t coming back. He didn’t know what that meant for the rest of his life. He kept asking when he could go home. He was sitting on the floor with his school bag beside him. He’d packed it himself. I don’t think he knew what you’re supposed to pack. His schoolbooks. A pencil case. Two shirts. A photograph of his parents folded inside an exercise book. He asked me if he could keep it with him. I said yes.” He was looking at their hands.

Isla’s chest had tightened. She didn’t let it into her voice. “Was anyone asking what he wanted?”

“The adults were trying to be sensible. One relative or another, here or somewhere else, which school. Nobody asked him. I asked him. He wanted somewhere he knew. His school. His friends. He wanted to know whether he could go to the same classroom on Monday. I told him he could stay with me.” Wei Long’s fingers closed round hers.

“Just like that?”

“I was fifteen. I didn’t have much to offer. A room. Some savings. A grandfather who was still alive. I could cook four things. I could get him to school,” he said, correcting her sense of the size of it.

“You were fifteen, Wei Long. You were a child.”

“Yes,” he said.

“What did your grandfather say?”

“He asked whether I understood what I was agreeing to. I said yes. I didn’t. Not all of it. I understood Yu Chen needed somewhere to sleep and was frightened, and that if I said I’d look after him I couldn’t change my mind in the morning. I didn’t understand how long it would go on or what it would change.”

“Did you regret it?”

“No… I regretted that he needed me to. I didn’t want him growing up thinking he was a parcel nobody wanted to sign for. He asked whether I was sure. I said yes.” The no came immediately; the rest after a moment.

“Even though you weren’t?”

“I was sure of that part.”

She understood. He hadn’t known how to raise a child or what would happen to his own life. He’d known exactly what he wanted an eight-year-old to hear. Yes. You can stay. Nobody’s sending you anywhere.

“Did your grandfather help?”

“Yes. He didn’t tell me I was too young or to leave it to someone else. He did the papers. He made sure Yu Chen had what he needed for school.”

“Did he ever tell you that you didn’t have to?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“I don’t know.”

“Perhaps he thought you already knew.”

“Perhaps. The first night Yu Chen slept in my room. I slept on the floor,” said Wei Long. He was quiet a while.

“On the floor?”

“He was afraid to sleep alone.”

“And the obvious solution was to give him your bed.”

“Yes.”

“You were fifteen.”

“You’ve mentioned it.”

“You’ll hear it again. Did he sleep?” She kissed the corner of his mouth.

“Eventually.”

“Did you?”

“No. I lay there listening to him breathe. I thought if I stayed awake I could make sure nothing else happened.”

She shut her eyes. “That wasn’t yours to do. Not all of it.”

“He was there. And I was there,” said Wei Long.

That was the part he’d never needed to explain. Two boys in a house that had got too big for one of them and too frightening for the other. He hadn’t known how to make the world safe. He’d decided to stay.

✦ ✦ ✦

“What were the four things you could cook?” she said, after a while.

“Rice. Eggs. Noodles. Soup.”

“What kind of soup?”

“Whatever there was.”

“That isn’t a recipe.”

“It worked. He liked eggs. He didn’t like vegetables. He still doesn’t.”

“Did you make him eat them?”

“I cut them smaller.”

“How diplomatic.”

“It was practical. Sometimes I ate after him. To make sure he’d had enough.”

She didn’t say anything to that. “Did you have anyone to talk to?”

“Not much. I didn’t tell my friends.”

“Why not?”

“I didn’t want anyone to think I couldn’t manage.”

She looked at him. Because they might have taken Yu Chen away. Because the boy had already lost his parents and Wei Long wasn’t going to let him lose his home as well. He didn’t say it. He didn’t need to.

“Did you ever cry?”

“I don’t remember.”

“That’s not the same as no.”

“No,” he agreed.

“Did he ever see you?”

“I don’t know.”

“Did you ever tell him how hard it was?”

“He was a child.”

“So were you,” said Isla.

He lifted her hand and kissed the knuckles, and put it down. “I don’t think I knew how to be anything else. Once I’d told him he could stay, I had to make sure I could keep it.”

“You were a good cousin. You gave him something he needed. You were allowed to need things too.” She touched his face.

“I didn’t know that,” he said.

“I know,” said Isla, and kissed him, not to stop the talking, just because she wanted to.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she drew back her eyes went to his right hand on the sheet. She’d seen the scar before: a pale, uneven band across the knuckles that showed when the light was from the side. It wasn’t dramatic. It didn’t seem to need a story. She’d always wondered.

“This,” she said, and turned his hand over to the light. “Can I ask?”

“Kettle.”

She blinked. “A kettle?”

“I was sixteen. Yu Chen was nine. I came home late from school and Grandfather was on duty and Yu Chen was at the table doing his homework. I’d boiled water for noodles and the kettle was too near the edge of the counter. I reached for it. The handle slipped.”

She winced. “On your hand?”

“Across the knuckles. I turned the stove off and put it under the cold tap. Yu Chen came in and asked what had happened, and I said nothing.”

“Nothing.”

“He was frightened.”

“So you lied to him.”

“Yes. He went and got the first-aid box. He knew where it was. He stood in the kitchen holding it and kept asking whether I needed a doctor.”

“Did you?”

“It was a minor burn.”

“You are not allowed to classify your own injuries while I’m asking,” said Isla.

He looked at her. “Understood.”

“Did you finish the dinner?”

“With the other hand.”

“Of course you did.”

“I’d already started it,” he said, and she lifted the hand to her mouth and kissed the scar.

He went entirely still. Her lips touched the pale line and moved along the back of his hand. She kissed it again. “That was a lot for sixteen.”

“It was only a kettle.”

“You were cooking for two,” she said against his knuckles, and held his hand there a little longer, and then lowered it and kept it between both of hers. “Did he eat?”

“He said the noodles were too soft.”

“At nine?”

“I made them again the next day.”

“Of course you did.” She kissed the skin beside the scar, and his palm, and the inside of his wrist, and he drew one slow breath.

“Isla. You don’t have to.”

“I know. I want to.”

He moved closer and kissed her, with his hand still caught in hers, and she let go of it only to put her own on his face.

✦ ✦ ✦

Around half past three his phone buzzed on the bedside table. She sighed. He read it once, then again, and she watched his face settle into its old stillness.

“Elara?”

“Not directly. Something I can’t discuss.”

“Then don’t. When you first told me about the Lins, I thought you kept your distance because of the work.” She waited until he’d put it away.

“I did.”

“It was more than that.”

“Yes.”

“And now you’re the one investigating what happened outside the house your grandfather told you never to go into.”

He said, “I didn’t put that together until much later. Some of the people I have to talk to knew my grandfather. Some of them knew me when I was a child.”

“And now they have to answer questions.”

“Yes.”

“Then that’s what you do. Her case. Not the whole history of the house. Did you ever go through the red door? After your grandfather died?” She settled her hand on his chest.

“Not as a guest.”

“Do you still think of it as the red door? Not the Lin house?”

“Yes.”

“You remember it as a line.”

“Perhaps. I remember standing outside it.”

“What did you want then?”

“To know what was inside. Now I want to know what happened outside it.” He looked at the window.

The difference was small. She heard it. He wasn’t the boy waiting at the end of a shift any more, or the fifteen-year-old who’d promised a child he could stay. He was a policeman with a case and a life that had slowly turned into something other than duty, and he’d come home to her with it.

She lifted his hand and kissed the scar once more and put his palm against her cheek. “Sleep.”

“You’re awake.”

“So are you. We can be awake together.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At 4:18 he woke when she moved. Her hand had come off his chest in her sleep and found his right wrist, and her fingers lay loose across the scar. He turned his hand so his palm covered hers. The phone stayed in his pocket. The case would be there in the morning, and the questions. Next door to the Lins the house had someone else’s screens in his old room, and Yu Chen had his own life, and the red door was still red.

He thought about his grandfather on the beat, knowing every staircase and face. About a boy on a floor with a school bag, asking if he could keep a photograph. About a kettle going over, and a frightened child holding a first-aid box, and two bowls of noodles on a table. About the woman asleep beside him, who’d never once asked him to be useful before she loved him.

He put his mouth to her hair. Then he shut his eyes, and for once he didn’t stay awake to make sure nothing else happened.

chapters.title: The Neighbour Asks for Nothing
chapters.desc: Visiting Yu Chen, he’s stopped at the garden wall by Lin Jian, who asks him for nothing, which is worse than asking. Both men know Wei Long knows his daughter is the Eraser, and that the man who knifed Elara is in Wei Long’s cells. Isla, waiting in the car, reads his face.
chapters.epigraph: “That’s worse, isn’t it?”
chapters.content:
Lin Jian was standing by the garden wall when they pulled up on Sunday morning, doing nothing in particular. One hand rested on the stone coping. The other held a white porcelain cup, and steam came off it into the cold. He wore a dark jacket over a pale shirt, the kind of clothes that look ordinary until you notice how carefully they’ve been chosen. Behind him the Lin estate was quiet and the red door was shut.

Isla had driven, because Wei Long had worked until three, and because she had told him that accepting help wasn’t a criminal offence. She stopped the car at the Song gate and reached for her phone. “I’ve a call at half ten. I’ll come in after.”

“All right.”

He got out. The path from the road to Yu Chen’s front door didn’t pass the Lin wall. He could have walked to the steps without looking at it. Lin Jian looked up.

“Inspector Song.”

Wei Long stopped. “Mr. Lin.”

Lin Jian glanced past him at the car, at the woman in it on her phone, and back. “Visiting your cousin.”

“Yes.”

“On a Sunday. When you were a boy you sat on those steps on Sundays with your schoolbooks and pretended not to watch my door.”

Lin Jian nodded and drank his tea. Wei Long knew who he was. Not just the name, or the place he had in his family. He knew how the Syndicate’s goods moved and who moved them for this man, and which harbour businesses existed to make that look like trade. He knew the youngest daughter, who had stood in the doorway of his old bedroom in November and told him he could visit whenever he liked. He knew the sentence she had said down the phone to him in September: My name is Eliana Lin. I’m the Eraser. He knew Magpie and Calder Risk Partners and what had happened to both after that call. And he knew what Qu Wenjun had said to him across an interview table in December, in a flat sailor’s voice, about a night in 2002 and four boats and a family that had burned.

Lin Jian knew he knew all of it.

“How is the investigation?” said Lin Jian.

“Which one?”

The older man’s face hardly moved. “The one in my alley.”

“Elara Wang’s case is ongoing.”

“How is it going?”

“We have a man in custody.”

“I know.”

He hadn’t asked whether the police had found the man. He’d asked how it was going.

“The evidence is being reviewed. The procedures are being followed,” said Wei Long.

“Is he still talking?”

“Mr. Qu has made a number of statements.”

Lin Jian looked down into his cup. Then up. He didn’t ask what the statements were. He didn’t ask what they said about him, or whether they’d been written down, or who had read them. He nodded once, as if Wei Long had told him the time, and that was worse than any question he could have asked.

“How is her hand?” he said.

“You’d know better than I would.”

“I’d like to hear it from someone who isn’t trying to spare me.”

Wei Long considered him. “The surgeons say it will take a year to know.”

Lin Jian nodded again. He put the cup down on the coping.

“Your grandfather used to stand about here. He didn’t like the wall. He thought it made the street look divided,” he said.

“He never said.”

“He was a policeman. He didn’t like a great many things. He did his job.” Lin Jian’s eyes rested on him.

“Yes.”

“How’s Yu Chen?”

“Well.”

“Still at the hospital?”

“He’s a junior doctor.”

“You’re still correcting people.”

“When they’re inaccurate.”

The corner of Lin Jian’s mouth moved. “He’s a good young man. Eliana thinks so too.”

He hadn’t asked anything or accused anyone. He’d put a sentence down between them with great care. Lin Jian knew his daughter lived on the other side of this wall with Wei Long’s cousin. He knew that the inspector in front of him had known who she was long before she rang him, and hadn’t used it against the two of them, and could have.

“They’re adults. They make their own decisions,” said Wei Long.

“That’s what I’m told. Thank you for answering my questions, Inspector.” Lin Jian picked his cup up again.

“Mr. Lin.”

He had turned for the steps when the older man said, “Inspector Song,” and he stopped.

“Take care of yourself.”

The words were ordinary. The voice wasn’t.

“You too,” said Wei Long, and walked on.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Chen opened the door before he reached the top step. “Ge. Come in. Auntie Tsoi made lunch. Eliana says give her five minutes.”

“For what?”

“Something about a computer.”

“It’s not just a computer!” from upstairs.

The house smelled of rice and ginger. Three bowls were already laid. Yu Chen talked about the hospital: a patient who’d mistaken him for a consultant and asked him to explain a procedure he’d never done on his own.

“Did you tell him?”

“Of course. Ge, I’m not going to pretend to be a specialist.”

“I didn’t say you would.”

“You looked like you were going to.”

Auntie Tsoi put fish in Wei Long’s bowl. He ate it. Then Yu Chen said, too casually, “Was someone outside?”

“Lin Jian.”

Yu Chen’s chopsticks stopped. “What did he want?”

“He asked how the case was going. He asked how you were.”

“Me?”

“I said you were well.”

Yu Chen looked at his rice. He didn’t ask why Lin Jian had wanted to know. He’d grown up on this side of the wall too. “Ge. If anything happens...”

“Yu Chen. Your life with Eliana is yours. My work is mine. Don’t put yourself between them.”

“I won’t.”

“Good.”

“Yu Chen!” from upstairs.

Yu Chen shut his eyes. “Yes?”

“Can you come here?”

“What’s happened?”

“Nothing. I need you.”

Wei Long kept eating. “Go.”

“Don’t finish the fish.”

“I won’t.”

“You’re lying,” said Yu Chen, and went. Wei Long heard Eliana say something about a file, and Yu Chen explaining that she’d opened the wrong folder. He looked at the empty chair opposite. For years he had been the one who answered when Yu Chen called. Now Yu Chen answered when somebody else called, and that was right, and he was still learning to sit at a table without feeling he ought to be doing something.

✦ ✦ ✦

Isla came in at eleven, said hello to Auntie Tsoi, accepted tea, and listened to Yu Chen and Eliana argue about whether the folder had been labelled correctly, by a reasonable person.

“You’re staying for tea. You’ve had lunch, so it’s tea,” Eliana told Wei Long.

“That sounds reasonable. You saw him,” said Isla, and Eliana went to the kitchen. Isla waited until she’d gone.

“Yes. By the wall.”

“What did he want?”

“Nothing.”

She looked at him. He looked back. “What did he ask?”

“How the case was going. How her hand was. How Yu Chen was.”

“That’s all?”

“Yes.”

“I believe you. I don’t think that’s all.” She drank some tea.

He said nothing. Through the window the red door showed over the wall, its colour softened in the winter light.

“Does he know that you know? About her? About other things?” Isla didn’t say the name.

“Yes.”

“Did he ask you for anything?”

“No.”

“Did he hint at anything?”

“No.”

“Did he threaten you? Or Yu Chen?”

“No.”

She nodded slowly. Then, low, “That’s worse, isn’t it?”

“Yes,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

They left after noon. Eliana and Yu Chen walked them to the gate and Eliana said, “Next week,” and Wei Long said, “If I’m free,” and she said that wasn’t an answer and she’d ask Yu Chen, because Yu Chen was easier to persuade, and Yu Chen said that wasn’t true, and Wei Long said it was. Auntie Tsoi gave Isla a container of food and told her not to let him leave it in the car.

Lin Jian wasn’t by the wall any more. The cup was gone. A faint ring of damp on the stone showed where it had stood. Wei Long slowed for half a step. Isla didn’t look at the house. She took his hand, and they walked on.

In the car she started the engine and adjusted the mirror and looked at him. He was facing the windscreen. His face was composed. His shoulders weren’t. She’d learned the difference.

“Seat belt.”

He fastened it. She drove. For a few streets neither of them said anything. A delivery van stopped outside a shop. Someone crossed with a paper bag. At a red light she put her hand on his thigh, and he looked down at it and covered it with his.

“Do you want to talk about it?”

“Not yet.”

“All right.”

His phone buzzed. He read it and put it away. She didn’t ask.

She knew some of it. She knew the man who had cut Elara’s hand was waiting for his trial, and that Wei Long would have to go on working through statements and evidence in a case full of people who’d known him since he was a boy doing sums at a station desk. What she understood, watching his hand on hers, was that Lin Jian had asked him for nothing, and that he couldn’t put that down. If the man had asked for something, the answer would have been easy. No. If he’d asked Wei Long to bend the case, no. To protect his family from what they’d done, no. To tell him what Qu Wenjun had said, no, without a second’s hesitation. He knew exactly what he would have to do if he were ever asked. He’d refuse. But Lin Jian had stood by the wall and asked about a hand and a young doctor and said take care of yourself, and left him nothing to refuse. Only the knowledge that both of them understood the same things, and the silence between those things, which was where Lin Jian had put him.

“You’re thinking loudly,” said Isla.

“Am I?”

“You don’t have to tell me what he said. You don’t have to explain the case. But you can tell me what you’re worried about.”

“I don’t know what he wants.”

“And if he wanted something, you’d know what to do.”

“Yes.”

“And because he didn’t ask, you can’t say no.”

He looked at her. She shrugged without taking her eyes off the road. “You’re not hard to read when you’re unhappy.”

“I’m not unhappy.”

“Fine. You’re thoughtfully uncomfortable.”

He looked out of the window for a while. “If he asks, I know my answer. I won’t touch the case. I won’t give him anything. I won’t use what I am to protect his family.”

“I know.”

“He knows I knew about her before she rang me. He knows I could have done something with it.”

“Could you?”

“Yes.”

“But you didn’t. So he knows that too.”

She left it there. She didn’t tell him what Lin Jian might be thinking, or pretend to understand him. She put the facts where they belonged and left them.

“I don’t want Yu Chen involved. I don’t want her made to pay for her father. I don’t want this following them into their house,” said Wei Long.

“Then don’t take it into their house. You’re allowed to leave work outside a door, you know. I’ve mentioned it.” She gave him a smile.

“Several times.”

“And yet.”

He lifted her hand off his thigh and kissed the knuckles. “Thank you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At home he put the food in the fridge, washed his hands and took his watch off. She went to put the kettle on. He stood at the counter looking at it, an ordinary steel kettle, and she knew what he was seeing: a boy of sixteen, and boiling water going over, and a frightened child in a doorway with a first-aid box. She came back and took his right hand without a word and kissed the scar across his knuckles.

“You’re home. Not at the wall. Not in that conversation. Here,” she said.

He drew her in and put his forehead against hers. “If he asks, I’ll refuse.”

“I know.”

“And if he never does?”

“Then you don’t have to answer,” said Isla, and kissed him.

The kettle clicked off behind them. Neither of them moved to it.

“Do you want to know what Qu said? About 2002. I can’t tell you. I’m asking whether you want to know,” he asked, against her hair.

She thought about it properly, because he’d asked properly. “No.”

“Why?”

“Because if I knew, you’d have to watch me knowing it every time we went to that house. You’d watch me pass Lin Jian at the wall and wonder whether my face gave anything away. You carry enough. I’m not going to make you carry me as well.” She leaned back to look at him.

He didn’t answer. His thumb moved along her jaw.

Isla said, “I’ll tell you what I do want. I want you to drink this tea, and then lie on the sofa with your head in my lap while I read, and fall asleep there for two hours, because you got in at three and you’ve been standing up straight all morning for a man with a cup.”

“That’s a lot of instructions.”

“I’m a consular officer. We have procedures.”

He drank the tea. He lay on the sofa with his head in her lap while she read, and her fingers went into his hair at the end of every page, and somewhere around the fourth page he stopped being able to tell whether she was turning them. When he woke the light had moved across the room and she was still there, on the same chapter, with her hand still in his hair.

chapters.title: The Case That Kept Him Away
chapters.desc: A week in a surveillance flat watching a smuggler. She sends him a photograph every night of what he’s missing, none of them of food. Home at dawn on Sunday he doesn’t take his coat off: explicit, fast, against her front door, then slow in bed.
chapters.epigraph: “I promise I’ll come home to you.”
chapters.content:
The first photograph arrived at 11:03 on Monday night. Wei Long was in a folding chair by a window that had been painted shut, watching a flat across the street through a gap in a brown curtain.

The surveillance flat was over a tailor’s shop that had closed down years ago, two doors from a laundry that stayed open till midnight. The man they were watching lived on the second floor above the laundry: Wat Chi-ming, forty-six, who for six months had been moving restricted goods through the paperwork of a dozen honest shipping manifests and a nest of companies that existed mainly on letterheads. The room smelled of old cigarettes, damp plaster and instant coffee. Someone had left a newspaper on the counter three weeks ago. The sofa was missing a cushion. He’d been there since six.

Thank You (Paid): You look like you need a distraction.

It was a photograph of her collarbone. The hollow under it, the open neck of the black blouse she wore to work, and a thin gold chain at her throat he knew, because he’d done up the clasp for her that morning when she couldn’t get her fingers round it.

He looked at it longer than was necessary, and then at the window. Wat’s lights were on behind drawn curtains. He’d gone out at 8:17 and come back just before ten. The team could see the street door but not the room. They logged visitors, deliveries and movements, and didn’t guess at what happened behind the curtains.

Wei Long: I’m working.

Thank You (Paid): I know. That’s why I sent it. Did you look?

Wei Long: Yes.

Thank You (Paid): Good.

Across the room Sergeant Liu had his binoculars on the laundry and hadn’t said a word in twenty minutes. “Sir. Your phone.”

“What about it?”

“Nothing. Just checking.”

“Check the entrance.”

Around half past eleven Wat’s lights went out. Wei Long wrote down the time. Around half past eleven he looked at his phone again, and there was nothing new, and he didn’t know why that disappointed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tuesday’s arrived at eleven exactly. A black stocking, one knee bent, the hem of a skirt at the edge of the frame. Behind it, unmistakably, their bedroom.

Thank You (Paid): I thought you might like something better to look at than that wall.

He was in the stairwell of the surveillance building, where the signal was better and the others couldn’t see his screen without making an effort. The wall was a unpleasant beige.

Wei Long: The wall isn’t the problem.

Thank You (Paid): No? What is?

He took a while.

Wei Long: You.

Thank You (Paid): That sounds promising.

He went back upstairs. Liu glanced at him. “Everything all right, sir? You look...”

“Don’t.”

Liu didn’t.

On Wednesday a white van belonging to a small haulage firm parked outside the laundry for eleven minutes and left with its back end noticeably lower than when it arrived. They photographed it, logged it, and asked for the traffic cameras through the proper channel. Wat didn’t go out. Just after eleven she sent a picture of his white shirt, the one with a cuff button missing. She was wearing it, sitting on the edge of their bed with the collar falling off one shoulder and her hair still damp.

Thank You (Paid): I stole something.

Wei Long: I noticed.

Thank You (Paid): You left it here.

Wei Long: I own it.

Thank You (Paid): Not tonight.

He put the phone in his pocket with some deliberation.

“Sir, the van’s back,” said Liu.

“Time?”

“Twenty-three fourteen.”

Two men got out. One went to the back doors. The other went in through the laundry’s service entrance. Wei Long reached for his radio, and for the next forty minutes there was no room in his head for anything else.

✦ ✦ ✦

By Thursday the flat had become a bad copy of a home: two mugs on the sill, three empty coffee packets in the bin, printed photographs on the table, his notes in his small upright hand. Wat’s routine was taking shape. Out at eight. Into the laundry twice a day, never for long. The van every other evening. A third man, not yet named, using the back stairs. They needed another day, perhaps two.

He rang her in a break. She answered on the fourth ring with traffic behind her.

“Inspector. Are you ill?”

“No.”

“You’re ringing me in the middle of an operation. Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

He looked at the empty coffee cup. “Food.”

“How informative.”

“Rice.”

“With what?”

“Something.”

She sighed. “I miss you.”

He stopped looking at the window. “Isla, I miss you too,” he said.

Her voice went gentle. “I know you can’t tell me much. Can you tell me when you’re coming home?”

“Sunday morning. If it goes the way it’s planned.”

“If.”

“If.”

“Then I’ll keep Sunday morning. Don’t tell me not to wait up. That isn’t yours to decide.” He heard her indicator ticking.

“No, it isn’t,” he said.

At eleven a photograph came with no words at all. Her hand on his pillow, the fingers curled loosely over its edge. He looked at it for a long while. Then he saved it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Friday was the longest day. At 6:40 a.m. Wat came out with an overnight bag and the follow car took him at a distance to a wholesale market, where he spent nine minutes talking to a man who handed him nothing, took nothing, and had been named in an earlier case as a director of one of Wat’s shells. Wei Long watched the footage twice and asked for the market’s outside cameras. At 10:30 Wat came home.

At eleven that night she was standing in front of the bedroom mirror in a dark slip dress with her hair over one shoulder.

Thank You (Paid): I was going to wear this tonight.

Wei Long: You look beautiful.

Thank You (Paid): That isn’t what I was asking.

Wei Long: I know.

Thank You (Paid): What were you going to say?

Wei Long: That I wish I were there.

Thank You (Paid): Better. I’m leaving it on the chair. You can see it when you come home.

“Sir, I think we’ve got the second vehicle,” said Liu, without turning round from the laptop.

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday was the fourteenth of February, which the city marked with red balloons in the windows of every restaurant on the street below and roses in buckets outside the convenience store, and which the surveillance team marked with a delivery driver who went into the laundry just after seven and came out just after seven with a flat cardboard package. His van stopped next at a storage unit leased to another of Wat’s companies. They had enough. Not enough to improvise with. They spent the night building the operation: warrants, entry teams, car positions, the handling of the evidence, who did what and in what order. Wei Long went through it twice.

Just before eleven his phone buzzed.

Thank You (Paid): Happy Valentine’s Day, Inspector. Are you still awake?

Wei Long: Yes.

Thank You (Paid): Stupid question.

Wei Long: Not stupid.

Thank You (Paid): I miss your hands.

He looked down at them. They were resting on the printed operational plan, one finger marking the entry sequence.

Wei Long: Sunday.

Thank You (Paid): Promise?

He checked the timings. The storage unit at 4:30. The arrest at the flat when the positions were confirmed. If it ran to schedule he could be home before seven.

Wei Long: I promise I’ll come home to you.

Thank You (Paid): All right. Go to bed. Try not to get arrested.

Wei Long: Unlikely.

Thank You (Paid): You’re confident for a man who hasn’t been home in six days.

✦ ✦ ✦

Sunday began at 4:18. The storage unit went first: shipping documents, laptops, phones, and several containers whose contents had nothing to do with what the paperwork said. Everything was photographed before it was moved. Wat was arrested in his flat just after five in a vest and pyjama trousers. He didn’t resist. He did insist that he had no idea what the police were talking about. Wei Long had heard that sentence in several languages from several hundred people and didn’t argue with it. He made sure the cautions were recorded, had the electronics left in place for the examiners, and by 6:48 had handed the scene over.

Just after seven he was driving home with his coat on the passenger seat, his shirt creased, a red line across his forehead from the edge of the chair he’d slept against for under an hour, unshaved. He hadn’t sent her a message. He wanted to see her face.

The flat was quiet. The bedroom door was open and the lights were off. A book lay face down on the coffee table. Then he heard her.

“You’re late.”

She stood at the end of the hallway, barefoot, in the white shirt from Wednesday’s photograph, her hair loose, one hand on the door frame, looking as though she’d only just woken. For a few seconds neither of them moved. Her eyes went over his face and his shoulders and the coat he’d put back on in the car park.

“You’re home,” she said.

“Yes.”

“You look terrible.”

He shut the door behind him. She came down the hall, and he’d imagined this a dozen times in the stairwell, in pieces: putting his things down, washing, changing, coffee. He hadn’t imagined getting further than the hall.

“Did you eat? Did you sleep? Did you...” she said, reaching for his lapels.

He kissed her.

The question stopped against his mouth. She was surprised for half a second and then her hands closed on his coat and she kissed him back so hard the week between them felt like a year, every night he’d put the phone away and gone back to the window landing in it at once. He held her face and then her waist and walked her backwards until her back met the front door with a soft thud, and braced one hand on the wood beside her head.

“You’re exhausted,” she said into his mouth.

“Yes.”

“And you’re still kissing me like this.”

“Yes. I missed you.” He pushed her hair off her face.

“I know.”

“I don’t think you do. I missed coming home and finding you in the kitchen. I missed you talking while I’m trying to read. I missed moving your things off my side of the bed.” He kissed the corner of her mouth.

“My things are not on your side.”

“They are. I missed you in the morning.” He kissed her throat.

Her hands went inside his coat. She pulled his shirt out of his trousers and got her palms on his bare back, and he made a sound into her neck. She unbuckled his belt with her fingers shaking, and he didn’t take the coat off. He didn’t take anything off. He undid the buttons of her shirt, his shirt, one after another, and opened it, and she had nothing on under it, and he looked at her in the grey hallway light and said her name.

“Here. Now. Don’t you dare take me to bed,” she said.

He lifted her. She wrapped her legs round his waist and her back hit the door again, and his coat hung round both of them like a tent, and she reached between them and freed him and guided him into her, and they both stopped dead. He held her there pinned against the door with his forehead on hers, breathing.

“Move,” said Isla.

He did. It was fast and rough and not the least bit organised. Her heels dug into his back and the door rattled in its frame with every stroke and she didn’t care. She held on to his shoulders under the coat and bit her lip and then didn’t, and said things to him in English, and then in French, and he didn’t understand the French and didn’t need to. She came first, all at once, clenching round him, her head back against the wood, and he followed her with his face buried in her neck and a groan she’d remember, and for a minute afterwards they just stayed there, held up by the door.

“You haven’t even taken your coat off,” she said, shakily.

“I noticed.”

“You’re usually much more organised.”

“Not at the moment,” he said, and carried her to bed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second time was nothing like the first. The coat ended up on the hall floor by the shoe cabinet, and the shirt somewhere between there and the bedroom, and he lay her down and took everything slowly that he’d taken fast. He kissed every inch of her that he’d seen in a photograph: the hollow under her collarbone where the gold chain lay, the inside of the knee from Tuesday, the curve of her shoulder where his shirt had slid off it on Wednesday. He put his mouth between her legs and kept it there until she was pulling his hair and begging, and then went on a little longer. When he finally came into her she was ready to weep with it. He moved inside her with long slow strokes, holding her hands down on the pillow beside her head, his fingers laced through hers, and watched every change in her face, and didn’t let her look away. She came with his name on her lips and his eyes on hers, and he came after her a long time later, almost without a sound.

Around half past nine the phone vibrated. Neither of them moved. Just after ten it went again. Just before eleven it rang, and he reached over her for it. It was Liu.

“Search complete, evidence secured, Wat’s in custody, nothing that needs you, sir. Sorry to ring.”

“Confirmed,” said Wei Long, and hung up, and Isla took the phone out of his hand, switched it to silent and gave it back.

“That’s my phone.”

“I know.”

“You’ve silenced it.”

“I have. Seven photographs. Seven evenings. You sent me about seventeen words back.” She looked pleased with herself.

“I was at work.”

“I wasn’t asking for a sonnet between surveillance logs. I wanted to know you were thinking about me.” She kissed his shoulder.

“Every night. Even when the van came. Even when he left with his bag.”

“I didn’t send you photos of my dinner,” said Isla, “because you’d have asked whether I’d finished it.”

“That’s a reasonable question.”

“Exactly. I wanted you distracted.”

“Liu asked whether I was ill.”

She laughed into his skin until he had to hold her still.

✦ ✦ ✦

At noon she was still in bed, lying on her stomach reading the book she’d abandoned on Saturday, one foot hooked over his ankle. He reached over and turned a page for her.

“Thank you. You’re not going anywhere today,” she said without looking up.

“No.”

“Not the station. Not the evidence. Not a report.”

“Tomorrow.”

“Good. It’s New Year’s Eve tomorrow. Auntie Tsoi has told Yu Chen to tell you that if you’re late she’ll give your fish to Yu Chen.” She turned another page.

“I won’t be late.”

“Next time,” said Isla, still reading, “tell me when it’s going to be a week.”

“I didn’t know it would be.”

“Then tell me when you know. And don’t say Sunday when you’re not sure.”

“I wasn’t sure.”

“I know. I wanted to hear you say it anyway.”

He understood that. “I’ll tell you what I know,” he said, “and what I don’t.”

She closed the book and looked at him. “You’re staring.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I can,” he said, and she put the book on the bedside table and moved into his arms, and kissed him without any of the week left in it.

“Welcome home,” she whispered, and he didn’t answer straight away. He pulled her in against him and shut his eyes, and for the first Sunday in a while there was nowhere else he had to be.

chapters.title: A Body in the Harbour
chapters.desc: A woman is pulled out of the water off the ferry pier: Koon Fan-ling, 26, a visa clerk at Isla’s consulate, strangled and weighted. Isla had lunch with her on Tuesdays. Dark: the post-mortem is shown plainly; Wei Long takes the case and is told he can’t, because of Isla.
chapters.epigraph: “Tomorrow. Don’t be late this time.”
chapters.content:
The call came at 6:18 on Wednesday morning. Isla was asleep with one hand under her cheek and the other on his chest, her hair across his shoulder. He reached for the phone without moving her.

“Song.”

“Sir. We’ve got a body. In the water off the ferry pier. Harbour patrol pulled her out just before six. Female, young. There’s a weight tied on.” Liu, awake and clipped.

Wei Long sat up. “Identity?”

“Not confirmed. There’s a handbag. Scene team has it.”

“Nobody moves anything else till it’s photographed. Get the coroner told. I’m coming.”

Isla opened her eyes. “Work?”

“A body in the harbour.”

The sleep went out of her face. “Who?”

“I don’t know yet.”

He dressed. She watched him from under the blanket, and when he bent to kiss her forehead she held his wrist for a second and said, “Be careful,” and neither of them knew that by lunchtime he would wish he’d let it ring.

✦ ✦ ✦

The morning was grey and the water under the pier was black. A section of the walkway had been taped off. She lay on a stretcher under a white sheet beside the recovery point, and two uniformed constables stood at the tape with their backs to her.

The weight was a cast-iron frying pan. Someone had tied it to her with nylon cord, round the waist and through the handle, and the cord had pulled tight into her clothes and held when the patrol launch brought her up. It was heavy enough to have kept her under.

“Caught on the lower structure about six metres out. Tide was going out,” said the recovery officer.

“Any sign she went in here?”

“Not yet.”

“Then don’t assume it.”

The scene officer lifted the sheet for him. She was young. Her dark hair lay wet and tangled across her face. One shoe was gone. Her hands had gone white and wrinkled from the water, the skin of the fingertips puckered like a washerwoman’s. Round her neck, above the collar of her blouse, ran a dark band, narrow and even, the colour of a plum. He crouched without touching anything and looked at it.

“Photograph that before she’s moved. The cord, the pan and anything on either of them bagged separately. The clothing recorded exactly as it came out of the water.”

The handbag came over in a sealed box. No purse. Inside, a lanyard and a work card in a plastic sleeve, and he read the name on it once, and then again. KOON FAN-LING. Visa Section.

Twenty-six. The consulate. He looked at the photograph on the card and knew the face. He had seen her on liaison visits, answering the internal phone when Isla was busy. She had once corrected his pronunciation of her surname with a patience he’d found formidable. And he had seen her outside a noodle stall near the market, on a Tuesday, because Isla had lunch with her on Tuesdays. Fan-ling says the stall’s putting less meat in the soup. She thinks they’re trying to make us pay more for the same bowl.

“Sir?” said Liu.
