Wei Long gave the card back to the evidence officer. “Confirm her through the proper channels. Nobody contacts her workplace until the family notification’s arranged.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The post-mortem began at 9:40. Dr. Hor was small and exact and had worked with the department long enough to know that he liked his answers straight.

On the steel table under the lamps the body had been photographed, undressed and washed. Without the wet hair across it the face was swollen and dusky above the line of the ligature and pale below it. Dr. Hor showed him the band round the neck first: a groove, fairly horizontal, running almost all the way round, bruised at the edges, the skin inside it dried and brown where the cord had pressed. She drew back the eyelids with a gloved thumb. The whites were spattered with tiny red points, like pepper.

She said, “Petechial haemorrhages. Eyes, and inside the lips. With the ligature mark that’s consistent with strangulation. I won’t give you a final cause until I’ve opened the neck and the tests are back.”

She opened the neck. He watched her do it, layer by layer, and watched her point to the bleeding in the muscle under the groove and the small bone at the top of the throat, the hyoid, unbroken, which at twenty-six it often wasn’t.

“Water in the airways?”

“Some. Immersion makes that hard to read. I can’t tell you yet whether she was alive when she went in. I’d say not, but I’ll want the lungs looked at.”

“Time of death?”

“A range, and not a narrow one. The water’s taken most of my clocks away.”

She turned one of the hands over. Two of the fingernails were broken off at the quick. There were bruises on the inside of the right forearm, three small ones close together.

“These may be defensive. They may be something else. I’m taking scrapings from under what’s left of the nails,” she said.

“And the pan?”

“It kept her down. It doesn’t tell you where she died.”

He wrote everything in his notebook and asked his questions: the cord, the bruises, whether any of it was older, what she could get off the pan. She said she’d prioritise whatever biological material she could find. Just after eleven she straightened up and pulled her mask down.

“Most likely ligature strangulation. I’ll give you the formal opinion when the results are in.”

“Thank you.”

Liu was waiting in the corridor. “Superintendent wants you upstairs. Now. And the consulate’s rung. They’re asking whether it’s Koon Fan-ling.”

Wei Long said nothing.

“Is there a problem, sir?”

“Yes, there is,” said Wei Long.

✦ ✦ ✦

The superintendent had the identification report and the notes from the mortuary open on his desk, and pointed at the chair.

“You know the deceased.”

“Professionally. Through Ms. Ren. They worked together and had lunch on Tuesdays. I’ve met Ms. Koon several times. I had no personal relationship with her.”

“Have you discussed her with Ms. Ren?”

“Not about anything relevant.”

“Then you’ll understand why you can’t lead this.”

“I understand the concern. I don’t agree that it stops me running the first stage.”

“It stops you running any of it. The victim was your partner’s colleague. Your partner may be a witness. She may know things about the dead woman’s movements, her friends, her state of mind. You can’t interview her as an independent officer. You can’t decide what she tells you is important. You can’t handle evidence that may bear on her.” The superintendent didn’t raise his voice. He didn’t need to.

“I haven’t spoken to her about it, and I won’t.”

“That isn’t the point either. It’s not whether I trust you to be professional. It’s whether this investigation can survive a defence barrister asking why the detective inspector in charge was sleeping with a witness. Detective Superintendent Chiang will take it. Give him your notes. Then stay away from it. This isn’t discipline, Inspector. I’m protecting the case. And you.” The superintendent closed the file.

“Understood,” said Wei Long, and stood up.

Just after twelve he handed it over. Chiang was a tall, unhurried man with half-moon glasses, and he listened to the whole of it: the pier, the pan, the cord, the band on her neck, the nails, the question of where she’d gone into the water and how.

“And your connection?”

“She was my partner’s friend. They had lunch on Tuesdays.”

“Have you told your partner?”

“No.”

“Keep it that way until my team contacts her.”

The case went on without him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He rang Isla from the corridor at half past twelve. She answered at once.

“Are you alone?” he said.

“Yes. Why?”

“Have you heard from Fan-ling today?”

There was a silence. Then, carefully, “No. Why?”

“Isla. I need you to sit down.”

She didn’t. “Is it Fan-ling?”

“Yes. She was found in the harbour this morning. She’s dead.”

The silence after that was a different kind. It took up the whole line.

“How?”

“We’re treating it as murder.”

“Was she... Was she hurt?”

“Yes.”

“Do you know what happened?”

“I can’t talk about the investigation.”

“I know. She was supposed to meet me yesterday. Tuesday. She sent me a message on Monday about the new place by the market. I told her I couldn’t, I had a meeting. She sent me a picture of the menu.” Her voice had gone small. Her breath caught.

“Keep it. Don’t delete anything she sent you. The investigating team will want to see it. They’ll contact you properly.”

“You’re not running it?”

“No. Because you knew her and I’m with you. It was taken off me at noon.”

“Are you angry?”

He looked at the hand holding the phone. “Yes.”

“Did she... Did she suffer?” She stopped again.

He could have told her the case was ongoing and the post-mortem incomplete. He told her what he could. “She was strangled. There was a weight tied to her. The pathologist hasn’t finished.”

“Oh. She was twenty-six. She always complained about that noodle stall. She was going to make me try another one,” said Isla. Something moved on her end, a chair, a hand on a desk.

“I know.”

“I don’t know what to do.”

“Don’t do anything now. The consulate’s been told. Let them handle the notifications. You don’t have to do all of it yourself.”

“Will you come home?”

“Yes.”

“When?”

“As soon as I can. I’m sorry,” he said, because it was too small and it was all he had.

“I know,” she said, and rang off.

He stood in the corridor for a minute. Then he collected his things and went home.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was sitting on the living-room floor with her back against the sofa. On the coffee table was a photograph on her phone: two bowls of noodles, one a little out of focus, a hand holding up a pair of chopsticks at the edge of the picture.

“She sent it last Tuesday. She said the chilli oil there was better than the place near the office. She was wrong. She insisted,” said Isla.

He sat down on the floor beside her. She showed him the messages. The menu. A complaint about the soup. A voice note, twelve seconds long, in which a young woman laughed and said Isla was incapable of choosing a restaurant. And the last one, from Monday afternoon.

Tomorrow. Don’t be late this time.

“I was late the week before. Seven minutes. She said seven minutes was late,” said Isla.

“She knew you’d come.”

“I should have gone yesterday. I could have moved the meeting.”

“You didn’t know.”

“I could have...”

“Isla, you didn’t know,” he said, and she stopped.

Her face broke. He pulled her in against him and she folded into his chest. She cried without any noise, which was worse. Her breathing went ragged and her shoulders shook and she kept trying to say things and not finishing them. He held her and didn’t tell her it would be all right.

“She used to save me the seat by the wall. She said I got distracted by people walking past and never finished my lunch,” she said at last, into his shirt.

“She was kind to you.”

“I didn’t know she was in danger.”

“Neither did I,” he said, and they sat on the floor with the photograph of two bowls of noodles on the table between them until the light changed.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t go to the investigation meetings. He didn’t ring Chiang. When the case file appeared on the shared system he didn’t open it, and he didn’t ask the officers on it what they’d found. It was deliberate and it was hard. He knew the questions he’d have asked and the order he’d have asked them in: her last known movements, who had keys to her building, where a cast-iron pan could be bought within a mile of the pier, how a body got to the end of a ferry pier at night without anyone seeing. He knew all of it and did none of it.

Chiang’s team interviewed Isla on the Friday. She gave them the messages and the menu and told them what she knew about Fan-ling’s life, which was Tuesdays, and work, and that Fan-ling had seemed entirely herself the week before. He didn’t ask how it had gone. He waited for her to tell him.

“They were professional. They asked whether anyone had been bothering her. Whether she’d been worried about money. Whether she’d seemed frightened,” she said that night.

“Had she?”

“Not to me. I keep thinking I’ll remember something I should have seen.” She was quiet a while.

“People don’t usually announce that they’re in danger.”

She looked at him. “You say that as if you have to remind yourself.”

“Sometimes.”

She leaned against him. “I don’t want her to turn into a file.”

“She won’t. The people who knew her won’t let her.”

Some nights after that she talked about Fan-ling and some nights she didn’t, and he learned not to treat silence as a request for questions. Fan-ling had once taken three buses across the city to bring her a document she’d forgotten, because the courier had gone home. Fan-ling was learning French and said grenouille so badly that the two of them had laughed for ten minutes in the stairwell. The stories were small. He kept every one. He also kept the pan, and the cord, and the band on her neck, and Dr. Hor’s level voice. Some nights he woke before Isla did and lay still listening to her breathe, and didn’t tell her why.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday the twenty-seventh he stood in court for a different case. Qu Wenjun, who had come to the Lins’ red door on the last night of November with a knife, stood in the dock in a grey sweatshirt and pleaded guilty. The facts were read into the record. Six years. It was pronounced without any drama at all, and Wei Long wrote it in his notebook and closed his file.

Outside in the corridor a clerk went by with a trolley of documents. Somewhere a child was crying. One case was finished, as far as a criminal case ever is. Another was open in a room he wasn’t allowed into.

Thank You (Paid): How was court?

Wei Long: Guilty plea. Six years.

Thank You (Paid): Good. Are you coming home? I bought noodles.

Wei Long: From the stall near the office?

Thank You (Paid): No. A different one. I don’t know if it’s good yet.

When he got in she was at the counter reading the instructions on the side of the takeaway bag as if the restaurant had issued a set of operating procedures.

“How was it?” he said.

“I haven’t tried them. I was waiting. And Fan-ling?” She looked up.

“I don’t know yet.”

She nodded. “Every Tuesday I expect her to message me.”

“You’ll probably go on expecting it for a while.”

“Yes.”

“That’s all right,” he said, and kissed her temple, and took the containers to the table. She got the chopsticks out of the drawer. For a while they moved round each other in the small kitchen doing the ordinary work of dinner: two bowls, two pairs of chopsticks, and a Tuesday lunch that neither of them could fill.

chapters.title: She Is a Witness
chapters.desc: He has to interview her properly, on tape, across a table in Interview Three, and can’t touch her for an hour. She lies to protect a colleague who sold visas, and he catches it. After the tape stops: a furious kiss in the corridor, her back to the wall, teeth.
chapters.epigraph: “She was a person.”
chapters.content:
Just after eight on Monday a message came from Detective Superintendent Chiang. My office. Koon case. 08:30. Wei Long read it twice and finished fastening his watch.

Isla was pouring coffee in the kitchen. “You’re early.”

“Chiang wants me.”

“About Fan-ling? Has something happened?” She set his cup down.

“I don’t know yet.”

“You haven’t been sleeping.”

“Neither have you.”

“That’s different. I’m allowed to worry about you. Come home tonight. And don’t say yes if you don’t know.” She reached up and straightened his tie and her fingers stayed on the knot.

“I know.”

“Good,” she said, and he kissed her, and neither of them mentioned that in under an hour he would be sitting across a table from her with a recording light on and a caution to read.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chiang wasn’t alone. Inspector Yik from the investigation team was there with a thin file and the grey face of a man who’d spent his weekend in bank statements.

Chiang said, “We’ve found something in the visa stock. Blank visa foils recorded as issued that never turn up as finished applications. Eleven so far. One name comes up in the stock movements again and again. Chik Wai-kit, Visa Section. Two deposits that don’t match his salary. Messages on a buyer’s phone about ‘the man inside’.”

“Not by name.”

“Not by name. We’ve also recovered the cloud backup of the dead woman’s phone. There’s a message to Ms. Ren from Wednesday the fourth of March that matters. On Friday Ms. Ren gave us a first account. Today we need a formal recorded statement, and she’s said she’ll give it, but she’s asked that you be the one who takes it.” Chiang slid a sheet across.

Wei Long looked at him. “You know the problem.”

“I do. So does the superintendent. He’s authorised it under written conditions. Inspector Yik in the room throughout. Every minute on tape. You see only what you need to put the questions. You make no decisions on what comes out of it. Yik does all the follow-up, and the recording goes to an independent reviewer.”

“Why me?”

“Because she asked, and she has things to tell us, and she says she’ll tell them to the person who knows what Fan-ling was like. That’s not a reason. The superintendent decided it’s enough. Are you comfortable doing it?” Chiang took off his glasses.

“No.”

“Neither am I. Do it properly,” said Chiang.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was waiting outside Interview Three in a dark jacket over a pale blouse, with her hair tied back and a folder on her knee. When she saw him she put her phone away.

“Inspector.”

“Ms. Ren.”

Her eyes went to Yik. “Good morning, Inspector Yik.”

Interview Three was smaller than the suspect rooms. A table, three chairs, a camera high in the corner, a recorder set into the desk. Plain, and meant to be. She sat opposite him. Yik sat to her left. Wei Long put the file down and looked at her, and there was a good deal he could have said. Had she slept. Had she eaten. Did she want water. He said none of it. He switched on the recorder and the red light came on.

“Interview Three. Monday the sixteenth of March 2026, 09:06. Present: Inspector Song Wei Long, Inspector Yik, and Ms. Isla Ren. Ms. Ren, you’re here as a witness in a criminal investigation. You’re not under arrest and you’re not a suspect. You’re asked to answer truthfully. Do you understand?” He gave the case reference, and looked straight at her.

“Yes.”

“The interview is recorded and the recording may be used in evidence or disclosed in later proceedings.”

“Yes.”

He read her the caution anyway, slowly and in full, as the conditions required, and told her she could ask for anything to be explained, ask for a break, or ask for legal advice at any time.

“I understand. I’m willing to go on.”

“State your name and occupation.”

“Isla Ren. Consular officer. Just over three years in this post.”

She described her work exactly: detained citizens, liaison with the local authorities, documents, welfare, emergencies. She said the job brought her into the visa section often but gave her no authority over its stock.

“Did you know Koon Fan-ling?”

“Yes. Since I joined. Colleagues, then friends. We had lunch most Tuesdays, near the market.”

“How would you describe her?”

Isla paused. “Competent. Quick. Funny as anything when she wasn’t pretending not to be.”

“Did she complain about anyone at work?”

“Everyone complains about someone at work. Supervisors. Workloads. People who don’t read instructions.”

“Did she mention Chik Wai-kit?”

Her eyes dropped to the table for a second. “Yes. She said he was difficult. Careless with paperwork. Didn’t like being corrected. Asked other people to do his work.”

“Did she ever tell you he was taking blank visa foils out of the stock room?”

“No.”

“Selling them?”

“No.”

“Did she mention any discrepancy in the stock records?”

“No.”

“Did she ever appear frightened of him?”

“No.”

The answers came fast. Not impossibly fast. She was used to formal questions and careful with words. But he knew the difference between her care and her avoidance, and he wrote down a time.

Yik asked about procedure, and she explained the difference between blank stock, issued foils, spoiled foils and completed applications, and corrected his terminology without blinking. Around half past nine Wei Long went back to Chik.

“Did you know he had access to the secure stock room?”

“Yes. He worked in the section.”

“Did Koon Fan-ling?”

“Yes.”

“Did you?”

“No.”

“Who held the keys? Did you ever see Mr. Chik take a foil out of the stock room?” She named two senior staff. He wrote them down.

“No.”

“Did Koon Fan-ling ever tell you she had?”

“No.”

“You’re certain.”

“Yes.”

Too quickly. He didn’t react. He went on.

✦ ✦ ✦

By 09:46 they’d been in the room forty minutes. He’d taken her through the Tuesdays, Fan-ling’s last known week, the messages, the photograph of the menu sent on Monday the ninth, the lunch Isla had missed on the tenth for a meeting. Nothing she said disagreed with anything the team had. Then he put a photograph on the table.

A still from an internal camera: a corridor outside a door marked SECURE STOCK, a man half turned away.

“Do you recognise him?”

“Mr. Chik.”

“Thursday the fifth of March, 18:42. His shift ended at half past five.”

“I don’t know why he was there.”

He put a second still beside it. Chik with a flat document envelope under his arm.

“Does that look like the envelopes used for visa stock?”

“I can’t tell from this.”

Her hands were folded on the table. Her right thumb moved once along the side of her left forefinger, a small movement. He knew it.

“Ms. Ren. I’m going to ask you something different. On Wednesday the fourth of March, did Koon Fan-ling tell you she had seen Mr. Chik take blank foils out of the stock room?”

“No.”

“Did you receive a message from her that evening at 21:16?”

She didn’t answer at once. “Yes.”

“What did it say?”

“I don’t remember the exact words.”

He looked down at the page and read it aloud. “I saw him take three. I don’t know where they’re going. If I report it he’ll know it was me.”

Her face didn’t change. Her thumb stopped.

He let the silence stand. “Do you remember it now?”

“Yes.”

“Why did you tell me she’d never mentioned missing stock?”

“I didn’t know what she meant.”

“You said she’d never told you she’d seen him take them.”

“I didn’t know if she was sure.”

“That wasn’t the question.”

“I was trying to be careful.”

“Then you should have said you weren’t sure. Did you answer her?” He went on in the same level voice.

“I told her not to confront him. To talk to her supervisor.”

“Did she?”

“She said she’d think about it. I asked her the next day. She said she hadn’t decided.”

“Did she tell you she was frightened?”

Isla’s eyes went to the red light. “She said she didn’t know what he might do.”

“Did you believe she was frightened of him?”

A long pause. “Yes.”

He put his pen down. “Then why did you tell me she’d never raised any concern about him?”

“Because I didn’t want you to think she was involved.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“She wasn’t involved.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I know Fan-ling.”

“Knowing someone isn’t knowing everything they did.”

Her face sharpened. “She was trying to do the right thing.”

“Then why didn’t you tell us?”

“Because I didn’t want her name used to build a case against her. Because I didn’t want people asking why she’d waited, as if waiting made her part of it.”

“She’s dead, Ms. Ren.”

He said it without raising his voice, and for the first time that morning her composure went.

“I know.”

“She could have been a witness.”

“She was a person.”

“She was both,” he said, and she looked away.

Yik asked whether there were any other messages or conversations she hadn’t mentioned. There weren’t. Had she deleted anything? No. Would she hand over the original thread for the team to preserve? Yes.

Just before ten Wei Long asked the last question. “Is there anything else you think the investigation should know about Koon Fan-ling’s concerns about Mr. Chik?”

She looked at him a long moment. “No.”

Just after ten he gave the time for the tape and switched the recorder off. The red light went dark. The room stayed exactly as it had been. Then she pushed her chair back and left without looking at him.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was by the fire door in the corridor with her arms folded tight across her chest when he came out.

“Isla.”

“Don’t.”

He stopped. He saw the woman who had sat across from him for fifty-six minutes and answered every question with perfect composure and lied about the one thing she didn’t want to give him. He saw the woman who’d sat at a noodle stall every Tuesday with a friend who was now in a drawer at the mortuary. He kept his voice low.

“You shouldn’t have lied.”

“I know.”

“You kept back evidence that matters.”

“I know.”

“Then why...”

“Because I didn’t want them turning her into a suspect. She told me because she trusted me. She didn’t want the whole office looking at her. She was afraid of losing her job.”

“She may have been in danger.”

“I know that now.”

“You knew she was frightened then.”

“Don’t talk to me like I’m one of your officers.”

“I’m not.”

“You sounded exactly like it in there.”

“Because I was interviewing you.”

She laughed once, without any humour. “Yes. I noticed. You read me the caution. You looked at me for an hour as if you’d never met me.”

“I knew you.”

“Not in that room. You have no idea what it’s like to sit there and hear you ask whether she told me she was frightened.” Her voice cracked.

“She needed someone to tell her what to do.”

“She needed someone to listen.”

“She needed both.”

Her eyes filled. “Yes. Yes. She did,” she said, almost angrily.

He moved a step towards her and stopped himself. Not here, not with Yik on the other side of the door and the case open and her a witness in it. She saw him stop.

“You’re not going to touch me?”

“Not here.”

“Because I’m a witness?”

“Because you’re upset, and I don’t want anybody mistaking what happened in that room for something it wasn’t.”

She stared at him. Then she grabbed his tie.

“You’re unbelievable.”

“That isn’t new information.”

She pulled him down. The kiss was angry and sudden and nothing like the careful kisses they gave each other in corridors. She kissed him hard enough that he took a half step back and his shoulder hit the wall, and her fist stayed tight in his tie. He caught her waist. He didn’t move, and then she kissed him again and he answered her. She bit his lower lip, not lightly, and he drew back an inch to look at her.

“You’re angry.”

“How observant.”

“At me?”

“At everything.”

“All right.”

“That’s all?”

“I’ve been reasonable for an hour,” he said, and she made a furious sound and pulled him back by the tie, and this time he kissed her with no restraint at all, his hand in her hair, her back against the wall now instead of his, both of them clumsy with it, neither pretending the anger had gone anywhere. When they broke apart her forehead was against his.

“Don’t do that again. Look at me like a stranger,” she whispered.

“I was doing my job.”

“I know. I know.”

“Then understand this. If you know something that matters to an investigation, you tell the people investigating it. Even when it’s uncomfortable. Especially then. You can’t decide what evidence the police get because you’re protecting someone. Even someone you loved.”

“I loved her,” said Isla.

“I know.”

“Am I a terrible witness?”

“You’re a witness who lied once,” he said, “and now has to tell the truth. Tell them what she said. Add nothing. Leave nothing out.”

She looked down at his tie, twisted in her fist, and let it go. “You make it sound simple.”

“It isn’t.”

The door of Interview Three opened. Yik came out with the file and looked at them, and at Wei Long’s tie, with complete professional neutrality.

“The tape’s secured. We’ll take the thread off your phone this afternoon, Ms. Ren. Sir, Chiang wants the summary before lunch.”

When he’d gone Isla said, “He’s going to know.”

“He already knows.”

“About the tie? Sorry.” She looked at it.

He fixed the knot. “Don’t be.”

“Are you angry with me?”

“Yes. And I’m not going anywhere.” Her face fell, and he went on.

“Even after that?”

“After that, yes. Come home tonight.” He touched her cheek once.

“I live there.”

“I know. I want you there.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At 12:41 he sent Chiang the summary. He wrote down what had happened without interpretation: that the witness had first denied any knowledge of missing stock; that a message from the deceased contradicted her; that she had then accepted receiving it and explained why she hadn’t disclosed it; that she had agreed to hand over the thread. He didn’t soften withheld. He didn’t call her confused. He didn’t leave out the lie. Chiang rang ten minutes later.

“Read it. Good. Are you all right?”

“Fine.”

“That wasn’t what I asked. Keep away from the case. And don’t take that room home and have the whole thing again over dinner,” said Chiang, and sighed.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was on the sofa when he got in, with two cups of tea on the table, one untouched.

“Are you still angry?”

“Yes.”

“All right. I keep thinking about what you said. That she needed both. I didn’t see her face when she sent it. Only the words. I thought I could give her time to decide.” She picked up her tea and put it down.

“That was your decision.”

“Now I wish I’d told her to report it that night.”

“Would she have?”

“I don’t know.”

“Then don’t make a certainty out of something you can’t know.”

“You’re being reasonable again.”

“Would you prefer I wasn’t?”

“Sometimes, I asked for you because I thought if it was you I could tell you everything. Then I didn’t want to see what you’d do with it. I didn’t want something she told me in confidence typed into a report,” said Isla, and let him take her hand.

“That’s what a witness statement is for.”

“I know that. Knowing what’s right and being able to do it aren’t always the same. You know that better than anyone.” She looked at their hands.

He did. He didn’t tell her she was wrong. He lifted her hand and kissed the knuckles. “Next time tell me before it turns into a lie.”

“Next time don’t read me the caution.”

“I can’t promise that.”

“I know. Did I hurt you? In there?” She leaned into his shoulder.

He thought about it honestly. “Yes. A little.”

“I’m sorry.”

“I know,” he said, and kissed her hair, and after a while she lifted her head.

“Your tie. I nearly strangled you with it.”

“It’s still wearable.”

“You’re welcome,” said Isla, and when she smiled he smiled back, which he didn’t do often, and which neither of them mistook for everything being fine.

chapters.title: He Breaks Protocol Once
chapters.desc: Someone follows her home three nights running. He stays in her flat with his weapon on the coffee table, against orders. On the third night she won’t let him stay on the sofa. On the fourth morning he reports himself.
chapters.epigraph: “Let me look after you, for once.”
chapters.content:
The first time, on Thursday, Isla thought it was coincidence. She’d left the consulate late and stopped at a pharmacy and was walking the last stretch home in the rain with a paper bag in one hand and her phone in the other, and there was a man across the road. Dark jacket, pale shirt, no umbrella. She noticed him because he was standing still while everybody else hurried. When she reached the door of her building she looked back, and he was still there. She went in, and forgot about him by the time the lift came.

The second time, on Friday, she knew his shoes. She’d gone a different way, through a bookshop and out by its back door, and two streets on he was at the crossing. He didn’t come near her. He didn’t speak. He followed her at the same distance to her building and when she stopped under the awning to look at him he turned away before she could see his face.

She rang Wei Long from the lobby.

“Where are you?”

“In the lobby. There’s someone following me.”

The silence lasted about a second. “Did you see his face?”

“No.”

“Stay in the lobby. Don’t take the lift on your own. I’m coming.”

He was there in twenty-three minutes. He didn’t make her tell it twice at the door. He spoke to the building’s security desk, asked for the camera footage to be kept, wrote down times and places, rang the station. Then he took her upstairs. In the kitchen, with his phone in his hand, he said, “Chiang’s sending a car past through the night and someone will put an alarm in tomorrow.”

“And you?”

“I’m told to leave it to them. You’re a witness in a case I’ve been taken off. I’m not your protection,” he said.

“But you live here.”

“I live here,” he agreed, and went on dialling.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 10:16 he took his service pistol out of his jacket, in its holster, and set it on the coffee table.

Detectives carried their weapons personally; they didn’t draw them from an armoury at the start of each shift and hand them back at the end. The rule was that off duty, at home, a personal-issue firearm lived locked in an approved safe. His lived in the steel box in the wardrobe. It didn’t live on a coffee table.

Isla watched him from the sofa. “You’re not supposed to do that.”

“I know.”

“Then why is it there?”

“Because I’m staying up.”

“That doesn’t answer the question.”

He moved it back from the edge of the table so that it sat squarely in front of him. “I’m not leaving you alone tonight.”

“I’m not alone. You’re here. You’d be here if that thing were in the wardrobe.”

“Not as fast,” he said.

She looked at him: work trousers, dark shirt, sleeves rolled, jacket over a chair, no dinner, not having sat down properly since he came in. “Have you told your superintendent?”

“I’ve told the duty officer I’m at home.”

“That isn’t the same.”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because I know what he’ll say. That I should leave it to the officers assigned to it.”

“Would he be wrong?”

He didn’t answer. She sat down beside him.

“You’re not the only person who can protect me. I don’t want you deciding things because you’re frightened.”

“I’m not frightened.”

“You’re sitting in our living room with a gun on the coffee table.”

He looked at it. “That isn’t an answer either.”

“No,” he said.

She tucked herself against his shoulder. He put his arm round her, and his eyes stayed on the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday, coming out of the grocer’s on the corner, she saw the man’s face. He was reflected in the shop window behind her, close enough that she could make out the shape of his jaw. She turned. He stopped. For one second they looked straight at each other. Then he walked away.

She didn’t follow him. She went back into the shop, asked the owner to ring the security desk at her building, and rang Wei Long. He came in fifteen minutes, and when he saw her his face did something she’d learned to read, smaller and harder than panic or surprise.

“Did he come near you? Speak? Touch you?”

“No. Wei Long, I think I know him. He’s a driver at the consulate. He waits by the staff entrance sometimes. I don’t know his name.”

“Are you sure?”

“Not completely. I thought it was someone else on Thursday.”

He rang it in. Then he took her home, and the pistol went back on the coffee table, and he slept for less than an hour. She woke at 3:12 and found him sitting upright on the sofa with one arm along the back of it and his eyes on the dark hall.

“Come to bed.”

“I’m fine here.”

“I didn’t ask if you were fine.”

“I’ll come later,” he said, and she knew better than to argue with him when his mind had hold of something it couldn’t put down, so she went back to bed alone. Just after four she woke again, and he was still there.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday morning Chiang’s team put a name to the face from the consulate’s staff list. Yiu Kar-fai, thirty-eight, one of the consulate’s contracted drivers: scheduled runs, airport pickups, sometimes documents across the city. He knew which entrance the staff used, what time they left and which way they walked.

And he was in the Koon file already. He’d been the go-between. Chik Wai-kit took the blank foils out of the stock room, and Yiu took them out of the building and to the buyers. The messages on a buyer’s phone that talked about “the driver” were his. There was more, and Chiang read it to Wei Long over the phone because the superintendent had decided he had a right to know who was standing across the road from his home. Messages that showed Yiu knew by the sixth of March that Fan-ling had seen Chik at the stock room. A car registered to him on a camera a hundred metres from the consulate at twenty past seven on the tenth, the night she didn’t come home. And a cast-iron frying pan, of the make and size of the one on the pier, bought at a kitchen shop near the fish market on the eighth with a card in his name.

“He sold the visas. She found out. He killed her,” said Wei Long.

Chiang said, “That’s where the evidence is going. We went to his flat at two. It was empty. Wardrobe cleared out, phone off since Saturday afternoon. There’s a warrant. Every unit has his face. Your instructions haven’t changed.”

Wei Long looked at the man’s photograph on his phone and remembered him, not from a shop window. From the consulate lobby. A man who’d held a car door while Isla got in. Who had nodded to him once by the lift.

“Find him,” he said, and hung up, and went back into the living room and sat down on the sofa beside the gun.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, the third, she came out of the bedroom just before twelve in a cotton nightdress with her hair down, and stood in front of him.

“Come to bed.”

“Go ahead. I’ll be there.”

“No. Not tonight.”

He put his phone down. She sat beside him and took his hand, and his fingers were stiff. She turned the palm up and pressed her thumb into the middle of it.

“You’ve been holding yourself like this for three days. As if the second you stop paying attention something terrible will happen.”

He didn’t answer. She looked at the coffee table. Then she lifted his hand off his knee, where it had been resting an inch from the holster, and moved it away, and held it in her lap.

“Come with me.”

“Isla...”

“Please.”

She stood up with his hand in hers. He went. In the bedroom she shut the door and he looked at it, and she saw him look.

“You’re still listening.”

“Yes.”

“I know. Then listen to me as well. I don’t want you on that sofa all night thinking being awake is the same as keeping me safe. I don’t want to be a room you have to guard. And I don’t want you on your own with this because you’re the one with the gun.” She put both hands flat on his chest.

“While I’m here, I’m responsible for your safety.”

“I’m responsible for mine too. Let me look after you, for once.”

He stood still. She put her hand on his cheek.

“Come to bed, Wei Long.”

He kissed her. Carefully at first, almost asking. She held his face and kissed him back, and something that had been held tight in him for three days gave way all at once. He pulled her in against him by the waist so hard she lost her footing and he held her up. She pulled his shirt open. He tugged her nightdress up and over her head and she stood in front of him with nothing on, and he looked at her as if she were the only thing in the city still standing.

She pushed him down onto the bed and climbed over him and unbuckled him, and he lifted his hips to let her pull everything off, and she straddled him and took him in her hand. He was hard and hot and his breath went ragged at her touch.

“You’re exhausted,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Then lie still and let me have you.”

She sank onto him. He groaned, low, and his hands closed on her hips. She rode him slowly, leaning down to kiss him, her hair falling round both their faces, and he moved with her, his eyes on hers. Even now he hadn’t stopped listening. When a car door slammed in the street below his whole body went still for half a second, his head turning a degree towards the hall, and she felt it, and didn’t stop and didn’t tell him to stop listening. She took his hand and laced their fingers and held it against the pillow, and rocked on him, and kissed the side of his neck, and waited, and felt him come back to her. Each time he came back a little further.

He rolled her under him without leaving her. He pushed deeper, slower, his forehead on hers, one forearm braced by her head, and said her name into her mouth. She wrapped her legs round him. His hand slid between them and found her and stayed there, patient, until she was shaking, and when she came she cried out and he covered her mouth with his and swallowed the sound, and kept moving through it, and came himself a few moments after with his whole body taut and his face pressed into her hair.

Afterwards he lay half over her with his head on her breast, heavy, his arm across her. She stroked his hair. His breathing slowed. Even then, she could feel the part of him that was still turned towards the hall, the part that would wake at a footstep. She didn’t ask him to stop it. She kept her hand in his, and some time after one he was asleep, properly asleep, for the first time in three nights.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke first. He was asleep with his face turned into her pillow and his arm round her waist, the line between his eyebrows almost gone. She touched his cheek and he was awake at once.

“What’s wrong?”

He looked at the door. She caught his face in both hands. “Nothing’s wrong.”

He seemed not to know what to do with that. Then he shut his eyes again.

“You slept.”

“Four hours.”

“That’s almost respectable,” said Isla, and kissed his cheek, and his phone buzzed on the bedside table, and it was Yik. No contact overnight. Search ongoing. Car stays on your street.

“He’s still out there,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Then go and tell them what you did.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At 8:30 on Monday he walked into the superintendent’s office without being sent for.

“Inspector.”

“Sir. I need to make a report. From Friday night until this morning, after Ms. Ren reported being followed, I kept my service weapon out of its safe at home, on a table, holstered and under my control, while I stayed awake as her protection. That was against your instruction that her protection was for the assigned team. I didn’t seek authorisation. I told the duty officer I was at home. I didn’t tell you. The weapon wasn’t drawn or discharged.” He stayed standing.

The superintendent closed the file in front of him. “Why didn’t you report it properly?”

“Because I believed she was at risk, and I decided before I’d made the notification.”

“Did you think you were within policy?”

“No.”

“Then why?”

“Because someone was following her.”

“That explains your concern. It doesn’t explain your decision.”

“No, sir.”

“Did you take any part in the search for Yiu? Ask for anything you weren’t given? Touch the investigation?”

“No.”

The superintendent studied him. “Your firearm isn’t a personal security measure, Song. Your judgement doesn’t replace procedure because the circumstances are personal. You were taken off the Koon case for exactly that reason, and then you made yourself part of a witness’s protection without approval.”

“Yes, sir.”

“You’ll give me a full written account. It’ll be reviewed. Until it’s decided, you’ll make no security arrangements for Ms. Ren in any official capacity. If there’s a threat, you report it, and the assigned officers deal with it. Being worried about someone doesn’t exempt you from the rules.”

“No, sir.”

“Anything to add?”

“No.”

He turned for the door. “Song. Is she safe?” The superintendent’s voice was lower.

“Yiu’s still at large. There’s a car on the street and the building security’s been reviewed.”

“That wasn’t quite what I asked.”

“She’s safe this morning,” said Wei Long.

“Go and write your report,” said the superintendent.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was at the counter when he got home. “How bad?”

“A written account. A review. Not suspended.”

“Disciplined?”

“Not decided.”

“You’re not going to tell me it was worth it?”

“No. It wasn’t a good decision.”

“But you’d do it again.”

He was quiet. “If I believed you were in immediate danger, I’d find it hard not to.”

“That isn’t the same as saying you’d put the gun on the coffee table again.”

“No.”

“Good. You frightened me too, you know. Not just him. Watching you turn into someone who couldn’t sleep or sit still or look at the door without thinking something was about to come through it.” She smoothed the front of his shirt, a crease that wasn’t there.

“I didn’t want him near you.”

“I know. Next time we do it properly. You tell the people who need to know. You let them do their job. And you come home to me.”

“All right.”

“That was suspiciously easy.”

“I’ve already had one conversation with a superintendent today.”

She laughed, and kissed him, and his hand came up to the back of her head and stayed. When she drew back she said, “Bedroom tonight? Not the sofa?”

“Bedroom.”

The pistol went back into the steel box in the wardrobe, and the box was locked, and the key went on his ring beside the one with the white tag. The coffee table was empty. Somewhere in the city a man with a cleared-out wardrobe was still loose. For the first time in four nights Wei Long lay down beside her without looking at the front door first, and the effort it took him was the only thing she didn’t say anything about.

chapters.title: The Arrest
chapters.desc: He finds Yiu in a car-park stairwell with a knife at a second clerk’s throat and shoots him twice. Shown, not softened: the sound, the smell, the man dying on the concrete steps. A long night afterwards; he’s silent for forty minutes, then says it twice.
chapters.epigraph: “I’d do it again.”
chapters.content:
The call came at 6:31 on Friday evening, while Wei Long was the duty inspector for the district and nobody’s protection at all.

Man with a knife holding a woman, multi-storey car park on Lantern Lane, stairwell C, level four or five. Caller says the man is Yiu Kar-fai.

The car park was the one the consulate’s staff used, two hundred metres from their building. He was four minutes away with Constable Choy beside him in the car, and he didn’t think about what the superintendent had said about Isla’s protection, because this wasn’t about Isla, and he didn’t think about the Koon case, because it wasn’t his. There was a knife and a woman on a staircase, and he was the nearest armed officer in the district. He thought about the stairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

Stairwell C was bare concrete, lit by caged bulbs, smelling of exhaust and old rainwater. They came up it fast and quiet. On the landing between four and five Yiu Kar-fai stood with his back to the wall and one arm locked round a young woman’s chest, and a kitchen knife under her jaw.

Wei Long knew her from the file Chiang had let him see: Lip Mei-ting, twenty-eight, Visa Section, due to go through the stock records with Yik on Monday. She had one shoe on. Her other foot was twisted under her on the step, and her face had gone the colour of the concrete.

“Police! Drop the knife!”

Yiu’s head turned. For a fraction of a second Wei Long saw it in his face, not surprise or confusion. Recognition. Yiu knew him. He’d seen him in the consulate lobby. He’d seen him outside Isla’s building. He’d known exactly whose attention he had and he’d followed her home anyway.

“Stay back.”

“Put the knife down. Let her go.”

“Stay back!” The blade moved. Mei-ting made a small choked sound.

Wei Long had his weapon up. He could see the angle of the knife and Yiu’s wrist and the woman’s shoulder against the wall. He could see the distance, four steps, and that Choy behind him had no line at all.

“Yiu. Listen to me. Put it down.”

“You think you’re walking out of here? She knows. She saw the records. She was going to tell them. Same as Fan-ling,” Yiu laughed, short and breathless and ugly.

“Put it down.”

Yiu’s arm tightened. His wrist turned, a small movement, and the point of the blade went in under the angle of her jaw and a line of red ran down her neck. Wei Long fired.

The sound in that concrete box was nothing like the range. It hit the walls and came straight back into his ears and his teeth. Yiu jerked. His arm loosened. The knife didn’t fall. Mei-ting dropped against the wall and Yiu lurched sideways over her, and the blade came round again towards her face. He fired a second time.

Yiu went over. He hit the edge of the landing, rolled down two steps and stopped on his side with his cheek against the concrete and the knife still in his hand. Nobody moved. Then Mei-ting began to scream.

“Knife! Don’t move! Mei-ting, get away from him. Down the stairs. Keep going. Don’t touch anything.” Wei Long kept his weapon on him until he could see both hands.

She scrambled backwards on her hands with one of them pressed to her neck. Choy caught her on the lower landing and took her down and out. Wei Long went down two steps.

The smell came up at him: the burnt sharpness of the rounds, and under it the car park’s damp, exhaust and rain, and under that something warm and coppery. Yiu’s eyes were open. There was a hole in his shirt below the collarbone and another lower, on the left side, and the blood was coming fast out of the second one, dark, spreading across the step under him and into the seam of the concrete. His mouth moved once. Nothing came out of it. His chest lifted, and lifted again, shallower, and then a long rattling breath went out of him that didn’t come back.

Wei Long kicked the knife clear of his hand and holstered his weapon and knelt.

He knew what he would find. He checked anyway. Two fingers on the side of the neck. Nothing. He moved his fingers half a centimetre, as if a different place might give a different answer. Nothing.

“Yiu Kar-fai,” he said.

There was no answer. He looked at the face. The man who’d followed Isla home. Who had tied a frying pan to a twenty-six-year-old woman and put her in the harbour. Who’d had a knife in another woman’s throat ninety seconds ago. Wei Long stayed on his knees on the step beside him until the paramedics came, and didn’t look away once.

✦ ✦ ✦

They were there in six minutes. He stood back and gave them room and told them who he was and that the weapon was holstered and the knife clear. The first one checked Yiu, and checked again. The second put the pads on, and the monitor showed them a flat line, and they worked anyway, because that was their procedure, for eleven minutes. Then the senior one sat back on her heels and looked at her watch.

“Time of death, 18:47.”

Wei Long heard it. When he was asked he repeated it.

After that it went as it was supposed to go. A uniformed sergeant arrived to take him off the scene. He unloaded his weapon and handed it over, with its magazine and its two empty spaces, and watched it go into a bag. He was asked not to talk about what had happened with Choy or anyone else until he’d given his first account, and he didn’t. A welfare officer called Mrs. Mau sat with him in the back of a van and gave him water. Photographs. Measurements. Yellow markers on the steps. The knife photographed where it lay. The stairwell closed. Mei-ting was taken to hospital with a cut to her neck that needed stitches and would leave a scar, conscious, frightened, able to speak. She turned round once in the ambulance doorway before they shut it, and looked at him, and he nodded, and the doors closed.

Around half past seven he gave his first account. Just after eight he gave it again to the officer from the discharge review. Just before nine he was asked to describe the moment Yiu’s wrist turned. Just after nine, the distance. Just after ten, whether he’d warned him before firing. Just before eleven, where Choy had been. The questions were necessary. A police officer had fired twice and killed a man, and every part of it had to be examined by people who weren’t him: the weapon, the rounds, the scene, the witnesses, his account set against all of it. He answered every one.

Just before eleven his hands started to shake. He was holding a paper cup of water and it rattled against the table. He put it down. Nobody mentioned it.

Just after eleven the review officer asked what he’d done after Yiu fell.

“Waited until the threat had ended. Approached. Checked for a pulse.”

“Did you believe he was alive?”

“No.”

“Then why check?”

Wei Long looked at the table. “Because I needed to know.”

“Did you check a second time?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

His hands were under the table now. He could feel them going. “Because I wanted to be certain.”

“We’ll take ten minutes,” said the review officer.

In the washroom he ran the cold tap over his hands. They went on shaking. He held on to the edge of the basin and looked at himself in the mirror. No mark on his face. No blood on his shirt. He looked exactly as he had that morning, and that was the part he couldn’t understand.

✦ ✦ ✦

Around half past twelve he was released for the night, his weapon kept for examination, told not to discuss the incident with any witness and to stay contactable. He signed what he was given and walked out of the station into air that had gone cool. There were three messages on his phone.

Thank You (Paid): Are you still there?

Thank You (Paid): Wei Long?

Thank You (Paid): Please tell me you’re all right.

He rang her. She answered before it had rung.

“Where are you?”

“Outside the station. I’m not hurt.”

A pause. “Something happened.”

“I fired my weapon.”

The silence on the line was total. Then, low, “Is the other person alive?”

“No.”

She breathed in. “Don’t move. I’m coming.”

She came just after one. The car stopped at the kerb and she was out of it before the engine had settled, and she stopped in front of him, and looked at his face and his shoulders and his hands.

“Are you hurt?”

“No.”

“Have you eaten? Sorry. That isn’t...” Then she shut her eyes.

“I’m all right.”

“No, you’re not,” said Isla, and he didn’t argue.

She put him in the passenger seat and got in and didn’t start the engine.

“Where do you want to go?”

“I don’t know.”

She drove to a multi-storey that stayed open all night, a different one, three streets from the station, and took the ramp to the top, and parked in the far corner where there were no other cars. The city lay spread out below the parapet. Lit windows in far-off towers. A few cars on the road. A motorbike going by somewhere underneath them and fading. She switched the engine off and turned to him.

“Tell me.”

He told her the way he’d told the review officer: the call, the stairs, Mei-ting, the knife, the warning, the first shot, the second. His voice was steady. It sounded like another statement. Then he stopped.

“He went down the steps. They won’t stop.” He was looking at his hands.

She took them. They were shaking hard. She held one between both of hers.

“Look at me. You’re in my car. You’re not in the stairwell. You’re here.”

“I know.”

“Then stay here with me,” said Isla.

Just after two he told her about the pulse. At 2:47, the second check. Just after three he told her about the sound of the first shot, which had stayed with him more than anything he’d seen: the crack off the concrete, the second after it, the noise of a man breathing and then not breathing. At 3:52 she asked whether he wanted water and he shook his head. At 4:16 she took his coat off him and folded it onto the back seat. Just before five she put her arm round him and he let his head go down on her shoulder. He didn’t sleep. She held his hands until the shaking eased, and it came back, and she held them again. Once he tried to pull away and she didn’t let go.

“I’m all right.”

“You’re allowed not to be.”

He turned his face into her shoulder. She kissed his temple.

✦ ✦ ✦

Around half past five the sky started to go grey over the towers. He’d been silent for forty minutes. Then he said, without lifting his head, “I’d do it again.”

“I know.”

“If he had the knife in her neck again and moved like that again, I’d fire. I didn’t have anything else. I couldn’t wait.”

“I know.”

“I’d do it again,” he said, and it came out differently the second time, less like a statement and more like something he was trying to make himself believe.

She lifted his face. “You can know you did the right thing and still be hurt by it. You can be certain you’d do it again for her and still not be untouched. Those aren’t against each other.”

“I checked his pulse. I knew. I still checked.”

“Of course you did,” said Isla.

His face broke. Not all at once. His eyes filled first and he looked away, his jaw working. Then his breath caught, and he put one hand over his eyes, and bent forward in the seat, and made no sound at all, and then he began to cry. Almost silently at first, controlled. His shoulders moved once, and again. She put both arms round him and held him in the passenger seat while the sky got light, and he didn’t apologise, and she didn’t ask him to stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after six his phone rang. The superintendent.

“Where are you?”

“With Isla.”

“Are you fit to come in?”

“No, sir.”

“Then don’t. The review officer will ring you later. You’re off duty until you’ve been seen. Have you been checked over?”

“Yes.”

“Get some sleep, Song,” said the superintendent, and rang off, and it was the gentlest thing Wei Long had ever heard him say.

At seven she made him get out of the car. Not to go home yet, only to walk. They went down in the lift and across to a café just pulling its shutter up, and he ordered tea and she ordered coffee and something to eat, and he held the cup in both hands because one wasn’t enough to keep it still. She sat beside him, not across.

“Have you ever done this before?”

“Fired outside training? Once. A warning shot, years ago. Nobody was hurt.”

“And this time someone died.”

“There’ll be another statement. The review. They’ll look at the weapon, the rounds, the scene, the cameras. They’ll talk to Choy. They’ll decide whether it was necessary and proportionate.”

“Will you be all right?”

“I don’t know,” he said, and it was the first thing he’d said all night that didn’t sound rehearsed.

She put her hand over his on the cup. “Then we’ll deal with that when we know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At home he showered and changed and she made him eat, and he managed half a bowl and put his chopsticks down, and she didn’t push it. The television was on in the corner with the sound low, because she couldn’t stand the quiet, and at eleven the news ran a short item about a racing driver called Serafina Song who’d married at the city registry at ten past nine that morning, a photograph of a woman in white with a tall man beside her on the steps.

“Song,” said Isla, looking at it. “Any relation?”

“No, people ask,” said Wei Long.

Nobody had expected him at a registry office that morning, and he wasn’t there, and she changed the channel.

At 12:46 a message came from the superintendent’s office: the discharge review was ongoing, he wasn’t required today, welfare support had been arranged. He read it and put the phone down. She was standing by the window.

“Do you want to sleep?”

“No.”

“Do you want me to stay?”

“Yes.”

He sat down on the bed and she stood between his knees, and he put his forehead against her stomach the way he had the morning of the missing boy, and her hands went into his hair.

“I keep hearing it,” he said.

“It’ll take time. You don’t have to make sense of it today. Sleep. Eat when you can. Let somebody else ask the questions for a while.” She bent and kissed the top of his head.

He breathed out something that might, in another week, have been a laugh. “You’re demanding.”

“Somebody has to be.”

She stayed until he slept. At 14:20 the department rang to say he’d be interviewed again the following week. Just after three he woke, and lay looking at the ceiling with her hand still in his. He could still hear the two shots. He could still feel the concrete under his knees and the place on a man’s neck where there was nothing under his fingers. And he could feel her hand, warm, holding on, and for now that was enough to keep him in the room.

chapters.title: A Posting to Lima
chapters.desc: Cleared by the review, he’s given a commendation he doesn’t want. The ministry offers Isla the posting she asked for two years ago: three years in Lima, deputy head of consular. She doesn’t tell him for four days. He finds the letter; she kisses him before he can speak.
chapters.epigraph: “She kissed me before I could speak.”
chapters.content:
The letter came on Thursday, the seventh of May. Isla read it twice at her desk, once standing at the window and once sitting down, as if a second reading might turn up a different sentence between the official paragraphs. It didn’t. The ministry was pleased to confirm her appointment to the consular section of the embassy in Lima, for three years, from September, subject to the usual formalities. Deputy Head of Consular. The job she had applied for two years ago, before she’d ever stood in a wet terminal arguing with a printer. She put the letter back in its envelope and put the envelope in the second drawer of the desk in the spare room at home, under a stack of correspondence, and didn’t tell him that night.

On Friday she meant to tell him over dinner. He came home late from the station with a commendation in a blue folder that he put face down on the hall table like an unpaid bill, and she decided the evening didn’t need another difficult conversation in it.

The discharge review had finished on Monday the fourth. It had looked at his first account, Choy’s statement, the cameras on levels four and five, the marks on the stairs, the examination of his weapon and the rounds, and the order in which it had all happened. Yiu Kar-fai had held a knife to a woman’s throat. Wei Long had told him repeatedly to drop it. Yiu had cut her. The first shot hadn’t stopped him. The second had been fired while he was still a danger to her. The finding was that the use of force had been necessary and proportionate, and the review was closed.

The superintendent had watched him read it. “You’re cleared, Inspector. There’ll be a commendation.”

“I don’t need one.”

“That isn’t what I said. Ms. Lip has sent in a written account. She wanted the department to know she understood what you did.” The superintendent turned a page of his own copy.

Near the back of the file was a copy of it. Mei-ting described the knife and the concrete at her back and the moment she’d been certain she was going to die. She remembered him telling Yiu to put it down. She remembered the first shot, and the second. At the end she had written: I know he fired a gun. I know a man died. I also know that I am alive.

He read that sentence twice and closed the folder.

“Take the rest of the day,” said the superintendent.

“I have work.”

“That wasn’t a question. You’re not being rewarded for working through it. Go home.”

On Friday the commendation was given in the superintendent’s office in front of four people, and that evening he told Isla about it in the kitchen.

“So it’s over.”

“The review is.”

“And they said you did the right thing.”

“They said I did what I was supposed to do.”

“How do you feel?”

He thought about it. “Relieved. Not pleased. I don’t want anyone to congratulate me.” He looked at the blue folder through the doorway.

“Then I won’t,” said Isla, and drew his hand to her mouth and kissed the knuckles, and neither of them mentioned Lima, because only one of them knew it existed.

On Saturday she took the letter out again and read the reporting date and the relocation arrangements and looked at the words three years until they stopped being a length of time and turned into a distance. On Sunday she nearly told him in the kitchen. He was making coffee and she was behind him with her arms round his waist. He asked if she wanted breakfast and she said yes. Then she asked whether he’d slept, and he said he had, and she knew he was lying, and let the moment go. By Monday morning the letter had been in the drawer for four days.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found it on Monday afternoon looking for the spare passport wallet. She’d asked him to keep it somewhere she could find it, because she was tired of turning up important documents in places that only made sense to him, and he’d put it in the second drawer of the desk in the spare room. He opened the drawer. The wallet was under a folder. The envelope was under the wallet, with the ministry’s crest in the corner, already opened, the letter inside folded once so that its heading showed.

He didn’t read other people’s post. He saw her name, and under it, Appointment: Deputy Head of Consular, Lima. He stood with it in his hand for several seconds. Then he read it. The date was Thursday. Three years. September.

He heard the front door. She came in with a paper bag and her handbag, kicked off her shoes and called towards the study.

“Wei Long?”

“In here.”

She came to the doorway. He was standing by the desk with the letter. Her eyes went to it. Neither of them said anything. Then she crossed the room.

“Don’t.”

“Isla...”

She reached him and kissed him. Not a small kiss. She took his face in both hands and kissed him before he could get past the first syllable of her name, before he could ask the question she’d spent four days hearing in her head. He stood still for a second. Then his free hand came to her waist. She kissed him again, slower, no less deliberate, and when she finally drew back she kept her forehead against his.

“Hi,” she whispered.

“Hi.”

“You’re going to ask me about the letter.”

“Yes.”

“I know.”

“Then why did you kiss me?”

“Because I wanted to.”

“That doesn’t answer the question.”

“It answers one of them. It came on Thursday. I wanted to tell you.” She stepped back with her hand still round his wrist.

“But you didn’t.”

“No.”

He folded it along its crease. “Why?”

“Because I was afraid. Not of the posting. I want it. I’ve wanted it for two years. I was afraid of telling you what it meant.” She looked at the floor.

“Three years. September. Deputy head of consular. Congratulations,” he said. He nodded once.

Her head came up. “Don’t.”

“Why?”

“Because you’re being polite. You haven’t said anything about us. You’re angry.” She searched his face.

“A little.”

Her fingers tightened on his wrist. “Because I applied?”

“No.”

“Because I accepted?”

“You haven’t formally accepted.”

“That’s not what I mean.”

“I know. I’m angry that you had it for four days and decided I couldn’t hear it.” He put the letter on the desk.

“I didn’t decide you couldn’t.”

“You decided not to tell me. Those are close enough.”

She shut her eyes. “I know.”

“Did you think I’d ask you not to go?”

“No.”

“That I’d tell you to choose me?”

“No.”

“Then what were you afraid of?”

She took a breath. “That you’d look at me differently. That you’d start hearing September in everything. That dinner would turn into a conversation about flights. That when I asked you to stay in bed another hour you’d hear a deadline in it. I didn’t want four months to turn into a countdown before I’d even said it out loud.” She gave a small laugh with nothing in it.

“You think I haven’t thought about September?”

She blinked.

“I know your posting cycle. I know you’ve been waiting for this. I wrote a paragraph about it and read it to your parents last July. I’ve thought about what three years means since then. And for the last hour, in detail.”

She laughed, startled, and pressed her lips together.

“You should have told me,” he said.

“I should have.”

He took her hand. “I don’t want you to stay here because you’re frightened of what leaving would do to us.”

“I don’t want to stay.”

“Good. You want to go. Then go.”

The plainness of it seemed to frighten her more than an argument would have. “You’re making it sound easy.”

“It isn’t. Three years is a long time. I don’t know how often I can come. I don’t know what your hours will be, or mine by then. I know the time difference is thirteen hours.”

“Thirteen,” she said.

“I checked. Peru doesn’t change its clocks. Neither do we. This isn’t a surprise. You’ve been working towards it. I’m not going to ask you to give it up.” He brushed his thumb over her knuckles.

She looked at him. “Would you come with me?”

He didn’t answer at once. Not because he was deciding whether he wanted to. Because he understood what she was asking.

“Do you want me to?”

“That’s not the same question.”

“No.”

Isla said, “I want you there. I don’t want you to throw away your work because I’ve got a chance. I don’t want you to resent it in a year. I don’t want you to come to prove something. I want to know whether you’ve thought about it. Not a promise. Not today.”

“I have. I don’t know yet. But I want to find out what’s possible. A transfer. Leave. Visits. I have a team and work here and I won’t pretend I can just walk out of them. I need to know what the arrangements are before I tell you what I can do.” He watched her take that, and saw it wasn’t the answer she’d hoped for, and went on.

“You’re planning already.”

“I’m trying to be accurate.”

“You’re terribly romantic.”

“I’ve been told.”

“By whom?”

“You. Repeatedly.”

She laughed, and this time it sounded like herself. He held her eyes.

“I don’t think three years is the end of anything. I want to go on with this. In Lima, here, or wherever we have to arrange it.”

“You make it sound like an operation.”

“It will need planning.”

“Will there be a briefing?”

“Probably.”

“Will I get a written report?”

“If you request one,” said Wei Long, and she put her forehead on his chest and laughed into his shirt, and he put his arms round her.

“I was so happy when it came. And then I was terrified. I practised telling you. I have some news. Then I thought that sounded like a performance review. You remember the position in Lima? Then I thought you’d ask whether I wanted it,” she said into the cotton.

“Which you do.”

“I wanted you to be happy for me before I had to tell you how frightened I was.”

He tipped her face up. “I am happy for you. And I’m frightened too.” Her eyes filled.

“You’re not supposed to say that.”

“Why?”

“Because I’ve spent four days trying to be the only one.”

“You don’t have to,” he said, and her fingers curled into the back of his shirt, and she kissed him again, and this time he met her before she got there.

✦ ✦ ✦

They didn’t talk about arrangements that night. They ate at home and she told him about the appointment process, the medical, the security checks, the formal acceptance she hadn’t sent yet. He asked sensible questions.

“Will you supervise the consular team directly?”

“The head of section runs it. I’m deputy. Staff, cases, emergencies, detained nationals, deaths abroad. The usual, with more of it mine.”

“After something big, a disaster, who runs the response?”

“The ambassador and the senior team. Consular finds our people and looks after them. Local authorities, hospitals, families at home, other posts.”

“That’s a lot. You’re qualified,” he said.

“Thank you. I was hoping you’d say you were proud of me.” She turned her glass.

He put his chopsticks down. “Isla. I’m proud of you.”

It came slowly over her face. “Thank you.”

“You should have told me on Thursday.”

“I know.”

“On Friday. On Saturday. On Sunday.”

“All right, Inspector, I’ve understood the pattern.”

He lifted her hand and kissed it. “Next time tell me before you spend four days being afraid of me.”

“Next time?”

“Your career isn’t going to stop producing difficult news. I’d rather hear it from you.”

Later she stood at the wardrobe taking out clothes to sort, and he sat on the bed with his notebook open and wrote nothing for several minutes.

“Are you working?”

“Thinking.”

“About Lima?”

“Whether the flat would be hard to sublet if I were away for long periods.”

She stared at him and started laughing. “You’ve known for six hours.”

“It’s a practical consideration.”

“We haven’t even decided if you’re coming.”

“I know. What were you thinking about?” He watched her come and sit beside him.

“How much I want to show you the coast. It isn’t what people think. It’s all cliffs and grey sea, and from June the sky goes grey for months and stays there. There’s a fine mist they call the garúa that never quite becomes rain. You’d hate it for a week and then you’d love it.”

“Then I’ll see it.”

She lifted her head. “You’ll come?”

“I said I’ll see it.”

“That isn’t a date.”

“No. Isla. I want to visit you in Lima. I can’t tell you when yet.” He looked at her.

Her face went soft. “That’s enough for tonight. What did you write?” She reached for the notebook.

He handed it over. The page was empty except for the date at the top. 11 May 2026. She gave it back.

“Write that I got the job. Write that I’m going to Lima. Write that you were unbearably handsome when you found the letter.”

“I don’t think that needs recording.”

“It does.”

He wrote while she watched. 11 May 2026. Isla got the appointment she wanted. Three years. Lima. Deputy head of consular. He paused, and added a line. She was afraid to tell me. I wish she hadn’t been.

Her fingers rested on his wrist. “That’s not all.”

“What else?”

“That I kissed you before you could ask me anything.”

He considered it, and wrote: She kissed me before I could speak.

“Better,” she whispered, and kissed him again, and he put the pen down. Outside, the evening came down over the city. September was four months off. For tonight Lima was a name on a letter, a place she’d wanted for two years, and a future they had finally started to say out loud.

chapters.title: He Says Go
chapters.desc: The start is moved up to the first week of July and she tells him after six hours, not four days. He says he’s unhappy, out loud, then says go, and means it. The first “I love you” is hers, in passing; his comes straight after. He books his leave and tells no one.
chapters.epigraph: “I love you, Isla”
chapters.content:
The argument began with a spreadsheet. Isla had it open on the dining table after dinner on the last Tuesday in May, the ministry’s relocation portal in the next tab: columns for accommodation, reporting dates, flights, temporary housing, the hundred small things she had to settle before she took up a post on the far side of the Pacific. Wei Long stood behind her chair reading over her shoulder.

“That flight’s on a Tuesday.”

“Yes.”

“You’d land Wednesday.”

“Yes.”

“Have you allowed for the time difference?”

“Thirteen hours. We’ve discussed it.”

“I’m confirming.”

She tipped her head back to look at him upside down. “Inspector, are you interrogating my flight?”

“I’m checking it.”

“On what grounds?”

“Leaving without adequate sleep.”

She laughed and changed the date. There was a small stack of paper beside the laptop: the appointment letter, a list of documents, a handover schedule for her cases here. She’d been at it an hour. He’d been standing behind her for twenty minutes.

“Sit down. You’re looming.”

“I’m standing.”

“You’re an enormous standing person. There’s something else. They’ve moved it,” said Isla, and he pulled out the chair beside hers and sat.

“Moved what?”

“The start. The deputy I’m replacing is leaving early for family reasons. They want me there for the first week of July instead of September. I got the email this afternoon. I’ve known for six hours. I’m telling you after six hours, not four days. I’d like that noted.” She didn’t look at him.

“It’s noted. July.” He looked at the screen, at the new date in its cell. Five weeks.

“July. My parents think I should take it. My mother has sent me three articles about Lima. Two of them were about restaurants. Hao says I should stop behaving as though accepting a job makes me personally responsible for the end of civilisation.” Her voice wobbled on it and steadied.

“Does he always talk like that?”

“Always.”

“He’s consistent.” He waited, because she’d stopped.

“And you?” she said.

She half closed the laptop. He didn’t answer straight away.

“Wei Long.”

“Go. Go. I’ll be here,” he said. She looked at him.

The room went quiet.

“Are you sure? Don’t say it because you think it’s what I need.”

“I’m not.”

“You can tell me if you’re unhappy.”

“I am unhappy. I don’t want you to leave. I don’t want three years of thirteen hours. I don’t want to work out whether you’re awake before I ring you, or spend the days that matter looking at a screen. But I want you to have this job. I want you to be deputy head of consular. I want you to have the life you wanted before you met me. So go.” Her lips parted. He went on in the same even voice. He took her hand.

She was quiet a long time. “And you’ll be here?”

“Yes. Especially when it’s difficult. I won’t pretend I’ll enjoy it. I won’t pretend it won’t hurt. I won’t make you feel guilty for going.” He rubbed his thumb over her knuckles.

She leaned over and kissed him, gently, and rested her forehead on his.

“You’re making it hard not to cry.”

“You can.”

“I’ve been crying all week.”

“I know.”

“How?”

“Your eyes,” he said, and she laughed, and the first tear went down, and he wiped it off with his thumb.

✦ ✦ ✦

He booked his leave on Wednesday at his desk after the briefing, while the squad room was quiet. The portal showed what he’d accrued and what he was entitled to over the coming year, which was a great deal, because he’d hardly taken any of it in six years. He looked at the roster first. He looked at his team’s cases and the court dates and the weeks his absence would hurt least, and he put the requests in in blocks, with room round them for operations and emergencies. Some in September. Some at Christmas. Some in the spring. Some on dates that meant nothing yet, except that they might turn into days when Isla was in Lima and he could be there too. He booked every day he was owed.

He didn’t tell her. He didn’t tell Yu Chen. He didn’t tell Liu, who would certainly have asked why an inspector who took three days a year had developed an interest in the leave system. Application received. Pending approval. He closed it and went back to his case file.

She found him in the kitchen that evening waiting for the kettle, and came up behind him and wrapped her arms round his waist.

“How was your day?”

“Ordinary. One arrest. Considerable paperwork.”

“Any handsome women distracting you?”

He turned his head. “One.”

“Did she cause trouble?”

“Frequently.”

“Did you arrest her?”

“No. I like her,” he said, and she laughed and kissed him between the shoulder blades. “How was yours?”

“They’ve started looking for someone to take my files. I have to write a transition document. It makes it real. Do you ever wish I hadn’t applied?” She leaned her cheek on his back.

“No. I wish it were closer.”

“Me too,” said Isla, and the kettle clicked off, and neither of them moved to it.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the end of May they could talk about Lima without lowering their voices. She told him what she’d be doing: part of the consular operation for a whole country’s citizens, detentions and deaths and emergencies, learning the local procedures, the people in the ministries, the hospitals. She talked about it with growing excitement and he listened and asked about the team and the reporting lines and the first months.

“Will you travel outside Lima?”

“Sometimes.”

“Security?”

“Standard.”

“Briefed on local risks?”

“Yes. You’re not going to ask me to send you my itinerary every time I leave the city.” She narrowed her eyes.

“No. I’m going to ask you to tell me when you arrive somewhere. And when you leave. And if your plans change.”

She put her fork down. “Are you writing a reporting protocol for your girlfriend?”

“I’m making a request.”

She leaned over the table and kissed him. “Approved. Would you like it in triplicate?”

“One copy is sufficient.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The last Thursday in May wasn’t marked on any calendar. No dinner, no booking, no flowers. Rain on the windows and a half-finished book on her bedside table. She came out of the bathroom in one of his shirts and stopped in the doorway. He was sitting on the bed taking his watch off, and he looked up, and neither of them said anything at all.

She crossed the room. He put the watch down as she stepped between his knees. Her hands went to his shoulders, his to her waist. She touched his face and he turned his head and kissed her palm, and she bent and kissed him, and there was no teasing in it, no French, no instruction, nothing to make him smile first. He stood without letting go of her. The backs of her legs met the mattress. He looked at her once, and she touched his cheek, and he understood.

He undid his own shirt on her, button by button, and pushed it off her shoulders and let it fall. He laid her down and took his time, the way he always did, but differently tonight, as if he were learning her by heart without letting it turn into a goodbye: the hollow under her collarbone, the soft skin inside her elbow, the curve where her waist went into her hip, the backs of her knees. His mouth went everywhere his hands went. When he moved down the bed and kissed the insides of her thighs she put her hand in his hair and didn’t say a word, and when his tongue found her she arched and bit her lip and still didn’t, and he held her hips and went slowly until she shook apart under him with her breath caught in her throat. Whenever he seemed to go somewhere else, somewhere five weeks off, she put her hand on his face and he came back.

She drew him up and over her and into her, and they moved together with nothing said, her heels on the backs of his thighs, his forehead on hers, his breathing and hers the only sound in the room besides the rain. When he came it was with his face in her neck and his whole body taut over her, and she held him through it with her arms locked round his back.

Afterwards she lay with her cheek on his chest. His hand moved over her spine. She lifted her head and kissed him and he answered at once, and the night hadn’t finished with them.

The second time was slower still. She was on top of him, rocking, his hands on her hips, and halfway through she laughed, once, without meaning to, at nothing, at how much she loved the face he made, and the laugh broke in the middle and turned into tears. He went still.

“Don’t stop. Don’t stop. I’m all right,” she said, and caught his face between her hands.

He looked up at her, searching, and she kissed him, and he understood that the tears weren’t asking to be comforted instead. They were just there, mixed up with laughing and wanting him, the impossible happiness of loving someone while knowing something was about to change. He sat up with her in his lap and held her, still inside her, and moved with her like that, his arms round her back, her tears on his neck, until she came gasping into his shoulder, and he came after her with her name.

✦ ✦ ✦

She lay across him afterwards with one leg over his and her hair over his shoulder, smiling, with wet eyes. He kissed the corner of one.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re crying.”

“I know. I’m happy. I’m sad. I’m tired. I love you. I hate July.” She laughed.
