He went still underneath her. She hadn’t said it before. Not like that, in passing.

“I love you,” he said.

It was the first time. They both knew it. He’d told her brother he wouldn’t say it to anyone else before he’d said it to her, and he hadn’t said it to anyone.

She touched his mouth. “Say it again.”

“I love you.”

Her smile trembled. “Again.”

“I love you, Isla,” he said, and she kissed him, and he held her until the rain stopped.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning she woke first and watched him sleep on his side with his hand near her waist. His face looked younger without its usual concentration. The line between his brows was still there, faint. She touched it with her fingertip and his eyes opened.

“Did I wake you?”

“Yes.”

“Sorry.”

He caught her hand and kissed the fingers. “Don’t apologise. Coffee?”

“Yes, please. One more minute.” He started to get up and she caught his wrist.

He lay back down. One minute became several. She tucked herself against his side.

“Do you know what I want to do when you come? Take you to the coast. The grey sea, the cliffs. The places I think are beautiful, not the ones in the guidebooks. The markets. And I want to complain about the weather with you.”

“You can do that here.”

“Not in the same language. There,” said Isla, and he smiled, and she pointed at him, delighted.

“I do that sometimes.”

“Not often enough.”

“Then give me more reasons,” he said, and she kissed his shoulder and said she intended to.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday she put the key on the table between them at breakfast. The plain silver one with the white tag, HOME, PROVISIONAL, in her handwriting, which had gone a little soft at the edges from living in his pocket for seven months.

She said, “I’m not giving up the flat. The ministry will house me in Lima. The lease here has two years left, and I’m keeping it, and I want you to stay in it.”

“It’s your flat.”

“It’s ours. You told me so in November. You were extremely definite. I don’t want you going back to that place you sleep in. I want you here, with my books and my terrible tea and your grandfather on the bedside table, and I want to know exactly where you are when I ring. That’s my request. One copy is sufficient.” She pushed the key an inch towards him.

He picked the key up and looked at the tag. “Do you want to change the label?”

“No. Not yet. That’s for when I’m home,” said Isla.

He put it back in his pocket, and she watched it go in, and some part of her that had been clenched for a week let go.

✦ ✦ ✦

Over the next few days the leave requests came back approved, one block at a time. He didn’t mention them. They weren’t a promise he could be in Lima whenever she wanted him there, and they weren’t proof against an operation or a court date. They were days he’d decided to keep. He looked at the calendar once and closed it and went to work.

At home she had started on her books. Three piles on the living-room floor: take, leave, undecided.

“How many undecided?”

“Eleven.”

“That’s a lot of indecision.”

“Don’t judge me.”

He picked one up. “You’re taking this.”

“Why?”

“You’ve read it twice.”

“Three times.”

“Then you’re taking it,” he said, and she took it from him and put it on the right pile and reached for his hand, and he stood beside her looking down at the three heaps of her life.

He’d told her to go. He still meant it. He’d mean it when the bags were packed, and when he stood at the terminal watching her go through the gates, and when he came back to this flat without her voice in it, and on the days when he hated every kilometre between here and there. He squeezed her hand.

“What?” she said.

“Nothing.”

“You’re doing that thing again. Thinking too much.”

He bent and kissed her, and she put her arms round his neck, and for the moment neither of them went anywhere.

chapters.title: The Airport, the Wrong Way Round
chapters.desc: The terminal where they met, raining again. He can’t go through security without a ticket, so he sits on a dead check-in counter at aisle forty until she laughs; she kisses him through the security barrier.
chapters.epigraph: “Come home when you’re ready.”
chapters.content:
She woke him at four, which wasn’t necessary, because he was already awake.

“You’re watching me,” she said into the dark.

“Yes.”

“For how long?”

“Since three.”

She rolled over and put her face in his neck and they lay like that without talking while the window went from black to grey. At five she got up and showered and he made coffee, two cups, and she drank hers standing at the counter in her travelling clothes looking round the kitchen as if she were memorising where the spoons lived. Her case was by the door. She’d packed it twice and he’d checked it once, which she’d allowed.

“I’ve left you a list. On the fridge,” she said.

He went and read it. 1. Eat. 2. Water the plant by the balcony (once a week, not once a day, you’ll drown it). 3. My mother will ring you. Answer. 4. Sleep on my side if you want, I won’t know. 5. Don’t sleep on my side, I’ll know. 6. The tea is for you too. 7. Ring me.

“Seven items,” he said.

“I thought you’d like the format.”

“Item four contradicts item five.”

“That’s deliberate,” said Isla, and put her cup in the sink, and came and stood in front of him and fixed his collar, which didn’t need it, and then they carried her case down to the car.

✦ ✦ ✦

It had rained on the day they met, and on Thursday the second of July it rained on the day she left. Isla noticed first. She stood under the departures board with her passport in one hand and her phone in the other, watching the water blur the terminal windows and the ground crew in their yellow jackets steering baggage carts across the wet apron.

“Of course,” she said.

Wei Long looked up from the documents he was checking. “What?”

“Rain. Same terminal. Same weather. How romantic.”

“You said you liked the rain.”

“I like rain when I’m indoors and not leaving the country. Well?” She watched him fold the papers away.

“Your flight’s on time.”

“That wasn’t the reassurance I wanted.”

“What did you want?”

“That you’ll miss me.”

“I will,” he said, so plainly that she had no room to tease him, and she smiled, a little sadly, and said, “Good.”

They’d come early. She’d insisted, partly because she hated rushing and partly because she wanted the time, and he hadn’t pointed out that they were nearly three hours early. He knew. She knew he knew. Her case was checked through to Lima by way of a long connection. Her passport and boarding pass were in the leather folder she carried everywhere, the posting papers in her handbag with the little notebook of names she had to ring when she landed. Everything was ready. That was the trouble. There was nothing left to do but go.

They found two seats at the end of the hall near the security entrance and she leaned on his shoulder.

“How many times have you checked the time difference?”

“Enough.”

“That means more than once.”

“Yes.”

“What’s your plan for ringing me?”

“It depends on your hours.”

“How diplomatic.”

“I’m trying to be considerate. I don’t want to wake you. I don’t want you to feel you have to answer.”

“Then ring when you can and I’ll ring when I can. Look at us. Negotiating a long-distance relationship like a bilateral agreement.” She put her hand in his.

“Would you like a memorandum?”

“Only if you sign it.”

“I can,” he said, and she laughed and he kissed her hair.

People went past. Families with children asleep on trolleys, men in suits, a couple standing too close to the board, a man arguing with an airline clerk about a suitcase. Isla watched the escalator that went down to arrivals.

“Do you remember the first time we were here?”

“Yes. Downstairs. The custody desk.”

“You forgot to thank me.”

“I remember.”

“I thought you were the rudest man I’d ever met.”

“I was occupied.”

“You were rude and occupied. I left you a card.” She looked up at him.

“Your handwriting was small. The card was damp. Your hair was wet. Your coat was navy. You had a folder against your hip and three documents and a black notebook. You corrected the record, spoke to four people in three languages, and left before I could thank you.” He turned her hand over and drew his thumb across her knuckles.

“You make it sound like a witness statement.”

“I remember it,” he said, and she leaned over and kissed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after nine they walked down the hall towards security. The queue had started to form. At the end of the last check-in aisle, number forty, there was an empty airline counter with its screen switched off and a stack of baggage tags beside it, and Wei Long looked at it, and then at her.

She knew that face. “No.”

He walked over to it.

“Wei Long.”

He put one hand on the edge of the counter, and with exactly the deliberation he’d have used to sit at his own desk, he got up and sat on it, and folded his hands in his lap.

“Comfortable,” he said.

She pressed her lips together. He looked at her. She tried to hold it, and then she burst out laughing, not the polite laugh she gave strangers or the amused one she gave him at dinner, but a real one, bent over with her hand on her mouth.

“You’re ridiculous.”

“You told me once the desk was where it started.”

“I did not.”

“You told your parents.”

“That isn’t the same thing. You’re sitting on an airline counter. People can see you. You’re an inspector.”

“Off duty,” he said, and a man going past with a trolley stared at him, and he didn’t move.

She stood in front of him smiling so widely that he could see the little creases at the corners of her eyes. He held out his hand and she stepped between his knees.

“You’re going to get us removed.”

“Then we’d have more time.”

“That’s not how airport security works.”

“I know. You’ve sat on my desk for sixteen months. Today I’m sitting on yours. Ten minutes.” He took her face in his hands.

She stopped laughing. She put her arms round his neck and kissed him there on the counter in the middle of the departures hall, and for ten minutes the world waited, and nobody removed anybody.

“Thank you. For making me laugh,” she said when she pulled back.

“You’re welcome.”

Around half past nine her boarding group was called on the board. He got down off the counter.

“Flight number?” she said.

“Yes.”

“Arrival time? Address? The name of the person meeting me?”

“Yes. Yes. Yes.”

“Don’t make me feel I’m being handed to another department. Eat properly. Not just coffee. Don’t work till midnight every night.” She straightened his collar. It was already straight. He let her.

“I can’t promise that.”

“Try. Ring me. Tell me when something happens. Not three days later.”

“I’ll tell you.”

She put both hands flat on his chest. “All right.”

He covered them with his. “All right.”

She kissed him. It was meant to be short, one last kiss before the barrier and the long flight and the new city, and it didn’t stay short. He bent and she caught his face in both hands, her fingers at the back of his neck, and he kissed her with the restraint he’d been holding all morning, and she felt it give a little in the way his hand closed on her waist.

“Don’t look so serious,” she said.

“I’m looking at you.”

“That isn’t helping.”

He moved a strand of hair off her face. “Go, Isla.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She joined the queue. At the front a woman checked her passport and boarding pass, and she put her bag in a tray and walked through the arch and collected her things on the other side, and turned. He was still there. He didn’t wave. She lifted her hand and he lifted his.

She walked on towards the next checkpoint and stopped and turned again. He’d moved up to the barrier, to the exact place where the staff would have told him to stop if he’d come any further. She laughed under her breath and walked back.

The barrier was glass and steel, with a narrow gap where passengers went through once their papers had been checked. She came right up to it on her side. He came up to it on his.

“You’re not supposed to come through,” she said.

“I’m aware.”

She reached through the gap and put her hands on his shoulders, and he bent his head, and her fingers went into his hair, and she kissed him through the barrier. It was awkward, the angle and the steel edge and the people behind her, and neither of them cared. She held his head in both hands. His hand came up to the side of her face. For a few seconds the airport went away.

“Thirteen hours,” she whispered, with her forehead on his.

“Yes.”

“Don’t forget me.”

“Isla. I know where you are. I know where you’re going and when you land. I know your address and the name of the man meeting you. That isn’t what you meant.” She laughed, wet.

“No.”

“I won’t forget you,” he said, and she kissed him once more and stepped back.

✦ ✦ ✦

Thank You (Paid): I miss you already.

Wei Long: You haven’t left yet.

Thank You (Paid): Exactly. Terrible situation.

Wei Long: Board when called.

She sent a photograph of herself in a window seat with the passport folder on her knee.

Thank You (Paid): Bossy.

Wei Long: Safe flight.

Thank You (Paid): I love you.

He put the phone in his pocket. Then he took it out again.

Wei Long: I love you too.

At 10:16 the plane pushed back. He watched it from the terminal window. The rain had got heavier and ran down the glass in crooked lines, smearing the aircraft’s lights. Downstairs, under his feet, was the custody desk, the same counter, the same fluorescent strip lights, and he could see it plainly: a woman in a soaked navy coat arguing with a printer.

Thank You (Paid): I’m on the plane. I can see the terminal.

Wei Long: I can see your plane.

Thank You (Paid): Can you see me?

He considered it.

Wei Long: No.

Thank You (Paid): Good. I look terrible.

Wei Long: You look beautiful.

Thank You (Paid): You can’t even see me.

Wei Long: I remember.

The plane turned for the runway and went out of sight behind the building. At 11:03 he left the airport and drove back through the rain. The passenger seat was empty. He’d known it would be. He’d watched her pack and checked her papers and carried her case down and driven her here, and he still hadn’t expected the quiet in the car to arrive so fast.

At a red light his phone buzzed and he left it until he’d pulled in at the next junction.

Thank You (Paid): I forgot to tell you something. You looked unbearably handsome sitting on that counter.

Wei Long: Airport staff would disagree.

Thank You (Paid): Then do it at home.

Wei Long: Come home when you’re ready.

Thank You (Paid): I will.

✦ ✦ ✦

He let himself into the flat with the key with the white label. Her side of the wardrobe was half empty. Her book from the undecided pile was on the bedside table, the one she’d decided to leave at the last minute so he’d have something of hers that wasn’t tea. There was the tea, in its tin on the shelf, the evening kind she liked, four packets left. He stood in the kitchen and looked at it for a while, and then made himself coffee, one cup, and got it wrong, and made it again.

She landed in Lima late the next morning by her clock and in the middle of his night, and the photograph she sent was of an airport window and a city lying pale and low under a sky the colour of wet concrete.

Thank You (Paid): Different terminal. Same weather.

He was awake. He’d been waiting.

Wei Long: Welcome to Lima.

Thank You (Paid): I wish you were here.

Wei Long: So do I.

He put the phone on the bedside table, face up, beside her book, and lay on his side of the bed and didn’t take up the rest of it. Then, around four, he moved over to hers, because the pillow still smelled of her shampoo and he was alone and nobody was keeping a record. At seven his phone buzzed.

Thank You (Paid): Item five.

He looked at it for some time. He hadn’t told her. There was no way she could know. He typed three replies and deleted all of them.

Wei Long: How?

Thank You (Paid): I didn’t. You just told me.

He put the phone away lay looking at the ceiling, and for the first time since the airport something in his chest that had been clenched like a fist opened by a finger’s width, and he laughed, out loud, alone in the flat, at himself. Nobody recorded it. He would tell her later, and she would be furious that she hadn’t heard it, and that seemed to him, at seven in the morning, like something worth looking forward to. On the other side of thirteen hours she was starting the life she’d wanted. He had told her to go. He meant it, and he meant it at three in the morning too, which was harder.

chapters.title: Thirteen Hours
chapters.desc: Thirteen hours apart. His night shift is her morning coffee. She runs her first death-in-custody case abroad. Language cards arrive in his post, one a week; calls get explicit and he hangs up blushing in a stairwell.
chapters.epigraph: “No tengo que hacerlo todo solo.”
chapters.content:
The first call came at eight in the evening, his time, which was seven in the morning in Lima, and he took it standing in the kitchen with a cup of coffee he’d made for two out of habit.

“Good morning. Good evening. I’m going to get that wrong for a month,” said Isla.

“You sound awake.”

“I’ve had coffee. The flat’s excellent. The water pressure is a rumour, the lift sounds like an animal dying, and the neighbour has a dog that thinks six in the morning is a reasonable time to discuss its feelings.”

“Does the dog have a point?”

“Not one I’ve been able to establish. What did you eat?” He heard a spoon on china.

“I was going to ask you that.”

“Bread, cheese, fruit. It’s breakfast, Inspector, not a confession. What’s your day been?”

“An interview at eleven. A file. Five hours’ sleep last night.”

“That’s a disappointing number.”

“It’s a number,” he said, and heard her smile. He could see her: the little table she’d sent him a photograph of, her hair wet, one foot tucked under her on the chair. Eleven days. He’d counted. He hadn’t written it down.

She said, “I’m going to ring you every morning. Seven mine, eight yours. Unless one of us is dead, unconscious or in a meeting that can’t be left.”

“Those are broad exceptions.”

“I trust you to read them sensibly. I miss you. Say something less practical.” A pause, comfortable; they’d become good at those.

He thought. “I’ve been making coffee for two.”

“That’s better.”

“I remember when I take the second cup out.”

She laughed, and the sound came down the line and settled somewhere under his ribs, and he stood in the kitchen for a minute after she’d gone, holding a cup that had gone lukewarm.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first language card came the following Thursday in an envelope with a Lima postmark and his name and address in her hand, the postcode underlined twice. A small cream card. On one side, in blue ink: ¿Ya comiste? On the other: Have you eaten? You ask me this every day. You should know how to ask it properly. And don’t say it like you’re reading a witness statement.

He propped it against his monitor. Liu saw it in the afternoon briefing.

“What’s that, sir?”

“Correspondence.”

“From Lima?” Liu reached for it. Wei Long moved it.

“Don’t touch my correspondence.”

“It’s a language card.”

“It’s still my correspondence.”

“What does it say?”

“Have you eaten.”

“That’s romantic, sir.”

“It’s a question.”

“From a woman thirteen hours away,” said Liu, and Wei Long slid the card into the back of his notebook and asked whether Liu had anything to say about the case.

That evening she made him say it down the phone. “No. Everything after the first syllable. Again. Better. Still sounds like you’re arresting the food.” A card came every week after that. ¿Quieres café? with a little drawing of a cup: useful in any country. Te extraño: you should know this one already. Estoy orgullosa de ti: I’m proud of you. He kept that one inside the notebook instead of on the desk. No tienes que hacerlo todo solo: you don’t have to do everything alone. On the back: This isn’t a translation exercise. It’s an instruction. He rang her that night.

“You’re becoming directive.”

“I’m told it’s one of my qualities. Did you read it? Did you understand it? Then say it.”

“No tengo que hacerlo todo solo.”

“Again.”

He said it again. His accent was careful and the words were clear. “Better. You’re a difficult student,” she said.

“I’ve been told I’m reliable.”

“Reliable isn’t the same as good at Spanish.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By August the calls were part of his evenings. He knew she had an early briefing when she rang five minutes late. She knew he’d been on an operation when he answered short and took a second longer to speak. Some calls lasted forty minutes and some lasted four, and neither of them demanded more. Once she rang while he was still at his desk and they talked while they both worked, her pages turning in Lima and his in the station, and she stopped halfway through a sentence.

“You’ve gone quiet.”

“I’m reading.”

“I can hear the pages.”

“Then you know I’m here.”

She was silent. “Yes, I do,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The death in custody began on a Tuesday. A citizen of hers, thirty-four, in Lima on business, had been held by the local police after a fight outside a restaurant. Hours later he was found unresponsive in a cell, and by the time the embassy was told he’d been taken to hospital, and soon after that he was dead.

She was called in before eight. It wasn’t her job to investigate. Her job was to find out what had happened to her citizen as far as the authorities were obliged to tell her, to make sure his family heard it properly, to explain what consular help was and wasn’t, and to see that the procedures were followed. The hospital was hard. The police were worse. They gave her a summary: a timeline, a medical emergency, his health. She wrote every word down, and then asked for the name of the officer who’d authorised his detention, the time he was put in the cell, the time he was last seen responsive, the time medical help was called and the time the ambulance came. The officer on the line got impatient. Isla didn’t.

“I understand that you’ve given me an initial account. I’m asking for the recorded times and the responsible officers. Those aren’t the same thing,” she said in Spanish.

She asked again, and that time she got them.

By noon she’d spoken to the hospital, the police liaison office, the emergency team at home and the family. His sister was in another country. His wife was at home in Canada waiting for a phone call she hadn’t understood would change her life, and Isla made it. She knew how to say a thing clearly and how to say it kindly and not to bury it in procedure, and not to offer explanations nobody had established yet, and not to promise that an investigation would produce an answer. She knew the woman would probably remember her voice for the rest of her life.

The wife asked whether someone could see him. Isla went that afternoon. The body was in the hospital mortuary, not the cell, in a cold white room with the refrigeration humming. A hospital administrator stood by the door and an official from the prosecutor’s office stood beside her. The man on the trolley looked younger than his passport photograph. His hair had been combed back and somebody had straightened his collar. There was a small mark at his temple, half under his hair. She didn’t touch him. She looked at his face long enough to remember it, and then asked whether the family would be allowed an independent examination, when they’d see the preliminary medical report, and who would decide the release of the body. Some of it was answered. The rest was deferred. She wrote down the names of the people who were deferring it.

Outside in the corridor she read her notes again. The times were still in the same order. The paper didn’t show that she’d just been looking at a dead man who’d come to Lima alive, or that a woman in Canada was waiting for her to ring back.

Wei Long: Seven o’clock. Are you free?

It was past eight at home. She rang him from her office with the door shut.

“Isla?”

“A citizen died in police custody. Yesterday they arrested him. Today he died.”

He said nothing for a second. “Are you handling the family?”

“I spoke to his wife. I saw him. In the mortuary. I know that’s not an investigation. I know what my role is.” She breathed.

“I didn’t say it was. Was it hard?” He’d got up; she could hear him walk to a window.

She laughed without anything in it. “That’s a strange question.”

“It’s the one I have.”

“Yes, it was,” she said.

“Have you eaten?”

“Don’t.”

“Have you?”

“No. I have two reports.”

“Eat first.”

“You’re a long way away to be telling me what to do.”

“I’m aware. Tell me about him.” He waited. She didn’t speak.

“His name was Daniel. Thirty-four. A wife and a little girl. He’d been here a week. That’s all I know for certain. She asked me if he was frightened. I said I didn’t know and I wouldn’t pretend to. She wanted something else.” Her voice went.

“She wanted her husband back,” said Wei Long, and Isla’s breath caught, and he didn’t fill the silence.

“I don’t want to turn into someone who can do this without feeling it.”

“You won’t.”

“You can’t know that.”

“No. But I know you.”

She pressed her fingers into her eyes. “I’m going to eat. Then finish the reports. Then go home.”

“Ring me when you get in.”

He stayed on the line while she found her bag and went down in the lift and out into the street, listening to her keys and the traffic, and didn’t ask her about the mortuary again. When she got in she rang him back, and he stayed with her while she ate.

✦ ✦ ✦

In September the distance stopped being new and became a fact, like weather. Some mornings she rang from the lift because she was late. Some evenings he answered in the station stairwell with his voice low because the corridor carried. Some nights she fell asleep halfway through a call and he stayed on until he was sure she was properly asleep. They learned to argue on a telephone. They learned that silence could mean a bad day, or a bad line, or one of them looking for the right word.

And then one Saturday morning at seven, which was six on Friday evening in Lima, the phone rang while he was still on the side of the bed with his shirt unbuttoned.

“I’m home,” said Isla. “I have the whole weekend. And I have a question. How’s your Spanish?”

“Some of it is there.”

“That isn’t confidence.”

“It’s an accurate assessment.”

“Then we’ll practise. Turn your camera on.”

He did. Her face came up on the screen, close, her hair loose on her shoulders, and the look in her eyes was the one he knew from nine o’clock in his office with the blinds down.

“Hello, Inspector.”

“Hello.”

“I wish you were here.”

“So do I.”

“Come closer. Closer. Better. Do you know what I miss most? Your hands. The way you touch me when you’re not thinking about it. When you’re reading or making coffee. You reach for me as if it’s the most natural thing in the world. Tell me you miss me. In Spanish.” He brought the phone nearer. She shifted against her pillows.

“Te extraño.”

“Again. Slower.”

“Te extraño, Isla.”

She watched his mouth. “Now tell me you want me.”

He was quiet. Then, “Te deseo.”

Her face changed. She put the phone on the pillow beside her, propped against something, so that he could see her lying on her side in a thin cream blouse, and she undid the top button of it while she watched him.

“Isla,” he said.

“I’m thirteen hours away. I have to use what I’ve got. I’m going to tell you what I’m doing, and you’re going to say it back to me. In Spanish. That’s the lesson.” She undid the next button.

“Is this on the syllabus?”

“It is now.”

She told him. She told him she was opening her blouse, and he said it back, slowly, and she corrected one word, and he said it again. She told him she was touching her breast the way he did, with his thumb, and he watched her do it on the small bright screen and said it back with his voice gone low. She told him she was sliding her hand down her stomach, and under the waistband of her skirt, and she shut her eyes, and he forgot the Spanish for something and she told him, breathless, and he said it. She told him she wanted him to touch himself too, and he hesitated, sitting on the edge of their bed in an empty flat with his shirt open, and she opened her eyes and looked at him through the screen and said please, and he did. She talked him through it, in English now because she’d run out of patience for grammar, what she was doing and what she wanted him to do and how she was imagining him, his weight, his mouth, and he answered her with the few words he had in her language, quiero besarte, te deseo, ven, and when she came she said his name so loudly that he heard the dog next door begin to bark through her wall, and he followed her a moment later with her name in his throat and his forehead against the cool of the window glass.

For a while neither of them said anything. She lay with her cheek on the pillow, looking at him.

“Now tell me you love me,” she said.

“Te quiero.”

“There’s another one.”

“Te amo. Te amo, Isla,” said Wei Long.

She whispered it back. Then she started laughing, helplessly, into the pillow.

“What?”

“The dog.”

“I heard.”

“I’m never going to be able to look at my neighbour again.”

“Are you blushing?” he said.

“Are you?”

“No. It’s warm.”

“It’s September.”

“Lima isn’t here,” he said, and she laughed until she had to put the phone down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Twenty minutes later the duty officer rang his work phone and he went in. He went straight to the stairwell to ring back about a file, and he was halfway through the call when Liu came through the fire door and stopped. Wei Long turned his back. Liu looked at his face and then at the phone and then at his face again.

“Sir. Are you blushing?”

“No.”

“Your ears are red.”

“Go downstairs.”

“Was that Lima?”

Wei Long ended the call. “Do you have an update on the case?”

“Not yet, sir.”

“Then go and get one.” Liu went down the stairs laughing, and Wei Long stood on the landing with his phone in his hand until it buzzed.

Thank You (Paid): I hope you didn’t forget everything I taught you.

Wei Long: Everything.

Thank You (Paid): Good. Next week’s card will be harder.

It came in the middle of the month, larger than the others and folded once. Cuando vuelvas, no voy a dejarte ir enseguida. When you come back, I’m not going to let you go straight away. I checked the grammar twice. You may not argue.

He rang her at seven the next morning, her time.

“Did you get it?”

“Yes. The grammar is correct. I checked.”

“Of course you did.”

He looked at the card. “When I come,” he said, “you won’t have to let me go at all. Not for a while.”

The silence on the other end was short, but he heard her breathing change.

“Is that a date?”

“Not yet.”

He had told her nothing about the leave, the blocks of days in the system, December, the spring. He wanted to know what he could actually give her before he put a date in front of her. But he’d started making it possible.

“It’s a beginning,” said Isla.

“Yes.”

“Then I’ll keep teaching you. You’re making progress at saying things nobody should say in a police station.”

“That isn’t on the syllabus.”

“It is now,” she said, and thirteen hours away she put the phone down and finished her coffee and started her day. The distance hadn’t got any smaller. It had a shape now: her voice in his kitchen, her handwriting in his post, Spanish in his notebook, and a date he hadn’t given her yet that he was already working towards.

chapters.title: The Ground Moves
chapters.desc: A major earthquake off the coast. Phones go down across Lima. He watches the news for twelve hours. Dark: collapsed blocks, the count rising, no word.
chapters.epigraph: “I love you. I’m waiting.”
chapters.content:
At three minutes past four on Thursday afternoon in Lima, Isla was standing in the doorway of her office on the sixth floor of the embassy when the floor moved.

At first it felt like a lorry going by underneath the building, a low hum up through the soles of her shoes. Someone at the end of the corridor looked up. Then the windows began to rattle in their frames, and the strip lights swung, and somebody said, “Terremoto,” quite calmly, as if naming a bird.

The second movement was much harder. The filing cabinet beside her desk walked six inches out from the wall. A stack of folders slid off a table and fanned across the floor. Somewhere below, a great deal of glass broke at once.

“Under the desks! Away from the windows!”

She went down under the nearest heavy table with one arm over her head and the other round its leg. The building groaned. She had never heard a sound like it: steel and concrete and glass and under it something enormous shifting in a direction it had never been meant to shift. Paulina from the visa section was under the table with her, breathing in small fast gasps.

“Stay down. Stay down. Hold the leg,” said Isla.

She had sat through the earthquake briefings. She’d read the procedures, learned the evacuation stairs and the assembly points, practised drop, cover and hold on in a training room while a man with a stopwatch counted the seconds in a bored voice. There was nothing bored about this. It went on for longer than seemed physically possible. When it eased at last nobody moved. They waited, because the briefing said to wait, and a smaller tremor came through the floor, and somebody down the corridor began to cry.

“Now, slowly. Out. Stairs. No lift,” called the floor warden.

Paulina had a cut on her forearm from a falling frame, shallow and bleeding freely. Isla wrapped it in a scarf. Someone else had cracked a knee on a desk. “Leave your bags. Stairs. Hand on the rail,” Isla said. Her phone was in her hand. No signal. She rang the emergency coordination number and it died before it connected. She rang Wei Long. Nothing. At 4:16 she typed a message on the third landing with Paulina leaning on her shoulder.

Earthquake. I’m safe at the moment. Trying to get out of the building.

One grey tick. She put the phone in her pocket and went on down.

The street was full of people standing in the middle of the road looking up at the buildings. Dust hung in the air and turned the afternoon light the colour of milk. A siren started somewhere beyond the junction, then another, then too many to count. Half the façade of the building opposite was lying on two parked cars. The embassy behind her was still standing, with a long crack across its front and its glass in the street.

“Everyone from our floor?” she asked the warden with the list.

“Almost. Not Hernán.”

“Don’t go back in. Check the assembly point first.”

The ground moved again, not as violently, and everyone on the pavement stopped talking at once. She waited until it passed. Then she started counting heads.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before six on Friday morning, thirteen hours ahead of Lima on the clock and thirty-eight minutes after the ground moved there, Wei Long’s phone rang on the bedside table and he had it before his eyes were open.

“Sir. Turn on the news. Earthquake in Lima. A big one. Off the coast. They’re saying there’s damage along the whole seafront.” It was Liu.

He was already out of bed. “Isla?”

“I don’t know, sir. I tried her. Nothing.”

The first footage was shaky, filmed on a phone from a pavement: people in the street, a row of buildings with their fronts torn off, dust everywhere. The presenter repeated the location and a magnitude that was being revised as she spoke. The map put the epicentre offshore, south-west of the city. Four o’clock local time. He looked at the clock. 5:44. He rang her. It failed. He rang again. He opened their messages. Hers was at the top, received just after five, half an hour ago: safe at the moment, and the word earthquake, and building. It had come through on some fragment of signal and there was nothing after it. He read it until the words stopped meaning anything. He rang her again.

“Liu. Find out which districts. Reliable sources only. No social media.”

“Yes, sir.”

He rang the ministry’s emergency line for citizens abroad. A recorded voice in English and then French. He chose the option for emergencies and was put in a queue, and stood in the kitchen in his shirt with the television going and the hold music playing in his ear. When a person answered at last he used the voice he used at work.

“My name is Song Wei Long. I’m calling about an officer of yours posted to the embassy in Lima. Isla Ren, deputy head of consular. I need confirmation of her welfare and the status of the consular team.”

“Are you a family member, sir?”

“No.”

“Then I can only take your details and pass them through the proper channel.”

“Please put me through to the emergency coordination desk.”

“That line is busy.”

“Then please try again.”

It was 6:05. By half past six he was dressed. He hadn’t shaved. His coffee stood cold on the counter. He’d packed nothing, because he didn’t yet know whether there was anywhere he could go.

✦ ✦ ✦

He rang again and got a different person, and changed his approach. He stopped being a private man asking for news. He gave the information in the order a duty officer would want it: name, post, role, date of arrival, last known contact, the time of that contact, its exact words, the fact that it had never been acknowledged. He didn’t exaggerate. He didn’t say she was missing. He didn’t say she was hurt. He said that he had no confirmation of where she was or how she was, and asked for the enquiry to be logged for follow-up.

“Someone will contact you if we have information.”

“When?”

“I can’t give you a time.”

“Then tell me who’s responsible for the follow-up.” He wrote down the name and a reference number in his notebook, and the time beside it, and thanked the man, and put the phone down, and picked it up and rang again.

Just after seven the first casualty figure appeared. It was small enough to be called preliminary and real enough to be a number. He read it twice and checked where it came from and when. Deaths in several districts, hundreds injured, buildings down. He opened a map of Lima. He knew where her flat was. He knew the route between it and the embassy. He knew the cliffs she’d described and the market and the building with the lift that sounded like a dying animal. He didn’t know which streets were standing. He scrolled back through their messages to the night before. A photograph of a plate of food: I have eaten. Don’t ask. I was going to ask. A picture of the empty plate: Evidence. Insufficient. No timestamp. She’d called him ridiculous. He’d said she was welcome. An ordinary conversation. He’d have given anything to have another one.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past eight Liu found him in the briefing room in front of the big television with his phone in one hand and his notebook in the other. There were numbers on the page with times beside them. One was crossed out. One was underlined twice.

Liu put a paper cup by his elbow. “Coffee, sir. You haven’t slept.”

“I’m aware.”

“Have you eaten?”

“Don’t.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You were going to.”

On the screen a street where the upper floors of a block had come down onto the lower ones like a concertina, and men in orange climbing over it, and a reporter behind a tape. The camera moved and for a second showed a kind of building he recognised from her photographs, narrow-fronted with balconies and shops underneath. His attention sharpened.

“Where’s that?”

Liu read the caption. “Near the centre, I think. I’ll check.”

He drank the coffee. It was cold. He drank it anyway.

At 9:46 he rang the ministry with his reference number. The enquiry was open. Lima hadn’t responded. The operator could request a callback.

“I have requested one. Please escalate it.”

“Sir, I appreciate that you’re worried, but...”

Wei Long said, “I’m not asking you to make an exception to your procedure. I’m asking you to tell me who is responsible for confirming the welfare of this officer. Please tell me who is responsible.” His voice hadn’t risen at all, which was what made it cut.

He was put on hold. Just after ten a woman came on who said that the ministry was trying to make contact with all its people in the affected area and couldn’t give him individual information without authorisation, but would attach his enquiry to the emergency record.

“Has the consular team reported in?”

“Not at this stage.”

He thanked her. Liu was watching him.

“You should sit down, sir. You’ve been standing for five hours.”

“That isn’t a medical condition.”

“It’s becoming one,” said Liu, and Wei Long looked at the screen and said, “I need to know where she is,” and Liu didn’t answer, because there was nothing useful to say.

✦ ✦ ✦

By noon the figures disagreed. One source gave a lower number, one included the missing, one said teams were still searching buildings where people were thought to be trapped. He kept a record of every update and wouldn’t use a number until he knew who’d issued it and when. The distinction mattered. It didn’t make the numbers any easier to read. At 1:40 his phone buzzed.

Ren Hao (Civil): I’ve seen the news. Have you heard from her?

Wei Long: No. Her last message was 4:16 p.m. Lima time. She said she was trying to leave the building.

Ren Hao (Civil): Have you called the ministry?

Wei Long: Four times. There’s an enquiry open.

Ren Hao (Civil): I’m calling everyone I can reach.

Wei Long: Don’t pass on anything unverified.

Ren Hao (Civil): I know. Wei Long. Tell me if you hear anything.

Wei Long: I will.

At 3:15 the confirmed dead passed a hundred. Just after four, two hundred. The news showed a residential block that had collapsed floor onto floor, and the camera stayed back, but you could see the scale of it, and the people behind the barriers holding photographs up at the rescuers, and a man in a dressing gown sitting on the kerb with his face in his hands.

He’d spent his career separating what he knew from what he suspected. He knew the time of the earthquake. He knew the districts. He knew the phone network was down. He knew she’d sent one message saying she was safe at that moment and trying to get out. He didn’t know whether she’d reached the street. He didn’t know whether she’d gone home, or whether she was hurt, or whether she was standing somewhere with a dead phone in her pocket thinking of him. The message was still on his screen and its simplicity had become unbearable. Just after five that evening, exactly twelve hours after it was sent, he opened it again. One grey tick. He touched the screen. There wasn’t.

At half past five the superintendent came down himself and told him to go home and do his waiting there, and Wei Long didn’t argue, because there was nothing he could do at the station that he couldn’t do in the flat. He drove back with the radio on. The count had passed three hundred. He put his keys in the dish and turned the television on before he’d taken his coat off.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after eight Ren Hao rang.

“Anything?”

“No.”

“I got through to their overseas desk. Same answer. They’re trying to account for their people. Have you eaten?” A pause. Ren Hao’s voice changed.

“Yes.”

“Don’t lie to me.”

Wei Long looked at the takeaway on the table, untouched. “No.”

Ren Hao breathed out. “She’s going to be furious with both of us when they find her. She’ll tell me to stop ringing everyone and she’ll tell you to sleep, and she’ll be right.”

“Yes.”

“Wei Long.”

“I’m here.”

“Ring me the second you hear. Even half of something,” said Ren Hao, and rang off, and Wei Long realised that in fifteen months he’d never once heard Ren Hao leave a silence alone, and tonight he had.

The phone went around half past ten and he was on his feet before the first ring finished.

“Mr. Song? This is the emergency coordination desk, about your welfare enquiry. We’ve had an update from the consular team in Lima. Some staff have been located and are safe. We’re still confirming individual names.”

“Is Isla Ren among them?”

“I don’t have her name confirmed yet.”

“Then what can you tell me?”

“That the team is working from an established assembly point, and we’re waiting for the next staff list.”

“Where?”

“I can’t give you that on this call.”

He shut his eyes. “Injuries?”

“I don’t have that. Your enquiry stays open.” He heard her turn a page.

“Please don’t close it.”

“We won’t,” she said, and he thanked her and wrote down 10:41 p.m. Consular team at assembly point. Not confirmed by name. Hardly an answer, but the first sign that there was somewhere for an answer to come from. He rang Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two in the morning he’d stopped sitting at the table. He was on the sofa with his phone in one hand and the remote in the other, turning the sound down and then up again whenever a presenter began a new report. He knew which channels were repeating themselves. He’d learned not to trust a photograph without a date on it.

At 2:47 he rang her. Failed. At 2:48 he wrote: I’m here. Ring when you can. At 3:12: I’ve spoken to the ministry. They’re accounting for the consular team. At 3:56 he rang again. He put the phone down on the table, face up, and the screen stayed dark.

He’d imagined a great many versions of her coming home. Her walking into the flat with her case, complaining about the flight, putting her bag down in the wrong place, telling him his Spanish had got worse while she’d been gone, and him kissing her before she’d finished the sentence. Meeting her at arrivals. The two of them arguing over who got to take the first holiday. He hadn’t imagined this.

He opened the photograph she’d sent the week before: a market stall, fruit in bright rows, her hand at the edge of the frame. I found the best peaches. You said that last week. These are better. Evidence? She’d sent him a picture of herself eating one, laughing, juice on her chin. He looked at it, and then he held the phone flat against his palm with his hand closed over it, the way you’d hold someone’s hand in a hospital corridor.

By four in the morning at home it was three on Friday afternoon in Lima, nearly a day after the ground first moved, and the ministry hadn’t confirmed her name. He was standing in front of the television. The count was past three hundred and rising. He had spent the night calling, checking, asking, recording and waiting. He’d spoken to the ministry in three different voices: the measured voice of a professional asking for information, the exact voice of a man who knew precisely how an emergency enquiry ought to be handled, and the voice of a man trying not to beg a stranger to tell him whether the woman he loved was alive. None of them had brought her back to him.

He rang her once more. The line failed. He didn’t swear. He didn’t throw the phone. He stood there listening to the dead tone until it stopped, and then he opened their messages. I’m safe at the moment. He’d spent years in rooms with people waiting for news they couldn’t control. He knew what not knowing did to a mind; how it took every empty space and filled it with something terrible. Knowing that didn’t help at all.

At 4:16 he sent one more.

Wei Long: I love you. I’m waiting.

He put the phone down beside him on the sofa, and the television went on talking, and on the far side of the world the ground had still not entirely stopped moving.

chapters.title: She Calls From the Embassy’s Shelter
chapters.desc: Two minutes on a satellite phone from the embassy’s shelter. “I’m fine.” He hears the sirens. Four hundred of her citizens are unaccounted for. “I’m coming.” “You can’t.” “Watch me.”
chapters.epigraph: “Watch me.”
chapters.content:
Isla hadn’t seen daylight since Thursday night.

The engineers had cleared the embassy’s lower floor a little after nine, and the staff and the citizens who’d come to the gates had been brought in off the street into the reinforced shelter under the building: concrete, no windows, emergency lighting, water in pallets along one wall. Upstairs a section of the façade had come down, one stairwell had been closed after an inspection, and nobody was allowed above the third floor. Down here people sat against the walls in foil blankets with phones that had been dead for hours. A child slept on a pile of coats. A man in a business suit kept asking anyone who passed whether the airport was open.

She’d spent the night with two colleagues and a laptop on a generator, building a list. Every citizen who’d turned up at the gates. Every name a family had rung through to the ministry at home before the lines failed. Every hotel register they could get. By the middle of Friday the number on the screen was four hundred.

Four hundred of her country’s people in the affected area whose whereabouts nobody could confirm. Not four hundred dead, not four hundred missing, even. Four hundred names nobody had yet been able to put a place beside. She had said that distinction out loud three times since breakfast, to three different people. It didn’t make the list any easier to look at.

“There’s another family at the door. Their son was staying near the seafront,” said Paulina, with her arm in a sling now.

“Get the reception team to take everything. Full name, date of birth, where he was staying, when anyone last heard from him, a number we can reach them on.”

“They want to know if we can send someone to look.”

“We can’t promise that until we know which streets are passable. Tell them we’re recording it and passing it to the local authorities tonight. And tell them I’m sorry. Say it in those words.” Isla rubbed her eyes.

Her phone was on nine percent. She’d been keeping it switched off between attempts, because the network was a rumour and there was no point spending the last of the battery on calls that died before they rang. At twenty to six in the evening one of the security officers came down the stairs with a satellite phone held up over his head like a trophy.

“We’ve got a window. Two minutes each. Staff first, then the citizens.”

She didn’t need to look the number up. She’d known it by heart since the night she typed Inspector Glacier into her contacts.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before seven on Saturday morning his phone rang with a number he’d never seen, a long string of digits that began with something that wasn’t a country.

“Hello?”

A burst of static. Then a voice.

“Wei Long?”

He stood up so fast the chair behind him hit the wall.

“Isla.”

“It’s me.”

He shut his eyes. He couldn’t say anything at all. Behind her voice there were other voices, a lot of them, and something that sounded like an alarm going somewhere far off.

“I’m here. I’m at the embassy. We’re in the shelter,” she said.

“Are you hurt?”

“No.”

“Are you certain?”

“Yes. I’ve got a cut on my hand from a window. It’s nothing. I’m not hurt.”

He looked down at the notebook on the table. For twenty-six hours he’d been looking at a message that stopped at safe at the moment. Now she was talking. He could hear her breathe. He could hear the room she was in. She was alive.

“Where were you when it happened?”

“In my office. We got everyone off our floor and down the stairs. The building’s damaged but it’s standing. We came back in when the engineers cleared the basement.”

“Your flat?”

“I don’t know. The roads to it are blocked.”

“Is there food? Water? A doctor?”

“Yes. Yes. There’s a medical team. Are you going to ask whether I’ve eaten?” He heard her laugh, faint and worn through.

“Yes.”

“Half a sandwich.”

“That isn’t much.”

“It’s what there was. Wei Long?” The line broke into hiss and came back.

“I’m here. Listen to me. I’m coming.”

A pause. Then, distinctly, “You can’t.”

“Watch me.”

“You can’t fly into a disaster zone because you couldn’t get hold of me.”

“I know.”

“Then don’t decide something because you’re frightened.”

He looked at the television. The banner under the pictures said three hundred and eighty-seven confirmed dead. Under that, a scroll of warnings and transport restrictions.

He said, “I’ve spent a day and a night finding out whether you were alive. I’m not going to pretend that hasn’t changed what I want to do.”

“I know. I want you here too.” She said the second part lower.

“Then let me come.”

“The airport’s half closed. Half the roads are cracked. We don’t know what next week looks like.”

“I can find that out.”

“You can find it out. You can’t make it safer by turning up without a plan.”

“Then I’ll make a plan. How long have we got?” The interference was coming in bursts now.

“A minute. Less.”

“Tell me what you need. Right now.”

She was quiet. “Your voice.”

He held the phone hard enough to hurt. “You have it.”

“I may not get the phone again for a while. If I can’t ring, don’t assume...”

“I won’t.”

“And don’t watch the news all night.”

He said nothing.

“Wei Long.”

“I’ll try.”

“That isn’t a promise.”

“No.”

She laughed, a small worn-out laugh. “Stubborn man.”

“Isla, I...”

The line went dead. He looked at the screen. Two minutes and eleven seconds. He put the phone down on the table, and sat down in the chair that had hit the wall, slowly, as if his body had only just remembered it was allowed to move.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before seven he rang Ren Hao, who picked up before it rang.

“Did you hear?”

“She rang. From the embassy shelter. She isn’t hurt.”

There was a sound on the line like a man letting go of a breath he’d been holding for a day. “Oh, thank God. Thank God. You spoke to her?”

“Two minutes. A satellite phone. A cut on her hand. Nothing else.”

“Two minutes,” said Ren Hao, and swore under his breath, and then laughed, and then didn’t say anything for long enough that Wei Long understood he couldn’t. “Are you going?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

“I need to know what’s flying. Whether the airport’s open. What the ministry advises.”

“I’ll make calls from my side.”

“Don’t get in the way of the response.”

“I’m not an idiot.”

“I’m aware,” said Wei Long, and Ren Hao laughed again, and said, “Say it.”

“Say what?”

“She’s alive. Say it out loud.”

He looked at the notebook. “She’s alive.”

“Good. Keep saying it till you believe it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

There was a missed call on his phone from three in the morning that he hadn’t seen, from a Vancouver number, and a voicemail he didn’t need to play. Item three on her list on the fridge: My mother will ring you. Answer. He’d been on the line to the ministry. He rang back.

It was four on Friday afternoon there. Her father answered on the first ring.

“Professor Ren. It’s Wei Long. She rang me twenty minutes ago. She’s at the embassy, in the shelter. She isn’t hurt.”

There was no sound on the line at all. Then, a long way off from the phone, her father said something in a voice Wei Long hadn’t heard him use on any video call, and he heard her mother make a sound that wasn’t a word, and then the phone was being passed, clumsily, and her mother was on it.

“You spoke to her? Her voice?”

“Yes. Two minutes. A satellite phone. She has a cut on her hand from a window and nothing else. She’d eaten half a sandwich.”

Her mother laughed and cried at the same time. “Of course she had. Of course you asked.”

“Yes.”

“Did she sound...” Her mother stopped.

“She sounded tired,” said Wei Long, “and like herself. She told me not to come.”

“Are you going to?”

“Yes.”

There was a pause on the line in which he could hear the house in Vancouver, a clock, a dog somewhere outside, the professor breathing behind his wife’s shoulder.

“Good. Thank you for ringing us. Thank you for answering. We rang you at three in the morning. I’m sorry,” said her mother.

“Item three,” he said, and she didn’t understand, and he didn’t explain, and her father came back on the line and said only, “Thank you, Wei Long,” in the voice of a man who had read a great deal and found that none of it was any use to him this morning, and rang off.

✦ ✦ ✦

By eight the flat was no longer a place he was waiting in. He had the travel advisories open on the laptop and a pad beside it. The airport was operating with restrictions and the airline couldn’t promise that a booking would turn into a departure. He rang the ministry and asked for whoever handled advice for staff families travelling into the affected area, and said he was Isla Ren’s partner and had direct confirmation that she was sheltering at the embassy, and wanted to know what was possible and what wasn’t. Non-essential travel was strongly discouraged. Travel for family members of posted staff was being coordinated case by case. He could register an intention to travel. He did.

Then he rang the emergency desk with his reference number and asked whether her location had been confirmed on the staff record. The woman wouldn’t read him the record, but she confirmed that Isla Ren had checked in at the embassy shelter. He wrote it down.

17 October, 08:37. Isla Ren confirmed at embassy shelter.

He looked at the sentence until the words stopped being words. Not the same as seeing her, but something he could put his hand on.

✦ ✦ ✦

In Lima it was Friday night, and the list was still four hundred long, give or take a dozen who’d turned up at a hospital or rung a cousin. Isla worked through it with a colleague at a trestle table under the emergency lights. You had to be careful not to count people twice when they’d been reported through three different channels. You had to tell apart the people who were genuinely missing from the people who couldn’t reach anyone. You had to write down where every report had come from. A name on the list wasn’t a death. A call that didn’t connect wasn’t an injury. A message from a sister saying I think he’s at the Hotel Costa wasn’t confirmation that anyone had found him.

“This one. Last seen at a hotel by the cliffs.”

“Has the hotel answered?”

“Not yet.”

“Pending. Don’t move her into missing until we know the hotel has actually checked its rooms, floor by floor, with a person and not a computer.”

At ten a woman came down the stairs with her husband holding her up and asked whether the embassy could send someone to find their daughter, who’d been at a language school in the centre and hadn’t been heard from since Thursday. Isla wanted to say yes. She wanted to promise somebody would go now, that the authorities would find the girl, that the next call would be good news.

She said, “We’re coordinating with the local emergency services. I’ll make sure everything you’ve told me goes to the team doing the welfare checks tonight. I won’t promise you something I can’t guarantee.”

The woman began to cry. Isla stayed with her. She didn’t look at her phone, which had died at nine, or think about the man at the other end of the world who’d said watch me in the voice he used for things he’d already decided.

Later, at the trestle table, a colleague put a wrapped meal and a bottle of water down in front of her.

“You need to eat.”

“I know.”

“You said that yesterday.”

“Then I’m consistent,” said Isla, and opened it, and found that her hands were shaking.

Somebody had a power bank and she sat against the wall with her phone plugged into it, and at 11:20 by her clock, for about forty seconds, a single bar of signal came up in the corner of the screen. She had a message from him. It had been sitting in a queue on some broken mast since four in the morning his time.

I love you. I’m waiting.

She read it with the phone pressed against her mouth. Then she typed as fast as she’d ever typed anything.

Thank You (Paid): I’m still in the shelter. I’m safe. We’re working the list. I wish you were here.

The bar went. The message hung, and went, and showed one grey tick, and then two.

✦ ✦ ✦

It reached him around half past twelve on Saturday afternoon, at the station, where he’d gone in his own clothes on his day off to see the superintendent.

He read it standing in the corridor outside the superintendent’s door. Two ticks. She’d seen his. He typed back.

Wei Long: So do I. I’m working on it.

It sat on one tick. He didn’t mind. She’d get it when the mast let her. He put the phone in his pocket and knocked on the door with a leave application in his other hand that he’d filled in at the kitchen table at half past seven, in his neatest capitals, with the dates left blank, because for the first time in his working life he didn’t yet know when he’d be back.

chapters.title: He Takes Leave for the First Time in Six Years
chapters.desc: He takes leave for the first time in six years. His sergeant takes the cases without being asked. Ren Hao books the only seat left and pays for it, loudly; he’s on a break from Song-Zhu and badly needs something to fix.
chapters.epigraph: “Six years is a long time, Song. Don’t make it seven.”
chapters.content:
The superintendent read the leave application twice, which Wei Long had seen him do only with confessions.

“The dates are blank.”

“I don’t know when I’ll be back, sir. I’ll fill them in when I have a flight.”

“You’ve confirmed she’s safe?”

“At the embassy shelter. Confirmed on the ministry’s record at 8:37 this morning.”

“And you understand that getting to Lima may not mean getting to her. That you may not be allowed into the affected districts at all.”

“Yes.”

“Then what exactly are you asking me for?”

“Leave. And to be sure I can go without leaving a hole in the team.”

The superintendent put the form down. “You’ve already decided.”

“Yes, sir.”

“I’m not going to tell you not to go. I’ll tell you not to make yourself another person their emergency services have to account for. Don’t go into restricted areas. Don’t try to talk your way through roadblocks. Don’t turn up at the embassy and expect them to stop what they’re doing to escort you anywhere. You have no warrant card in Lima. You’re a man with a passport.” He folded his hands on the desk.

“I know.”

“Keep us informed. Now go and find Hau before he finds you.” He signed the bottom of the form without filling in the dates.

✦ ✦ ✦

Station Sergeant Hau was waiting outside the door. He’d been at the station for twenty-two years and on Wei Long’s floor for six, and he was the only man in the building who called the inspector by his surname to his face when he thought he was being an idiot.

“Song.”

“Hau.”

“Six years. Six years since you took proper leave.” Hau looked at the form in his hand.

“I’ve taken days.”

“You took a day when the station flooded, a day when you’d had your appendix out, and a day when the superintendent sent you home with a fever of thirty-nine and you came back after lunch. Who’s taking your cases?” Hau followed him into his office.

“I’ll prepare a handover.”

“I didn’t ask you to prepare a handover. I’ll take them.” Hau held out his hand for the case list.

“You have your own caseload.”

“I do.”

“There’s an interview on Monday.”

“I’ve seen it.”

“The evidence review on the harbour fraud...”

“Is with Yik. The robbery file’s with Sham. I’ll do the custody applications. Liu can take the witness follow-ups, provided you stop giving him things that need three forms and a magnifying glass. He has to be allowed home now and then.” Hau took the list off the desk himself.

Wei Long looked at him. Hau looked back, with the expression of a man who had made up his mind about something on Thursday morning while watching the inspector stand in front of a television for six hours.

“Thank you,” said Wei Long.

“Don’t thank me. I haven’t seen your handover notes.”

“They’re complete.”

“Of course they are. Six years is a long time, Song. Don’t make it seven.” Hau went to the door, and stopped.

The handover took him an hour. He’d spent years making sure any of his files could be understood by someone who wasn’t him: notes current, exhibits referenced, enquiries listed, every deadline marked. Hau read the first two pages and looked up.

“You’ve put the next court date beside every file. And the officer. And the outstanding actions.”

“Yes.”

“Did you think about adding a line that says Sergeant Hau can read?”

“I didn’t think it was necessary.”

“I’ll be reachable for urgent...”

“No. You’re on leave. If something’s genuinely urgent the superintendent rings you. You’re not going to be sitting in Lima reading statements at three in the morning. Take your work phone off.”

“I need it for the...”

“You have a personal phone.”

Wei Long looked at him, and took the work phone out of his pocket, and put it in his desk drawer, and locked the drawer.

“Thank you,” said Hau.

“For what?”

“Making my morning harder than it needed to be. Go to Lima.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao rang at a quarter past one. “Where are you?”

“Home.”

“Don’t move. I’m coming over.”

“Why?”

“Because you are apparently incapable of booking a plane without turning it into a three-day administrative project.”

He arrived twenty-three minutes later with a laptop bag and a paper cup of coffee and the face of a man who had decided everyone around him was being inefficient, and took one look at the dining table, the advisories, the pad, the itineraries in Wei Long’s small handwriting with their connection times underlined, and stopped.

“You haven’t booked.”

“The airport’s under restrictions. The connection isn’t guaranteed. The ministry advises against...”

“I know. Wei Long. I’ve been awake since five. I’ve spoken to two people at the ministry, one airline, and a man who seemed to think the status of an airport was classified. There’s one route that gets you there without a forty-hour wait. One seat left on it. Tonight, five to midnight, through the Pacific hub, into Lima at half past twelve tomorrow afternoon their time. The last leg is scheduled to operate.” He opened the laptop.

Wei Long looked at the screen. “It’s business class.”

“It’s the only seat.”

“I can go economy.”

“Then go economy next time. I’m paying.” Ren Hao’s hands were already on the keys.

“I can pay for my own ticket.”

“I know you can. I’m paying.”

Wei Long caught his wrist. Ren Hao looked up. Neither of them said anything.

“Let me do this. Please. I need to fix something. Let it be this,” said Ren Hao, and his voice had gone quiet in a way it never went.

Wei Long let go. The payment went through. A booking reference came up on the screen: one passenger, one seat, Lima, and the thing he’d been arranging in his head for two days had become a fact.

“Thank you,” he said.

“Don’t. Bring her home when she’s ready. And I’m not telling her I paid. She’ll say I spent too much.” Ren Hao picked up his coffee.

“She’ll know.”

“Then it was a business expense. I run a global risk firm. I can make anything a business expense.”

Wei Long nearly smiled, and Ren Hao saw, and said, “Good. At least one of us can still look alive.”

✦ ✦ ✦

There was something wrong with him. Wei Long noticed it when Ren Hao sat down and didn’t immediately start talking. His phone lit up twice beside his coffee and both times he glanced at it and turned it over.

“What’s happened?”

“Nothing.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

Ren Hao laughed, short. “You sound like her.”

“I’m told that’s a problem.”

“Sometimes. Song-Zhu and I are on a break. Since the nineteenth of September.” He looked at the window.

Wei Long waited.

“That’s all? You’re not going to ask why?”

“Do you want me to?”

“No.”

“Then I won’t.”

“That’s surprisingly considerate.”

“I’m capable of it.”

“I know. Isla keeps telling me. It’s the crash. The jet that went into the sea on approach on the second of August. She’s leading the recorders. A hundred and eighty people, and the data stops eleven seconds early, and she hasn’t slept since, and I kept... organising her. Food. Drivers. Making her sleep. She told me she was my girlfriend and not my equipment. She was right. She usually is. I keep wanting to know when she’ll be finished, whether she’s eaten, whether she’s sleeping. I know how that sounds.” Ren Hao turned the phone over and over in his fingers. He rubbed his face.

“It sounds familiar,” said Wei Long.

Ren Hao stared at him, and then laughed, once, under his breath. “Right. Fair. We didn’t stop caring. We just couldn’t keep having the same argument.” He was silent.

“Do you want to be with her?”

“Yes.” No pause at all.

“Then I hope you work it out.”

“That’s it?”

“Would you prefer a written statement?”

“Maybe. You’re good at those. Sorry. Too soon.” Ren Hao grinned.

“Your sister will ask about her. She’ll tell you to stop behaving like an idiot. Then she’ll ask whether you’ve eaten,” said Wei Long.

“She’ll be unbearable.”

“Yes,” said Wei Long, and for the first time that afternoon Ren Hao looked properly amused.

✦ ✦ ✦

Packing took less time than he’d expected. One case, one carry-on, documents, chargers, a change of clothes. He checked his passport and his ticket twice. Then he opened the kitchen cupboard.

The tea was on the second shelf, in its tin. The evening kind she liked, that she’d left in the flat in July. Four packets had become three; he’d had one in August on a bad night, and not told her. He took the tin down and put it in the carry-on.

Ren Hao was in the doorway. “What are you doing?”

“Packing.”

“Is that tea?”

“Hers.”

“You’re taking her tea to Lima.”

“She might want it.”

Ren Hao looked at the case, and the carry-on, and the tin. “One bag and a bag of tea. That’s your entire packing strategy.”

“I don’t need much.”

“She’s going to laugh at you.”

“Probably.”

Ren Hao smiled, and then didn’t. “Bring her back when she can come. And don’t make her feel she has to leave before she’s ready.”

“I won’t.”

At the door at four he held out his hand, and when Wei Long took it, pulled him into a short, hard hug that Wei Long, this time, returned.

“Ring me when you land. Don’t go into restricted areas. Don’t argue with the local police. Don’t buy a car.”

“Why would I buy a car?”

“I don’t know. You seem like the kind of man who’d decide walking was inefficient and purchase a vehicle. I’m covering possibilities. Thank you for going.” Ren Hao stepped back.

“She’s my partner.”

“I know. That’s why I’m thanking you,” said Ren Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight the satellite phone came through again. It was seven on Saturday morning in Lima and the line was better than the day before, a faint crackle under her voice instead of a storm.

“Are you packed?”

“One case. A carry-on.”

“What’s in the carry-on?”

“Documents. Chargers. Your tea.”

There was a silence on the line, and then she laughed, really laughed, for the first time in two days. “My tea? You’re bringing my tea all the way to Lima?”

“You asked me to bring something from home.”

“I meant something sentimental.”

“It is sentimental. It’s your tea.”

She laughed again, and he could hear how tired she was underneath it. “Hao says he paid for your seat.”

“He did.”

“I told him you could pay for yourself.”

“So did I. He ignored both of us.”

“That sounds like my brother. Is he all right? He sounds like a man who needs something to fix.”

“I think he found it.”

“He told you about Song-Zhu.”

“Yes.”

“I don’t know what’s going to happen with them,” she said.

“You don’t have to know tonight.”

Someone called her name somewhere behind her. “I have to go. The list’s down to three hundred and twelve. Hospitals, cousins, a man who’d been in a bar in Miraflores the whole time with no battery and didn’t think to tell anyone.”

“Have you slept?”

“A little. Wei Long. You know you might land and not be able to get to me straight away.”

“I know. I’ll follow the ministry and the local police. If I can’t reach the embassy I’ll wait until I can.”

“Look at you. Following instructions,” said Isla.

“I’m capable.”

“Sometimes. I wish I could be at the airport when you land.” Her voice dropped.

“I know.”

“I want to hold you.”

He looked at the case by the door. “So do I. Don’t stay awake all day.”

“That’s my line.”

“I’m borrowing it.”

“I love you,” she said.

“I love you,” said Wei Long, and the line went.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten he stood in the bedroom with the lights off. His work phone was locked in a drawer at the station. His ticket was on his phone, his passport was in his jacket, and the tea was packed. He checked the passport again. He didn’t need to check it a third time, and didn’t.

For six years he’d treated leave as something you put off. There was always another interview, another operation, another report to sign. Next week would be quieter. Next month would be better. There would be time. He had never been much good at imagining the work going on without him. Now Hau had taken the cases without being asked, and the station would run, and the reports would get written and the witnesses interviewed, and the world wouldn’t stop because Inspector Song wasn’t at his desk. He found that uncomfortable to understand, and found it a relief.

On his way out he stopped at the fridge. Her list was still there under its magnet, seven items in her handwriting, the paper curling at one corner from the steam off the kettle. He’d done most of them. He’d watered the plant once a week, not once a day. He’d answered her mother. He’d slept on her side, and been caught. He took the pen out of his jacket and wrote underneath, in his small square capitals, an eighth item.

8. I’m coming. W.L.

He looked at it. It was the first thing he’d ever added to a list of hers without being asked, and it looked strange there, his handwriting under hers, the way his books had looked on her shelf the first night. He took a photograph of it and sent it, knowing it would sit on one grey tick somewhere over the Pacific until a mast in Lima let it through, and that she’d see it on Sunday morning with her coffee, or on Sunday afternoon when he was already standing in front of her, whichever came first.

He locked the door with the key with the white label, and put it in his pocket, and went down to the taxi in the rain.

chapters.title: He Flies to Her
chapters.desc: His warrant card means nothing at the checkpoint. He finds her asleep on a desk on the ninth floor, a list under her cheek, slides it out without reading it, and waits. She wakes and kisses him before she’s sure he’s real. Then he carries water up nine flights for nine hours.
chapters.epigraph: “I didn’t come to take you home.”
chapters.content:
His warrant card was the first thing he put away.

At the airport in Lima it had been some use, as a way of explaining to a tired immigration officer who he was and why a man with one case and no hotel was arriving into a city that had been told not to expect visitors. At the police checkpoint two streets from the embassy it was worth less than his passport. The officer looked at the photograph, looked at him, and handed it back with a courteous face that made the distinction perfectly clear. Whatever it meant at home, it didn’t travel. He wasn’t an inspector here. He had no jurisdiction and no rank and no business inside a building where people were running an emergency. He was a man who’d crossed half the world because the woman he loved was in a city that had stopped behaving predictably, and he understood the difference.

He showed his passport, gave her name, and waited by the barrier with his case against his leg while somebody rang somebody. The ground was cracked across the road in a long zigzag that had been painted round in orange. The building opposite had lost its front and you could see into its rooms like a doll’s house: a bed, a picture still on a wall, a kitchen tap hanging from a pipe.

The woman who came out to meet him had the face of somebody who’d slept four hours since Thursday.

“Inspector Song?”

“I’m not here in any official capacity.”

She looked at his passport. “Mr. Song, then. She’s inside. The consular section’s working from the ninth floor since its own offices were damaged. There are restrictions on where you can go in the building.”

“I’ll follow them.”

“And you understand that you can’t take part in any decision or see any record.”

“I understand.”

She seemed relieved not to have to explain it twice. “Come with me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The building smelled of dust and disinfectant and too many people living on too little sleep. Handwritten arrows on paper were taped to the walls: AGUA, MÉDICO, a red cross. Boxes stood in corridors where they’d become useful instead of in the way. People sat against the walls in blankets. A man slept upright in a plastic chair. Every movement had a purpose and every conversation seemed to end with a name.

“She’s had breaks when we made her. She’s hard to persuade,” the woman said on the stairs.

That sounded familiar.

The lift had a notice taped across its doors. They climbed. On the ninth floor the woman opened a door into a room that had been an open-plan office and was now a collection of desks and folding tables and extension leads. Someone was talking low into a headset. Someone was sorting paper into piles on the floor. A printer produced a page every few seconds with a small mechanical complaint.

“Wait here. I’ll tell her.”

He looked past her and saw Isla. She was asleep at the far end of the room, folded forward over a desk with one arm under her head. A printed list lay under her cheek, its edge creasing the skin. Her hair had come down from whatever she’d done with it that morning. There was still a pen between two of her fingers.

He didn’t move. He’d watched the footage of the streets until it repeated itself. He’d listened to people say the numbers in more and more careful voices. None of it had prepared him for her asleep in a chair too low for the desk, in a room that smelled of paper and dust, with a list of missing people under her face.

“She dropped off about twenty minutes ago. We tried to move her to the rest room. She said she’d only close her eyes for a minute,” said the woman, low.

“Has she eaten?”

The woman gave him a look.

“I’ll take that as no.”

“She’s been safe since Thursday. The cut on her hand was cleaned and dressed. She’s all right, Mr. Song,” said the woman, and her voice was kinder.

“Thank you,” he said, and she left them with a glance.

He put his case down by the wall and walked across the room. He’d imagined this a dozen times between the hub and Lima, and in none of them had she been asleep.

He pulled a chair up beside the desk without scraping it and sat down. Then, so as not to wake her, he lifted the corner of the list off her cheek and slid it out from under her and laid it on the clear part of the desk without reading it, keeping the pages in their order. There was a red line on her cheek from the paper. The cut on her right hand had a clean white dressing. He wanted to touch her. He took his jacket off instead and hung it on the back of the chair, and sat, and waited. He’d waited three days. He could wait twenty minutes more.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke the way people wake when they didn’t mean to sleep: a frown first, then her fingers moving, then her head coming up off her arm. She looked at the desk, at the list that wasn’t under her face any more, at the chair beside her. Then she looked at him, and for one suspended second she didn’t seem to understand what she was seeing at all.

“Isla,” he said.

She didn’t stand up, or ask how he’d got there, or whether he’d been delayed, or any of the things he’d prepared answers to. She reached for him. Her chair went back with a scrape that made half the room look up, and she caught his face in both her hands and kissed him, and she still wasn’t sure he was real. He could feel it. She kissed him as if checking, her fingers trembling on his cheeks, as if the whole distance between them had been a clerical error that could be corrected by pressing her mouth to his. He stood up and caught her round the waist, and for several seconds neither of them did anything but hold on.

Then she pulled back far enough to look at him.

“You’re here.”

“Yes.”

“You’re actually here. How?”

“Plane.”

A laugh broke out of her, so close to a sob that he tightened his arms. “Did you eat?”

“On the aircraft. Technically,” he said, and she laughed again, with more air in it, and put her forehead against his chest, and he told her, into her hair, that he had her tea.
