She went still. “You brought it.”

“It was in the bag.”

“That isn’t the same as denying it.”

“I’m not denying it.”

Her hands went round his back and closed in the cloth of his shirt, and for a while he didn’t ask her anything, and she held on.

“I thought I’d have to do all of this without you. I kept thinking, if I can just get through the next hour I can ring you properly. And there was another list. Another family. Another hospital. I couldn’t stop,” she whispered.

He said, “No, I don’t know what it was like. Not exactly. I know you were frightened and kept going. And I know you should have been allowed to sleep somewhere better than that chair.”

She laughed shakily. “That’s what you’re angry about?”

“I’m not angry. I’m tired.”

“You look as if you’ve flown here to arrest the furniture.”

“I might,” he said, and she laughed into his shoulder and then kissed him again, slower, with her thumbs on his cheekbones, until she made a small sound and leaned all her weight into him.

“Stay. I can’t leave yet,” she said.

“I know. I didn’t come to take you home.”

“Even though you want to?”

“Yes. I came because you said you wished I was here. And because I wanted to be.” He rested his forehead on hers.

For the first time since she’d woken she stopped holding herself up by force, and leaned on him, and the room went on round them, a phone ringing, a chair moving, somebody asking for a list. Nobody interrupted. After a while she looked down at the desk, and he watched the work come back into her face almost faster than he could follow.

“I have to finish reconciling this batch.”

“Then finish it. What do you need?”

That stopped her. She looked at him, and then at the water station at the far end of the room: a table of empty bottles, a handwritten notice on the stairwell door. AGUA. PISOS SUPERIORES. NO USAR EL ASCENSOR.

She said, “Water. We’re running out up here. The deliveries come in at the ground floor and the lift’s dead and the mains haven’t been tested yet, so it all goes up by hand. Nine floors.”

“I counted them.”

“You’ve just flown here.”

“I can carry water.”

“Your shoulders...”

“Isla, you have work to finish. Tell me where the water is,” he said, and she stopped.

She looked at him, and at her list, and at the empty bottles. “Ground floor, by the storeroom. Don’t use the west stairwell, it’s closed. Don’t carry more than you can manage. And if anyone tells you to stop...”

“I’ll stop.”

She narrowed her eyes. “You’re suspiciously agreeable.”

“You asked me to help,” he said, and she reached up and kissed him once more, and said thank you, and he touched her cheek where the paper had marked it and told her to finish her list.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first trip took longer than he’d expected. Not the weight. The route. The ground floor storeroom had become a supply point and the one open staircase was narrow, and there were people in it going both ways: staff carrying boxes down, volunteers carrying boxes up, a stretcher coming through, a family being led to the shelter. He asked where the water was needed and did what he was told. He didn’t organise anyone. He didn’t give an order. He didn’t try to be useful by acting. He picked up the water.

A carton was twelve bottles. He carried it to the ninth floor, set it down where the sign said, and went back down. By the sixth trip a woman with a clipboard had handed him a pair of work gloves without a word. By the eighth he’d stopped looking at his watch.

On the seventh-floor landing in the third hour Isla came round the corner with a clipboard against her chest, in the middle of a sentence to another officer, and stopped dead. He had a carton in his arms and his sleeves rolled up and dust down one leg, and a red line across one palm from the cardboard.

“What are you doing?”

“Water.”

“I can see that.”

“Then the answer was unnecessary,” he said, and the other officer studied her clipboard.

“Three hours. Put it down. Come with me,” said Isla, when he told her.

She took him to a small room with two folding chairs, a box of medical gloves and a tray of sandwiches, and sat him in one chair, and put a bottle of water in front of him.

“Drink. Slowly.”

“I know how to drink water.”

“I’m aware. I’m reminding you because you’ve apparently become a delivery service. This isn’t fine.” She turned his hand over. There was a scrape at the base of his thumb, bleeding a little into the dust.

“It’s a scrape.”

She cleaned it and put a dressing on it, and he watched her do it with the same hands that had held a list of four hundred names. “You have other things to do,” he said.

“I can put a plaster on your hand and still have other things to do. Eat.”

He ate a sandwich. She watched him eat half of it.

“I’ve put you to work,” she said.

“I came here to be with you. That doesn’t mean sitting in a chair watching you. I can carry water for a few hours. You’ve been doing this for three days.” He touched her fingers.

Someone called her name from the corridor, and she kissed him and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

The hours turned into a rhythm. The cartons weren’t all the same weight. Some had been opened and half emptied. The stairwell got warmer as the afternoon went on and the dust caught at the back of his throat. He moved aside on the landings. He held doors. A young volunteer in a university sweatshirt asked him in careful English whether he was from the embassy.

“No.”

“Then why are you doing this?”

“Because the water needs to go upstairs.”

The volunteer thought about that, and handed him another carton.

Thank You (Paid): Are you still carrying water?

Wei Long: Yes.

Thank You (Paid): How much?

Wei Long: I haven’t counted.

Thank You (Paid): Of course you haven’t. I love you.

He stood on the fifth-floor landing with the phone in his hand. Seeing it arrive in the middle of a message about water made something in his chest come loose.

Wei Long: I love you too. Finish your work.

Thank You (Paid): You’re bossy for a man who’s been carrying bottled water all afternoon.

Wei Long: I learned from you.

There was a strange comfort in it. For three days he hadn’t been able to do anything useful at all. He’d watched maps and numbers and a phone that wouldn’t connect, and sat with the knowledge that wanting to reach her didn’t mean he could. Now he could carry something: not much, water in cardboard up nine flights of stairs, but somebody needed it. Somebody would drink it at a desk without having to get up from a list. He could do that. So he did.

At the ninth hour a woman at the storeroom told him the next delivery was delayed until morning and there was nothing left to take up. He set the last carton down. His shoulders were stiff and his palms raw from the cardboard and his hair had fallen over his forehead and stayed there. He went upstairs and found her at a table with a phone between her shoulder and ear, writing.

She looked at his empty hands. “Finished?”

“For now.”

“How many hours?”

“Nine.”

She put the phone down. She took both his hands and looked at them and pressed the curling edge of the plaster back down with her thumb, and then she put her arms round him and pressed her face into his chest in the middle of the consular section, and nobody asked them to move.

“I was asleep. You came all that way and I was asleep at my desk. I wanted to be the first thing you saw,” she said.

“You were. You were the first person I came to see. I found you. That was enough,” said Wei Long.

She lifted her head. She kissed him then on purpose, with everything she hadn’t been able to say all day while she was working, and he kissed her back with one hand at the back of her neck.

“I don’t want you to leave tomorrow,” she said.

“I’m not leaving tomorrow.”

“How long?”

“I have leave. As long as I can.”

She let out a breath. “Why did you do it? The water?”

“Because you were here.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That night they were given a small room where staff slept between shifts: two narrow camp beds, a desk, a window that wouldn’t quite shut, a blanket folded at the foot of one bed and a light over the door that flickered when the air conditioning came on. Isla shut the door. They were alone for the first time since he’d arrived.

“Take your shirt off. I want to see whether you’ve hurt yourself. And not only for that,” she said.

He undid the buttons. She ran her hands over his shoulders, careful round the places that were sore, and kissed the one that hurt most, and then the side of his neck, and he shut his eyes and put his hand on her waist.

“You’re going to ache tomorrow.”

“Probably.”

“I’ll find you something for it.”

“You don’t have to look after me every minute,” he said, and then, “But you can.”

“That’s better,” said Isla, and kissed him, standing in the flickering light, until her knees reminded her how long she’d been on them. There was no need to hurry, no need to make up three months in one evening. They didn’t make love. She was too tired to stand up straight and he’d carried water for nine hours, and they both knew it, and neither of them minded. He took the tin out of his bag and gave it to her, and she turned it over and read the label.

“I left this at home.”

“You did.”

“But you brought mine,” she said, and held it against her chest and her eyes went warm, and she put it on the desk and pushed the two camp beds together with her foot, and lay down with him on the join between them, which was uncomfortable, and neither of them said so.

Into his shoulder she promised to show him the coast tomorrow, if she was free.

“And if you’re not?”

“Then you’ll come with me when I am.”

“All right.”

“I’m glad you’re here,” she said, and fell asleep in the middle of his answer, before the light over the door had flickered again. He lay with her weight on his sore shoulder and didn’t move it. This time he didn’t have to imagine where she was. He could feel her breathing.

chapters.title: The Glacier in a Foreign City
chapters.desc: He can’t read the signs; she translates everything and reconciles a whole country’s missing against hospital lists. She finds the last name alive: a student in a field hospital, written down the way her surname sounded. A borrowed room with a cracked wall, an aftershock mid-way, and neither stops.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m proud of you.”
chapters.content:
By the end of October Wei Long had learned three things about Lima. It had more hills than he’d expected. The word desvío appeared on an unreasonable number of signs, usually with an arrow pointing somewhere he hadn’t meant to go. And Isla could read anything put in front of her, including notices printed on damp paper, handwritten instructions taped to barriers, and announcements from a loudspeaker that sounded as if it had been thrown down a staircase. He could read the numbers. He couldn’t read the signs.

“Not that way,” she said one morning, catching his sleeve on a corner by the embassy.

“The arrow points left.”

“Because the road’s closed on the right.” When he went on looking at the sign, she told him it was Spanish, and took his hand and steered him across the road.

The pavements were broken in places. Some buildings still had fencing round them, and the streets near the worst of it were divided into sections for the engineers. There were notices about water points, shelters, medical stations, closed roads; some printed by the city, some written in marker pen by people who’d decided waiting for an official sign was a waste of time. She translated as they walked.

“Water point. Medical station. Unsafe building, do not enter.”

“I can read that one.”

“Because of the red cross?”

“Because of the picture of the building falling down,” he said, and she laughed, and he understood why she found it so easy to tease him here. At home he knew every street, every station door, every shortcut that saved three minutes. He could walk into a room and know who was in charge, where the exits were, and who was trying not to be noticed. Here he was a man who needed directions to a pharmacy. He found it humbling. She found it entertaining.

The laughter came more easily now than in the first days. Not because the work was easier or the city had recovered; it hadn’t. There were still families without answers. The dead were still being identified, and the hospitals were still full. But she’d stopped sleeping at her desk. She ate meals at something like regular hours. She complained about the coffee. She’d started telling him which streets she liked and which buildings she thought were ugly, and he’d learned that she disliked one particular local pastry and had eaten it three times to be polite, and that she couldn’t be stopped buying fruit.

“You don’t need six oranges.”

“They’re good.”

“You bought six yesterday.”

“Those were also good.”

“You haven’t eaten all six.”

“I’m working through them. Slowly. I’m not the only one round here who eats slowly,” she said, and he moved the bag into his other hand.

He had no answer to that.

✦ ✦ ✦

The register was kept in a room on the eighth floor, and it had been arranged with great care. One wall held the working list. Another held the names of citizens who’d been confirmed safe, in columns: hospital, shelter, family, other. A third held the reports still waiting to be checked. The names of the dead were kept on their own, on a board by the door, and nobody wrote on that board except the head of section or Isla.

She’d explained the system to him in his first week, carefully. Someone reported missing wasn’t someone dead. An unverified report wasn’t a confirmed identity. A name on a hospital list didn’t mean someone had been found until the details matched. He understood why she was so exact about it. The register changed every day. Names moved across the walls. The working list had been four hundred names long on the Friday after the earthquake. On the last Tuesday in October it was twenty-three.

He sat at a spare table while she worked through a batch of hospital admissions with a pen in one hand and a phone in the other. He’d learned not to ask whether she was nearly finished.

“There’s a mismatch. Same surname. Different dates of birth. One says admitted on the fifteenth, one on the sixteenth,” she murmured.

“Two people?”

“Or one person written down wrong.” She rang the hospital, and he listened to her do it in Spanish, calm, exact, asking for the original intake record, asking a nurse to say it again more slowly. He’d heard her talk to her parents and translate witness statements and handle frightened families on the phone at home. This was something else. There wasn’t one person at the end of the line who needed her. There were hundreds, each of whom had to be understood separately. A hospital recorded a patient one way and a shelter another. A family reported someone missing under a nickname. Someone arrived at a field hospital with no papers and was written down as best the nurse could manage. Someone on the missing list had rung his mother on a borrowed phone and the message hadn’t reached anyone with a pen. She was translating systems into each other, one name at a time.

“Different people. The second record had the wrong year,” she said, and wrote in the margin.

There was a red dent on her middle finger where the pen sat. He slid a cup of water over to her and she drank it without looking up.

“How do you do it?” he asked.

“I don’t know. I do the next thing. I make the next call. I don’t look at the whole wall at once.” She thought about it properly, because he’d asked properly.

He knew that answer. It was how he worked a case when there was too much evidence and a family waiting and no use in standing still. He hadn’t understood the size of her job until he’d watched her hold a country’s worth of other people’s worst week in her head and do it one line at a time, a little tired, her hair tied back, a pen behind her ear and a line between her brows whenever a record didn’t match.

✦ ✦ ✦

The last missing name stayed on the wall for two more days.

A student. Twenty-one. A language exchange, a room in a shared flat in one of the districts on the coast that had come down worst, no contact since the fifteenth. The hospital lists had been checked. The shelters had been checked. The field hospitals had sent their admissions, though several records were incomplete and one had come in with no full name at all. Isla had circled that one in pencil.

She said, “Here. A date, half a surname and a hospital reference. No date of birth. It came through one of the field stations in the first night, when they were treating people before anyone had time to ask who they were.”

“Why hasn’t it been matched?”

“Because the half a surname doesn’t look like the surname. Unless the nurse heard it, and didn’t read it.” She picked up the phone.

It took a long time. She asked for the patient register at the field hospital. She explained the problem. The person at the other end went away. Isla waited with the receiver against her ear for eleven minutes, and Wei Long watched her write a number and ask another question, and another, and then her face changed. Not much. Her shoulders didn’t drop. She didn’t smile. But something in it shifted.

“Can you confirm the first name? And the date of birth? Yes. That’s the same. Is the patient conscious? Able to speak? Thank you. Gracias.” She checked it against the report. Her hand tightened on the pen. She listened, and shut her eyes.

She put the phone down and didn’t move.

“Isla?”

“Alive. Admitted on the night of the fifteenth with no papers. A broken pelvis and a head wound. They wrote her surname down the way it sounded when she said it, half-conscious, to a nurse who didn’t speak English. Her family’s been searching under the real spelling for three weeks. She’s awake. They’ve confirmed who she is.” She looked at him. She looked at the paper.

She picked the phone up again. “I have to ring her mother.”

He stepped back and gave her room. He heard the careful introduction and the confirmation of identity and she’s alive, said twice, and Isla explaining she couldn’t give a medical report herself but would make sure the hospital rang. There was a long silence. “Yes, I understand. You’re welcome,” Isla said, low.

When she’d put the phone down she stood up and went to the wall and took a pen and drew a line through the last name in the missing column, and wrote it again in the hospital column with the reference and the date. Her handwriting was as neat as ever. Then she capped the pen and sat down, abruptly.

He crouched beside her chair. “Are you all right?”

“I don’t know. I kept thinking there’d be one more. Another name that didn’t match. Another family asking me to check one more hospital.” She looked at their hands, his over hers.

“There may be.”

“I know. But this one’s alive.”

Her eyes filled and she pressed her lips together to hold it, and he stood and pulled her up out of the chair and into his arms, and she held on with her face in his chest.

“I thought we’d lost her,” she whispered.

“You found her.”

“We found her.”

“Yes, I’m proud of you,” he said, and held her until she was ready to let go, and when she lifted her head he brushed his thumb under her eye.

She’d sent him that sentence on a cream card, in Spanish. She hadn’t expected to hear it from him in a room full of paperwork with the last missing name crossed off the wall.

“Go home tonight,” he said.

“I still have to update the record and notify the ministry and make sure the family has the hospital’s number.”

“Then do that. And then go home.”

“You’re learning.”

“I’m observing.”

“Is that what you call it?” said Isla, and finished the entry, and for once didn’t start another.

✦ ✦ ✦

Home that night was a borrowed room. Her flat was still being used to sleep staff on rotation, so they’d been given a room on the top floor of an apartment block near the embassy that had been inspected and cleared for temporary use. It wasn’t beautiful. The curtains didn’t meet in the middle. A long crack ran diagonally up the wall beside the bed from the corner of the window frame almost to the ceiling. It had been marked in pencil at both ends and photographed, and the engineer’s notice was taped to the back of the door.

Wei Long read the notice twice. Isla translated it both times.

“The engineer’s signed it off. You won’t find a different answer by staring at it,” she said, watching him read it a third time.

“I’m checking the date.”

“You checked it downstairs.”

“I wanted to be certain.”

She came up behind him and put her chin on his shoulder. “The room’s safe.”

He looked at the crack. “It’s still a crack.”

“Buildings crack in earthquakes. Stop interrogating it,” she said, and kissed his cheek, and he put the paper down.

She took her shoes off and stood in the middle of the room and looked at him.

“What?” he said.

“Nothing. I’m allowed to look. I’ve spent weeks trying not to count how long it’d be before I could have you to myself in a room with a door. I’ve been extremely professional about it.” She came and loosened his collar.

“I noticed,” he said, and framed her face with her hands, and she kissed him.

They had kissed in the consular section with the room full of people and the next call waiting, and between lists, and once through a barrier at an airport. This was a quiet room with the door shut and nobody asking her for a name, and she held on to him. He backed her towards the bed with his hands on her waist and she pulled his shirt up out of his trousers and over his head, and he undid her blouse, and they undressed each other without any hurry, though there was nothing restrained in the way she reached for him. There was relief in it, and three months of saying goodnight to a screen.

She pushed him down onto the bed and lay on him, skin against skin from shoulder to knee, and kissed him until he groaned, and then she sat up astride him and took him inside her with one slow sinking movement that made him grip her hips hard. She rode him with her palms flat on his chest. He watched her face. Outside a dog barked in the street and a car went by on the cracked road, and she leaned down and kissed him, and he rolled her under him and drove into her, deep and slow, her legs round his waist, her nails in his back.

The aftershock came while he was inside her.

A low hum through the floor first. The water in the glass on the bedside table shivered. She lifted her head off the pillow. Then he felt it, the bed shifting under them, a picture frame ticking against the wall, the crack by the window seeming to widen in the dim light, though he knew that might only be the shadows moving. He went completely still, braced over her on his forearms with his body between hers and the wall, his head turned towards the window. Something tapped. A far-off car alarm began.

“Wei Long.”

“Wait.”

It lasted perhaps five seconds. The lamp stayed standing. The glass didn’t fall. Nothing came off the ceiling. The building gave one last faint shudder and was still. He looked at the crack, at the pencil marks at either end of it. Neither had moved.

“It’s passed,” she said, under him.

“For now.”

She put her hand on his cheek and turned his face back to hers. “Do you want to move?”

“Do you?”

“No. Not unless they tell us to. Don’t stop.” Her heels pressed into the backs of his thighs.

He looked at her for a second longer, and then he didn’t stop. He moved in her again, slowly, and then less slowly, and it came back with a different urgency, not panic, not pretending the ground hadn’t moved, but the plain need to hold one another while they could. She said his name against his mouth. He kissed her throat and her breasts and her mouth again, and she came with her arms locked round his neck and her face turned into his shoulder, and he came a moment after her with his whole body shaking and her name said into her hair.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later she lay with her cheek on his chest and his hand moving over her back.

“You didn’t stop,” she said.

“I checked that you were safe.”

“I know. If the building had been unsafe you’d have had me out of that door before I’d found my shoes.”

“Yes.”

“I’m not saying you should have done anything differently. I was frightened when it came. Not of the room. That something would happen before I’d had enough time with you. That sounds selfish. There are people who’ve lost everything and are still waiting for answers, and I was lying here wanting another hour with you.” She lifted her head. She looked down.

“Isla. You don’t have to earn the right to be here. You’ve worked for weeks for people who needed you. Wanting an hour with me doesn’t take anything away from them. You’re allowed to be tired, and frightened, and to want something that has nothing to do with the work.” He moved her hair off her forehead.

She looked at him a long time. Then she kissed his chest. “I love you.”

“I love you too.”

“How long are you staying?”

He’d known she’d ask. “As long as the leave allows. I haven’t set the date to go back.”

“You can’t stay for ever. You have a job, and people who depend on you.”

“Yes.”

“I don’t want you to lose anything because you came.”

“I won’t.”

“Promise?”

“I won’t promise something I can’t control.”

She smiled against his skin. “That’s the man I know. Set the date tomorrow. Not tonight.”

“No. Tonight I’m here,” he said.

In the morning the crack was still there. He looked at it while she was in the shower, at the pencil marks and the floor beneath it, and didn’t touch it.

“Are you interrogating the wall again?” she said from the bathroom door.

“It’s still a crack.”

“How observant.”

They went down together into a city that wasn’t restored but was going on: fences round the damaged blocks, traffic moving carefully, two men unloading boxes from a van on the corner. At the foot of the stairs there was a notice taped to the door, and she took his hand and started to translate it, and he listened.

“What does it say?”

“That the lift’s still out of service.”

“I knew that one.”

“Congratulations,” said Isla, and he had come to Lima thinking he’d spend his days waiting for her to finish work, and he’d learned that the work was part of the woman he loved, and he followed her down into the street, reading nothing, understanding a great deal.

chapters.title: He Asks Her What She Wants
chapters.desc: On the cliff path at dusk he asks her what she wants. Nobody has asked her in years and she doesn’t know. He waits. She answers with her mouth on the sea wall, then says she’ll keep the posting for now. On Friday she drives him to the airport.
chapters.epigraph: “What do you want, Isla?”
chapters.content:
The sea was grey. Isla had warned him it usually was at this time of year, under a lid of cloud that the city had a word for and he’d already forgotten, and that it could also be blue or silver or a colour she’d described with three Spanish adjectives and a comparison to a French cheese. This afternoon it was grey, and it moved against the bottom of the cliff with a slow weight he recognised. It looked like the water at home on a day when nobody had told the harbour to perform.

He’d booked his flight on Wednesday. Friday, the twentieth, a connection through the hub, home on the Sunday morning. He’d told her in the kitchen of the borrowed flat while she was cutting an orange, and she’d said all right, and finished cutting the orange, and given him half. Since then she’d been quieter than usual. Not unhappy. She’d stirred her coffee too long at breakfast. In the taxi to the coast she’d looked out of the window instead of telling him which buildings she disliked. He’d noticed, and hadn’t asked. Sometimes a question was useful. Sometimes it only made a person produce an answer so the question would go away, and he’d spent eleven years watching people do that across a table.

She’d promised him this walk a week ago. He’d reminded her twice. She’d accused him of keeping a register of her promises, and he’d said he did, and she’d laughed and found them an evening.

The path along the top of the cliffs was full of people doing the ordinary things that cities did once the worst was over: couples with ice creams, a man running with a dog that clearly didn’t want to, two girls taking photographs of each other against the rail. Below them the surfers sat on their boards past the break, waiting. Part of the path near the lighthouse was still fenced off, with an engineer’s notice on the fence that he could now partly read. A cyclist rang his bell behind them and Isla moved against his side without looking round. He took her hand.

At the far end, where the path widened and the crowd thinned, there was a low wall above the drop. She sat on it, put her bag beside her, and took out her phone, and looked at it, and put it away again.

“It’s strange. Being somewhere without checking this every thirty seconds,” she said.

“You just checked it.”

“I looked at it. That’s different. I didn’t unlock it.”

He sat down next to her. She leaned her shoulder against his arm. The sun had gone behind the cloud and left a thin pale line along the horizon, and the water below them turned the colour of a pencil drawing.

“What do you want?” he said.

She turned her head. “For dinner? There’s a place near here...”

“Not dinner.”

She looked at him then, properly, and he kept looking back at her.

“What do you want, Isla?”

She could have told him the sea, or coffee, or a shower that lasted an hour, or twelve hours of sleep with the curtains shut. She could have told him to kiss her. All of it was true and none of it was what he’d asked. She opened her mouth to say something reasonable and found there was nothing there.

“I don’t know,” she said.

“All right.”

She waited for the rest of it, and there wasn’t any.

✦ ✦ ✦

People asked her things all day. What she’d arranged. Whether a hospital had confirmed a name. Whether the family had been rung, whether the statement had been translated, whether she could cover the duty phone on Saturday. Her head of section asked what she needed, and meant staff. Her mother asked whether she was eating. Her father asked what she was reading and then told her what he was reading. Hao asked whether she was happy, in the middle of a story about something else, and was wounded if she noticed. Wei Long, every night for three months, had asked whether she was safe.

Nobody had asked her what she wanted since the ministry’s interview board, when the answer had been Lima, a posting abroad, the consular section, the thing she’d worked towards since she was twenty-two. She’d known then. She’d been sure enough to tell a panel of five people with a straight face.

She said, “I used to know. I was quite good at it. I wanted this. I wanted to be good at it. Then the ground moved, and every day was a list of things that couldn’t wait, and I didn’t mind. I still don’t. But somewhere in it I stopped thinking about what happens after the next thing is finished. I didn’t notice I’d stopped.” She tipped her head at the city behind them. She turned her phone over in her lap.

He didn’t tell her that was understandable. He didn’t tell her anything. He sat beside her and looked at the water and let her have the silence, the way he’d let witnesses have it, except that nobody was writing anything down, and she found she could breathe in it.

“What if I don’t know for a while?” she said.

“Then you don’t.”

“What if I want something that doesn’t make sense?”

“Then you tell me, and we work out whether it can.”

“We?”

“If it involves me. I’d like it to involve me.” He considered.

She laughed, and it caught in her throat on the way out. Below them a surfer finally stood up on a wave, rode it for three seconds, and fell off, and his friends cheered.

“I’m frightened,” she said, so low he leaned to hear it. “You’re going on Friday. I thought that when it was over I’d want things to go back to normal. Proper meals, normal hours, a building that stays still. And now I keep thinking about the kitchen on Saturday morning when you’ve gone, and I don’t know what normal is supposed to be.” She made herself look at him. “What if I want you to stay?”

“Then tell me you want me to stay.”

“That’s it?”

“No. Then we’d have to talk about my leave and your posting and my job, and what staying would mean, and it might not be possible. But I’d want to be asked.” He turned her hand over and ran his thumb along the edge of the dressing she still wore on her palm, though the cut underneath had nearly healed.

“You wouldn’t be angry?”

“I’d be disappointed if I couldn’t. That isn’t the same thing.”

She looked down at their hands. He’d made no promise, only an offer to hear the question, and that turned out to be what she’d needed and hadn’t known how to ask for.

She brought one knee up onto the wall and turned to face him.

“Your turn. What do you want?”

He didn’t answer straight away. She watched him think about it the way he thought about everything, as if it deserved to be got right.

He said, “I want to see what your life here looks like when it isn’t an emergency. Which coffee you complain about. Which streets you take when you’re not in a hurry. I want to come back to this wall when they’ve taken the fence down. When the posting ends I want to go home with you. I want to see you at your desk and in your kitchen and losing an argument to your brother. I don’t know how much leave I’ll get or how often. I want to try.” He looked at the fence, and then back at her.

“How long have you been thinking about this?”

“Since before I came.”

“And you didn’t tell me?”

“I wanted to be sitting next to you.”

Her throat closed. She put her hand flat on his chest, over his heart, the way she’d done in the consular section to make sure he was really there, and he put his own hand over it.

“I don’t want you to decide anything because you’re afraid I’ll go. And I won’t decide anything for you because I’m afraid you’ll stay,” he said.

She thought about the last missing name, and the line she’d drawn through it on the wall, and how long it had taken her to put the pen down.

✦ ✦ ✦

She kissed him instead of answering. The first one was slow. She cupped his jaw and leaned in and found his mouth with a care that made him go still on the wall, his fingers tightening round hers. When she drew back she only went as far as she needed to see him.

“Is that the answer?” he said.

“Part of it.”

“And the rest?”

“I’m still working on the rest,” said Isla, and kissed him again, and this time she didn’t stop. Her free hand went to the back of his neck and pulled him down to her, and he turned on the wall and gathered her in with his hand spread across her back. Her knee pressed his thigh. She opened her mouth under his and he made a low sound into it that she felt more than heard, and she wound her fingers into his hair, which she’d been wanting to do since the taxi. The wall was cold through her trousers. The wind came off the water and blew her hair across both their faces and neither of them did anything about it. Somewhere behind them a couple went past laughing, and somebody whistled, and she kissed him harder.

When she finally pulled back she was out of breath and he had her hair caught on his collar.

“I’m glad you asked,” she said.

“I should have asked sooner.”

“No. You asked when I could hear it.”

He untangled her hair from his collar with great concentration. “Then I’ll ask again in a month.”

“You’ll be in another hemisphere in a month.”

“There are telephones.”

“I want to keep the posting. For now. I worked for it for years. I don’t want the earthquake to be the reason I give it up. But I want a life here, not just the work. And I want to see you when nothing terrible has happened. I want you to come at Easter and complain about the signs,” she said, and heard herself say it, and knew it was true.

“I can read the signs.”

“You can’t.”

“Agua. Cerrado. Desvío,” he said.

“Water, closed, detour. You’ve learned the Spanish for a crisis.”

“I’ve learned the Spanish I needed.”

“Te extraño,” she said.

He’d had that one on a cream card propped against his desk lamp since August. He didn’t say so. He said it back to her, badly, every consonant arrested, and she laughed into his shoulder and didn’t correct him.

✦ ✦ ✦

They stayed on the wall until the lamps along the path came on, one after another, and the sea went from grey to nothing at all, only sound. She told him other things she wanted, as they came to her, and none of them were large. To stop feeling guilty when she sat down. To ring her parents because she missed them and not to prove she was alive. To have dinner without her phone face up on the table. To sleep through one night without an alarm. He didn’t comment on any of them. He listened, and said yes to one and good to another, and when she said she wanted him to admit he liked the sea he said he didn’t dislike it.

“You’ve been staring at it for an hour as if it’s withholding evidence.”

“I’ve been observing it.”

“You’ve been observing me too.”

“Yes,” he said, and that was apparently the end of the subject.

When it got too cold to sit, she stood up and pulled him up after her.

“Where are we going?” he asked.

“You said dinner.”

“You choose.”

She looked at him. He’d asked her the large question and now he was handing her the small ones too, one at a time, so she could practise.

“There’s a place two streets back. The fish is the best I’ve had here, the music is terrible and the chairs hurt,” she said.

“Why would we go there?”

“Because I like it.”

“Then we’ll go,” said Wei Long.

She set off. Three steps along the path she stopped, came back, put both hands on his chest and caught his collar and kissed him once more, quickly, in the lamplight, with a family of four going round them on either side.

“I want this. You. The hard parts too, if we can keep choosing each other through them,” she said.

“I choose you.”

“I know you do. That’s what frightens me,” she said, and took his hand, and pulled him on towards the terrible music.

The restaurant was as bad as promised. The chairs hurt. She ordered for both of them without asking and he let her. Halfway through the fish her phone lit up on the table, and she looked at it, and he watched her decide, and she left it where it was until the plates had gone. It was a colleague asking whether she could cover the duty phone on Saturday. She said yes. Then she looked across the table at him and said, “Saturday morning. After you’ve gone. I’d rather be busy,” and he understood that this, too, was something she wanted, and nodded, and paid the bill while she wasn’t looking.

On Friday she drove him to the airport in a borrowed car with one wing mirror held on with tape. She didn’t cry in the car. She didn’t cry at the drop-off either. She kissed him by the doors with her hands in his coat, and told him to eat on the plane, and said te extraño before he’d even gone, which he pointed out was premature.

“I’m practising,” she said, and got back in the car.

He stood on the kerb with his case and watched the taped mirror until the car turned the corner by the car park, and then a little longer, and then he went in.

chapters.title: She Asks for a Transfer Home
chapters.desc: She asks the ministry for a posting home: for herself, not for him. Her head of section, Ruth Ferreira, asks if it’s a man. Wei Long is back in Lima for his last eleven days of leave, and she tells him only when it’s sent, on a bench above the park.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to do anything to keep me.”
chapters.content:
The application took Isla three weeks to write, and none of that was because it was difficult.

The ministry had a form for it. There was a box for the post requested and a box for the preferred date and a section, half a page long, headed Professional and personal reasons for the request, which was where she kept getting stuck. She’d filled in everything else before Christmas and saved it under a file name so dull nobody looking over her shoulder would open it, and then she’d left it alone while the office emptied for the holidays and Lima went from grey to blinding in a week.

Nobody had warned her about the summer. The lid of cloud that had sat over the coast since she arrived had lifted in December as if someone had taken it away to be cleaned, and now the sea was a hard bright blue and people walked the cliffs in sunglasses. The fences were still up round the worst of the blocks. But the city had started to look like a self she hadn’t met yet, and she’d found she wanted to be in it.

That was part of what made the half page so hard.

The first version she wrote was too vague. The second read like a resignation. The third was so careful that it seemed to have been written by someone who didn’t want anything in particular and would be grateful for whatever she was given, and she read it twice on Monday morning at her desk and deleted it, and typed the heading again.

Request for consideration: home posting.

She looked at the word home for a while.

For most of her life it had meant a house in Vancouver with too many bookshelves and a dog who barked at the recycling. Then it had meant wherever the ministry put her. Then, for two years, without her quite noticing, it had come to mean a city with no snow and a harbour that never performed for anyone, a brother on the thirty-second floor who said I love you the way other people said hello, and a desk in a police station where a man looked up at nine o’clock.

She’d wanted Lima. She’d asked for it, worked for it, and been prouder of the letter than she’d admitted to anyone but him. She wasn’t sorry she’d come, and she wasn’t sorry about what she’d done here. But somewhere between the sea wall and the last name on the list she’d understood that wanting to go somewhere wasn’t the same as having stopped wanting to go back.

She began to type.

She didn’t ask to be released early. She acknowledged the needs of the post and the recovery work still under way after the earthquake. She asked to be considered for a position in her home city at the next suitable opportunity, or sooner if the ministry could arrange it without leaving the section short. She said she intended to stay in consular work, that the last six months had taught her more about emergencies than the previous four years, and that she wanted to build on it somewhere she could also build a life.

She didn’t write his name. She didn’t need to; the half page wasn’t about him, and she wanted it to be true.

At twenty past ten she saved it. At half past, an email arrived from her head of section asking whether she could come by.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ruth Ferreira had been running consular sections for twenty years, in four countries, and had the face of a woman who’d heard every possible reason for every possible request and believed about a third of them. After the earthquake she’d slept in her office for six nights and sent Isla to the rest room twice by direct order. Isla liked her enormously and was a little afraid of her.

The draft was on the desk, printed, with two paragraphs marked in pencil.

“You saw it,” said Isla.

“You saved it to the shared drive. Sit down.”

Isla sat.

“You’re asking for a home posting.”

“At the next suitable opportunity.”

“You’ve been in Lima six and a half months. The posting is three years. You applied for this job. You were appointed to a senior role two grades early. You did more in October than most deputies do in a whole posting. So help me understand why you want to come off it before you’ve seen a second winter.” Ruth tapped the first pencil mark.

“I’m not asking to come off it. I’m asking the ministry to think about my next assignment.”

“That’s a distinction without much difference.”

“It’s a difference to me.”

Ruth leaned back. The telephone by the window rang, stopped, and rang again, and neither of them looked at it. “Your family’s well?”

“They’re well. My parents are in Vancouver. My brother’s in the home city.”

“So this isn’t an emergency.”

“No.”

“Is it a man?”

The question was perfectly reasonable, and Isla found she disliked it more than anything anyone had said to her in a month.

She said, “There is someone. You know there is. He was carrying water up your stairwell for nine hours in October. He’s part of my life, and I’m not going to pretend he isn’t. But he isn’t the reason I’m asking, and I’d rather the committee didn’t read it that way.”

“Committees read things however they like. I’m going to say something you won’t enjoy. People in this service make sacrifices. They know it when they apply. Relationships and overseas postings don’t always fit, and I’ve watched good officers leave a career every time one got difficult.” Ruth’s pencil moved to the second mark.

“I’m not leaving because it’s difficult. It is difficult. That isn’t why.”

“Then perhaps it’s the earthquake. People come out of something like that and want to go home. It passes.”

Isla thought of the ninth floor. The list under her cheek, the coffee ring in the cup. Ringing a mother on a Tuesday afternoon in October to say she’s alive, twice. The kitchen of the borrowed flat on the Saturday after he’d gone, where she’d covered the duty phone because she couldn’t bear the quiet, and taken nine calls, and been glad of every one.

She said, “It changed me. I don’t think that’s the same as a reaction that passes. I want this work. I want more responsibility, not less. I also want to have a life in the place I think of as home, and I don’t accept that I have to choose. Those things aren’t opposites. They only look like opposites on a form.”

Ruth looked at her until the phone by the window had stopped ringing.

“Revise the paragraph about timing. Make it clear you want the next assignment cycle and not an early release, or they’ll bin it. Send it through the formal channel. I’ll attach my assessment,” she said at last.

“Thank you.” Isla was at the door when she turned back to ask whether he was happy there.

That was a different question. Isla gave it the time it deserved.

“Yes, in a lot of ways. That’s why it took three weeks,” she said.

Ruth nodded, without looking convinced, and picked up the ringing phone.

✦ ✦ ✦

She revised it in the afternoon. The new paragraph was cleaner and the dates were plain, and the half page that mattered stayed in her own words. At four thirty-six she read it again. At four forty-two she attached it to the formal request. At four forty-four she checked the address, and at four forty-five she sent it, and the confirmation came back before she’d taken her hand off the mouse.

Your request has been received and forwarded to the assignment team for consideration.

No decision. No promise. But it wasn’t a dull file name on a shared drive any more. It existed somewhere she couldn’t take it back from.

She’d expected to feel frightened. What she felt was lighter, the way she’d felt the first night in Lima she’d slept without the alarm set. Her phone buzzed on the desk.

Inspector Glacier: Have you eaten?

She laughed out loud, and the junior officer at the next desk looked up.

He’d been in Lima a week. He’d flown home on the twentieth of November as planned, and she’d said Easter, on the sea wall, and meant it. On the second of January he’d rung to say Easter was a long way off, and he had eleven days of leave left that would lapse in March, and Hau had already moved the cases. He’d arrived on the eleventh with one bag and her tea, and spent the week getting lost on purpose and cooking her dinners from recipes on packets he couldn’t read. Three had been excellent. One had been made with icing sugar.

Isla: Not yet.

Inspector Glacier: Why?

Isla: Work.

Inspector Glacier: That doesn’t sound like a reason.

She looked at the confirmation on her screen. She could tell him now: the head of section, the pencil marks, the committee, the months it might take, the vacancy there might not be. She could hand him every uncertainty down a phone line and let him hold them while she finished her report.

She didn’t want to. She wanted to tell him when it was done, to his face, so that whatever he felt about it she’d see it.

Isla: Dinner? The place with the terrible chairs.

Inspector Glacier: I’ll be there at seven.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was standing outside the restaurant when she came round the corner, hands in his pockets, reading the notice on the door with the expression he used on suspects who hadn’t yet decided to talk.

“It says they’re closed on Tuesdays,” she said behind him.

“It’s Monday.”

“I know. I thought you might like to know about Tuesdays.”

He turned, and took her bag off her shoulder without asking, and told her she was late, and she said “Three minutes,” and he said he’d noticed, and then, when she was opening her mouth to tease him about counting, “I missed you,” so plainly that she forgot what she’d been going to say and kissed him in the doorway instead.

They ate slowly. She told him about a hospital that had lost a patient’s passport in its laundry and found it three days later, ironed. He told her that Ren Hao had sent him a photograph of an extremely expensive coffee machine and the single word Thoughts?, and that he’d replied Why?, and that Ren Hao hadn’t spoken to him since.

“He wanted you to tell him to buy it.”

“I don’t know whether he should buy it.”

“He doesn’t want an honest answer, he wants permission.”

“Then he shouldn’t ask me,” said Wei Long, and finished his fish, and she watched him do it and thought that she had never in her life been so sure of a person’s face.

He noticed she was quiet on the walk back. He didn’t say so. He shortened his stride to hers and waited, and three streets from her flat, where a bench faced the dark slope of the park, she stopped.

“Can we sit down?”

They sat. The air was warm, and the streetlamps had come on, and somewhere below them in the dark a dog was barking at the sea.

“I sent a request today. To the ministry. I’ve asked to be considered for a posting at home,” she said.

He didn’t answer straight away. She watched his face, which did almost nothing, and she knew it well enough now to see what that little was.

“Not now. The next assignment cycle. It isn’t guaranteed, and it could take months. Ruth called me in. She asked if it was a man,” she said.

“What did you tell her?”

“That you’re part of my life and you’re not the reason.”

He looked at her hands in her lap. “Why didn’t you tell me before you sent it?”

She’d known he’d ask. She’d had three weeks to work out the answer.

“Because I wanted it to be mine. If I’d asked you whether you wanted me home, you’d have said yes, and I’d have spent the rest of my life wondering whether I’d done it because you said yes.”

She turned to him. “I didn’t want to make you responsible for it. So I decided first. And now it’s sent,” she said.

He was quiet for a while. “Do you want to come home?” he said.

“Yes.”

“Why?”

That was the question he’d asked her on the wall, put the other way round, and she answered it the same way, a piece at a time.

“Because I want my family closer than an aeroplane. Because Hao books dinner with me six months in advance and I’d like to be shouted at in person. Because I want to keep doing this work and I don’t want every important part of my life to be somewhere else while I do it. And because I want to be with you. Not because I can’t manage without you. I can. I’ve been doing it. But I don’t want distance to be the shape of us for ever if there’s another shape.” She looked at the park.

He took her hand off her knee and held it.

“Are you happy? Tell me honestly,” she said.

“Yes. And worried. That they’ll say no, or that it’ll take longer than you want, or that they’ll give you something that isn’t good enough for you.”

“But you’re happy I asked.”

He said, “I’m happy you decided. I want you home. I want you to come home because you want to, and not because you think it’s how you keep me. You don’t have to do anything to keep me.”

She didn’t trust her voice, so she kissed him instead, on the bench, in the warm dark, with his hand coming up to the side of her neck and his thumb resting under her ear where her pulse was. She kissed him until the dog below them stopped barking, and then a little longer, and when she drew back she kept her forehead against his.

“If they say no,” she said.

“Then we’ll decide what to do next.”

“You always say we’ll decide.”

“Because we will.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In her flat she showed him the confirmation on her phone. He read it as carefully.

“It’s only an acknowledgement. They haven’t approved anything,” she said.

“I understand.”

“You’re terribly calm about it.”

“What would you prefer?”

“I don’t know. Some enthusiasm.”

He gave her the phone back, and then, before she’d put it down, he picked her up. It wasn’t graceful. He got one arm under her knees and the other round her back and lifted her off the floor of her own kitchen with no effort at all, and she shrieked and grabbed his collar and laughed until she couldn’t breathe.

“Is that enthusiastic enough?”

“Put me down.”

“No,” said Wei Long, and carried her to the bedroom, and didn’t.

He laid her on the bed in the light from the hall and undressed her the way he did everything when he’d decided to do it properly, without hurry. Her sandals. The button at her waist. Her blouse, one button and then a kiss below it and then the next. She tugged at his shirt and he let her have it. When he was bare to the waist she sat up and pressed her mouth to the centre of his chest and felt his heart going under it much faster than his face had admitted to on the bench.

“You were nervous,” she said against his skin.

“You were quiet all through dinner.”

“So you were nervous.”

“Yes,” he said, and pushed her gently back down and kissed her stomach, and then lower, and she stopped asking him questions. He used his mouth on her slowly, with his hands holding her hips still when she tried to move, and she pushed her fingers into his hair and said his name to the ceiling, then in Spanish, then not in any language. She came with her heels in the mattress and her whole body lifting off it, and he didn’t stop until she pulled him up by the hair.

He came into her in one long push that made them both stop breathing. She wrapped her legs round him. Neither of them hurried. He moved in her deep and steady, braced on his forearms, watching her face. She’d sent a form. That was all she’d done today. She’d sent a form and he was shaking.

“Isla,” he said, like a question.

“Yes,” she said, which wasn’t an answer to anything, and dug her nails into his back and held on while he came, with his face in her neck and her name broken in half.

Afterwards he lay with his head on her stomach and her hand in his hair, the way he had in his own flat a long time ago, and the sea sounded far off through the open window.

“Six weeks. That’s what Ruth thinks. Maybe longer,” she said.

“I’ll count.”

“Of course you will.”

“I have nine days left. Then I’ll count from there,” he said.

She didn’t say anything. She lay looking at the ceiling with her fingers moving in his hair, and found she was already making a list in her head of what she’d have to give back to Lima, and that it was long, and that she’d miss most of it.

chapters.title: The Ministry Says No
chapters.desc: The ministry says no to the deputy job and yes to an emergencies desk at the consulate: a step down on paper. She takes it because she wants the work. He meets her at arrivals with ranunculus, asked for by name; she jumps. His fridge list is still up.
chapters.epigraph: “It was still true.”
chapters.content:
The email arrived at 9:17 on a Monday morning, between a man at the front counter explaining in increasingly desperate Spanish that he’d submitted the same certificate three times and a colleague crossing the corridor with a box of files held against her chest.

Isla read it once, and then again, and then closed it and sat with her hands on the keyboard.

The ministry regretted that it couldn’t support her appointment to the post of deputy head of consular in the home city. The post had been allocated to another officer whose current assignment and experience made them the preferred candidate. However, following consideration of her request and present staffing needs, an alternative position was available. Emergencies desk. Consular section. Home city. From the next transfer window, subject to formal acceptance and handover.

She opened it again, in case it had changed.

The deputy post was the one she’d imagined when she wrote the half page. It was the natural next step after Lima: a wider remit, a team, the recognition that came with having run something hard and run it well. The emergencies desk was a desk. It was the first phone that rang when a citizen was arrested, admitted, missing or dead, and the person who answered it spent their days telling frightened people what happened next. She knew exactly what it was. She’d been doing a version of it since October. It was important, and on the organisation chart it was a grade below the job she had now.

She’d asked to come home. The ministry had found a way to bring her home. She couldn’t decide whether she was supposed to feel grateful or insulted, and was annoyed with herself for needing to decide. Her phone lit up beside the keyboard.

Inspector Glacier: Good morning. Has the answer come?

She’d mentioned it once, a week ago, in passing. He’d put it in the notebook. She knew he had.

Isla: Yes.

The dots came and went twice.

Inspector Glacier: Do you want to ring?

Isla: Not yet.

Inspector Glacier: All right. I’m here when you do.

He didn’t ask what it said. He didn’t tell her it would be fine before he knew whether it was. She put the phone away and opened a new document and wrote a list of questions, because that was what she did with things she couldn’t yet feel properly. The reporting line. The grade. The length of the assignment. Whether accepting it would count against her the next time a deputy post came up, and whether anyone would tell her the truth about that.

She didn’t intend to accept a job she didn’t understand. She didn’t intend to turn one down because its title was smaller, either.

At eleven she went to see Ruth, who had read the email before she arrived.

“You’re disappointed,” said Ruth.

“Yes.”

“You’re allowed to be. There were four of you for that post, and the one who got it has been waiting longer. That’s all it is. It isn’t a comment on Lima. The desk is a grade down. I won’t pretend it isn’t. You’d be doing work you’ve already proved you can do, and the next senior vacancy could be a long way off.” She turned her pen over.

“Do you think I should take it?”

“I think you should decide what matters to you.”

“You say that when you don’t want to give an answer.”

“I say it because it’s usually right. If you take it, take it because you want the work. Not because you’re grateful they let you go home. People who take jobs out of gratitude are miserable in them by the second year, and they make everyone round them miserable too.” Ruth put the pen down.

Isla went back to her desk and read the job description three times. The job was hospitals that answered quickly and hospitals that didn’t, and police liaison officers who needed a request in writing, and families who wanted answers she wouldn’t have, and the long patient business of making sure nobody was forgotten in a system that was built to forget people. There’d be calls she’d take home with her. There’d be nights.

By the third reading she knew she wanted it, and was a little surprised.

✦ ✦ ✦

She rang him at twelve minutes past six, Lima time. He answered on the second ring, which at home was a quarter past seven the next morning, and she could hear the kettle.

“They said no to the deputy job,” she said.

There was a short silence. “I’m sorry.”

“They offered me the emergencies desk. At the consulate. At home.”

His silence changed. She couldn’t have described how, but it did.

“Home,” he said.

“Yes.”

“Is that what you want?”

“I think so. It’s a step down.” She leaned back until the chair creaked.

“On paper.”

“On paper is where people read it.”

“Do you want the work?”

She looked at the job description on her desk, with her own pencil all over it. “Yes.”

“Then I don’t think the paper is the only thing that matters.”

“You sound like Ruth.”

“Is that good?”

“I haven’t decided,” said Isla, and told him all of it: the grade, the reporting line, the questions she’d asked and the answers that had come back, the one that said accepting wouldn’t remove her from consideration for future posts, which wasn’t the same as saying it wouldn’t hurt. He listened without interrupting. She heard him put a cup down.

“Do you want to know what I think?” he said, when she’d finished.

“Yes.”

“I think if the conditions are acceptable and you want to do it, you should take it. And if in two years it’s wrong, you’ll know, and you’ll do something else.”

“You make it sound manageable.”

“I didn’t say easy.”

“You’ve got until Friday to stop sounding like a reasonable man,” she said, and he made the small sound that was the nearest he came to laughing on the phone, and she shut her eyes and listened to it.

On Thursday she accepted. She’d rung her parents first. Her mother had been delighted in a way she’d clearly been saving up since July. Her father had asked three sensible questions about the grade and then a fourth, which was whether she’d be nearer the good bookshop on the hill, and she’d said yes. Then Hao had rung her, before she’d told him, because their mother had.

“I’m organising dinner,” he said, instead of hello.

“I asked you not to.”

“I heard you. I’ve disregarded it. Are you happy?” There was a pause, and his voice dropped, which it almost never did.

“Yes.”

“Good. And if anyone asks, I had nothing to do with this.”

“I know you didn’t.”

“I’m serious. I didn’t want you to come home for me. I wanted you to come home because you wanted to.”

“I do.”

“Then I’m happy. Don’t thank me. Bring me something from Lima. Something expensive,” he said, as easily as he said everything, and she had to stop and swallow before she could thank him.

“Goodbye, Hao.”

She sent the acceptance at eleven. Then she sent two words to the other side of the world.

Isla: I’ve accepted.

He rang inside a minute, from a corridor; she could hear a door bang and somebody shouting for a pen.

“You’re coming home,” he said.

“Yes.”

“When?”

“The window’s late April. The twenty-sixth, if the handover runs to time. Six weeks.”

He let out a breath, and she heard it: no louder than a man putting down something he’d been carrying since July.

“Six weeks is soon,” he said.

“Are you counting?”

“Yes.”

“Of course you are.”

“I’ll take the day off.”

“Don’t use all your leave, you’ll need it.”

“I won’t use all of it,” he said, which wasn’t the same thing, and she let him have it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The arrivals hall was busy on Monday evening, the twenty-sixth of April. Wei Long had been in it for forty minutes, which was thirty-five more than necessary. He’d checked the board four times though the flight had landed on schedule. His coat was buttoned. The flowers were in his left hand.

Ranunculus. Two years ago he’d forgotten their name between the florist’s and the car, and Isla had told him, and he’d written it on his palm in biro and that night in his notebook. Today he’d gone into the same shop by the restaurant and asked for them by name before the woman could open her mouth. She’d looked at him as if he’d done a trick.

The doors opened and closed. A family came through, then a man with two suitcases and his phone already at his ear, then a small boy who ran ahead of his parents dragging a stuffed dog by one leg. Somebody shouted a name. Somebody else cried. Then he saw her.

She had one big case and one small bag over her shoulder, and her hair loose and flattened on one side from the headrest, and she was scanning the faces at the barrier with the quick, methodical look she’d used on lists in October. She looked tired. She looked brown from a Lima summer. She was looking for him.

He stepped forward. She saw him, and stopped dead in the middle of the hall, and people swerved round her.

“Wei Long.”

He just had time to put the flowers down on the rail before she let go of the suitcase handle and ran. She didn’t slow. She came at him so fast that he had to take a step back to catch her, and then she jumped, and he caught her under the thighs and round the back, and her arms went round his neck and her mouth found his before either of them had said another word.

It wasn’t a careful kiss. She kissed him like an answer to every screen that had stood between them for nine months, her hands in his hair, her knees tight at his waist, her coat falling open. He held her off the floor and kissed her back with his eyes shut and the whole of arrivals going on round them, and he didn’t care, and he’d never in his life not cared about being looked at in a public place.

When she pulled back she was smiling so widely that he felt his own face do something he couldn’t stop.

“Hello,” she whispered.

“Hello.”

She kissed him again, shorter. He let her down slowly until her feet found the floor, and she didn’t let go of him. She put her hand flat on his cheek as she had in the consular section in October, checking. He let her check. Then she saw the rail.

“Ranunculus.”

“Yes.”

“You remembered.”

“I wrote it down.”

She picked them up and looked at them, and then at him. “Did you choose them, or did the woman in the shop tell you?”

“I asked for them by name.”

“That’s extremely romantic for a man who once forgot to say thank you.”

“I said thank you to the woman in the shop. Your suitcase is unattended,” said Wei Long. He glanced past her.

She stared at him, and then put her face in his coat and laughed until her shoulders shook.

“Three months,” she said into his lapel, “and that’s what you say.”

“It’s in the middle of the hall.”

“It’s been on worse floors. It’s been on a floor that moved.”

“Isla.”

She leaned up and kissed him again and said, “Fine, get my suitcase,” and he did, and she took his free hand and held the flowers against her chest with the other.

Outside the air was soft and wet and smelled of jet fuel and the harbour, and cooler than Lima. She stopped just past the doors and looked at the taxi rank and the flyover and the lit towers beyond it, all of it exactly where she’d left it, and didn’t say anything. He waited.

“I have a job. Not the one I wanted,” she said after a while.

“I know.”

“I’m still a bit disappointed.”

“You’re allowed.”

“I’m going to do it well.”

“I know you are.”

“And I’m going to apply for deputy again the next time one comes up, and I’m going to get it.”

“Yes.”

She looked at him. “You’re agreeing with everything.”

“You’re right about everything.”

“That won’t last,” said Isla, and put her hand in his coat pocket with his.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove her to her flat, which had been his for nine months and was still hers. She noticed at once that he’d kept it exactly as she’d left it and that he’d lived in it anyway: his boots by the door next to the space where hers went, his files stacked on her side table in a pile so square it looked machined, three of her tea’s four packets on the second shelf and the fourth gone. On the fridge, under the magnet shaped like a fish, the list she’d left in July was still there, with eight items on it now. The eighth was in his handwriting.

8. I’m coming. W.L.

She stood and read it with the flowers still in her arms.

“You didn’t take it down.”

“No.”

“October was six months ago.”

“It was still true,” said Wei Long, and took her coat off her shoulders from behind, and the flowers out of her arms, and put them in the sink in water because there was nothing else to put them in.

She turned round. The flat was too small for two people who both owned books; she could see that from the hall. They’d have to do something about it. Not tonight.

“Take me to bed. I’ve been sitting down for thirty-one hours,” she said.

He went to run her a bath first, because she’d been sitting down for thirty-one hours. When he came back she was asleep on top of the covers in her coat with one shoe still on, and a ranunculus, which she must have taken out of the sink on her way, lying on the pillow by her hand. He took the shoe off. He didn’t take the flower away. He lay down on his side of her bed, in his clothes, and watched her sleep until the bath had gone cold.

chapters.title: She Doesn’t Hate It
chapters.desc: She runs consular emergencies for the whole city, and the station learns her direct line. Nine o’clock, his desk, ten minutes, again. They sign a lease on a bigger flat together, with boxes for furniture: explicit. He takes Qu Wenjun’s one line to Camphor Hill.
chapters.epigraph: “I forgot I was allowed to like the work.”
chapters.content:
The first call came just before eight on her second Tuesday, while the kettle was still deciding whether to boil.

“Ren.”

“Officer Ren, sorry it’s early. We’ve got a citizen of yours detained overnight. A tourist. Some kind of fight outside a hotel.”

“Is he hurt? Has he been charged? Which station?” She had the laptop open before the kettle clicked. By a quarter past eight she’d confirmed where he was held and that he’d seen a lawyer. By half past she’d rung his mother in Ottawa, where it was the evening before, and explained what the consulate could do and what it couldn’t. Around half past eight his mother asked whether Isla could make the police let him go.

Isla said, “No, I can’t tell the police to release him. I can make sure he has a lawyer, that he’s being treated properly, and that you hear from me the moment I know something real.”

“But you’re the consulate.”

“Yes.”

“Can’t you do something?”

“I am doing something, Mrs. Carter. I promise you I am,” said Isla, gently, and looked at the page of notes in front of her, and at the coffee she hadn’t made.

By the end of April the station had her direct line.

She found this out on a Wednesday just before nine in the morning, when the phone rang and a voice like gravel being poured said, “Officer Ren? Station Sergeant Hau. French national in the cells, asking for consular notification, and your section’s down as the contact.”

“Send me the custody reference and I’ll check whether he’s ours.”

“I’ll do that. And Inspector Song asked me to tell you the nine o’clock appointment is still in effect.”

She looked at the clock. “Is that an official police communication, Sergeant?”

“No, Officer Ren.”

“Then tell him I’m grateful for the reminder.”

Hau made a noise that might have been a cough, and rang off.

She walked into the station at 9:02. Nobody on the front desk asked who she was. The newest constable, who’d been at the station three weeks and had clearly been briefed, pointed down the corridor without being asked, and two detectives at the coffee machine became fascinated by the coffee machine.

He was reading a report. He looked up the moment the door opened, which she noticed, because two years ago he’d made her wait for it.

“You’re late.”

“Two minutes. I was protecting a man from his mother’s phone calls.”

“Did it work?”

“No. She thinks I personally run the justice system. Good morning.” She sat on the edge of his desk, where she’d sat the first time, and moved her bag before he could tell her it was on his files.

“Good morning,” said Wei Long, and she leaned down and he came up to meet her, one hand at her waist, and the kiss was brief and familiar and made the rest of the day look better than it had any right to.

“Eating?” he said.

“Mostly.”

It wasn’t an answer, and they both knew it.

“It’s the one you’re getting. Are they still running the book?” Somebody walked past the open blind, slowed, and walked on with great determination. She tipped her head at the corridor.

“I don’t know what you mean.”

“Inspector, I have eyes. I’ve had eyes since March two years ago.”

He looked at her over his tea. Then he smiled, properly, not the twitch at the corner the squad had spent two years trying to photograph, and she touched the corner of his mouth with her finger as though she were marking it on a map.

“Go back to work. You have a call at half past,” he said.

“How do you know that?”

“You told me yesterday.”

She slid off the desk. At the door she turned. “Tomorrow?”

“Nine.”

“Don’t be late.”

“I work here,” said Wei Long. She left, and he picked up his pen, and the door opened again and her head came round it.

“By the way, I love you.”

“I love you,” he said, to an empty doorway, because she’d already gone.

From the corridor somebody made a strangled sound. Wei Long put his pen down and said, without raising his voice, “Sergeant Hau. If the sheet’s still on the noticeboard tomorrow I’ll take it down.”

Hau’s face appeared at the blind. “Which sheet, sir?”

✦ ✦ ✦

Not every day was a tourist and a cross mother.

In May a fishing boat brought a body in from eleven miles out. By two o’clock she’d confirmed the identity, and by four she was on the phone to a woman in Halifax who’d been married to him for twenty-six years. Was he alone. Did he suffer. Can you find out. Isla said she didn’t know yet, and that she’d ask, and then said nothing at all while the woman cried, because there was nothing she could say that would be any use and she’d learned in Lima that saying it anyway was for her own sake and not the family’s. After a while the woman apologised. Isla told her not to. “He loved the sea. He loved it more than me, some years,” the woman said. Isla wrote that down too, though it wasn’t for any form.

She got to the station just after nine that night. He took one look at her face and moved a folder off the chair beside his.

She sat in the chair instead of on the desk. He didn’t ask about the case. He put a cup of warm water in front of her, not tea, because she’d mentioned a headache at lunch and he’d written that down too, and went back to his report with his free hand left lying on the desk between them. After a minute she put hers on top of it. They stayed like that until her ten minutes were up, and then for another four, and nobody walked past the blind at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The lost child was at the cruise terminal on a bright Friday: five years old, separated from her grandmother in the crush off a ship, found by a terminal guard sitting between two luggage trolleys holding a stuffed rabbit with one ear.

“Hello,” said Isla, crouching. “I’m Isla. What’s your name?”

“Amelia. Are you police?”

“No. I’m from the consulate. It’s an office that helps people from home when they’re far away.”

Amelia considered this with suspicion. “My grandma walks slowly.”

“Then we’ll make sure nobody makes her hurry. Who’s that?” Isla nodded at the rabbit.

“Captain. He’s scared.”

“Has he been on a ship before?”

A nod.

“Then he’s qualified,” said Isla, and Amelia stopped crying long enough to look at her. The grandmother was found at the information desk ten minutes later, white to the lips and sitting down only because a security officer had made her. When she saw the child she dropped to her knees on the terminal floor, and Isla stood back and let them have it, and found she was holding her breath, and let it out.

“Captain did well,” she said, to nobody, and went back to the car.

The betting sheet came back the week after. She found it because she was looking for a stapler in the cupboard beside the station printer, pinned to the inside of the door behind a box of paper clips. At the top, in Hau’s capitals: HOW LONG BEFORE INSP. SONG SMILES WHEN OFFICER REN WALKS IN? Below it, names and dates and sums of money, and at the bottom in a different pen: He already does. You’re all two years late.

“Put it back,” said Wei Long from the doorway.

“Absolutely not. Who wrote the last line?”

“I don’t know.”

“It isn’t your writing.”

“No.”

“It’s Hau’s.”

He didn’t answer. She folded it into quarters and put it in her bag, and he watched her do it, and didn’t take it off her, which told her more than anything on the sheet.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the third week of May they signed a lease together on a flat three streets up from hers, with a second bedroom for books and a balcony that caught the evening. Her old flat had been too small for two people who both owned files; they’d known that the night she came home. The new one had both their names on the door and, for the moment, almost nothing else in it. Her things from Lima had arrived in crates. His had arrived in eleven boxes, all labelled, all square. The sofa had been delayed twice. So had the table and the shelves. The bed was a mattress on the bedroom floor.

“Which one is the sofa?” he said, on the first Saturday night, standing in the middle of the living room.

She pointed. “The big one.”

“That’s a box.”

“It’s a large box. It says BOOKS. It’s perfectly stable.”

He put his palm on top and pushed, and it shifted.

“Why would you do that?”

“To test it.”

“You tested my sofa.”

“I tested the box. Your furniture is extremely busy,” said Wei Long. He looked round at the crates and the cartons and the one real chair.

She laughed until she had to hold on to him, and then she didn’t let go.

“Have you eaten?” he said into her hair.

“No. I was waiting for you. Don’t.”

“I was going to ask what you wanted.”

“You,” said Isla.

He kissed her standing up in the middle of the boxes. It started as the kiss they’d learned for the end of the day, and she didn’t let it end; she pulled him down by the collar and kept him. He undid her blouse with more care than the buttons needed, and she pulled his shirt out of his trousers and up, and he got it the rest of the way, and when he went for the bedroom she shook her head.

“Here.”

He looked at the boxes. “Here?”

“Here. I’ve been looking at these boxes for a week. I want to like them.”

She pushed him back until his legs hit the one marked BOOKS and he sat down on it, and it held, just. She stood between his knees and let him take her skirt off and her underwear, slowly, his mouth following his hands down her stomach, and when she couldn’t stand it she climbed onto his lap with a knee either side of him on the cardboard and reached between them and opened his trousers. He was hard in her hand. She took him in by herself, an inch and then all of it, holding his face so he had to watch her do it, and the noise he made was one she’d never heard him make in the station or anywhere else.

The box gave way under them on the fourth stroke. It didn’t collapse; one corner went, with a soft crunch of paper, and they lurched sideways, and she clutched his neck and he caught them both with one hand flat on the next carton, and she was laughing so much she could hardly breathe, with him still inside her.

“Your sofa,” he said.

“Don’t you dare.”

He lifted her off it, still holding her, and put her down on the rug, and came down over her. The rug was thin. The floor under it was hard. Neither of them cared. He moved into her again, long and deep, her knees up at his ribs, and she pulled him down until his weight was on her and wrapped both arms round his back and held on. There was no hurry, and no flight in the morning, and no thirteen hours. There was the lamp they hadn’t unpacked lying on its side by the wall, and his breath at her ear, and the slow, heavy pull of him that went on until she was gasping, and she came under him with her heels digging into the backs of his thighs and his name coming out of her like something she’d been keeping since October.

He didn’t stop. He slowed, and waited, and kissed her until she was shaking again, and only then let himself go, with his forehead pressed to hers and a sound low in his throat.

The cold came up through the rug after a while.
