He got up and lifted her and carried her through to the mattress on the bedroom floor, and she said it wasn’t a bed, and he said it was functional, and she said “Honestly,” and he said “You chose me,” and lay down beside her, and she turned over and put her back against his chest and pulled his arm round her and found she was nearly asleep.

“We need a sofa,” she said.

“Tomorrow.”

“And a bed frame. And a table.”

“Tomorrow,” said Wei Long, against the back of her neck, and in the morning they bought none of them, because it rained and they didn’t get up.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Thursday after, he went to Camphor Hill in his long coat at seven in the evening and stood on Elara Wang’s step with an envelope.

He’d carried it since March of last year. Qu Wenjun had given it to him in the interview room after the plea, folded once, and asked for it to reach her on the day she married again. He’d read it, because he read everything that passed through his hands in a case. One line. He’d put it in an envelope of his own and kept it in his desk drawer apart from the case papers, because it wasn’t evidence and he’d never have forgiven himself if it had become evidence by mistake.

“He asked for this to reach you on the day. I read it. You don’t have to,” he told her, when she opened the door.

She looked at it without moving before she took it. Xing Yue was behind her in the hall. Neither of them asked him in, and he hadn’t expected them to.

On Saturday he was in the hospital garden at twenty to six, at the back with the night staff in their scrubs, because Eliana had texted him at eleven the night before: If you’re late I’ll drag you down the path myself. Yu says you always disappear. Yu Chen found him at the gate with two coffees and gave him one, and said, “You came,” and Wei Long said, “I said I would,” and Yu Chen said he knew, and stood beside him while the grass went from grey to green.

Isla came at six exactly, with her hair pinned and the betting sheet still in her bag from a fortnight ago, and slipped her hand into his.

“Did I miss it?”

“Yes.”

She stopped dead. He looked at her.

“You’re joking.”

“Yes.”

She hit his arm, not lightly, and then the bride came out of the old block in white, and the garden went quiet, and Isla stopped hitting him and held on to his arm instead.

He didn’t go forward afterwards. He stood at the back while everyone else did, and watched the woman whose case he’d carried for eighteen months laugh with her head thrown back under the window her mother had once looked out of. He didn’t know what she’d made of the line. It wasn’t his to know. He’d brought it because he’d been asked, and the rest was hers.

“Are you happy?” said Isla, under the noise.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

At nine that evening she walked into the station in a plain dress with a paper bag of pastries and sat on his desk.

“You’re late,” he said.

“One minute.”

“Yes.”

“I like the job. I didn’t think I would. Not all of it. Some days are awful. But when someone’s frightened, I can tell them what happens next, and I know who to ring. I was so busy minding about the title that I forgot I was allowed to like the work,” she said, out of nowhere, with her mouth full. She brushed sugar off her fingers onto his blotter.

“You didn’t forget. You were disappointed.”

“That’s generous.”

“It’s accurate,” said Wei Long, and took the other pastry.

When she’d gone at twelve minutes past, he went out to the noticeboard. The old sheet had been replaced with a new one, in Hau’s capitals.

HOW LONG BEFORE INSP. SONG ASKS OFFICER REN TO MARRY HIM?

He read it twice. He went back to his office and shut the door and sat for a while with his hands flat on the desk.

Hau, passing the blind a minute later, glanced in, saw the inspector’s face, and walked on without stopping. He didn’t put any money on the sheet that week. He didn’t tell anyone why.

chapters.title: The Same Interview Room
chapters.desc: Inspector and consular officer, one case, opposite sides of the same table: a citizen of hers accused of manslaughter in a case of his. She won’t tell him what her citizen said. Afterwards, in his car, both of them right, a hard kiss.
chapters.epigraph: “I know where your side is. I sat opposite it today.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Isla noticed was the name. The second was the word manslaughter.

The notification came through the duty system at ten past eight on a Monday in July while she was standing at the printer. One of her citizens had been arrested over the death of a crew member on a privately chartered yacht in local waters. The dead man was a foreign national. Her citizen was the skipper.

Adrian Vale, 43. Yacht skipper. Arrested Sunday 14:20. Legal representation requested. Requests consular assistance and family notification.

She rang the custody desk.

“Officer Ren, morning. Yes, we’ve got him. He’s asked for you. His lawyer’s been called, not here yet.”

“Who’s the investigating officer?”

“Inspector Song.”

Her hand stopped on the keyboard. She’d known it was his station. She’d known that sooner or later one of hers would be in one of his cells. She’d thought she’d be ready.

“Thank you. I’ll come over when the lawyer’s arrived.”

She took her phone out.

Isla: I have a consular case at your station.

Inspector Glacier: I know.

Isla: You’re running it.

Inspector Glacier: Yes.

There was nothing in that. Two officials confirming a fact. They’d worked in the same city for three months and their jobs touched most weeks. She read it three times anyway.

Inspector Glacier: Are you free for dinner tonight?

Isla: You’re asking me that while you’re investigating my citizen?

Inspector Glacier: I’m asking before the interview. I thought it was better than after.

Isla: It isn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

The dead man was Rhys Mercer, thirty-four, deckhand, employed by Vale for fourteen months. The yacht had come back into harbour just after dawn on Sunday. Vale had reported that Mercer went over the side in the dark during an argument about the boat, that they’d searched for forty minutes, and that he’d then called the marine police. The body had been found at nine, a mile down the coast.

The first account said accident. The boat said other things. A section of the aft rail was bent outward. A stanchion fitting had been found on the deck, sheared. One crew member said she’d heard shouting, and another said that afterwards Vale had ordered everyone below and kept them there for twenty minutes before anyone touched the radio.

Nobody knew yet what had happened. Isla had dealt with enough deaths abroad to know how fast a first account turned into the only story a family ever remembered, and she didn’t intend to help it.

Station Sergeant Hau met her at the front counter.

“His solicitor’s here, Officer Ren. Interview Three. The inspector’s inside.”

“I assumed he would be.”

“Shall I tell him you’ve arrived?”

“He knows,” said Isla.

Through the narrow window in the door of Interview Three she could see Wei Long on the far side of the table with a file open in front of him and his jacket on. He looked up as she came down the corridor. For one second their eyes met through the glass. Then he stood and opened the door.

“Officer Ren.”

“Inspector.”

His face was perfectly composed. She’d watched him wear that face across a table at other people, and once, in Interview Three, at her. It was strange to be on the same side of the door as it.

Vale was at the table beside his solicitor, a tanned man with grey coming in at the temples and the hands of someone who’d worked ropes all his life, clasped hard together. When she came in he said, “Thank God,” as if she’d come to take him home.

She sat in the chair opposite the inspector, beside her citizen, which was where the procedure put her and where she’d never sat before.

“Mr. Vale, I’m Isla Ren, from the consulate. I’m here to explain what we can do for you.”

“Can you get me out?”

“No. I can’t arrange your release, and I can’t take part in the investigation. I can make sure you have a lawyer, that you’re being treated properly, that your family knows where you are. And I’d like to speak to you privately for a few minutes about what you need from us. That’s separate from the police interview.”

Vale looked across the table. “Is that allowed?”

“Consular access is permitted. The interview won’t start until it’s done,” said Wei Long.

“Thank you, Inspector,” said Isla.

He inclined his head. That was all. She’d known him for two years and four months and she’d never once heard him say Officer Ren in that voice, and she didn’t like it, and she knew it was right.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the consultation room Vale was frightened, and angry, and had been awake for more than a day, and couldn’t yet tell the difference between being suspected of something and having already lost everything.

She went through it with him: the lawyer, the consular role, the call she could arrange to his sister in Calgary.

“Can you tell her I’m innocent?”

“I can tell her you’ve been detained and that there’s an investigation. I can’t say anything about the facts.”

“You don’t believe me.”

“Mr. Vale, I’m not here to decide whether you did anything. I’m here for what you need.”

He looked at the wall. Then he said, low, “We argued. Rhys and I. He’d been skipping safety checks for weeks and I told him he’d get someone killed, and he said I was the one who... I grabbed his arm. He pulled away. And then he wasn’t there.” His solicitor had stepped out to take a call. Vale’s hands came apart and went together again.

Isla kept her face still. “Mr. Vale, I can’t give you legal advice and nothing you say to me is privileged. Please don’t tell me any more about Sunday night. Tell your solicitor.”

“Did I push him? I don’t know if I pushed him,” he said, in case she knew.

“Tell your solicitor,” said Isla again, and stood up, and asked him whether there was anything else he needed from the consulate.

He asked for his sister. At the door he said, “Do you think I’m a bad person?”

“I think a man is dead and you’re in a frightening place. It isn’t my job to decide who you are,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The interview started at 11:20. She wasn’t in it. She had no part in the evidence and didn’t want one. She sat in the waiting area with her laptop and dealt with the sister in Calgary, who wanted to fly out that night, and a hospital across the harbour that had mislaid a citizen’s medication, and a funeral director who needed a form she’d already sent twice.

At 12:06 she went into the corridor to take a call and found Wei Long at the end of it with a file under his arm.

“Break?” she said.

“He’s been given a meal. His solicitor’s with him. Have you eaten?” He looked at her.

“Don’t.”

“There’s food in the staff room.”

“You’re interviewing my citizen for manslaughter and you’re asking me if I’ve had lunch.”

“Yes.”

“You don’t know when to stop being my boyfriend.”

“I do know. I’m choosing not to,” said Wei Long.

She went past him. Their hands brushed in the narrow corridor, his knuckles against hers. Neither of them looked down.

The interview ran another two hours. Vale went back to the cells pending further enquiries. Isla was writing up the welfare note when the inspector came out of Interview Three with his sleeves turned back once and a crease between his eyebrows she knew from the bad cases.

“Can I talk to you?”

“About what?”

“The case.”

“Then no.”

“I’m not asking you to disclose anything. I need to know whether he’s raised any welfare concerns that bear on custody. Self-harm. Anything he said to you.” He stopped by the custody desk, out of the officer’s hearing.

“You can ask the custody officer. You can ask his solicitor. You can ask him, under caution, through the proper process.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you asking me?”

“Because you were in the room with him for twenty minutes and I wasn’t. And because I know you. If there were something I needed to know, you’d tell me.” He held her eyes.

She felt it go through her, cold and quick.

“No, Wei Long. That’s exactly what I won’t do. You know the rule. What you don’t understand is what happens if I make an exception because it’s you asking. If I tell you something he said to me in a consular interview, I’m not his consular officer any more. I’m your source. There’s an article in the Vienna Convention, forty-four, that says I’m not obliged to give evidence about what I learned doing my job. I’m not going to give it to you in a corridor instead.” She kept her voice level; the custody officer was six metres away.

“I wasn’t asking you to be a source.”

“You just did.”

The corridor went silent. A phone rang in the custody suite and somebody answered it.

He nodded. Once. “All right.”

“He has access to his solicitor. He’s asked for his sister and we’re arranging it. That’s all I can tell you.”

“That’s sufficient.”

“Good,” said Isla, and walked away, and he didn’t follow her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stayed at her desk till half past six and wrote up the day in the dry language the record wanted. Lawyer present. Family notified. Welfare checked. She didn’t record the twenty minutes in the consultation room as an account of anything. She didn’t pass it to anyone. She sat for a while with her hands on the keys and thought about a man saying I don’t know if I pushed him, and about another man saying I know you, and which one she minded more.

Her head of section, Marc Pelletier, stopped by her desk on his way out.

“How was the yacht?”

“Busy. He’s got a lawyer. The sister’s flying in Wednesday.”

“And Inspector Song?”

She looked up.

“You were both on it,” said Pelletier mildly. “Different jobs, same building. It’s hard when they overlap. Did you keep it clean?”

“Yes.”

“Then go home. It protects him as much as you, you know.”

“I know,” said Isla, and shut her laptop.

Just after seven her phone buzzed.

Inspector Glacier: Are you still at work?

Isla: Leaving now.

Inspector Glacier: I’m outside. I’ll wait.

Isla: You don’t have to.

Inspector Glacier: I know.

His car was at the kerb with the engine off. He was still in his work shirt, sitting bolt upright behind the wheel. She got into the passenger seat and put her bag at her feet and didn’t say anything, and neither did he, and the lights of the street moved over the windscreen.

“You were right. I shouldn’t have asked you,” he said at last.

“No.”

“I told myself I was asking about his welfare.”

“You were.”

“I was also asking because I wanted to know what he’d said to you. I’m sorry.” He turned his head and looked at her.

He didn’t explain that the case was hard, or that it might matter, or that he’d meant well. He said what he’d done and stopped. She’d always loved that about him, and she was still angry.

“I’m angry with you,” she said.

“I know.”

“Not because you asked a question. Because you made me prove I could be trusted by refusing to answer it. In front of a custody officer. In your building.”

His jaw moved. “I didn’t mean it like that.”

“I know you didn’t. It’s how it felt. I trust you. I love you. Neither of those is a reason for me to hand you something that belongs to a man who came to me for help. And I can’t walk into your station every time a citizen of mine is in your cells and wonder whether you’re looking at me and thinking I’m holding something back.” She looked at the windscreen.

“I won’t.”

“How do you know?”

“Because I know what your job is. And I know why you do it. It’s the same reason I do mine,” said Wei Long.

She looked at him. Then she reached across the console and took a fistful of his shirt.

He looked down at her hand. “Isla.”

“I’m still angry.”

“I know.”

“I’m also glad you waited.”

She pulled. He came. The kiss was hard, nothing careful in it and nothing kind, her fist in his shirt and her other hand at his jaw and her teeth catching his lip, all the things she hadn’t been able to say in the corridor going into it at once. He answered in kind. His hand went to the back of her neck and held her there, and he kissed her, which he had been waiting since twenty past eleven to do, leaning across the console until the handbrake was digging into her hip and she didn’t care. Somebody walked past on the pavement. Neither of them stopped.

When they broke apart she was breathing badly and her forehead was against his.

“Are you still angry?” he said.

“Yes.”

“All right.”

“You’re not supposed to agree.”

“Would you rather I argued?”

“No.”

“Then I agree,” said Wei Long, and she laughed, against her will, into his mouth.

“We were both right,” she said.

“Yes.”

“And it was horrible anyway.”

“Yes. Next time you say you can’t discuss something, I won’t ask why.” He took her hand out of his shirt and smoothed the creases she’d made and kissed her knuckles.

“Next time I’ll be on my side of the table. You’ll be on yours,” said Isla.

“I know where your side is. I sat opposite it today.”

She sat back. Her hip hurt where the handbrake had been. Her mouth felt bruised. “Take me home. I’m starving.”

He looked at her.

“I know. Don’t,” she said.

He started the engine. At the first red light she put her hand on the gearstick over his and left it there, and he turned his hand over under hers when the light changed, and drove the rest of the way with one hand, badly, which in two years and four months she’d never once seen him do.

chapters.title: Her Brother Approves, Finally
chapters.desc: Ren Hao approves, finally, in an eleven-minute toast nobody asked for at a dinner nobody wanted. Wei Long holds her hand under the table the whole time. Ren Hao catches them in the corridor and leaves loudly.
chapters.epigraph: “I want the people who love you to know I love you properly.”
chapters.content:
Ren Hao had called it a small family dinner, and Isla had believed him, which she’d later describe as the only truly stupid thing she did in 2027.

The restaurant had a private room on the top floor with a table for twelve, a printed menu with the date on it, flowers down the middle, and a seating plan in a little silver frame on an easel by the door. There were eleven names on the seating plan. She read it in her coat with her bag still on her shoulder.

“Why am I sitting there?”

“Because you’re my sister,” said her brother, appearing at her elbow in a suit that cost more than her first car.

“That’s not a reason. I’m on your left. Wei Long’s on your right. You’ve put yourself between us.”

“I’ve arranged the table.”

“You’ve separated us.”

“Don’t be dramatic. It’s a seating plan, not a custody battle,” said Ren Hao, delighted.

“You once threatened to have him investigated.”

“That was before I knew him.”

“It was eight months after you knew him.”

“Details. Inspector,” said Ren Hao, and turned with his arms out, because Wei Long had come up the stairs behind her with a small paper bag in one hand and his tie done up to the top.

“Ren Hao.”

They shook hands. It was perfectly civil, and went on slightly too long, and Isla watched it the way she’d watch two ministers who’d been told by their governments to get on.

“Where am I?” said Wei Long.

“Beside me.”

“All right.”

She stared at him. “You’re accepting that?”

“It’s a chair.”

“It’s a strategic position.”

“It’s still a chair,” he said, and Ren Hao clapped him on the shoulder hard enough to move him and said, “You see? This is why I like him,” and walked into the room before either of them could ask him to say it again.

✦ ✦ ✦

The dinner began well, which was the first warning.

Her brother was charming. He asked Wei Long about work without asking anything that touched a live case. He listened to Isla’s account of the emergencies desk and asked a good question about the hospitals. He told a story about a client who’d mistaken a ninety-page risk assessment for a restaurant review and given it three stars, and Yu Chen laughed into his water, and Eliana laughed harder, and two of Hao’s oldest friends, who’d come up from the other end of the table to hear it, laughed so loudly that a waiter looked in. Even Wei Long’s mouth moved.

Song-Zhu sat opposite Hao and laughed less than anyone, and Isla, watching, saw him check on her between every course without seeming to. The final report on the crash had come out twelve days before. Isla had seen the photographs from the memorial: the families in rows by the sea, her brother in the front with Song-Zhu’s hand in his, both of them in black. Song-Zhu had come tonight anyway. She was eating slowly and listening, and once, when Hao was mid-story, she reached across and straightened his collar without stopping him, and he didn’t stop.

Under the table, Wei Long’s hand found Isla’s. She slid her fingers between his. He didn’t look at her. His thumb moved once across her knuckles and then lay still, and stayed there through the fish and the second bottle of wine and an argument between Hao and Song-Zhu about whether a soup he’d sent back three years ago had been supposed to be cold.

“It was supposed to be cold,” said Song-Zhu.

“It was too cold.”

“That’s not a thing.”

“It is a thing. I’m a man of standards. Inspector. Were my expectations reasonable?” He appealed to the table.

Wei Long considered it. “What were they?”

“Room temperature.”

“For a cold soup?”

“You see? This is the question I appreciate. A man who gathers the facts,” said Hao.

“He’s agreeing with me,” said Song-Zhu.

Isla saw her brother’s eyes go down to the tablecloth, where nothing was visible but where he’d clearly worked out exactly what was, and then come back up to his glass. He didn’t say anything. That was so unlike him that she nearly asked if he was ill.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was over the main course that he got to what he’d come for.

“Isla tells me,” he said, “that you’re still doing the nine o’clock thing.”

“The nine o’clock thing,” said Wei Long.

“She goes to your office every evening.”

“Not every evening.”

Isla turned in her chair. “Excuse me?”

“Some days you have work,” he said to her, reasonably, and gave Hao ten minutes.

“Always ten minutes?”

“Usually.”

“Usually?”

“Sometimes longer.”

Isla felt her face heat. Her brother lit up like a city.

“How much longer?”

“That’s enough,” said Isla.

“I’m asking about a timetable. Do you feel interrogated, Inspector?”

“Slightly.”

“Then we’re making progress,” said Hao, satisfied.

Across the table Song-Zhu caught Isla’s eye and shook her head minutely, as if to say she’d been through this herself, in a French restaurant with candles, and had survived it by laughing. Hao leaned back, and looked at his sister.

“You used to complain about him. Don’t deny it. You rang me from the station car park in the first month and said he was impossible to read.”

“He was impossible to read.”

“Was?” said Wei Long.

“Don’t get comfortable.”

“And now you defend him to me.”

“I defend people when they’re right.”

“She’s usually right,” said Wei Long.

Isla turned to thank him.

“Not always,” said Wei Long.

Hao laughed so loudly that Yu Chen dropped his fork. “There. There. That’s what I wanted to see. Somebody who can disagree with her and live.”

“I’ve learned when to do it,” said Wei Long, and Isla kicked him under the table, and he didn’t move his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter past nine, with the dessert on the table and nobody yet daring to eat it, her brother stood up.

“Sit down,” said Isla.

“No.”

“Hao. Sit down.”

“Everyone,” said Ren Hao, lifting his glass, and across the table Song-Zhu took out her phone, set it face up beside her plate, and touched the screen.

“Are you recording this?”

“No, I’m timing it,” said Song-Zhu.

The table laughed. Hao gave her a look of deep betrayal and carried on.

He’d rehearsed. Isla knew within a sentence. He went back to the beginning, to Vancouver, to a four-year-old who wanted to do everything herself and fell off everything and got up and said she was fine. He said he’d known her twenty-seven years. She said twenty-six, he’d been away at a sailing camp the summer she was born. He said that counted, morally, and went on. He told the table about the year she decided to learn French out of spite because a boy at school said she couldn’t, and the year she learned the northern language properly because their grandmother had cried when she’d got a tone wrong, and the day she’d rung from the ministry to say she’d got Lima and he’d had to go into the stairwell on the thirty-second floor so that nobody would see him.

He told them about October.

He didn’t tell it well. He kept stopping. He said that for a day and a night nobody could tell him if his sister was alive, and that the only person who’d answered his calls every single time was a police inspector he’d once tried to have investigated, and that on the Saturday the inspector had tried to pay for his own plane ticket and Hao hadn’t let him. “Best money I ever spent. And I’ve bought a boat,” he said.

Nobody laughed. Under the table, Wei Long’s hand had tightened on hers until it hurt.

Ren Hao said, “I wanted her to be happy. I also wanted whoever stood next to her to understand what that means with her, because it doesn’t mean quiet, and it doesn’t mean small. Inspector. You’ve never tried to impress me. You’ve never promised her anything you couldn’t keep. When she decides something, you let her decide it, which I’ve never once managed in thirty years. And I’ve watched her get happier. Not quieter. Not smaller. Happier. So, finally, and officially, after an unreasonable length of time: you have my approval.” He turned. He raised his glass a little higher.

The table erupted. Yu Chen banged the table. Eliana whistled through her fingers, which nobody had known she could do. One of Hao’s friends shouted “About time!” from the far end, and Isla put her free hand over her face.

“Eleven minutes, and fourteen seconds,” said Song-Zhu, looking at her phone.

“That’s not bad,” said Hao.

“It’s longer than a state banquet.”

“Then I should go into public speaking.”

“No,” said the whole table.

“He practised it on me. Twice. On Thursday it was nine minutes. He added the boat,” Song-Zhu told Isla under the noise, putting her phone away.

Wei Long stood up. The room went quiet faster than it had for Hao, which Isla could see her brother noticing.

Wei Long said, “Thank you. I know what she is to you. I know you wanted to be sure. I can’t promise nothing hard will happen. I can promise I’ll tell her the truth and that I’ll respect what she decides. I love her. To Isla.” He looked at Hao and not at anyone else. He picked up his glass.

Hao held his eyes across the flowers. “All right,” he said, and that was all, and it was more than the eleven minutes.

“To my sister.”

“To dinner being over,” said Isla, standing up between them with her eyes stinging, and they drank to that too.

✦ ✦ ✦

By eleven the photographs were done (one of everyone, one of the siblings, one of the couple with Hao standing beside them until the photographer asked him to move, and then another because he claimed he’d blinked, and Song-Zhu checked the screen and said he hadn’t), and Yu Chen and Eliana had gone home, and Hao was arguing with the manager about a coat that had been put in the wrong cupboard. Isla and Wei Long went out into the corridor that led to the lifts. It was carpeted, and empty, and had a window at the end over the street.

“Eleven minutes,” she said.

“And fourteen seconds.”

“He gave a speech at my graduation. Three minutes.”

“He had less material.”

She laughed and stopped by the window. “You were nervous.”

“Yes.”

“You didn’t need his permission.”

“I know. I wanted it anyway. I want the people who love you to know I love you properly.” He moved a strand of hair off her cheek with one finger.

She kissed him before he could say anything else. It was meant to be short. It wasn’t. His hand came to her waist and she stepped in until there was no space at all, her fingers in the front of his jacket, and he kissed her slowly, the way he did when he’d decided nothing else was happening, and for a while she forgot that she was standing in a public corridor with her brother on the other side of a door.

“Well,” said a voice behind them.

They came apart. Ren Hao was at the far end of the corridor holding his coat. He looked at them, and at their hands, and at their faces, and raised both palms.

“No, no. Don’t stop on my account.”

“You could have rung,” said Isla.

“I did. Twice. Inspector. I approved you.” He pointed at Wei Long.

“I’m grateful.”

“Don’t make me regret it.”

“I won’t.”

“Good. Carry on.” He turned on his heel and walked off down the corridor, and every step was louder than the last. From round the corner his voice came back at the volume he used across trading floors.

“I’M GOING TO THE CAR.”

Isla put her face in Wei Long’s jacket.

“AND I’M NOT COMING BACK.”

“Is he upset?” said Wei Long.

“No. He’s making sure we know he saw.”

“Ah.”

She lifted her head. “Ah?”

“It’s a technique. I’ve used it,” said Wei Long.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car she let her head drop onto his shoulder at the lights and left it there.

“He loves you now. You know that,” she said.

“He said he approved.”

“In front of eleven witnesses. He’ll want another dinner to confirm it.”

“I’ll go.”

“You don’t have to say yes to everything my brother asks.”

“I know. He was worried about you. That whoever you chose would make your life smaller,” he said, and turned onto the coast road.

“I know.”

“I won’t.”

“I know that too. Eleven minutes and fourteen seconds. We should make him do it again at our wedding,” she said. The lights of the bay went by. She played with his fingers on the gearstick.

She heard it after she’d said it. It had come out the way you’d mention the weather.

He didn’t laugh. He didn’t pretend he hadn’t heard. He drove for another hundred metres, indicating carefully round a parked van, and then he said, “Would you like that?”

Her heart did something inconvenient. “Yes.”

“All right.”

“That’s all?”

“I’d like it too,” said Wei Long.

She looked out of the window so he wouldn’t see her face, and then decided she didn’t care whether he did, and looked back at him. He was watching the road with great concentration. There was colour along his cheekbones.

When they got home he went to his desk in the second bedroom, the one with the books, to put his watch in the drawer where he always kept it. She heard the drawer open. She lay on the bed in her dress with her shoes off and listened, and the drawer didn’t close, and didn’t close, and she found she was smiling at the ceiling.

chapters.title: Back to the Terminal
chapters.desc: The airport where they met. He proposes by the custody desk at arrivals with a prepared written statement. She says yes into his collar.
chapters.epigraph: “I have loved you in every place between this desk and here, and here is this desk.”
chapters.content:
The airport had changed its chairs. They’d redone the arrivals hall in the summer: new floor, new lighting, the information counters moved to the other side, everything paler and brighter and lower to the ground. Wei Long had sat in one of the new chairs at a quarter to seven and found his knees nearly level with his chin. He’d stood up again after a minute and stayed standing.

Isla’s flight was due at 7:40. She’d been at a regional consular meeting for two days, two hours’ flight away, and her return had been put back an hour by weather somewhere over the sea. He’d said he would collect her. He hadn’t said where he’d be standing. That was the first problem.

The second was the three sheets of paper folded in his inside pocket, which he’d checked six times since he’d parked. The third was the small box in the other pocket, which he’d checked four times, because he’d decided early on that checking it more often than the paper would be a sign of something.

He wasn’t nervous about the ring. He was nervous about the statement. He’d written it himself over five evenings at the desk in the room with the books, while she thought he was doing overtime. He’d revised it three times and printed it twice, and chosen the second version, because in the first he’d found a sentence that began At approximately and had had to stand up and walk round the flat.

It was three pages. He’d thought about cutting it, and decided not to. If he was going to say something that mattered, he was going to say all of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 7:46 she came through the doors with her case in one hand and her phone at her ear.

“No, I know. I’ll send the revised schedule tomorrow. Yes, I’ve got the papers. Thank you.”

She rang off and looked up, and saw him, and her whole face changed, the way it had in this hall six months ago and in a stairwell in Lima before that.

“Wei Long,” she said.

He took her case. She kissed him, quick and warm, and then stepped back and looked round, and frowned.

“Why are you standing here? The car park’s the other way.”

He looked past her. She followed his eyes.

At the far end of the hall, behind a new glass screen, was the police custody desk. They’d replaced the counter and moved the screen a metre to the left. But it was the same corner, under the same stretch of window, with the same rain coming down the glass, because it was the fourth of October and it was always raining when he needed it not to.

“Oh,” said Isla.

“I asked the duty sergeant for five minutes. He didn’t ask why,” said Wei Long.

She looked at him. Something in his face must have told her, because her free hand went slowly to her mouth.

“Come with me,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The duty sergeant at the airport post had been a constable in Wei Long’s first squad. He let them through the side gate in the glass screen with a face like a locked door, said “Five minutes, sir,” and went to stand at the far end of the counter reading a clipboard so hard it might have been in a foreign language.

The desk was empty. Rain ran down the window above it. Isla stood where she’d stood two and a half years ago with a soaked coat and a folder of the wrong forms, and he stood where he’d stood with a fraudster on a chain and no idea what was about to happen to him.

He put her case down. He took the paper out.

“What’s that?” said Isla.

“A statement.”

“A statement?”

“Yes.”

“Are you interviewing me?”

“No.”

“Do I have to sign it?”

“No. I wrote it. I’m going to read all of it. Then I’m going to ask you something.” He unfolded it, and his hands were steady, which surprised him.

Her eyes went to his other hand, where the box was, and then back to his face. She didn’t say anything. She nodded. He read.

He read it the way he read evidence into a record, standing straight, in his ordinary voice, without looking up. It was set out in numbered paragraphs, because that was how he knew how to make sure nothing was left out.

1. On Monday 3 March 2025 at this desk you corrected a form that wasn’t your mistake, in three languages, in eleven minutes. I stood here and said “Correct.” I didn’t thank you. You left a card under my windscreen wiper that said so. I still have it. It is in my wallet behind my warrant card.

Isla made a small sound. He didn’t stop.

2. On Friday 7 March you sat on my desk on top of a stabbing file and told me the world could wait ten minutes. You were right. It has waited ten minutes on four hundred and nineteen evenings since then. I have the dates.

3. I didn’t know I was lonely. I thought it was quiet. You came in and switched off the scanner and I found out the difference, and I would like it on the record that I wasn’t grateful at first.

He told her, in paragraphs four to eleven, things he’d never said aloud. That he’d read her consular file the week they met and that it had told him nothing he wanted to know. That the night after the stairwell he’d sat in the car outside her building for an hour and not rung the bell, because he’d thought that if he rang it he’d never want to leave, and he’d been right. That he’d told her to go to Lima because she wanted to, and had gone home and stood in her kitchen and not known what to do with his hands. That during the day in October when nobody could reach her he’d made a list on the back of a case file of the things he’d never told her, and that this was the list, put in order.

12. You have never once needed me to tell you what to do. I don’t want to be a man who decides things for you. I don’t want you to be smaller or quieter or less difficult to make room for me. I like the difficulty. I’ve got used to it.

13. I would like ordinary mornings. I would like to know which tea you’re drinking and whether you’ve eaten. I would like to argue about the heating. I would like to make plans and change them when your phone goes, and I’d like you to do the same when mine does. I would like to come home and find you there, and I’d like you to come home and find me.

14. We will get this wrong sometimes. We have already. In July I asked you a question in a corridor that I shouldn’t have asked. You told me so. I would like you to keep telling me so for the rest of my life.

By the bottom of the second page Isla was crying. Not loudly. She had both hands pressed flat against her mouth, and tears were running down over her fingers, and she was trying to hold still so he could finish.

15. I love you. I loved you when you sat on my desk, and in the stairwell, and in your car the night of Lantern Lane when I couldn’t make my hands stop. I loved you when you went to Lima and when you came back. I loved you in a room with a cracked wall. I have loved you in every place between this desk and here, and here is this desk.

16. I would like to keep doing it. For the rest of my life, if you’ll let me.

17. Veux-tu m’épouser? Quiero que te casas conmigo.

That is all.

He folded the paper. He didn’t put it away. He held it in one hand and the box in the other, and standing there with the rain on the window and the sergeant at the end of the counter not breathing, he seemed to have forgotten what came next. Isla laughed through her fingers, wetly.

“You wrote that. All of it,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Three pages.”

“Yes.”

“With numbers.”

“Yes.”

She took her hands down from her face. He opened the box. The ring was plain: a single clear stone in a narrow band, nothing round it, no ornament at all. He’d spent three Saturdays choosing it and in the end chosen the first one he’d been shown, because it was the one he’d kept looking back at.

“Isla Ren,” he said. “Will you marry me?”

She didn’t answer straight away. It wasn’t that she didn’t know. She’d been sure since a bench in Lima in January, possibly since a stairwell in March. It was that every word she had in any of her languages had gone somewhere behind her ribs and wouldn’t come out.

She stepped forward instead and took the front of his coat in both fists and pulled herself against him, hard, and put her face into his collar.

“Yes,” she said into it.

He didn’t move. “What?”

“Yes. Yes, Wei Long. Yes. I’ll marry you.” She held him tighter.

For one second he was absolutely still. Then his arms came round her, one hand spread on her back and the other cupping the back of her head, and he held on to her with a kind of relief she’d only ever seen in him once before, on a ninth floor in October, and she felt him let his breath out against her hair.

“Thank you,” he said.

“Don’t thank me. I’m saying yes because I want to. Because I want the mornings, and the arguments about the heating, and you reading things to me in paragraphs. And because I want you.” She pulled back far enough to look at him.

He held up the ring. She held out her hand, and it was shaking, and he noticed.

“Are you all right?”

“I’m getting married. I’m allowed to shake.”

He slid it on. It fitted. He looked at it on her finger for a second and then at her face.

“Is it comfortable?”

“That’s your first question?”

“I wanted to make sure.”

She kissed him then, with her new ring catching the light at the back of his neck and her case on its side by the custody desk, and he kissed her back as if there were nobody in the terminal at all, and at the far end of the counter the duty sergeant turned a page on his clipboard and then, without a sound, put the clipboard down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao rang around half past eight. Isla was in the passenger seat holding her left hand up in front of the dashboard lights. She looked at the screen, and at Wei Long.

“Answer it,” he said.

“Are you sure?”

“He’ll find out. Better from you.”

She put it on speaker. “Hello.”

“Where are you?”

“In the car. Hao, I’ve got news.”

There was a pause of the kind her brother almost never allowed. “What news?”

“I’m engaged.”

Silence. Then, with great care: “To whom?”

“Hao.”

“I know to whom. I want to hear you say it.”

“To Wei Long. He asked me at the airport. At the custody desk. Where we met.”

The silence went on long enough that she thought the call had dropped. Then: “Put him on.”

“You’re on speaker.”

“Inspector.”

“Ren Hao.”

“You proposed.”

“Yes.”

“Did you have a ring?”

“Yes.”

“Did you say anything? Or did you just hold it out like an exhibit?”

“I read her a statement.”

Another silence. Isla put her hand over her mouth.

“A statement?”

“Three pages. Seventeen paragraphs,” said Wei Long.

The noise Ren Hao made was half a laugh and half something else, and went on for some time. When he spoke again his voice had dropped all the way down.

“Good, I’m happy for you. Both of you. And don’t tell Mum and Dad, I want to tell them,” he said.

“Hao, it’s six in the morning in Vancouver.”

“Then I’ll wait till seven,” said her brother, and hung up, and she was laughing and crying at once and couldn’t have said which she’d started first.

“He’s going to tell everyone,” she said.

“Yes.”

“He’ll make a speech about it.”

“Yes,” said Wei Long. At the next light he lifted her left hand off her knee and kissed the ring, and put the hand back where it had been, and drove on. She looked at the paper folded on her lap, and opened it, and read the last paragraph again in the light from the street, and frowned.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the twenty-third of October, at a wedding across two back gardens in the Walled City, under a persimmon tree and a string of lights that Yu Chen had hung crooked, Isla stood beside him in the second row with her ring turned inward so it wouldn’t take attention from the bride. It took attention anyway, later; Eliana spotted it across the first dance and stopped dead in Yu Chen’s arms and mouthed WHAT, and Isla mouthed later.

At the reception her brother took the microphone, as everyone had known he would, and told the gardens that Yu Chen was the luckiest man in the city and that Eliana was terrifying in the best way, and didn’t mention his sister once, which she knew had cost him. Afterwards, at the drinks table under the lights, with a glass in his hand and the triplets and Nainai and two of the Lin sisters round him, he made up for it.

“Seventeen paragraphs. Numbered. At the custody desk. Paragraph two had a statistic in it.” Isla heard him say.

“Your brother’s telling them,” said Wei Long.

“He’s exaggerating.”

“Paragraph two did have a statistic.”

She leaned against his shoulder under the persimmon and watched Yu Chen try to dance and Eliana steer him. Yu Chen found them later, with his tie undone and his wife’s hand in his, and looked at Isla’s ring and then at his cousin.

“Ge, you really did it,” he said.

“Yes.”

Yu Chen didn’t say anything else. He put his arms round the man who’d raised him, in the middle of the garden, for longer than either of them was used to, and Wei Long let him, and stood straight as a post inside it, and when Yu Chen let go his eyes were wet and Wei Long’s weren’t, quite.

“She corrected his Spanish,” Isla told Eliana later, by the gate, when she’d been made to hold out her hand under the lights and turn it.

“In the airport?”

“In bed. That night. It’s a long story,” said Isla.

chapters.title: She Corrects His Proposal
chapters.desc: She corrects his proposal in three languages, at home, in bed. Engaged, the first night: explicit, slow, playful; he writes it again on a card, correctly.
chapters.epigraph: “One letter is the difference between a fact and a wish.”
chapters.content:
By the time they got home, Isla had found the mistake.

It had taken her forty minutes. Not because it was hard to find; it was in the last line, and she’d heard it at the custody desk with tears running into her fingers and filed it somewhere for later. But she’d been busy. She’d been looking at her hand. She’d been listening to her brother make a noise down the phone that she’d never heard him make. She’d read the statement once in the car at the lights, once in the lift with her shoulder against his, and once more in the hall while he was taking his shoes off, and by then she was certain.

She stood in the bedroom doorway with the three pages in her hand.

“There’s a problem.”

He was undoing his cuffs by the wardrobe. He looked up. “With what?”

“Your proposal.”

His hands stopped. He looked at the ring on her finger, and back at her face. “You said yes.”

“I did. I’m not taking it back. But paragraph seventeen. Quiero que te casas conmigo.” She held up the last page.

“Yes.”

“Your subjunctive is wrong, mi amor.”

There was a silence in which she watched him not be offended, which was one of the most attractive things she’d ever seen a man do.

“Which part?”

She laughed out loud. She couldn’t help it. She crossed the room and gave him the page and stood at his elbow and pointed.

“Quiero que. I want that. After quiero que with a different subject, the next verb goes into the subjunctive, because it’s something you want to happen and hasn’t happened yet. So it’s not te casas, which is you marry, as in a fact. It’s te cases. Quiero que te cases conmigo. I want you to marry me.”

He looked at the line. “One letter.”

“One letter is the difference between a fact and a wish.”

“It is a fact. You said yes,” said Wei Long.

She stared at him. Then she took the page out of his hand and put it face down on the chest of drawers with great precision, and turned round.

“I’m going to correct the whole thing. All three languages. You’ll learn it properly,” she said.

“Now?”

“Now.”

“I’ve got work in the morning.”

“So have I. Sit down.”

He sat at the foot of the bed. She stood in front of him, between his knees, in the dress she’d travelled in, with her shoes off and her ring on, and took his face in her hands as though it were a page she was about to mark.

“English first.”

“We’re speaking English.”

“I’m starting with the easy one. Paragraph fifteen. You said here is this desk. That’s not how anybody says it. Nobody in the world says that sentence except you.”

“It was accurate.”

“It was beautiful,” said Isla, “and it’s staying in exactly as it is, and that’s the only correction you’re getting in English. French.” She bent and kissed the corner of his mouth. “Say it.”

“Veux-tu m’épouser?”

“The u in tu. You’re saying it like a policeman. Round your mouth.”

He tried again. She kissed him on the mouth this time.

“Better. Again.”

“Veux-tu m’épouser?”

“Again.”

“You’re kissing me every time I say it.”

“It’s a teaching method. It’s extremely effective. Ask any child in Vancouver.” She sat down on his knee, sideways, and put her arm round his neck.

“I’d rather not.”

“And in yours?”

“Mine I can do,” said Wei Long, and said it, a few plain words in the language he’d grown up in, will you marry me, close to her ear.

She repeated it to show she could. He shook his head.

“The third word. You’ve made it go up.”

“It goes up.”

“It goes down and comes back. You’ve asked me whether I’ll marry a horse.”

“I have not.”

“Not a horse. But not me,” he conceded.

He said it again, slowly, and she said it after him, and got it, and he nodded once, the way he’d nod at a constable who’d finally filled in a form correctly.

“Better,” he said.

“Don’t you dare turn this round.”

“You started the lesson.”

“Spanish, the question, not the wish. If you want to ask someone in Spanish, you say ¿Quieres casarte conmigo? Do you want to marry me. Say it,” said Isla, with dignity.

He said it. The r was terrible. She told him so. He said it again, and it was less terrible, and she slid off his knee and climbed onto the bed behind him and knelt there and put her mouth against the side of his neck, under his ear, where she’d once kept him from signing twelve pages of testimony.

“Again,” she murmured.

“¿Quieres casarte... Isla.” His voice went. She’d found the place with her teeth.

“That’s not Spanish.”

He turned round on the bed and caught her by the waist and put her on her back in one movement, without any hurry, and looked down at her with his tie still on and his cuffs still undone.

“Are we finished studying?”

“Almost. You haven’t done the most important part,” said Isla.

“Which is?”

“Asking me properly. Without paper. Not yet. When I tell you.” She pulled at his tie until the knot gave.

✦ ✦ ✦

She undressed him first. She took her time about it, because she was entitled to, and because he let her: the tie, the shirt, the vest underneath that she’d teased him about since the first night and that he still wore in October. She kissed his collarbone. She kissed the scar on the back of his hand, the kettle when he was sixteen, which she’d kissed at two in the morning in a different flat and asked about and been told. She undid his belt and the button and pushed the rest down and off and threw it on the floor, and he lay on her bed in the lamplight with nothing on, looking at her with an expression she’d learned over two and a half years to read and which a squad room had spent the same time failing to photograph.

“You. Your turn,” he said.

“I know whose turn it is.”

She stood up beside the bed and unzipped the dress herself and let it go, and then the rest, and stood there in nothing but the ring until he sat up and reached for her.

She didn’t let him take her. She pushed him back down with a hand flat on his chest and climbed over him, a knee either side of his hips, and sat on him without taking him in, so that he was hard against her and couldn’t do anything about it. He made a sound. His hands came up to her thighs and held them.

“Now, ask,” said Isla.

He looked up at her. Her hair had come down. It fell round both of them and closed out the lamp. There was no paper, and no duty sergeant at the end of a counter, and no rain on the window, only her weight on him and her hands on his chest and the new ring catching the light every time she breathed.

He reached up and pushed her hair back behind her ear, the way he had a hundred times, and left his hand there.

“Isla Ren.”

“Yes?”

“I love you.”

“I love you too.”

“I want to marry you. Will you marry me?” He didn’t look away.

She bent down and kissed him, and lifted herself, and reached between them and took him in her hand and guided him, and sank down onto him slowly, all the way, until there was nothing left to take and they were both breathing.

“Yes,” she said, against his mouth.

He laughed. It came out of him under her, low and astonished, and she felt it where they were joined, and it was the best thing she’d ever felt in her life, and she told him so in French, which he didn’t understand, and then in English, which he did.

“Thank you,” he said.

“Wrong. Don’t thank me.” She lifted and came down again, and his hands went tight on her hips.

“Then what?”

“Try again.”

He thought about it, which was absurd and which she loved. She moved on him slowly while he did, rising and sinking, her palms on his chest, watching his face lose its order a line at a time.

“I’m glad you said yes,” said Wei Long.

“Better.”

“I’m glad you’re going to marry me.”

“Better still,” said Isla, and stopped talking.

She rode him without hurry, the lamp warm on her back and his hands moving from her hips up her sides to her breasts and back, and every time she came down he pushed up to meet her, so that it was slow and deep and went through her like a long note. He sat up after a while, because he couldn’t not, and put his arms round her and held her against him and kissed her throat and her shoulder and her mouth, and she wrapped her legs round his back and kept moving in his lap, smaller now, closer, her forehead pressed to his. Neither of them said anything in any language. She came first, with her arms locked round his neck and her face turned into his hair and the ring pressed into the back of his shoulder hard enough to mark it, and he held her through it and then laid her back on the pillows and came into her again, deep, and followed her a minute later with her name and then, under his breath, unmistakably, te quiero, with the r exactly right.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay on his chest with one leg over his and traced the edge of the mark the ring had left on his shoulder.

“You’ve been practising,” she said.

“No.”

“Your r was perfect.”

“It was an accident.”

“Liar.”

He didn’t answer, which was an answer. She lifted her head to look at him and he was looking at the ceiling with an expression of great innocence that wouldn’t have fooled a first-year constable.

“Since when?”

“Since the cards. I kept them,” said Wei Long.

She went still.

“The ones from Lima?”

“Yes.”

“All of them?”

“Twenty-six. They’re in the notebook. I say them in the car. Not te casas. That one wasn’t on a card. I wrote it myself. I should have checked.” He was still looking at the ceiling.

She didn’t say anything for a while. She put her head back down on his chest and listened to his heart, which had slowed almost to normal, and thought about a man in a car at red lights saying ¿Ya comiste? to the windscreen, badly, every day for nine months, so that one day he’d be able to say it to her properly.

“Why didn’t you ask me. For the Spanish,” she said.

“Because then you’d have known.”

At a quarter past midnight he got out of bed.

“Where are you going?”

“To get something.”

“Is it urgent?”

“No.”

“Then come back.”

“In a minute.”

“That’s what people say before they disappear for twenty minutes.”

“Not me,” said Wei Long, and went through to the room with the books. She heard the desk drawer, and then a pen being uncapped, and then nothing for a long while but the scratch of it. She lay and listened and didn’t go and look, which took more self-control than anything she’d done at the terminal.

He came back with a white card, the size of the ones she’d posted from Lima. He sat down on the foot of the bed and gave it to her without a word.

On the front, in his square careful hand, three lines.

Isla Ren. I love you. Will you marry me?

Isla Ren. Je t’aime. Veux-tu m’épouser?

Isla Ren. Te quiero. ¿Quieres casarte conmigo?

She read them all twice. Every accent was where it belonged. He’d put the upside-down question mark at the start of the Spanish, which most people forgot, and he’d gone over it once, so that it was darker than the rest.

“I checked it this time. Against the cards. And the dictionary,” he said.

“Where did you get the card?”

“The drawer.”

“You keep blank cards in your desk drawer.”

“For notes.”

“Of course you do,” said Isla, and found that she couldn’t see the writing properly any more.

He waited. Then he said, “Is something wrong?”

“No. Nothing’s wrong. Lie down.” She put the card on the bedside table, against the lamp, next to the three folded pages.

He lay down. She pulled the sheet over both of them and put her cheek on his shoulder, on the mark the ring had made, and looked across him at the bedside table: a three-page statement with seventeen numbered paragraphs, a card with the same question in three languages, and a ring on her hand that had nothing round it at all.

“What’s next,” she said. “A formal letter?”

“I can write one.”

“Don’t you dare.”

“I’ll need to do the forms. There are forms for marriage. Two nationalities,” he said.

“I know there are forms. I process them.”

“I’ll check every box twice.”

“And I’ll check you,” said Isla. She was nearly asleep. She felt him turn his head and press his mouth to her hair, and stay there.

“Your French was better the second time,” she murmured.

“Thank you.”

“Your Spanish was good.”

“Thank you.”

“Don’t thank me,” said Isla, and slept, and he lay awake a while longer in the lamplight, looking at a card on a bedside table, until he was sure of every word on it and could turn the lamp off.

chapters.title: The Forms
chapters.desc: The most romantic paperwork either of them has ever filled in: a notice of marriage, two nationalities, one registry. He reads the declaration three times; she helps the old couple on the bench. A kiss at window four.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s different because we did something about it.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Wei Long did in the entrance hall of the marriage registry was check the folder. The second was check it again. The third was ask her whether she’d brought her passport.

“It’s in my bag,” said Isla.

“I know.”

“You watched me put it there. You checked it at the door. You checked it in the lift.”

“Yes.”

“So why are you asking?”

He looked at the folder. “Confirmation.”

She took his arm, and tried not to laugh, and failed. It was the second Tuesday in November and raining in the soft, steady way that meant it would rain all day. The hall had a long wooden bench against one wall and a notice on the other listing the documents required for a notice of intended marriage, in two languages, with a mistake in the second one that she’d noticed the first time she’d come here for work and still hadn’t reported. A couple in their sixties sat on the bench holding hands and a single shared form. A young man in a suit too big for him was filling his in on his knee with enormous care, his tongue between his teeth, while a girl in a yellow raincoat beside him read every word over his shoulder and corrected nothing. Behind the counter a printer was making a noise like something being slowly strangled.

“You’ve put the documents in date order,” she said.

“Yes.”

“With coloured tabs.”

“Yes.”

“You printed the appointment confirmation twice.”

“One’s a spare.”

“Are you nervous?”

“No,” said Wei Long, and handed her the spare, so that she’d have one too. She folded it into her bag next to her own copy, which she’d also printed, and which she decided he never needed to know about.

She’d sat on the other side of a counter like this a hundred times. She’d explained the notice period to Canadians marrying locals and locals marrying Canadians, and checked certificates of no impediment, and once spent an hour on the phone to a registry in Manitoba about a decree absolute that had been filed under a dead man’s middle name. She knew exactly what would happen in the next forty minutes and which box people always got wrong. She’d never once thought about what it would be like to be the one holding the folder, with her name on the forms, waiting for her number.

It was better than she’d expected. It was also more frightening.

The woman on the bench leaned over before their number came. “Excuse me. You look as if you know about these. Is it the surname as it is now, or the surname at birth?”

Isla knew. She couldn’t help it. She took the form and found the box. “As it is now, and the one at birth goes in section C, here. Have you been married before?”

“To him. In 1986. We divorced in 1999. We were idiots. Now we’re doing it again,” said the woman, and nodded at her husband, who smiled at the floor.

“Complete idiots,” the man agreed.

Isla said, “Then you tick previously married and put the same name in both places, and the clerk will look at you over her glasses, and you mustn’t mind.”

“We won’t,” said the woman, and took the form back, and patted Isla’s hand as though Isla were the one who needed it. Wei Long had watched the whole exchange without moving. When Isla sat back he said, low, “You’re working.”

“I’m not working. I’m helping.”

“You checked her surname history.”

“Somebody had to,” said Isla, and he looked at the old couple bent together over their single form, and didn’t say anything else, and she saw him put it away somewhere, the way he put things in his notebook.

✦ ✦ ✦

Their number came up after eleven minutes. The clerk at window four was a woman with reading glasses on a chain and the calm of someone who’d seen every kind of couple there was.

“Good morning. Identification, please.”

He had the passports on the counter before she’d finished the sentence. Then the proofs of address, both of them. Then the appointment confirmation, the original, with the spare left in Isla’s hand. The clerk looked at the tabs, and then at him, and then at Isla, and Isla looked back at her without any expression at all, and the clerk’s mouth moved a fraction at one corner.

“Mr. Song, you’re a local national. Ms. Ren, Canadian?”

“Yes,” said Isla.

“As you’re of different nationalities there are a few extra questions. Full names as they appear on your passports.” The clerk turned a page.

They gave them. Dates of birth. Current address, which was the same, which the clerk noted. Previous marriages: none, none. Whether either of them was related to the other within the prohibited degrees. Wei Long said “No” so firmly that the young man on the bench looked up. Whether either of them was entering into the marriage under any pressure.

“No,” said Isla.

“No,” said Wei Long.

“Have you both read the declaration?”

“Yes,” he said. “Could I read it once more?”

“Of course.”

Isla turned to him. “You’ve read it twice.”

“I’d like to read it again.”

“Do you think it’s changed since Thursday?”

“No. I don’t want to make a mistake.” He looked at the paper, and then at her, and his voice went down so that the clerk wouldn’t hear.

She’d been going to tease him. She didn’t. She put her hand under the edge of the counter, out of sight, and found his, and he turned his palm up under hers and held on, and read the declaration all the way through for a third time, with his lips not quite moving.

“Here are your forms. Separate sections each. Sign at the bottom. Take them to the table by the window,” said the clerk.

✦ ✦ ✦

For a while there was nothing but two pens.

He wrote his name in the square capitals he used for evidence labels and checked it against the passport letter by letter. He wrote his date of birth and checked that too.

“You know your own date of birth,” said Isla, without looking up.

“I know I know it.”

“Then why...”

“Because the one time I don’t check will be the time it’s wrong,” said Wei Long, and she couldn’t argue with that, because it was exactly what she said to her junior officers.

She finished first. She always did; she’d filled in more of these than he’d filled in parking tickets. She put her pen down and watched him work his way down the second page with his finger beside each line, ticking each box and then going back to the top and checking every tick.

“What’s that one?” she said, leaning on his shoulder.

“Confirmation of identity.”

“Correct.”

He ticked it.

“And that?”

“Marital status. Never married.”

“Correct.”

“And this one?” He’d stopped. It was the box she’d known he’d stop at: the declaration that each party consented freely to the marriage. He read the sentence twice.

“Voluntary consent. Extremely voluntary. Put that down,” she said, and put her cheek against his arm.

“There isn’t a box for extremely.”

“Write it in the margin.”

“You can’t write in the margins of a statutory form.”

“I know. I’ve rejected people for it. Tick.” She put her finger on the box beside his.

He ticked it. Then he looked at her for a second longer than the form required, and she saw what was in his face, and had to look away out of the window at the rain.

✦ ✦ ✦

The clerk read every page with her glasses on the end of her nose and said, “Everything’s in order.” She explained the notice period, which Isla could have recited, and what they’d need to bring on the day, which Isla could also have recited, and that the notice would be put up on the board in the public hall for the required number of days. Wei Long asked two questions. Both were sensible. One was about the board.

“Anyone can read it?” he said.

“Anyone. That’s the point of it.”

He nodded, accepting that, and Isla knew, with total certainty, that he would come and read it himself on the way to work tomorrow, and the day after, to make sure it was still there.

The clerk gathered the papers, stamped the receipt twice, and pushed it across the counter. He took it with both hands.

“Done?” said Isla.

“Submitted. It isn’t the same thing. The notice still has to run.”

“So you’re telling me, Inspector, that our marriage hasn’t yet been approved.”

“I’m telling you the paperwork’s been lodged.”

“Terrible news.”

“You’re making fun of me.”

“A little. You look as if you’re waiting for a verdict.”

He glanced at the counter, at the stamp, at the clerk putting their forms into a tray marked IN. “I’d like it to be accepted. I’d like to do it properly. All of it,” he said.

She stopped smiling.

She reached up and kissed him at window four, in front of the clerk and the couple on the bench and the young man in the large suit, which was entirely inappropriate for a public counter and which she’d have asked anyone else to take outside. He kissed her back with the receipt still in both hands. When she let him go, the clerk had taken her glasses off.

“Congratulations,” said the clerk.

“Thank you,” said Isla.

“Thank you. For checking,” said Wei Long, because he’d been brought up to.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the steps outside she took the receipt from him, and he let her. She read it, though she knew what it said, and folded it in half and put it in the inside pocket of her bag, the one with a zip. Her phone buzzed.

Hao (Loud): Well??? Is it done? Did he check every box twice?

Isla: Three times.

Hao (Loud): Amateur. I’d have checked four.

The old couple came out behind them with their own receipt, holding hands, and the woman waved it at Isla like a ticket to something, and went carefully down the wet steps on her husband’s arm.

“It doesn’t feel any different,” she said. “Does it?”

He thought about it, in the rain, under the overhang, with people going up and down the steps round them.

“We’re still engaged. The day’s still in March. So no. It’s different because we did something about it.” He looked down at her.

She put both her arms round his waist inside his coat.

“Do you know what the most romantic part was?” she said.

“The forms?”

“No.”

“The clerk?”

“No.”

“The notice period?”

Isla said, “You checked every box twice. And then you checked them again. You did that for me. That was the most romantic thing anyone’s ever done in a government building.”

“You checked me.”

“Of course I checked you. I had to make sure you didn’t interrogate her.”

“I was listening.”

“With your police face.”

“What’s my police face?”

“The one that makes people confess to things they haven’t done. You’re going to be my husband.” She tipped her head back to see him.

He went still for half a second. She felt it under her hands. Then his hand came up and settled between her shoulder blades.

“Yes, and you’re going to be my wife,” he said.

“Say it again.”

“You’re going to be my wife.”

He bent and kissed her, on the steps of the registry, in the rain, with no counter between them and no form to sign, until somebody coming up the steps had to go round them and said something cheerful about it in passing that neither of them heard.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night he put the receipt in his desk drawer.

Not in the folder with the passports and the tenancy agreement and the policy for the contents of the flat. In the top drawer, on the left, with the three folded pages of a statement in seventeen numbered paragraphs, and a white card with the same question on it in three languages, and a folded sheet of paper from March two and a half years ago headed THE TEN-MINUTE OBSERVATION PROJECT that he’d confiscated as evidence and never given back.

She found him standing at the open drawer in the room with the books.

“You’re keeping everything,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Even the one with the grammatical mistake?”

“That one too.”

“Why?”

“It’s part of the record.”

She came up behind him and wrapped her arms round him and her chin on his shoulder, and laughed into his shirt. “That’s the least romantic thing you’ve ever said to me.”

He turned round in her arms. “Would you like another reason?”

“Yes.”

He looked at her. Then he kissed her, slowly, with the drawer still open behind him and the lamp on the desk making a circle on the wood.

“I want to remember how we got here. Every part,” he said.

“Even the paperwork?”

“You were there for the paperwork.”

She stood with her forehead against his chest and her eyes shut. Behind him, in the drawer, a receipt with two stamps on it lay on top of a sheet of squared paper that said, in Sham’s handwriting from 2025, Conclusion: subject alarmingly punctual.

“November, forms. Two nationalities,” she said into his shirt.

“One registry.”

“One marriage,” said Isla.

He closed the drawer with his free hand. Then he turned the lamp off, and took her to bed, and in the morning, on the way to the station, he went by the registry in the rain and stood in the public hall for two minutes reading a notice on a board with both their names on it, to make sure it was still there.

chapters.title: He Dances, Badly
chapters.desc: At the engagement party everyone films him dancing, and nobody posts it, because she asked. Superintendent Pun and Ren Hao arm in arm. Yu Chen and Eliana leave early for his six o’clock shift. Home, her shoes in his hand: explicit.
chapters.epigraph: “I danced with my fiancée. That’s all.”
chapters.content:
The first person to film Wei Long dancing was Ren Hao. The second was Yu Chen. The third was retired Superintendent Pun, who said afterwards that he’d only been checking whether his camera worked, and that it was a coincidence the inspector had been in the middle of the frame for three minutes and forty seconds.

By the end of the song at least six people had it. Every one of them deleted it eventually, or said they had. Not because Wei Long asked. Because Isla did.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her brother had hired the whole top floor of a restaurant on the waterfront for the engagement party and then said it was “a few drinks”. There were sixty people. There was a band, three musicians in a corner by the window who played old songs the way people liked them played at weddings. There was a cake with a sugar version of the airport custody desk on top of it, which Ren Hao had commissioned without telling anyone, complete with a tiny sugar inspector holding three tiny pages. Wei Long had looked at it for some time and then asked the pastry chef, gravely, whether the pages were edible. They were.

“Dance with me,” said Isla, at a quarter to ten.

He looked at the floor. It was full. Her brother was in the middle of it doing something with both elbows and his shoulders that had no relationship to the music and couldn’t have been more confident.

“No,” said Wei Long.

“Why?”

“I don’t dance.”

“Everyone dances. It’s our engagement party.”

“Your brother is dancing.”

“Hao’s having a wonderful time.”

“He’s been drinking.”

“He’s had one glass.”

“That may be enough,” said Wei Long, and she laughed and took his hand and said “Please,” and looked at him, and that was unfair. He knew it was unfair. She knew that he knew. Neither of them was going to say so. He put his glass down on the nearest table.

“One dance.”

“Two.”

“One.”

“We’ll negotiate later,” said Isla, and towed him onto the floor.

His first mistake was assuming there’d be instructions. There weren’t. The band started something slow with a clarinet in it, and she came in close and put his hand on her waist and her own on his shoulder, and he stood there, holding her correctly, waiting for some sensible indication of what was supposed to happen next.

“Relax,” she said.

“I’m relaxed.”

“Your shoulders disagree.”

He put them down.

“Now follow me.”

He looked at their feet. “Which way?”

“Don’t look at your feet.”

“I need to know where they are.”

“They’re attached to you. They’ll come.”

He followed her. Technically. He was a beat behind and his steps were too deliberate, as though each one had to be signed off before the next, and when he tried to turn her he nearly took them both into Sergeant Liu and his wife. Isla caught his shoulder, laughing, and brought him back.

“I nearly stood on you.”

“You didn’t.”

“I nearly did.”

“But you didn’t,” said Isla, and put her cheek against his shoulder. “Are you hating this?”

He thought about it, which she could feel. “No,” he said, surprised, and his hands settled on her back, and something in the way he was holding himself let go by a few degrees. He wasn’t good. He wasn’t anywhere close. But he stopped looking at his feet, and halfway through the second verse he turned her, slowly, without warning anyone, and nobody fell over.

Across the room Ren Hao had his phone up.

“Hao,” said Isla, over Wei Long’s shoulder.

“Don’t mind me. I’m documenting a historic occasion.”

“Don’t post that.”

Her brother lowered the phone and looked hurt. “It’s family history.”

“Then keep it in the family.”

“Fine,” said Ren Hao, and raised it again, and she let him, and Wei Long danced all the way to the end of the song with his eyes on her face, because she’d told him not to look at his feet and there was nowhere else he wanted to look.

✦ ✦ ✦

The most surprising thing about the evening was Superintendent Pun.

He’d arrived at eight in a dark suit with his medal ribbon on it, accepted one drink, and spent the first hour standing by the wall examining the decorations looking like a man who’d spent forty years deciding whether other people had done their jobs. Seventy-five, upright, with a voice that had once cleared a riot without a loudhailer. Isla had seen two of Hao’s colleagues come up to him, introduce themselves, and retreat.

Then Hao found him. Nobody knew exactly how it happened. One minute Pun was by the drinks table talking to Song-Zhu about runway lighting. The next, Ren Hao had an arm round his shoulders and both of them were laughing.

“He was always serious. Even at nineteen. I’d tell the other recruits a joke and they’d laugh and he’d write it down,” Pun was saying, as Isla came within earshot.

“Was he ever young?” said Ren Hao.

“He was fifteen when he took on that boy. Fifteen. My son at fifteen couldn’t remember his own lunch. I think he’s still learning the ordinary things.” Pun nodded at the corner where Yu Chen was standing with Eliana. He watched the floor. Wei Long was being turned, now, by Isla’s cousin from Calgary, with the face of a man doing his duty under fire.

Ren Hao looked at the floor too, and then laughed so much Pun had to take his glass off him.

“You’re filming,” said Pun.

“I’m filming him.”

“That’s worse,” said Pun, and didn’t take his arm away.

They stood shoulder to shoulder for the next forty minutes, the retired superintendent and the loudest man in the city, and at some point Hao’s arm stayed where it was and Pun’s went round Hao’s back in turn, and when the band played something fast they went onto the floor together. It wasn’t graceful. Pun had clearly decided that if he was going to do it he would do it without shame, and Ren Hao had never felt shame in his life. Someone started clapping. Then everyone was.

“Look,” said Isla, finding Wei Long at the edge of the floor.

“I see them.”

“Your teacher and my brother.”

“They’ve been talking for forty minutes.”

“That’s practically a friendship.”

“Yes, I think it is,” said Wei Long, watching Pun, who’d once stood in a hospital corridor at three in the morning with a nineteen-year-old recruit whose cousin had pneumonia and said nothing at all for two hours because nothing was needed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Chen and Eliana left early, because he had a six o’clock start in the emergency department and she’d decided, in front of witnesses, that he was going to bed whether he liked it or not.

“I’m fine,” said Yu Chen.

“You’ve been awake since four.”

“I’m a doctor.”

“That’s not a medical argument,” said Eliana, and took his coat off the back of a chair and held it open, and Yu Chen gave up and put his arms in it.

He came to Wei Long before he went. “Ge.”

“Drive carefully.”

“I’m not driving. She is. Congratulations again.” Yu Chen hesitated, and then smiled, the same smile he’d had at nine with jam on his face.

Wei Long put his hand on his cousin’s shoulder.

Eliana hugged Isla and looked at her ring, which she’d examined on four separate occasions since October.

“Enjoy being engaged. It goes faster than you’d think,” she said.

“I’m trying,” said Isla, and watched them go down the stairs together, Yu Chen’s hand on the small of his wife’s back, seven weeks married.

✦ ✦ ✦

Before she left herself, she went round the room.

She’d seen the phones. She didn’t mind the laughing. She didn’t mind people seeing him dance. But she knew what it would be on the internet by Monday: a station inspector everybody in the city’s crime pages knew by face, turning stiffly under fairy lights with his mouth set. She wanted it to belong to the people who’d been there.

“Hao.”

Her brother looked round.

“Ask everyone not to post anything. They can keep it. Just not online.”

His face changed, and he didn’t argue. He stood on a chair, which nobody had asked him to do, and announced in the voice he used across trading floors that the footage from tonight was private, and that anyone who posted so much as a frame would answer to him personally and also to the inspector, who had powers of arrest.

“Even the bit where he nearly fell?” called somebody.

“Especially that bit.”

Wei Long found her by the coats.

“You didn’t have to do that,” he said.

“I know.”

“People can post what they like.”

“I know.”

“Then why?”

She straightened his lapel, which didn’t need it. “Because I want to keep this one for us. And because I don’t want the whole city knowing how badly you dance.”

“It’s already known.”

“Not officially,” said Isla.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the time they reached the car she’d been in heels for five hours and was walking with the determined expression of a woman who would rather die than say her feet hurt.

“Shoes,” he said.

“They’re fine.”

“You’ve been walking differently for ten minutes.”

“Have you been watching my feet?”

“Yes.”

She laughed, and took them off on the pavement, one hand on his arm, and gave them to him. He carried them by the straps all the way to the car and put them on the back seat like evidence, and when they got home he carried them up as well, and into the bedroom, and set them side by side by the wardrobe.

She was taking her earrings out at the mirror. “You brought those up.”

“You’ll want them.”

“Not tonight I won’t.”

He came behind her and took the second earring out of her fingers and put it on the dresser with the first. Then he said, “Sit down.”

She perched on the end of the bed, amused, with her dress round her knees. He knelt on the floor in front of her in his suit trousers and his shirtsleeves and looked up at her.

“May I?”

“Please,” said Isla.

He pushed the hem of her dress up her thighs carefully, so it wouldn’t catch, until he found the lace at the top of her stockings. He undid nothing. He ran his thumbs under the edge of the lace and then bent his head and kissed the skin just above it, on the inside of her thigh, and she drew in a breath. Then he caught the top of the stocking between his teeth.

“Wei Long.”

He looked up at her with the lace in his mouth. She’d never in her life seen him look like that. He drew it down slowly, with his teeth and then his fingers, down over her knee and her calf and her heel, kissing each place it uncovered, and put it on the floor folded, because he was who he was.
