Then he did the other one. She’d stopped laughing by her second knee. By her second ankle her hands were in his hair.

“That isn’t remotely professional,” she managed.

“I’ve never claimed to be,” said Wei Long, against her instep, and pushed her back onto the bed.

He pushed the dress the rest of the way up, to her waist, and kept going with his mouth. She’d thought she knew all the ways he did this. He took his time in a way that felt like a promise, holding her open with his hands on her thighs while she pulled at his hair and said things in three languages, and when she came it was with her heel pressed into his back and her whole body lifting off the bed, and his name broken into two halves.

He stood up. She sat up after him and attacked his shirt buttons with fingers that didn’t work, and he helped, and she got his belt open and pulled him down onto her by the waistband. He came into her slowly, all the way, and stopped there, with his weight on his forearms and his forehead against hers, until she couldn’t bear the stillness and moved under him. Then he moved too, long and deep, nothing like the boxes or the first night with the ring: the rhythm of a man who’d danced badly all evening and now, in the one place where it mattered, knew exactly what he was doing. She wrapped her legs round him. The zip of her dress was digging into her back and she didn’t care. She came again, unexpectedly, with her mouth on his shoulder, and he followed her a few strokes later with a sound low in his throat that she felt more than heard.

They lay tangled in her dress, which was ruined at the hem now, and his shirt, which was still on one arm.

“Your dancing wasn’t that bad,” she said eventually, into his neck.

“That’s generous.”

“You kept going.”

“You asked me to.”

“I’ll ask you again.”

“Then I’ll dance again. Even if everyone films it,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 9:12 the next morning his phone buzzed on the bedside table, and then went on buzzing.

Ren Hao (Civil): Reminder that all footage from last night is PRIVATE.

Ren Hao (Civil): Especially the dancing.

Sir (Retired): Agreed.

Ren Hao (Civil): Superintendent, with respect, you were also dancing.

Sir (Retired): I have no recollection of that.

Yu Chen (Eaten?): I saw the video.

Next Door: So did I.

Ren Hao (Civil): Delete it.

Yu Chen (Eaten?): Already did.

Next Door: I’ve saved it. For the archive.

Ren Hao (Civil): Eliana.

Thank You (Paid): Nobody posts anything. I mean it.

Ren Hao (Civil): Yes, ma’am.

Wei Long read all of it lying on his back, with Isla’s head on his chest and her hair across his face. Then he typed one line with his thumb and sent it.

Wei Long: I danced with my fiancée. That’s all.

Isla read it upside down from where she lay.

“Excellent statement,” she said.

“Is it accurate?”

“Completely,” said Isla, and lifted her head, and kissed him, and for once there was nobody in the room to film it, and on the floor by the wardrobe her shoes stood side by side where he’d put them, and her stockings lay beside them, folded.

chapters.title: Ten Minutes
chapters.desc: Epilogue. Fifty weeks married (registry, Sat 25 Mar 2028). Four years and two days after the terminal, she sits on his desk at nine. He’s already looking. The world waits ten minutes; Hau and Choy bet coins on the windowsill.
chapters.epigraph: “You still look up.”
chapters.content:
Just before nine on a Monday evening in March, Station Sergeant Hau put a file on the inspector’s desk that didn’t need to be there.

“The corrected statement from the harbour case, sir. The witness has signed the amendment.”

“Leave it.”

Hau left it. Then he looked at the clock on the wall, which said 8:57, and at the inspector, and at the door, and didn’t move.

“Anything else?” said Wei Long.

“No, sir.”

“Then go home, Sergeant.”

“Yes, sir,” said Hau, and walked away with the air of a man who hadn’t come upstairs about a witness statement and wasn’t going home either.

Just before nine Constable Choy put his head round the door. “Sir, do you need the...”

“No.”

“I haven’t said what.”

“Whatever it is, tomorrow.”

Choy vanished. Wei Long looked at the clock. He closed the file. He moved it from the middle of the desk to the left-hand side, squared it, and moved his pen out of the way. At nine exactly, the door opened.

She didn’t knock. She never had. She came past the two desks nearest the door with her coat over her arm and a paper bag in her other hand and her hair tied low at the back of her neck, and lifted two fingers to the night shift as she passed, and they lifted theirs back. He was already looking at her. He’d been looking at the door since 8:58, which the night shift knew, and which he knew they knew.

“Hello,” she said.

“Hello.”

She sat on the desk. Not on the clear side, where he’d moved things for her. On the file.

He put a hand on her waist to steady her. “Careful.”

“I’ve been doing this for four years.”

“I know.”

“Four years and two days. It was a Monday too. It was raining.”

“I know,” said Wei Long, and she leaned down and kissed him, and he kissed her back without looking at the door or the clock or the file she was sitting on, and somewhere across the room someone cleared his throat, and neither of them paid it the slightest attention.

“Long day?” she said, when she’d sat back.

“Ordinary. Three interviews. One arrest. A witness who changed his mind about which way a car was facing.”

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Rice.”

“With?”

He considered. “Food.”

“I married an impossible man,” said Isla.

“You knew that.”

“I was optimistic. There,” she said, and touched the corner of his mouth with her thumb, where it had moved, the way she’d done in this office since the first spring.

“Hello, wife,” said Wei Long, against her thumb.

✦ ✦ ✦

They’d been married for fifty weeks.

Saturday the twenty-fifth of March, the year before, at the registry where he’d checked every box twice: a small room with blond wood and a window onto a courtyard tree, two witnesses, Yu Chen and Song-Zhu, and a bunch of ranunculus Isla had bought herself on the way because she’d wanted to choose them. He’d been more nervous than he’d been at the custody desk. He’d read the certificate before he signed it. The registrar, who’d been told by his clerk about the man with the coloured tabs, had waited without comment while he did.

Afterwards there’d been dinner for twenty at a long table in a back room above a noodle shop by the harbour that did the best fish in the city, because Isla had refused anywhere with a seating plan. Her parents had flown in and sat at one end, her mother holding Wei Long’s hand across the corner of the table for most of the meal as if she’d decided on the evening of a video call three years ago that she’d keep him. Her brother had given a toast that lasted long enough for Song-Zhu, who would propose to him on an airfield a week later, to check her watch twice. Her father had read a poem in the northern language that he’d translated himself, and got two lines wrong, and been corrected from the other end of the table by his wife. Pun had stood up at the end, in his medal ribbon, and lifted his glass, and said “About time,” and sat down again. Eliana had cried. Yu Chen had put his arms round his cousin outside on the stairs, and said nothing at all, and stayed.

That night Wei Long had put the certificate in the drawer, on top of the receipt and the card and the three folded pages and a squared sheet from 2025 with Conclusion: subject alarmingly punctual on it. She’d found him standing there.

“Are you checking it?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“To make sure it’s real,” he’d said, and she’d taken his face in both hands and kissed him until he stopped checking.

It was real. So was the year after it, which hadn’t been made of anything special. Her desk had become a deputy’s desk in September, at the consulate, at home, the next time a post came up, which she’d said she’d get and had got. His cases had gone on, the way cases did. Some evenings they ate together and some evenings one of them waited for the other at the table until the food went cold, and then ate it anyway. They’d argued about the heating, and about whether the bedroom needed a second lamp, and once, badly, in July, about a phone call he’d taken from her section that he shouldn’t have taken, and neither of them had been wrong, and they’d sat in the car outside the flat afterwards until it wasn’t. She’d given a toast in three languages at her brother’s wedding in October, and made two hundred people cry in one of them and laugh in the other two. He’d gone back to Vancouver at Christmas and been measured against the wardrobe door again by her mother, in case he’d grown, and lost at chess to her father three nights running and been delighted about it. He’d learned to make one Lima dish properly, and had made it for Ruth Ferreira when she passed through on her way to a new posting, and Ruth had eaten it in silence and then asked for the recipe in writing. She’d learned that when he said fine about a case it meant she should put the kettle on.

And there were still ten minutes, at nine, at his desk, when she could come. She came when she could. He looked up when she came. That was all. Every time.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 9:03 she opened the paper bag.

“I brought something.”

He looked in. Two small pastries in a box from the bakery near her office, the one with the egg tarts he’d once said were acceptable, which from him was a medal.

“You went out of your way.”

“I was passing.”

“You weren’t.”

“No,” said Isla.

He broke one in half and gave her the larger piece without thinking about it, because he’d been doing it for four years.

“You always do that.”

“Do what?”

“Give me the bigger half.”

“You like it.”

“So do you.”

“I’m aware,” said Wei Long, and ate his.

She looked down at the file under her. “Am I sitting on something important?”

“Yes.”

“Should I move?”

“No.”

She swung her foot and knocked her heel lightly against the side of his drawer, the top drawer on the left, which she knew the contents of better than she knew her own handbag. “Did you have a hard day?” he said.

“Not especially. A medical transfer for a man who’d had a stroke in a hotel lift. A woman whose passport was eaten by a dog, which I’d have thought was a story people made up, but she brought the dog. And an hour explaining to a gentleman from Winnipeg that a consular officer can’t make an airline change its schedule because he’s personally inconvenienced.”

“Did he understand?”

“Eventually. I may have used my police face.”

“You don’t have a police face.”

“I borrowed yours. I missed you,” said Isla. She put her forehead against his.

“You saw me this morning.”

“And at lunch.”

“That’s a lot of missing for one day.”

“Apparently,” said Isla, and kissed him again.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after nine the squad room had gone quiet, the way it did. Not because the work had stopped; the work never stopped. A phone was ringing two desks away and a printer was grinding and Sham and Tak were arguing in low voices over the wording of a charge. But nobody came near the inspector’s door. Nobody needed a signature. There were constables in this room who’d joined after Lima and had never known a station where nine o’clock didn’t belong to the inspector and his wife, and older officers who remembered the woman in the soaked coat and the inspector who’d forgotten to send her home.

Just after nine Constable Choy walked past the noticeboard and looked at the clock and then at Station Sergeant Hau, who hadn’t gone home and was sitting at a spare desk by the window pretending to read a duty roster.

“Sergeant.”

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You’re thinking it. Three minutes.” Hau didn’t look up.

“Two. He’s already moved the file.”

“Three. He hasn’t finished his tea.”

Choy put a coin on the windowsill. “Two.”

“Amateur,” said Hau.

Just after nine Isla shifted on the desk, and Wei Long slid the file out from under her without looking and put it on the side.

“Was that an important file?”

“Yes.”

“And you moved it for me?”

“You were sitting on it.”

“I’m your wife.”

“That doesn’t make the file less important.”

“It makes me more important.”

He looked up at her. “Yes,” he said.

She’d known he’d say it. It still stopped her, the way it always did, because he said it so plainly, one of the facts in a statement, checked twice.

“You’re good at that,” she said.

“At what?”

“Making me feel loved without making a speech about it.”

“I made a speech once.”

“Seventeen paragraphs. I’m keeping them,” said Isla.

“Two more minutes,” he said, with his thumb on her wedding ring.

“Five.”

“Two.”

“That’s a terrible rule.”

“I’ll review it.”

“I’ll appeal. Tonight.”

“After nine,” said Wei Long.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 9:10 he stood up, and helped her into her coat, and she straightened his collar, which didn’t need it, and kissed him properly, with her hand flat on his chest and his on her back, long enough that the printer finished its job and nobody started another one.

“Text me when you’re leaving,” she said.

“I will.”

“Don’t let Hau give you another file to take home.”

“I’ll try.”

She went. At the door she turned round, the way she always did.

“Love you.”

“I love you,” he said, without looking at anyone else in the room.

The door shut just after nine. On the windowsill Choy held out his hand, and Hau put a second coin in it without comment.

“Who won?” said Choy.

Hau looked at the inspector, who was already reading the next report with the face that made people confess to things they hadn’t done. On the corner of his desk was a paper bag folded flat, and on top of the file she’d sat on, held down by his pen, a sticky note in her handwriting that said Eat properly tomorrow. I mean it.

“Not you,” said Hau, and took the coin back.

✦ ✦ ✦

Around half past ten his phone lit up on the desk.

Thank You (Paid): Leaving yet?

Wei Long: Now.

Thank You (Paid): Liar. Hau says you’ve got the harbour file open.

He looked across the room. Hau, who should have gone home three hours ago, was putting his coat on by the window with great innocence.

Wei Long: Hau isn’t a reliable witness.

Thank You (Paid): Hau has never once been wrong about you. Come home.

He closed the harbour file. He put it in the drawer, the bottom one, not the top, and locked it, and switched off the lamp, and on the way out he passed the noticeboard, where somebody had pinned a new sheet in a new hand under the old ones, headed HOW LONG BEFORE SHE STOPS COMING AT NINE?, with every column underneath it left blank. Nobody had put any money on it at all.

He got home at a quarter to eleven. She was in the kitchen in one of his shirts, barefoot, stirring something on the hob that was about to boil over. He reached round her and turned the heat down.

“I’m capable of cooking,” said Isla.

“I know.”

“Then why are you interfering?”

“Because it was boiling over.”

She looked. “Oh,” she said, and leaned back against him, and he put his chin on her shoulder and his arms round her and took the spoon out of her hand, and she asked whether it had been a long day.

“Ordinary.”

“You used that one already.”

“It’s still accurate.”

She turned round inside his arms. She’d had her hair cut short in January, to her jaw, on an impulse she’d announced afterwards as a decision, and he still wasn’t used to the back of her neck. He kissed it to see if he was.

“Do you know what I like best about being married?” she said.

“What?”

“You still look up.”

“Every time,” said Wei Long.

She put her arms round his neck. The pot ticked on the hob. On the windowsill was the tin with ISLA’S TEA on the label in his handwriting and, underneath, smaller, in hers, and his. Outside it had started raining again, in the soft way it rained in March, and somewhere across the city a phone was ringing on a desk that would wait until morning.

chapters.title: He Announces the Back Hug
chapters.desc: A drama she makes him watch, a line in his notebook, and a week of planning. Then he tells her he’s going to hug her from behind, which ruins it. She turns round inside it and kisses him against the stove.
chapters.epigraph: “She prefers to know. Sometimes she needs not to.”
chapters.content:
It started with a television drama, which was Isla’s fault, and a notebook, which was his.

On a Sunday night in July she’d made him sit through an episode of the show her whole office was watching, about a cold-hearted heir and a cheerful pastry chef. She’d lain with her feet in his lap, eating grapes, giving him a commentary he hadn’t asked for. Twenty minutes in, the heir came up behind the pastry chef in her kitchen while she was icing something and put his arms round her waist from behind, and the pastry chef dropped her piping bag, and the music swelled, and Isla made a noise like a kettle.

“That. Everybody wants that,” she said, pointing a grape at the screen.

“Wants what?”

“The back hug. You come up behind someone and hold them while they’re doing something ordinary. It’s the most romantic thing in the world. Ask anyone.”

He’d looked at the screen. The heir had his chin on the pastry chef’s shoulder. The pastry chef had icing on her face.

“She’s holding a bag of icing,” he said.

“That’s not the point.”

“She’s going to drop it.”

“She does drop it. That’s the point. You wouldn’t understand.” Isla ate the grape.

He’d said nothing. When she went to bed, he’d taken out his notebook and written, under the date, Back hug. From behind. While doing something ordinary. Everybody wants it (Isla). Then he’d underlined Isla, because that was the part of the evidence that mattered.

✦ ✦ ✦

He waited a week. He wanted the conditions to be right.

The following Sunday she buzzed him up at seven and left her door on the latch, and he came into her kitchen with his car keys still in his hand. She was at the stove, in a T-shirt with a hole in the shoulder, stirring a pan of something red, and she didn’t turn round.

“You’re home.”

“Yes.”

“How was work?”

“Fine.”

“That’s your favourite word. Did you eat lunch?” She tasted the sauce and made a face at it.

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Lunch.”

She stopped, with the spoon in mid-air. “I’m going to start asking you for evidence.”

“Noodles. At the stall by the station. The one you like.”

“Better,” said Isla, and went back to stirring.

He put his keys down on the counter. He didn’t take his jacket off. He stood in the doorway and looked at her back, at the hole in the shoulder of her T-shirt, at her hair coming down out of its clip, at the spoon going round. Ordinary. Exactly the conditions. He’d been through it in the car. He knew how far away to start and where to put his hands.

She glanced over her shoulder. “What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re standing in the doorway like you’re about to serve a warrant.”

He considered this. It wasn’t entirely inaccurate. “I want to hug you,” he said.

Her face changed, warm and surprised. “Then come here.”

“From behind.”

She blinked at him. “Okay?”

He took one step into the kitchen.

“I’m going to do the back hug now.”

There was a silence. The sauce bubbled. Isla stared at him over her shoulder with the spoon dripping onto the floor, and he watched her understand, in stages, what he’d said and why he’d said it, and then she started to laugh.

“Wei Long.”

“What?”

“You’ve announced it.”

“I thought you should know.”

“It’s meant to be a surprise. That’s the whole... It’s meant to be a surprise!” She was laughing too hard to finish. She turned the gas down with her free hand before she set the kitchen on fire.

“I don’t think a surprise is necessary for a hug.”

“It’s necessary for that hug!”

“Do you want me to stop?”

“No. No. God, no. Proceed. Please. Proceed, Inspector,” said Isla, wiping her eyes with the back of her wrist.

He crossed the kitchen.

It was awkward at first. He’d misjudged the distance; she was standing closer to the stove than he’d planned for, and he was taller than the heir, and he had to fit himself round her and the handle of the pan and her elbow, which was still moving the spoon. He put his arms round her waist the way he’d seen it done. He drew her back against his chest, carefully, with the attention he’d give to approaching someone on a ledge.

Then his chin settled on her shoulder, by the hole in the T-shirt, and his hands came to rest flat on her stomach, one over the other, and Isla went completely still.

“Oh,” she said.

He turned his head and kissed the side of her hair.

“Is that acceptable?”

“Yes, entirely,” she said. Her voice had gone somewhere small.

He held her. The pan ticked. The sauce went on not quite boiling. She leaned her whole weight back into him, gradually, the way a person lets go of a rail, and her free hand came up and closed over both of his on her stomach and stayed there.

“You could have just done it. Without telling me,” she said, after a while.

“I know.”

“Then why did you announce it?”

He thought about it properly, with his mouth against her hair, because she’d asked properly.

“Because I wanted you to know it was on purpose. That I’d thought about it. That it wasn’t an accident,” he said.

She didn’t say anything until the pan had stopped ticking.

“You wrote it down. Didn’t you. Last Sunday. After the drama,” she said at last.

He didn’t answer.

“Song Wei Long. Did you write the back hug in your notebook?”

“It was relevant information.”

She turned the gas off. She put the spoon down on the side, deliberately. He felt her start to turn and loosened his arms to let her go, and she caught both his wrists and held them where they were.

“Don’t move.”

He stopped moving. She turned round inside the circle of his arms, slowly, until she was facing him, with his hands still at her waist and her back to the warm stove. She looked up at him. She had a speck of sauce on her chin and an expression he’d seen on her only once before, on a desk, in March.

“Your surprise is ruined,” she said.

“I noticed.”

“Would you like to try again?”

“How?”

She pulled his head down and kissed him.

He was still for the first second, because she’d taken the thing he’d planned for a week and done something with it he hadn’t planned at all. Then his arms tightened round her and he kissed her back, and she made a small sound into his mouth and pushed her hands up under his jacket, and he walked her back the one step there was until she was pressed against the edge of the stove, and he put one hand flat on the wall above it so she wouldn’t touch anything hot, and kissed her until neither of them had any interest in the sauce.

When she pulled away to breathe she was laughing again.

“That’s better,” she said.

“Was the hug insufficient?”

“No. The hug was perfect. I wanted a kiss as well.”

“You could have asked.”

“I turned round and kissed you. That’s practically a written request.”

“I don’t think that’s how requests work.”

“Then you’ll need more practice,” said Isla, and he gave her more practice, against the stove, until the sauce had formed a skin and she’d stopped caring about that too.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Are you always going to announce them now?” she said later, sitting on the counter, eating the sauce off a piece of bread because they’d let the pasta go to glue.

“Would you prefer that I didn’t?”

She pretended to think. She was hopeless at pretending to think; she looked at the ceiling and swung her feet and failed to hide the smile.

“No, I think I like knowing,” she said.

That surprised him. “Really?”

“It means I get to look forward to them. Nobody’s ever announced anything to me before. People just do things, and then you find out afterwards what they meant. You tell me first. It’s like being given the agenda.” She tore off another piece of bread.

He looked at her. Then he put his forehead against hers.

“I’ll remember that,” he said.

“Write it down.”

“I will.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next one came on the Wednesday, at her desk at the consulate, at lunchtime, where he’d come with noodles. She was bent over a file and didn’t hear him come in.

“I’m going to do the back hug now,” said a voice behind her, and she jumped so hard she knocked a stapler off the desk, and two colleagues at the next desks looked up, and she laughed so loudly that the head of the visa section came out of his office to see who’d died.

The third was in a lift. The fourth was in the queue at the fish stall in the market, where he announced it in a low voice that the fishmonger nonetheless heard, and the fishmonger said something to his wife that made her hit him with a cloth. The fifth wasn’t announced at all.

It was a Friday at the end of August, and she was at her own kitchen window with her phone, reading a message from Hao that had made her want to throw the phone into the harbour. She’d left the door on the latch for him and didn’t hear it open. She didn’t hear him cross the floor. She only felt his arms come round her waist from behind and his chin come down on her shoulder, warm and certain, and his hands settle where they’d settled the first time.

She went still. Then she reached back with her free hand and found his.

“You didn’t announce it,” she said.

“No.”

“Why not?”

“You looked as if you needed one,” said Wei Long, “more than you needed to know it was coming.”

She put the phone away leaned back into him and didn’t say anything at all, and neither did he. Later, when she went to bed, she found his notebook on the kitchen table where he’d left it open, which he never did, and on the page under the date, in his square hand, Back hug: announced (4). Unannounced (1). Both acceptable. She prefers to know. Sometimes she needs not to.

She closed it without reading any further, and went and got into bed beside him, and put her cold feet on his legs, and he didn’t announce that he minded.

chapters.title: Small Talk for Seven Detectives
chapters.desc: Superintendent Chiang asks the consulate for a session on rapport with frightened witnesses. Isla runs small talk for six detectives and a station sergeant in Interview Two. It goes badly for everyone; his score is last.
chapters.epigraph: “I only need to be good at talking to you.”
chapters.content:
It was the superintendent’s idea, which was the only reason anybody came.

After the au pair in March, the frightened girl who’d talked to Isla in French for forty minutes and to Wei Long’s detectives not at all, Detective Superintendent Chiang had asked the consulate whether one of its officers might give the squad an hour on rapport with frightened witnesses. The consulate had said yes. The consulate had then sent Isla, because she’d volunteered before anyone else could, and because her head of section had looked at her face and said, “You’ve been waiting for this.”

So at nine on a Tuesday morning in October she stood at the front of Interview Two with a whiteboard marker, and six detectives and one station sergeant sat round the table looking at her as though she’d announced a surprise weapons inspection.

“Good morning,” said Isla.

Nobody answered.

“Excellent. We’ve found our first problem.”

Sham looked at Sin. Sin looked at the ceiling. Station Sergeant Hau, who’d only come because Chiang had told him the coffee would be better than the canteen’s, folded his arms. At the far end of the table Wei Long opened his notebook.

“Your inspector’s prepared. Thank you, Inspector,” said Isla.

“He’s writing down your mistakes,” said Sham.

“I haven’t started,” said Wei Long, without looking up.

“Yet,” said Isla, and wrote across the top of the board: SMALL TALK. HOW TO TALK TO PEOPLE WITHOUT MAKING THEM FEEL ARRESTED.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’re excellent at questions. When you need information, you get it. What some of you seem to believe is that every conversation is an interview. With a witness who’s frightened, that’s the fastest way to make them stop talking. So this morning we’re going to practise the opposite. Not manipulation. Not technique. Ordinary conversation, the kind that makes someone feel safe enough to keep going. Pairs. Ask your partner one thing that isn’t about work. Thirty seconds,” she told them. Underneath the title she wrote three words. NOTICE. ASK. LISTEN.

“We already know each other,” said Tak.

“Then you should find it easy.”

“What if I don’t want to?”

“Then you’re going to have an educational morning. Sham and Sin, you first,” said Isla.

Sham turned in his chair. “How was your weekend?”

“Fine,” said Sin.

“What did you do?”

“Nothing.”

“Where?”

Sin looked at him. “At home.”

Sham turned to Isla with his hands out. “That’s a complete conversation.”

“That’s a hostage negotiation. Again. Something that invites an answer,” said Isla, and the room laughed for the first time, unwillingly.

“Did you do anything interesting this weekend?”

Sin thought about it with the suffering face of a man under caution. “I went fishing.”

“Wonderful,” said Isla. “Now, Detective Sham, what do you ask?”

“Did you catch anything?”

“Good.”

“Was it legal?”

She put the marker down. “Why would that be your next question?”

“Fishing regulations. There’s a size limit on grouper,” said Sham, reasonably.

“It’s a social conversation.”

“I didn’t catch anything,” said Sin.

“Then there’s nothing to regulate. Ask him something else,” said Isla.

Sham looked at his colleague for a long, hard moment. “Will you go again?”

Sin looked surprised. “Probably. Saturday. Early.”

“That,” said Isla, “is a conversation,” and wrote on the board: SHAM 4/10. IMPROVING. Sham objected to the four. She said he’d asked about the size limit on grouper. He said it was relevant. She said not to friendship, and moved on.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tak was paired with Constable Choy, who’d made the mistake of mentioning that he liked to cook.

“What do you cook?” said Tak.

“Simple things, mostly.”

“What ingredients?”

“Depends.”

“Do you measure?”

“Yes.”

“Precisely?”

Choy stared at him. “Are you investigating my kitchen?”

“Detective Tak,” said Isla. “Why did you ask about measuring?”

“I wanted to establish his process.”

“Did he ask you to?”

“No.”

“Then maybe he wanted to tell you what he likes to make.”

Tak considered this like a new line of enquiry. He turned back to Choy. “What do you like to make?”

Choy brightened. “Steamed fish. Ginger, spring onion, a bit of soy.”

“Do you use a thermometer?”

The room fell apart. Isla wrote TAK 3/10 on the board, and when Tak demanded to know why Sham was ahead of him, she said, “Because he didn’t ask anyone about their thermometer.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Hau had been waiting for his turn with the confidence of a man who believed himself naturally charming. Isla paired him with Sergeant Liu.

“Nice weather today,” said Hau.

“Yes,” said Liu.

Hau waited. Liu waited.

“Go on,” said Isla.

Hau cleared his throat. “Do you like this weather?”

“It’s weather,” said Liu.

“Sergeant Hau, tell him something about yourself.”

Hau thought. “I like rainy days.”

“Why?” said Liu, which was the first unprompted question anyone had asked all morning, and Isla nearly applauded.

“The roads are quieter. Fewer collisions. Fewer calls.”

“Less paperwork,” said Liu.

“Exactly.”

They looked at each other with something like respect.

“Good, now ask him something back,” said Isla.

“Do you like rainy days?” said Hau.

Liu considered it. “No.”

“Why not?”

“I get wet.”

Isla put her head down on the whiteboard and kept it there. When she lifted it the room was shaking with the effort of not laughing out loud, and she wrote, HAU 5/10. WEATHER-BASED DEADLOCK. HAS POTENTIAL.

Choy, on his second go, surprised her. He asked Liu whether he’d watched anything good lately, and Liu named a drama about a hospital, and Choy asked what it was about, and listened, and laughed in the right place, and then said he’d watched the first episode last night because Liu had mentioned it in the canteen last week. Liu, who hadn’t known anyone was listening in the canteen, looked.

“That. You remembered something he said, you followed it up, you gave him something to talk about. Eight out of ten,” said Isla, pointing her marker at both of them.

“Why does Choy get eight?” said Tak.

“Because he had a conversation.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Inspector Song, your turn,” said Isla, at a quarter to ten.

He closed his notebook. “I’m not participating.”

“You are.”

“Why?”

“Because you’re the hardest case in the room.”

There was a noise of collective agreement round the table that he received without any expression at all. She pulled a chair round and sat down opposite him, knee to knee.

“Ask me a question.”

He looked at her. “How was your day?”

“Good. I had lunch yesterday with a colleague and we spent the whole time arguing about a terrible film.”

“What was wrong with it?”

“The dialogue was awful.”

“Why did you see it?”

“She chose it.”

“Did you tell her it was terrible?”

“Yes.”

“Did she disagree?”

“She loved it.”

He thought about that. “Then you had different expectations.”

“Yes,” said Isla, and waited.

He waited too. Then he said, politely, “Was there anything else?”

Sham laughed until he had to put his forehead on the table.

“I’m not a witness, Inspector.”

“What should I have asked?”

“Something about the film.”

“You said the dialogue was awful.”

“Then ask me why.”

“Why was the dialogue awful?”

“Because nobody in it talked like a real person.”

He considered that with total seriousness. “Was it translated?”

She looked at him, and then she was laughing too, and then the whole room was, Hau with his hand over his eyes, and Wei Long looked from one of them to the other with the faint frown of a man who’d asked a reasonable question.

“You listen beautifully. You’re just terrible at sounding casually interested. You ask questions like you’re building a case,” said Isla, when she could.

“I’m trying to understand.”

“I know. Sometimes you don’t have to understand. You can just enjoy it. Try again.” She leaned in.

He looked at her. Then he said, “Would you recommend another film? Instead?”

She stopped. “That’s a good question,” she said, lower than she’d meant to.

“What’s my score?”

“Two.”

The room exploded. He sat back.

“That’s unfair.”

“It’s generous. You asked whether a film was translated.”

“It was relevant.”

She wrote it on the board: SONG 2/10. EXCELLENT LISTENING. SUSPICIOUS QUESTIONING STYLE.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten she read the final rankings aloud. Choy, eight. Hau, five. Sham, four. Tak and Sin, three each. Liu and Song, two.

“Why am I tied with the inspector?” said Liu.

“Because neither of you can do small talk.”

“Sin got three. He asked Sham where his sister works,” said Wei Long.

Isla said, “That’s not small talk, it’s a background check, and I’m not changing the scores. Your homework is one ordinary conversation this week without asking anyone about their work, their whereabouts, their schedule or whether they have anything to declare.”

“What if they volunteer it?” said Hau.

“Then you may listen.”

“And if it’s suspicious?”

“Then you may tell your inspector.”

“Reasonable,” said Wei Long, and she pointed her marker at him and said “Don’t encourage them,” and dismissed the class.

He waited by the door while they filed out, Sham still wiping his eyes, and then came back and picked up her bag.

“You were good,” he said.

“Thank you.”

“You made them take part. Tak will never ask anyone about cooking again.”

“That’s probably for the best. You know you came joint last.” She looked up at him.

“I noticed.”

“Are you embarrassed?”

“No, I don’t need to be good at small talk with everyone. I only need to be good at talking to you,” said Wei Long. He held the door for her.

For once she had nothing to say. She took his arm in the corridor, in front of the whole squad room, which was supposed to be against the rules and which nobody had ever enforced.

“That’s a terribly... that’s a good answer,” she said.

“Does it change my score?”

“No. You’re my boyfriend. You’re graded separately.”

“On what scale?”

“I haven’t decided yet. You’ll be the first to know,” said Isla.

✦ ✦ ✦

The following Monday Hau found a new sheet on the noticeboard, in Sham’s handwriting: SMALL TALK, FOLLOW-UP ASSESSMENT, seven names and a column for scores, and at the bottom, in a different pen, Most improved: Inspector Song.

Wei Long stood in front of it with his coffee for some time. Then he took out his pen and crossed his own name off.

“Sir?” said Hau.

“I’m not participating.”

“Why not, sir?”

“I’m having dinner with Officer Ren tonight,” said Wei Long, “and she’s asked me what I’d like to eat, and I’ve said I’d like her to choose.”

Hau considered this. “That’s good small talk, sir.”

“It isn’t small talk.”

“No, sir,” said Hau, and the inspector walked away, and for the rest of the morning the squad argued about whether he’d just made a joke, and Sham wrote 10 in tiny figures in the margin next to the crossed-out name, and nobody rubbed it out.

chapters.title: The Laugh Nobody Recorded
chapters.desc: Sham swears the inspector laughed. Nobody can prove it. Then a pigeon story at home and Isla has six seconds on her phone.
chapters.epigraph: “You sounded happy.”
chapters.content:
The trouble began with Detective Sham, who said the inspector had laughed.

“I heard it,” said Sham, on a grey Thursday in January, to the squad room at large.

“You heard something,” said Sin.

“I know what a laugh sounds like.”

“Do you?”

“I’ve worked for him for nine years. I’d know.”

“Exactly. Nine years. You’ve forgotten what one sounds like,” said Tak.

Across the room Wei Long went on reading a forensic report on a burglary in the hill district. He’d been aware of the conversation for about four minutes. He’d chosen not to take part in it, because in his assessment it was a waste of everybody’s time. The difficulty was that the squad had reached the point where his silence was being entered into the record as evidence.

“Yesterday. In the briefing. When Choy said the suspect had hidden the jewellery in his grandmother’s urn and his grandmother wasn’t dead,” said Sham.

“Was it a full laugh? With sound?” said Constable Choy.

“What do you think a laugh is?”

“I’m establishing the facts.”

“Did he smile first?” said Sin.

“I don’t know. I was looking at my file.”

“So you didn’t see it.”

“I heard it.”

Wei Long turned a page. “Can we go back to work?”

The room went quiet for about three seconds.

“Sir,” said Sham, “did you laugh yesterday?”

“No.”

Sin leaned over to Tak. “That’s not a denial. That’s a statement.”

“Sergeant Liu,” said Wei Long, not looking up. “Does the squad have any cases?”

“Several, sir.”

“Then perhaps the squad could attend to them.”

They dispersed. On his way back to his desk Sham muttered, “Nobody ever believes me,” and Wei Long heard him, and he also heard six people trying not to laugh, and went back to the urn.

✦ ✦ ✦

Isla found out that evening, because Sham’s wife was in a book club with one of Isla’s colleagues, and the city was smaller than anyone admitted.

She was on the sofa in the flat that had been hers and was now theirs, in one of his shirts, scrolling, when he came out of the shower with a towel round his neck.

“Your squad is investigating something,” she said.

“That doesn’t narrow it down.”

“Your laugh.”

He stopped in the middle of drying his hair.

She looked up, and her face lit. “Oh. So it’s true.”

“It’s nothing.”

“Apparently it’s a matter of great importance at the station. It’s reached the book club.”

“Sham has too much time.”

“Did you laugh?”

“No.”

She watched him. He watched her back, with the towel still over his head.

“That’s interesting,” she said.

“What is?”

“You’ve answered that question at least twice today, and both times you looked as if you were trying not to smile.”

“I wasn’t.”

“Of course not,” said Isla, and went back to her phone, with the patience of a woman who’d waited two hours outside a magistrates’ court for a witness to come out for a cigarette.

He hung the towel over a chair and came and sat down at the other end of the sofa, and after a minute, because she’d known he would, he said, “What did they say?”

“That it was in the briefing yesterday. Sham heard it.”

“Sham also once reported that a pigeon was following him.”

She put the phone down. “Was it?”

“It was eating out of his hand.”

“Was it following him?”

“It was eating out of his hand. For three streets. From a bag of chestnuts he’d bought outside the station. He filed a note.” He looked at the ceiling.

“A note?”

“Suspicious bird behaviour, Tanner’s Row, 14:20. He said it might be a trained courier.”

“Was he terrified?”

“He wasn’t terrified.”

“Was the pigeon?”

He looked at her. She was sitting with her knees up inside his shirt, her face perfectly solemn, and he thought about Sham walking three streets with a pigeon at his heels and a bag of chestnuts held out in front of him like a warrant, writing trained courier afterwards in his careful hand. He laughed.

Not the breath through the nose he sometimes allowed her when she said something absurd. Not the twitch at the corner of the mouth the squad had spent ten months trying to photograph. A real laugh, low and warm and slightly rough at the edges, as though it hadn’t been used in a while and had come out of storage, and it went on long enough that he heard it himself and stopped.

Isla’s eyes had gone enormous. She didn’t move. Then, by degrees, the way you’d approach a deer, she reached for the phone on the cushion beside her.

“Don’t,” he said.

She was already unlocking it.

“Isla.”

“Say something else. About the pigeon.”

“There isn’t anything else about the pigeon.”

“There’s always something else about the pigeon. Oh my God.” She looked at her screen. Her mouth fell open.

“What?”

“I’ve got it.”

He looked at the phone. “You recorded that?”

“Accidentally.”

“You were holding your phone.”

“I was scrolling.”

“You pointed it at me.”

“I have excellent instincts,” said Isla, and turned the screen round so he could see: a voice memo, red, still going, which she stopped with a flourish. 0:06.

“Six seconds,” she breathed.

He held out his hand. “Delete it.”

She clutched the phone to her chest with both arms. “No.”

“Isla.”

“Six seconds. Do you know how long I’ve been waiting for six seconds?”

“I didn’t know you were waiting.”

“Because you stop whenever you notice. Every time. I’ve had to rely on memory. Do you understand how unreliable memory is? You laugh, and I’m so surprised I forget to listen properly, and then it’s gone, and I’m left with a sort of shape where it was.” She was laughing too now, but it had changed.

He didn’t say anything. His face had changed. Not much, but she knew where to look now.

“It’s not that rare,” he said.

“Then why has nobody at your station managed to record it in nine years?”

He didn’t have an answer to that.

✦ ✦ ✦

He tried again after dinner. She was at the kitchen counter backing the file up to her laptop, which she’d decided to do in front of him, on principle.

“Give me the phone.”

“Are you going to arrest me?”

“I’m asking you to delete a recording.”

“It’s evidence.”

“Of what?”

“That you can be happy. Out loud,” said Isla.

“I am happy.”

“I know,” she said, so that he didn’t have a reply ready, and she lifted the phone between them and pressed play.

His own laugh came out of the speaker and filled the kitchen.

It sounded different through the phone. Smaller, and softer, and more surprised. Less like the man who sat behind a desk at the station and more like someone who’d been standing barefoot in a kitchen waiting for the kettle, which was what he was. He listened to all six seconds. He’d never heard it from outside before.

“It’s embarrassing,” he said.

“It’s lovely.”

“It’s six seconds of me laughing at a pigeon.”

“Exactly. Do you know what I like best? You didn’t look at me first. You weren’t checking whether I was watching. You just did it,” said Isla. She reached out and took his hand and pulled him towards her by it.

“You were watching.”

“I was.”

“Then it wasn’t strictly unobserved.”

“That’s your objection?”

“It’s a reasonable distinction.”

She held on to him. “Not yet.”

He stayed. She kissed him, short, and then again when he started to pull back, longer, with her hand at the back of his neck, until he’d stopped thinking about the phone on the counter, which was the point.

When she let him go he kept his forehead against hers.

“Have you deleted it?” he said.

“No.”

“Isla.”

She kissed the corner of his mouth. “No.”

“It’s private.”

“I know.”

“Don’t send it to anyone.”

“I won’t.”

“Not your brother.”

She made a face. “Why would I give Hao that kind of power? He’d make it his ringtone.”

He shut his eyes. “He would.”

“He’d play it at board meetings.”

“Delete it.”

She kissed him again instead, properly, slowly, her hands flat on his chest, and when she drew back he was looking at her with the face of a man who knew he’d lost an argument he’d never had any chance of winning, and didn’t, on balance, mind.

“That’s not an answer,” he said.

“It’s my answer.”

He looked at the phone on the counter. Then at her.

“Keep it. For yourself. Only you,” he said.

Her face went soft all at once. “Only me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning Sham came to his desk at half past eight.

“Sir. About yesterday.”

“Detective Sham.”

“I still maintain you laughed. I’m going to prove it.”

“Do it in your own time.”

Sham hesitated, then leaned in, lowering his voice to the register of a man asking about a terminal diagnosis. “Sir, was it a proper one?”

“Go to work,” said Wei Long.

At 9:17 his phone buzzed on the blotter.

Thank You (Paid): [audio, 0:06]

Thank You (Paid): You sounded happy.

He looked round. Nobody was near. He held the phone to his ear, low, under the edge of the desk, and listened once. Then again.

Wei Long: You’ve sent it to me.

Thank You (Paid): You’re not anyone. You’re you.

Wei Long: That isn’t how that works.

Thank You (Paid): It is today. I love you. Keep laughing.

He put the phone away. Across the room Sham was staring at him.

“Sir.”

“What?”

“You’re smiling.”

“I’m not.”

Sham turned to Sin with both hands out, appealing to the court. “I’m telling you. Something happened.”

“Leave it. Let the man have whatever it is,” said Sergeant Liu, from the next desk, without looking up from his screen.

Wei Long didn’t reprimand him, which the squad discussed at some length over lunch and failed to explain. And nobody saw him turn the phone over again at twenty past nine, when it lit up, and read it, and keep reading it a little longer than a single line needed.

Thank You (Paid): Ten minutes tonight. Don’t be late.

Wei Long: I work here.

Thank You (Paid): That’s not an excuse. It’s never been an excuse.

chapters.title: Arm Wrestling for Her Honour
chapters.desc: Her brother challenges him to arm wrestling across a noodle-shop table, best of five. He wins three, then loses two on purpose; she knows, and tells him in bed.
chapters.epigraph: “They’re yours.”
chapters.content:
Ren Hao had been challenging him for twenty minutes before anyone took it seriously.

It began, as most things with Ren Hao began, at a restaurant. A noodle place near the harbour on a Friday in November, with steamed-up windows and a menu on the wall and a television in the corner showing a football match that nobody was watching. Isla’s brother had booked it, arrived late, ordered for the table without asking, and then spent the soup explaining at length that his sister’s boyfriend was too quiet, too serious and far too comfortable sitting across a table from him without showing any sign of distress.

Wei Long had listened. Isla had eaten her noodles.

Ren Hao said, “It’s unnatural. Everyone’s frightened of me. My clients are frightened of me. My mother’s a little frightened of me. You’ve been sitting there for forty minutes like a man waiting for a bus.”

“I’m waiting for the fish,” said Wei Long.

“You see? That. I bet I could beat you at arm wrestling.” Ren Hao pointed his chopsticks across the table.

There was a pause.

“Why?” said Wei Long.

“Why? Because I want to.”

“That isn’t a reason.”

“It’s an excellent reason. It’s the only reason anyone does anything.”

Isla put her chopsticks down. “Oh, no.”

“Don’t start,” said her brother.

“I’m not starting. You’re starting.”

“I’m defending my honour.”

“Your honour?”

“And yours.”

“My honour’s doing perfectly well.”

“Not with this man. That! He just does things. Without a sound. It’s sinister. Arm wrestling. Best of five,” said Ren Hao darkly, and Wei Long reached over without a word and filled Isla’s teacup, and Ren Hao flung both hands up.

“Perhaps you’re too loud,” said Wei Long.

Isla choked on her tea. Ren Hao stared at him across the soup bowls, and then a slow, delighted smile spread across his face, the smile of a man who had finally been given something to push against.

“Best of five,” he said again.

Wei Long looked at Isla. She gave him the smallest possible shake of the head.

He looked back at her brother. “All right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The owner, who’d been watching from behind the counter with growing interest, came and moved the dishes to the next table himself. A man at the corner table turned his chair round. The football went on, ignored, on the television.

Ren Hao took off his jacket and rolled up his sleeves to the elbow. Wei Long didn’t.

“Are you going to take this seriously?”

“Yes.”

“Then roll your sleeves up.”

“They’re already above my wrist.”

“That isn’t the point!”

“I’m sorry,” Isla told the owner.

“Don’t be. This is better than the football,” said the owner.

They set their elbows on the table and clasped hands. Ren Hao’s grip was hard and dry and he squeezed first, on purpose, the way men in his line of work shook hands.

“Ready?”

“Yes.”

“Three, two, one.”

Ren Hao pushed.

Wei Long’s arm didn’t move. It wasn’t that it resisted; it stayed where it was, the way a wall stays where it is when you lean on it. Ren Hao’s face changed. He pushed harder. The tendons stood out in his forearm. Wei Long’s hand stayed exactly upright, and his expression stayed exactly the same, and after six or seven seconds Ren Hao’s wrist began, by small degrees, to bend.

“Wait,” said Ren Hao.

Wei Long put his hand down on the table. Gently.

“One,” he said.

Isla was looking into her bowl. Her shoulders were shaking.

“Again,” said her brother.

He did better the second time, because he planted his feet and leaned his whole weight in and gritted his teeth as if his family name depended on a restaurant table. Wei Long let his arm give, slowly, an inch, two inches, until Ren Hao’s face filled with hope, and then he stopped giving, and held it there, and Ren Hao strained against it with the colour coming up his neck.

“Are you all right?” said Wei Long.

“Don’t talk to me.”

“All right.”

Two.

By the third round Ren Hao had begun to negotiate. “Best of five is excessive.”

“You suggested it,” said Isla.

“I was being generous.”

“To whom?”

“To the competition.”

“Do you want to stop?” said Wei Long.

Ren Hao looked at him. “No.”

He held on for nearly ten seconds that time. He was sweating. Halfway through, Wei Long glanced at his shoulder with mild professional concern.

“Your shoulder’s tense.”

“I’m aware.”

“You should relax it, or you’ll...”

“I’m going to throw this glass at you.”

Isla was laughing too much and had to turn round in her chair. Three.

Ren Hao sat back and looked at his hand, opening and closing it. “I don’t accept this.”

“It’s three,” said Wei Long.

“I know how counting works.”

“Good.”

“Don’t be smug.”

“I’m not.”

“You are. You just do it in silence. It’s worse.”

Under the table, Isla’s hand found Wei Long’s wrist and closed on it. He looked down at her. She looked back up at him with her eyes narrowed, and he understood exactly what she was telling him, and also that she knew exactly what he was about to do.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao asked to switch hands for the fourth. Wei Long agreed. They clasped left hands, and Ren Hao pushed with everything he had, and this time Wei Long’s arm went down, steadily, all the way, until his knuckles touched the table. Ren Hao froze. Then his face cracked open.

“Yes! Did you see that?” He let go and pointed at his sister.

“I saw.”

“I won.”

“You won one.”

“I won one,” said Ren Hao, with the reverence of a man who’d won a war. Wei Long flexed his left hand and said, “Congratulations,” and Ren Hao narrowed his eyes.

“Why does that sound as if you’re congratulating a child?”

“Would you prefer I didn’t?”

“I would. Again.”

Isla didn’t look at Wei Long. She didn’t need to. She’d seen him carry an unconscious man down three flights of stairs in a fire drill at the station and hold a struggling suspect against a car with one hand while he took his own phone out of his pocket with the other. There was no world in which her brother had become stronger than him in the last ninety seconds. But her brother was smiling. And the man beside her, who’d spent eight months tolerating Ren Hao’s attempts to intimidate him with the patience of a lighthouse, seemed perfectly happy to let him have it.

“Last one. Decider,” said Ren Hao.

“It’s three-one. It can’t be a decider,” said Isla.

“It’s a moral decider.”

They clasped right hands. Ren Hao counted down from three. He pushed with his life on the table, his jaw locked and his face going dark red, and the man at the corner table started banging his fist on his own table in time, and somebody in the kitchen came out to watch. Wei Long resisted just long enough. Then his arm began to go: an inch, two, a long slow fall, until his knuckles met the wood.

“YES! I WON!” Ren Hao was on his feet.

The man at the corner table applauded. So did the cook. Isla clapped twice, gravely. “Congratulations, Hao.”

Her brother turned to Wei Long, still breathing hard. “Not so invincible after all, Inspector.”

“No,” Wei Long agreed.

Ren Hao’s eyes narrowed again. “Did you let me win?”

Wei Long picked up his napkin and wiped his fingers. “No.”

“Look me in the eye and say that.”

Wei Long looked him in the eye. “No,” he said.

Isla pressed her lips together and decided she would remember this for the rest of her life.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her brother was in a magnificent mood for the rest of the evening. He ordered dessert for the table and another for the man in the corner. He told the waiter he’d just beaten a police inspector at arm wrestling, and the waiter, who’d watched every round, congratulated him with a straight face. He offered to teach Wei Long a few techniques, and Wei Long thanked him, which made him even happier. On the pavement outside he clapped Wei Long on the shoulder hard enough to move him.

“Good match.”

“Thank you.”

“Next time I’ll beat you properly.”

“I look forward to it.”

Ren Hao looked between them, then pointed at his sister. “Don’t let him be smug about this.”

“I won’t.”

“I’m serious!”

“So am I,” said Wei Long, and Ren Hao seemed satisfied with that, and went off down the street towards the taxi rank with his jacket over his shoulder, already on the phone to someone and saying three-two in a voice that carried to the ferry pier.

In the car she waited until he’d done up his seat belt.

“I saw that.”

“Saw what?”

“The fourth. And the fifth.”

He started the engine. “I don’t know what you mean.”

“Song Wei Long.”

“Isla Ren.”

“You lost on purpose. Twice.”

He pulled out into the traffic. “Your brother was happy.”

“That isn’t an explanation.”

“It seemed important to him.”

“Would you rather have beaten him five times?”

He thought about it at a red light. “Would you rather I had?”

She considered it, honestly. “No. He’d never have recovered. He’d have had to move to another city,” she said.

The corner of his mouth went. “I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She brought it up again in bed, with the lights off, her cheek on his shoulder and his hand moving slowly up and down her back.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Yes.”

“Why did you really let him win? You could have won the fifth without hurting him. He’d have been fine at three-one.”

He was quiet for a while. His hand stopped moving and then started again.

He said, “Your brother wanted to feel he could still do something for you. He knows you don’t need him. He knows you can take care of yourself and you’ve been doing it since you were four. But he’s your older brother, and he’s spent eight months watching someone else get to look after you. Sometimes he needs to be the one who wins something. He wasn’t arm wrestling me. He was arm wrestling the fact that you’re happy and he didn’t arrange it.” He moved a strand of her hair off his collarbone.

She lifted her head and looked at him in the dark.

“That’s the most anyone’s ever understood my brother. Including my mother,” she said.

“He was showing off.”

“He was.”

“So I let him have it.”

She kissed him, once, and then again, slower, with her hand on his face, and he drew her closer and turned so that she was half under him and kissed her until she’d forgotten about her brother altogether, and then she remembered and laughed into his mouth.

“He’ll be unbearable now.”

“I know.”

“He’ll tell everyone. He’ll tell his clients.”

“I know.”

“He might challenge you again.”

“I’ll prepare,” said Wei Long.

“Prepare?”

“Next time I’ll make sure he wins four.”

She laughed until he had to hold on to her to keep her in the bed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after one the next afternoon the family group chat, which had existed for five weeks and which Wei Long had been added to without consultation, lit up.

Ren Hao (Civil): For the record, last night I defeated Inspector Song Wei Long at arm wrestling. Best of five.

Ren Hao (Civil): Final score 4–1.

Ren Hao (Civil): I expect this to be acknowledged.

Thank You (Paid): It was three–two, Hao.

Ren Hao (Civil): The first three were warm-ups.

Ren Hao (Civil): Inspector, confirm.

Wei Long, at his desk, read it twice. Then he typed.

Wei Long: Congratulations.

His phone buzzed again almost at once, from a different thread.

Thank You (Paid): You’re encouraging him.

Wei Long: He won.

Thank You (Paid): You’re impossible.

Thank You (Paid): Thank you for loving my family even when they’re ridiculous.

He looked at that one for some time, at his desk, with the squad room going on round him.

Wei Long: They’re yours.

chapters.title: Herbal Tea Replaces Coffee
chapters.desc: A slow conspiracy by a woman who thinks he drinks too much coffee: thirteen weeks of roasted barley in his grandfather’s green tin. He’s known since he descaled the machine in December.
chapters.epigraph: “You were making me tea.”
chapters.content:
The first time Isla replaced his coffee with something else, he didn’t notice.

The second time, he noticed it tasted different and decided the shop had changed suppliers. By the third week he’d privately concluded that the machine needed descaling, and descaled it, on a Sunday, with the instruction booklet open on the counter beside him and an expression of grave responsibility, while she sat at the table behind her book and bit the inside of her cheek until it hurt.

It had started with a perfectly reasonable observation, in November, eleven days after he’d moved his boots in next to hers by the door.

“You drink too much coffee.”

He was standing at the counter at half past six in the morning, waiting for the machine. “How much is too much?”

“Four cups yesterday.”

“Three.”

“I counted.”

“One was half a cup.”

“That’s still a cup.”

He considered this. “Two and a half, then.”

“That isn’t better, Wei Long. That’s arithmetic.”

He picked up his mug. “It isn’t a problem.”

“Of course not,” said Isla, and smiled, and he should have been suspicious of the smile, and wasn’t, because it was half past six and he hadn’t had any coffee.

✦ ✦ ✦

The coffee went on a Monday, after he’d left for the station. She tipped the beans into an airtight jar and put the jar at the back of the cupboard above the fridge, behind the rice cooker’s box, where he never looked because he was tall enough not to need to. In the coffee tin, the dented green one that had been his grandfather’s and that he’d brought from his flat with the scanner and the files, she put a blend she’d made up at the herbalist’s on the hill after twenty minutes’ consultation with a woman who’d plainly done this for other wives: roasted barley, a little chicory, a pinch of cinnamon. It went through the machine. It came out dark. It smelled, if you were half asleep and in a hurry and didn’t care, almost right.

He made his first cup of it on Tuesday. He took a sip. Then another.

“Something wrong?” said Isla from the table.

“It tastes different.”

“Different how?”

“Less bitter.”

“Maybe they’re better beans.”

He considered this possibility with the same care he’d give a witness’s alibi. “Perhaps,” he said, and finished the cup.

Isla turned a page she hadn’t read.

✦ ✦ ✦

By December the operation had three strands. Roasted barley in the mornings. Chamomile with a little lavender in the evenings, in the brown teapot, which he’d accepted without question as her tea and drank at her side on the sofa while she read. And a ginger blend for the nights he came home at one in the morning with his face grey and said fine about a case, which she made in silence and put in his hands without asking, and which he drank without asking either.

She kept the real beans. Not because she meant to give them back. She couldn’t bear waste.

He adapted with the stoical acceptance of a man who believed household appliances had moods. He did make one remark, in the second week of January, over breakfast.

“The coffee at the station tastes stronger.”

Isla nearly dropped her spoon. “Does it?”

“Yes.”

“Maybe their machine’s different.”

“It is different.”

“Mystery solved,” she said, and went on eating, and felt his eyes stay on her for a beat longer than they needed to.

“Have you changed anything here?” he said.

“No.”

That was technically true. She hadn’t touched the machine.

✦ ✦ ✦

What she hadn’t expected was what happened to his mornings.

He’d always drunk his coffee standing up. At the counter, at his desk, by the window, in the car at red lights. In his flat he’d drunk it in four minutes flat, looking at his phone, and gone. In January she noticed that he’d started bringing his cup to the table. He sat beside her while she ate her toast. Sometimes he read the news. Sometimes he answered a message from Liu. More and more often he did neither, and just sat with the cup going cold between his hands, listening to her talk about whatever had happened at the consulate the day before, the citizen with the parrot or the bishop who’d lost his passport in a sauna, and asked her questions about it, and waited for the answers.

He was perfectly content. Isla was so pleased with herself she could hardly stand it.

Then, on a Thursday morning in February, a week after he’d come home from seven nights in a surveillance flat over a laundry, he walked into the kitchen with the green tin in his hand.

“Isla.”

“Yes?”

“Where did you buy this?”

Her stomach dropped through the floor. “The coffee?”

He took the lid off, held it under his nose, and looked at her over the top of it.

“It isn’t coffee.”

There was a silence. A small, perfect, completely incriminating silence, with the kettle in it.

Isla put her toast down. “It’s a tisane.”

“I can see that.”

“Roasted barley, mostly.”

“I can smell that.”

“And chicory.”

He looked in the tin again. “There’s cinnamon.”

“Just a pinch.”

He put the lid back on. Then he said, with terrible calm, in the voice she’d heard him use once, through a door, to a man who’d lied about where he’d been on a Tuesday: “How long?”

She thought about lying. But she’d come so far without being caught in an actual lie, and it seemed a waste to spoil a clean record now with a clumsy one at the end.

“Since November.”

“It’s February.”

“Yes.”

“Three months.”

“Almost exactly. Thirteen weeks. I’ve got a chart,” said Isla, and lifted her chin.

He looked down at the tin, and then at her. “You replaced my coffee.”

“I substituted it.”

“Without telling me.”

“Because you’d have said it wasn’t necessary.”

“It isn’t necessary.”

“You see?”

He set the tin on the counter. He was quiet, and she began, for the first time, to worry.

She said, “I wasn’t trying to control what you drink. You work fourteen hours, you forget lunch, you come home and have another cup at midnight so you can read a file in bed. I thought if I changed it here, you’d have less without having to think about it. I wanted to make one thing a bit better for you. That’s all.”

He was still looking at the tin. “Did you keep the coffee?” he said.

“It’s in the cupboard. Behind the rice cooker box.”

“All of it?”

“I wasn’t going to throw away perfectly good coffee.”

He nodded slowly. Then he said, “You know I can tell them apart now.”

She blinked. “What?”

“The blends. The barley one’s better in the morning. The chamomile is too floral and I don’t like the lavender. The ginger is acceptable. I’d like the ginger on Tuesdays, because Tuesdays are the worst day.” He was entirely serious.

Her mouth fell open. “You knew?”

“Not at first.”

“When?”

“The descaling. Nothing changed. So it wasn’t the machine. And there’s only one other person who uses it,” said Wei Long.

“That was December.”

“Yes.”

“And you didn’t say anything for two months?”

He looked at her. Then at the green tin on the counter, his grandfather’s tin, full of barley.

“You were making me tea,” he said. “Every morning. Why would I stop that?”

She made a helpless noise, half a laugh and half something else. She came round the counter and took the tin out of his hand, or tried to, because he didn’t let go of it.

“You’re ridiculous.”

“I’ve been told.”

“You could have pretended to be surprised.”

“I was surprised. In December.”

“You let me draw a chart.”

“I didn’t know about the chart,” said Wei Long, and kissed her.

He kissed her with the tin still in his hand, his other arm round her waist, in the middle of the kitchen at a quarter to seven in the morning with her toast going cold and the kettle clicking off behind them. She hooked a hand behind his neck and held on to the front of his shirt. It went on: the kind he gave her when he’d decided something, slow and thorough, and when he finally let her go she’d forgotten what they’d been arguing about.

“What was that for?” she said.

“Three months of tea.”

“That’s generous payment.”

“I thought so.”

“Are you going to want your coffee back?”

He considered it. “Sometimes.”

“Then sometimes you can have coffee. And the rest of the time, tea,” said Isla.

“Reasonable.”

“Look at us. Negotiating terms.”

“Ginger on Tuesdays.”

“Ginger on Tuesdays,” she agreed.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening he came home with a small paper bag from the roaster’s by the station and put it on the coffee table in front of her.

She looked in. A quarter-kilo of beans. She narrowed her eyes. “Is this retaliation?”

“No.”

“A declaration of independence?”

“No.”

“Are you going to drink four cups tomorrow?”

“Two.”

“One.”

“Two,” said Wei Long, and went to change.

When he came back she’d put the green tin on the coffee table beside the bag. He picked it up, turned it over, and found the label she’d stuck to the bottom of it, in her handwriting.

For the man who won’t look after himself.

He looked at her across the room.

“I’m keeping this,” he said.

“Good.”

He sat down beside her and put his arm round her and took her book out of her hands and found her place in it and gave it back, and she leaned into him, and after a while said, “Tea tomorrow?”

“Yes.”

“And coffee?”

“One cup.”

“Promise?”

He kissed her hair. “One.”

In the morning she found him at the counter making coffee, his one cup, from beans he’d put into the green tin. He’d turned the label round to the front and written a new one underneath it, in square capitals.

ISLA’S TEA. DO NOT REPLACE WITHOUT PERMISSION.

“That’s your coffee. In the tea tin,” she said.

“It’s our tin.”

“You’ve labelled it Isla’s tea.”

“Because that’s what it’s for,” he said, and she laughed so loudly that the neighbour’s dog started barking through the wall, and took the pen out of his shirt pocket and, under his capitals, in her own small round hand, wrote two more words.

And his.

chapters.title: The Book on the Ten Minutes
chapters.desc: The squad’s betting book on Isla’s ten minutes, its whole life: Sham’s first sheet, confiscated; Hau running it from the front desk; Tak caught cheating; the entries for Lantern Lane and Lima; Liu winning on the proposal; and why the inspector keeps the first sheet and the last, blank one.
chapters.epigraph: “That you were there.”
chapters.content:
The book began on a Wednesday in March 2025, as a sheet of squared paper, and the inspector confiscated it inside a day.

Station Sergeant Hau heard about it the way he heard about everything in the building: from the canteen. Detective Sham had drawn a table. Five names had gone into it in five hands, Liu, Sham, Choy, Sin and Tak, each with a guess at how long the consular officer from the airport would spend on the inspector’s desk at nine o’clock with the blinds down. The inspector had come back from a meeting, found it beside his keyboard, read it with no expression whatever, and put it in his drawer.

“As evidence. He said nobody places bets on duty. And to stop calling it a project,” Sham reported, grievously, over his rice.

Hau had been at the station for twenty years by then, and on the front desk for eleven. He’d watched the inspector come up through the ranks from nineteen without, as far as Hau could tell, once looking at a clock except to log the time. He put down his chopsticks.

“Nobody on his squad,” Hau said, “places bets on duty.”

Sham looked at him.

“I’m not on his squad,” said Hau.

✦ ✦ ✦

So the book moved downstairs, to the front desk, which was outside the inspector’s chain of command and therefore, by Hau’s reading of the regulations, outside his jurisdiction. The first sheet was folded into quarters in the desk drawer. The second was written on the back of an old duty roster. By the third week Hau had bought a proper notebook from the stationer’s on the corner, black, with a red spine, and written on the cover in block capitals THE TEN-MINUTE BOOK, and underneath, smaller, Inspector Song’s nine o’clock visitor.

The rules were simple, and Hau kept them in the inside cover.

One: the inspector has to look up when she comes in.
Two: looking at the clock doesn’t count.
Three: looking at the door doesn’t count.
Four: looking at his phone doesn’t count unless it’s her.
Five: if he looks up before she comes in, all bets are void.
Six: if he looks up before nine, the odds go to hell.

There was a separate column for whether he smiled. Nobody ever collected on it. Twice someone claimed to have seen it and both times the claim was disallowed for lack of corroboration.

“Why are you doing this?” said Sin, one evening in May, leaning on the front desk.

Hau was writing the odds for the week in pencil. “Because it’s interesting.”

“It isn’t interesting. She comes every night.”

“Exactly. Consistency. You don’t get consistency in this building. You get burglaries.”

“What’s the difference between him looking up at 8:59 and nine?”

Hau looked at him over his glasses. “A minute of a man waiting,” he said, “for something he didn’t know he wanted,” and went back to the odds, and Sin went upstairs and didn’t bet that week.

✦ ✦ ✦

The book survived everything.

It survived the first time she brought dinner up, dumplings in a carrier bag, just after nine, and sat on his desk with her legs crossed and fed him with his own chopsticks. It survived the evening in late April when she caught him in the car park at quarter past six, and he came back up with his collar crooked, and Hau opened a new column headed Off-schedule. It survived the Thursday in May when her brother came through the front doors at a volume that set off the car alarm in the yard, and demanded the inspector by name and rank, and Hau, at the desk, said “Take a seat, sir,” in the voice he used on drunks, and Ren Hao sat, astonished, for the first time in what was clearly years. Hau told that one in the canteen for a month.

It survived a week in February 2026 when the inspector was in a surveillance flat over a laundry for seven nights running and nobody came at nine, and Sham ran an unofficial side bet on whether she’d come anyway, and she did, on the Wednesday, with a thermos, and was told by Liu at the top of the stairs that he wasn’t there, and said “I know,” and left the thermos on his desk, and went home.

It survived Tak cheating. That was in the summer of 2025. Tak had been texting Isla, under cover of asking about a consular form, to find out whether she’d be late, and placing his bets accordingly, and winning four weeks in a row, until Hau noticed that Tak always bet late on the evenings the visitor was in fact late. Hau confiscated Tak’s winnings for the station Christmas fund and barred him from the book for a month. The visitor, when she found out, brought Tak a box of pastries with a card that said No more insider trading. I. R.

Hau kept the entries in his own hand, in pencil, with the date.

12 Feb 2026. 8:57, insp. looked at door twice. She came 9:02. Five-minute delay. Insp. didn’t leave desk. Didn’t read a word on the page in front of him. Checked.

2 Jan 2026. 9:00 exactly. She brought him a pomelo. Nobody knows why. He peeled it at his desk and ate half and gave her the other half. Odds void (he looked up at 8:58).

24 Apr 2026. No visitor. Lantern Lane.

That one he wrote small, with nothing beside it. Nobody upstairs that month was in the mood for odds. They’d all heard the second shot over the radio.

17 Oct 2026. No visitor. Inspector on leave. Lima.

That one he wrote even smaller.

The building was different that autumn. They’d all seen the pictures from the coast. They all knew the inspector had spent a day and a half watching his phone not ring, and then packed one bag and taken the 23:55, and that the visitor’s brother had paid for the seat. Nobody made a joke about the missing ten minutes. For five weeks the book stayed in the drawer and Hau didn’t open it.

23 Nov 2026. Inspector back. No visitor (she’s still out there). He looked at the door at nine anyway. Then at the clock. Then at the door. Then went back to work.

Hau nearly rubbed that entry out afterwards, and didn’t.

28 Apr 2027. 9:02. First visit since July. She came in past the desk and said “Hello, Sergeant,” as if she’d been in yesterday. No odds accepted. He looked up before she reached his door. He’d been looking at it since 8:45.

✦ ✦ ✦

By 2027 the book had become a legend. Constables who joined that year heard about it before they knew what it was.

“Does the inspector know?” one of them asked Hau, a boy called Lun with a haircut that looked self-inflicted.

“Of course not.”

“Doesn’t he see you writing it?”

“He sees everything.”

“Then...”

“He chooses not to see this.”

Lun thought about it. “Why?”

Hau looked up the stairs. The inspector’s door was open. He was at his desk on the phone, and you could tell who was on the other end of it from the way he’d stopped typing.

“Because it does no harm. And because he knows we’re all waiting for the same thing he is,” said Hau.

Lun followed his eyes. “Oh,” he said.

“Yes. Oh,” said Hau.

In May, when she’d come home and Hau had moved the odds from his drawer to the stationery cupboard upstairs, because there was no point pretending any more, she found the smiling sheet pinned inside the cupboard door and folded it into her handbag in front of the inspector and walked out with it, and Hau let her, because it was hers. The sheet he pinned on the noticeboard after that, at the end of May, had a different question across the top in his own capitals.

HOW LONG BEFORE INSP. SONG ASKS OFFICER REN TO MARRY HIM?

He didn’t bet on it himself. He’d seen the inspector’s face the night it went up, through the blind, and he knew that some questions were already answered and only waiting for a date.

✦ ✦ ✦

Monday the fourth of October 2027, the inspector came in at half past seven in a shirt that had been pressed by someone who wasn’t a laundry. At 8:35 he opened his top drawer, looked into it, and shut it. Just before nine he read something on three sheets of paper that he wouldn’t let Liu see. At ten past five he signed out, which he never did before eight, and Hau, at the desk, said, “Off early, sir?” and the inspector said, “The airport,” and Hau said nothing, and wrote nothing, and sat without moving for some time after the door had shut.

The squad didn’t find out until the next morning. Hau found out at ten to nine that night, from the duty sergeant at the airport post, who’d been a constable in the inspector’s first squad and who rang the front desk on his break and said only, “He did it. At the custody desk. She said yes. He read her three pages first. I’ve never seen anything like it in my life,” and rang off before Hau could ask him what had been on the pages.

The settlement took place in the briefing room at eight the next morning, before the inspector got in. Hau put the black notebook on the table and the May sheet beside it.

“Ladies and gentlemen. The Ten-Minute Book’s last open question is closed.”

“Who won?” said Sham.

Hau ran his finger down the sheet. Liu had put October 2027 the day the sheet went up, which Hau knew because he’d watched him write it and wondered how. Sin had put never, she’ll ask him. Sham had put at the desk, at nine, in front of all of us, and he’ll forget the ring.

“Liu,” said Hau.

“How?” said Sham.

Liu, who’d been the inspector’s sergeant for six years and had once seen him take a ring catalogue out of his drawer, look at it, and put it back, only shrugged.

“I asked the jeweller on the corner,” he said, “in May, if anyone had been in.”

The squad stared at him.

“That’s not insider trading. That’s detective work,” said Liu.

✦ ✦ ✦

The last time the book was settled was a Tuesday morning, the sixth of March 2029, the day after the fourth anniversary of the wet terminal.

Hau came up the stairs at a quarter to eight with the black notebook under his arm, its red spine split now and mended with tape, and a sheet of paper folded on top of it that he’d taken off the noticeboard the night before. He put them both on the inspector’s desk. The inspector looked up.

“Sir, four years. I’m retiring the book,” said Hau.

The inspector opened it. He turned the pages slowly, in silence: the rules inside the cover, the odds in pencil, Tak’s confiscated winnings, Off-schedule, Lantern Lane small, Lima smaller, 23 Nov 2026 with the door and the clock and the door. He read every line. Hau let him.

Then he unfolded the sheet on top. Somebody had pinned it to the noticeboard the week before in a hand Hau didn’t recognise. HOW LONG BEFORE SHE STOPS COMING AT NINE? Underneath, ruled columns for names and dates and sums of money, every one of them blank. Nobody in the building had put a single coin on it.

The inspector looked at that until Hau had to look away.

Then, without a word, he opened the top drawer on the left and took out a sheet of squared paper, softened at the folds, in five hands, which said across the top THE TEN-MINUTE OBSERVATION PROJECT, and at the bottom, in Sham’s writing, Conclusion: subject alarmingly punctual.

Hau stared at it. “You kept that.”

“Evidence,” said the inspector.

“Of what, sir?”

The inspector put the three things side by side on his desk: the first sheet, the black book, the blank last sheet. He looked at them.

“That you were there. All of you,” he said.

Hau found, unexpectedly, that he had to look out of the window.

The inspector put the book and both sheets in the drawer, on top of a receipt with two stamps, a card in three languages, and three folded pages, and shut it, and didn’t lock it.
