“Thank you, Sergeant.”

“Sir.”

“The blank one. Leave it blank,” the inspector said, as Hau turned to go.

“Sir,” said Hau, and went downstairs, and at nine o’clock that night, when the visitor came in past the front desk with her coat over her arm and said “Evening, Sergeant,” as she’d said for four years, he didn’t look at his watch and he didn’t look up the stairs. He knew exactly where the inspector was looking. Everyone in the building did.

chapters.title: Language Cards in His Pockets
chapters.desc: After Lima she goes on writing him language cards, and leaves them in every jacket he owns. Twelve words, used at the worst moments. The twelfth is in his shirt pocket: rendirse. Explicit.
chapters.epigraph: “Not because you’ve lost. Because you trust whoever is holding you.”
chapters.content:
The first card was in his jacket on a Tuesday at the beginning of June, five weeks after she’d come home.

He found it outside the station, reaching for his car keys: a small cream rectangle, folded once, in her hand. He knew the cards. Twenty-six of them had come through his letterbox from Lima, one a week, and they lived in the back of his notebook in an elastic band, and he said them to the windscreen at red lights. He hadn’t expected them to go on now that she was here.

despacio

Slowly. For when you forget that not everything has to be done at once.

He stood by the car and read it twice. Then he put it back where he’d found it.

That evening he set it on the bedside table, face up. She was reading in bed and didn’t look up.

“You found it.”

“Yes.”

“Did you learn it?”

“Despacio.”

“Good,” said Isla, and turned a page, and the corner of her mouth went, and he understood that there would be more.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second was in his other jacket, the grey one, two days later.

cuidado

Careful. For when you think you’re made of steel.

He found it at the top of the station stairs before the morning briefing, and walked into the squad room with it in his hand just as Sham came round the corner with a stack of files up to his chin.

“Cuidado,” said Wei Long.

Sham stopped. “Sir?”

“Your files.”

Sham looked down. The top folder was halfway off the pile. He caught it with his chin. “Thank you, sir,” he said, deeply puzzled, and went on, and for the rest of the week the squad said cuidado to each other in the corridors in his exact tone of voice and believed he didn’t know.

At nine he showed her the card. “I used it.”

“On whom?”

“Sham.”

“What happened?”

“He nearly dropped a file.”

“How romantic,” said Isla, and kissed him on the desk until the blinds rattled.

✦ ✦ ✦

The third was in his raincoat.

todavía

Still. As in: still here, still waiting, still yours.

It fell out onto the hall floor on a wet Friday when he was hanging the coat up, and he bent and picked it up and read it standing there, dripping, with one shoe off.

“Too sentimental?” she called from the kitchen, because of course she’d heard it land.

He went and found her at the stove, and took the spoon out of her hand, and kissed her instead of answering, and she laughed into his mouth and said, “That’s not what I was cooking for.”

The fourth was in his work jacket, on a day he hadn’t eaten.

hambre

Hunger. For when you forget to have lunch. You’ve forgotten. I know you have.

He found it at ten past two, reaching for a pen. He looked at the word. Then at the sandwich in its wrapper beside his keyboard, which Liu had put there at noon. He unwrapped it.

Hau, coming in with a file, stopped in the doorway. “Sir? Are you eating?”

“Yes.”

Hau looked at the sandwich, and at the card on the blotter beside it. “Is that a new procedure, sir?”

“No,” said Wei Long, and took another bite, and photographed the card, and sent it.

Wei Long: Found it.

Thank You (Paid): Are you eating at your desk again?

Wei Long: Define desk.

Thank You (Paid): Show me the plate.

He looked at the half that was left, and took another bite.

Wei Long: In progress.

✦ ✦ ✦

The fifth was paciencia, in his navy suit jacket, the week he asked her four times in one evening where she wanted to go at the weekend. Patience. For when you want an answer immediately. She watched him find it, and read it, and look at her.

“It’s Tuesday, Inspector,” she said.

“I’m being patient.”

“You’ve lasted less than twelve hours.”

“I’m waiting for your answer.”

“Saturday, somewhere with a view,” said Isla, relenting.

The sixth was in his black jacket, after a late shift.

hogar

Home. Not only a place. Sometimes a person.

He found it at one in the morning, letting himself into the new flat, the one with both their names on the door and boxes still in the corners. She’d fallen asleep on the sofa, which had finally arrived, with a book on her chest and the lamp on and a blanket slipping off her shoulder. He stood in the doorway and looked at her for some time. Then he took the card out and read it again, and put it in his shirt pocket, and bent and lifted her.

She woke halfway to the bedroom. “You’re back.”

“Yes.”

She opened one eye. “Welcome home,” she said, and went back to sleep against his neck, and he stood in the bedroom doorway holding her for longer than he needed to before he put her down.

The seventh was sobremesa, and it came with a longer note than the others, because it had no English.

The time after a meal when nobody gets up. When the plates are empty and you stay at the table anyway, talking, because the company’s better than whatever you were going to do next. You’ve never once done this. Learn it.

He didn’t use it. He did it. That Sunday, after lunch, she started to clear the plates and he put his hand over hers on the table and said, “Sit down,” and she sat, and they stayed at the table until it got dark, talking about nothing, her feet in his lap under the table, the plates still there, and when she finally got up to turn on the light she was smiling in a way he’d have written down if he’d had his notebook.

✦ ✦ ✦

The eighth was travesura. Mischief. For when you know exactly what you’re doing. He found it on a Sunday morning, and she was sitting up in bed in his shirt looking far too pleased with herself, and he held it up and said, “Explain,” and she said, “Because you know exactly what you’re doing when you look at me like that,” and he looked at her like that, and she stopped explaining.

The ninth was in his formal suit, before an official dinner at the consulate.

deseo

Desire. For when you don’t know how to ask.

He read it in the car park of the hotel and put it away and didn’t mention it. That night, after the dinner, she was at the mirror in their bedroom trying to undo the clasp of a necklace.

“Can you help?”

He stood behind her and undid it. His fingers stayed at the back of her neck. She met his eyes in the glass.

“Deseo,” he said.

She went still. Then she turned round, slowly, with the necklace in her hand.

“You learned that one.”

“Yes.”

“Do you know what it means?”

“Yes.”

“And what do you want?”

“You,” said Wei Long, and she dropped the necklace on the floor, and neither of them picked it up until morning.

The tenth was in his travel jacket, before a three-day conference in another city. confianza. Trust. For when you have to let someone stand next to you. She was folding his shirts on the bed while he read it. He didn’t say anything. He slipped it into his wallet, behind the windscreen card from 2025 and the hambre one, which he’d also moved, she noticed.

“You’re collecting them now?”

“They’re useful.”

The eleventh was in his station jacket, on a day when he’d been in an interview room for nine hours.

siempre

Always. Because love isn’t only something you feel. It’s something you keep doing.

He read it just before nine at his desk. At nine she came in with dinner and he looked up before she’d reached the door, and held the card up between two fingers, and said, “Siempre,” and she stopped in the middle of the room as if she’d walked into glass.

“You remembered.”

“I remember all of them.”

“All eleven?”

“Yes. What’s the twelfth?” He caught her wrist as she came round the desk.

“Tomorrow,” said Isla.

“Why tomorrow?”

“Because I haven’t decided where to put it yet,” she said, and kissed his forehead, and left him there with his dinner going cold, wondering, which he did for twenty-two hours.

✦ ✦ ✦

The twelfth was in his shirt pocket. Not his jacket. His shirt.

He found it at eleven on the Saturday night after a shower, pulling on a clean shirt out of the drawer. A card folded small, tucked into the breast pocket where it would sit against his heart.

rendirse

To surrender. Not because you’ve lost. Because you trust whoever is holding you.

He read it twice. Then he looked at the bedroom door.

She was sitting up against the headboard with her hair loose and the lamp on, wearing nothing but another of his shirts, watching him.

“You found it.”

“Yes. Why this one?” He came and sat on the bed.

“Because you’ve learned eleven words about looking after yourself, and being patient, and trusting people, and coming home. This one’s about letting somebody look after you. You’ve never once done it. Not properly. Not without checking the door.” She took the card out of his fingers and turned it over.

He looked at her. “Rendirse,” he said.

The r was careful and not quite right. Her face changed anyway.

“Again.”

“Rendirse.”

“Better. Perfect. Now do it.” She put the card on the bedside table.

He didn’t ask what she meant. He lay back on the bed, on top of the covers, in the shirt he’d just put on, and let her.

She undid the buttons one by one, slowly, the way he did everything, and he lay still and watched her and kept his hands at his sides because that was what the word was. She kissed his chest. She kissed the burn across his knuckles, and the inside of his wrist, and the place on his ribs that made him catch his breath. She took the rest of his clothes off without his help and then her own shirt, and climbed over him, and took his wrists in her hands and pressed them down into the pillow beside his head, gently, with almost no weight at all.

“You could get up. Any time,” she said, against his mouth.

“I know.”

“Don’t.”

He didn’t. She kissed him until his breathing went, and then she reached down and took him in her hand and guided him and sank onto him, slowly, all the way, and held still there with her palms flat on his wrists, and he shut his eyes, and for once in his life didn’t open them to check anything. She moved on him at her own pace and no faster. When he lifted his hips to meet her she stopped, and waited, until he let go of that too. It went on and on. She leaned down and kissed his throat and his jaw and the corner of his mouth, and whispered things to him in Spanish, some of them on the cards and most of them not, and he lay under her and let it all happen to him, and found that it was the most frightening thing he’d ever done and that he wasn’t frightened at all.

“Rendirse,” she said in his ear, near the end.

“Rendirse,” he said back, and this time the r was right, and she let go of his wrists, and he put his arms round her and held on, and they came within a breath of each other, with her forehead pressed to his and his hands spread across her back.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday morning he put on his station jacket and reached into the pocket for his keys.

The first card was there. Then the second, the third. He checked the inside pocket. He checked his wallet. All twelve, in order, behind the windscreen card from the airport.

She was in the bedroom doorway with her coffee. “You’re taking them?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Useful vocabulary,” said Wei Long, and came and kissed her, and picked up his keys, and at the door turned round.

“Isla.”

“Yes?”

“Rendirse,” he said, low.

She looked at him over the cup. “Have a good day, cariño,” she said, and he went down the stairs to the car with twelve cards in his pockets and the thirteenth already, he was fairly sure, somewhere in the car.

chapters.title: The Stakeout Picnic
chapters.desc: She brings sandwiches and lychees to a surveillance van and is not allowed in. The suspect walks out while they’re kissing against it; he makes the arrest with mustard on his cuff.
chapters.epigraph: “But I can bring lunch.”
chapters.content:
Just before one on a Thursday in August, Detective Sham looked out of the side window of the surveillance van and said, “Oh, no.”

Sergeant Liu, in the back with the radio, didn’t look up. “What?”

“It’s the inspector’s girlfriend.”

Liu looked up. On the pavement opposite the van, beside a fruit stall and a parked moped, stood Isla Ren in a yellow summer dress with a paper carrier bag in each hand and a cardboard tray of iced coffees balanced on top of one of them, smiling at the van’s tinted window with the bright, total confidence of a woman who’d brought lunch and expected it to be welcomed.

“Don’t open the door,” said Sham.

“Why would I open the door?”

“Because she’s looking at you.”

Liu looked away so fast he hit his head on the radio shelf.

✦ ✦ ✦

They’d been in the van since half past eight. It was an unmarked white delivery van with a plumbing firm’s name on the side that didn’t exist, parked on a narrow street of low-rise flats in the east of the city, and the man they were watching lived on the third floor of the building opposite. Tou Ka-ming, thirty-eight, believed to be paying and directing a crew of burglars who’d taken eleven jewellery shops in five months. The instruction was simple: watch until he left the building or met anyone on the list, then follow or lift, as the situation required.

It was the most boring kind of operation there was. The van was hot. The air conditioning had died at ten. The coffee in the flask was a crime in itself.

Wei Long was in the passenger seat with a pair of binoculars on his knee and his eyes on the third-floor window. His phone buzzed.

Thank You (Paid): I’m outside the van.

Thank You (Paid): The one with the fake plumbers on it.

Thank You (Paid): You said you hadn’t eaten. I have proof.

“Sir,” said Liu, from the back.

“I know.”

“You can see her?”

“She told me.”

There was a silence.

“You knew she was coming?” said Sham.

“She said at breakfast she might bring lunch. I said not to. She heard not yet.” He lowered the binoculars.

“Are we allowed to accept sandwiches? On an operation?” said Choy.

“That’s not a procedural question.”

“I’m asking as a hungry man, sir.”

Outside, Isla knocked twice on the side of the van. Brightly.

✦ ✦ ✦

Wei Long slid the side door open six inches and put his head out into the heat.

“You can’t come in.”

“I don’t want to come in. It smells of men in there. I brought food.” She held up the bags.

“I can see that.”

“Sandwiches. Five. And coffee. And I asked the man at the stall and he says your suspect buys his oranges at nine every morning and hasn’t been down today, so you’ve probably got time.”

He looked at her.

“You asked the fruit seller about my suspect.”

“I asked him about oranges. He volunteered the rest. Take them.”

He took the bags. She didn’t let go of the second one.

“Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“When?”

He thought about it. “Earlier.”

“Define earlier.”

“Before nine.”

“That’s breakfast, Wei Long. It’s a quarter to one.”

He looked at her. She looked back, in the sun, with her eyebrows up.

“No,” he said.

“Thought not. There’s one for everybody. Yours is the one with your name on. Don’t let Choy have it.” She let go of the bag.

“I heard that,” said Choy from inside.

“Good!” said Isla, and then asked Wei Long, lower, whether he’d had water, because he looked tired.

He held the bottle up out of the cup holder by the door. She inspected it like a customs officer and nodded.

“Go home,” he said.

“I’m going,” said Isla, and pulled him down by the collar and kissed his cheek through the gap, and stepped back, and he shut the door, and the whole van looked at him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The sandwiches were excellent. This was agreed by everyone, unanimously, with their mouths full.

Sham had chicken. Liu had egg and cress. Choy had tuna and the remains of somebody else’s crisps. Wei Long’s was roast beef with mustard, on the bread from the bakery near the consulate that he’d once said was acceptable, wrapped in waxed paper, with a note tucked into the fold.

Eat all of it. I know you. I. R.

He read it and folded it and put it in his shirt pocket. Sham saw.

“What does the note say, sir?”

“Nothing.”

“Is it romantic?”

“Eat your sandwich.”

Liu unfolded his own wrapper. “Mine says Don’t let Choy steal yours.”

“Why does everyone think I steal food?” said Choy.

“You ate my biscuits,” said Sham.

“They were communal.”

“They were in my bag.”

For fifteen minutes the van was the most peaceful place in the city. Then the phone buzzed.

Thank You (Paid): Did you eat it?

He looked at the half sandwich in his other hand.

Wei Long: Yes.

Thank You (Paid): All of it?

Wei Long: Half.

Thank You (Paid): Half isn’t all.

He took another bite.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after two she came back. He saw her first, because he’d been watching the street more than the window since the second text, which he wasn’t going to examine. She was across the road by the fruit stall again, on her phone, not looking at the van with enormous concentration.

Thank You (Paid): I forgot the fruit.

Wei Long: You don’t need to bring fruit.

Thank You (Paid): I already bought it. From the man. He’s given me a discount because I’m “the plumber’s wife”.

Wei Long: Go home.

Thank You (Paid): I’m walking past.

She was, in fact, walking past, at the speed of a funeral. Sham watched her through the window.

“She’s back.”

“She’s going to get him into trouble,” said Liu, not unhappily.

“Watch the entrance,” said Wei Long.

“Sir, you’re watching her.”

“I’m aware.”

She stopped beside the van. He slid the door open.

“You said you were walking past.”

“I am.”

“You’ve stopped.”

“I wanted to see you. Lychees. Peeled. I peeled them on the bench. There’s a fork,” said Isla, and held up a plastic box.

He took them. She looked past him into the gloom.

“Hello, everyone.”

“Hello, Miss Ren,” said three detectives at once, like a school.

“Thank you for lunch,” said Choy. “Could you bring dessert next time?”

“Constable,” said Wei Long.

“I’m expressing gratitude, sir.”

Wei Long stepped down out of the van onto the pavement and pulled the door to behind him. The heat came up off the concrete. Across the street, the third-floor window was still shut, the blind still down.

“You should go,” he said.

She tilted her head. “Do you want me to?”

He looked at her in her yellow dress, in the sun, with her hair coming down and a smear of lychee juice on her thumb.

“No,” he said.

Her face went soft all at once. “Then don’t send me away so fast.”

He looked at the window. Shut. He looked at his watch. “Five minutes.”

“How generous.”

“I thought so.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The trouble with five minutes was that Isla had never respected one in her life.

She stood beside him in the strip of shade along the van with her hand in his. She asked if he’d liked the sandwich. He said it was fine. She said he always said that. He said it was usually fine. She reached up and straightened his collar, which didn’t need it, and then stopped.

“You’ve got mustard.”

“Where?”

She touched his right cuff. There was a bright yellow smear across the white. He looked at it.

“I’ll change later.”

“Elegant, Inspector.”

“It’s a surveillance van.”

“Still,” said Isla, and he put his thumb against her cheek, and she stopped talking, and leaned in, and he kissed her.

It was meant to be brief. It wasn’t. Her free hand went to the back of his neck and his went to her waist, and he kissed her again, slower, against the warm side of a van with a non-existent plumber’s name on it, as though the street and the operation and the third-floor window had all stepped out and left them alone.

Inside the van, Sham looked away. Liu looked at Sham. Choy looked at both of them.

“Are we supposed to be watching?”

“Not them,” hissed Liu.

Which was why none of them saw the street door of the building opposite open, and Tou Ka-ming come out with a black rucksack over one shoulder, check his phone, and cross the road towards the fruit stall, which would take him straight past the van.

Choy saw him at eight metres. “Sir, sir,” he said, to the tinted window.

Outside, the inspector was still kissing his girlfriend. Liu reached past Choy and rapped on the inside of the glass, twice, hard.

Wei Long lifted his head. Isla felt him change under her hands, completely, in less than a second: the man she’d been kissing was gone and someone else was standing there.

“Stay here,” he said.

“What...”

He was already moving. Tou Ka-ming was five metres away, looking at his phone.

“Police. Stand still.”

Tou looked up. For half a second he considered it. Then he turned and ran, and Wei Long caught him by the rucksack strap in two strides and turned him and put him face first against the side of the van with one forearm across his shoulder blades, not hard, not gently.

“Hands where I can see them.”

The side door crashed open. Sham and Liu were out before the man had finished swearing. It was clean. It was over in thirty seconds. Cuffs, caution, rucksack. In the rucksack, two phones, a band of cash and a jeweller’s loupe that would turn out to belong to shop number seven.

Only when it was all done, and Tou was in the back of the car that had come round the corner, did Wei Long look down at his right hand. Mustard. Across his cuff.

Isla was standing by the van with the box of lychees held against her chest. She looked at the cuff. She looked at him. Her lips pressed together until they disappeared. He gave her a look.

She turned round and faced the fruit stall and her shoulders started to shake.

✦ ✦ ✦

Sham came up beside him with the evidence bags. “Good arrest, sir.”

“Thank you.”

“Excellent timing.”

Wei Long looked at him.

Sham nodded, gravely, towards the woman in yellow by the fruit stall. “Efficient use of resources.”

“Detective Sham.”

“Sir?”

“Log the evidence.”

“Sir. Sir? Your cuff.” Sham went. At the van door he turned.

“I know.”

“Mustard.”

“I know.”

“Excellent mustard, apparently,” said Sham, and disappeared inside before anything could be done about him.

Wei Long went back to the fruit stall. Isla was still laughing. She’d stopped trying to hide it.

“You’re enjoying this,” he said.

“You arrested a jewel thief with mustard on your sleeve.”

“It didn’t affect the arrest.”

“I know it didn’t. I watched. Terrible for your reputation.” She took his wrist and inspected the cuff.

“I’ll survive.”

“You should go. You’re working,” she said.

“You’ve said that twice.”

“Because you keep coming back,” said Isla, and he looked at her, and bent and kissed her, quickly, by the oranges, in front of the fruit seller, who’d seen the whole thing and was now telling his neighbour about it with gestures.

“Was that thank you?” she said.

“For the sandwiches.”

“And the lychees?”

“Yes.”

“And the mustard?”

“The mustard most of all,” said Wei Long, and took the box of lychees out of her hands, and went back to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

The team chat, at 18:40:

Sham: Operation complete. Suspect detained 14:24. Evidence recovered. Inspector’s shirt sustained mustard damage in the course of duty.

Sham: Catering: excellent.

Liu: Confirmed.

Choy: Requesting repeat catering.

Wei Long: Delete the last three lines.

Nobody did. That evening Isla was on the sofa in her flat when he came in, in a clean shirt from his locker. She looked up.

“Any more arrests?”

“No.”

“Any more mustard?”

He sat down beside her, and she leaned into his shoulder.

“It wasn’t a picnic,” he said, after a while.

“It had sandwiches. And fruit. And a view.”

“It was a surveillance operation.”

“With sandwiches. That’s a picnic,” said Isla.

He put his arm round her. “You can’t come to an operation again. It isn’t safe.”

“I know.”

“You can’t stand next to the van.”

“I know.”

“Or kiss me against it.”

“I know. But I can bring lunch,” she said, and lifted her head.

He looked down at her. “Yes, you can bring lunch,” he said.

“Next time I’ll bring dessert,” said Isla, and he shut his eyes.

chapters.title: The Black Box Comes to the Station
chapters.desc: Song-Zhu, newly engaged to Ren Hao, brings a phone recovered from the harbour, and the glacier works with someone who talks faster than Isla. She takes nineteen of his ten minutes.
chapters.epigraph: “I married one.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Wei Long noticed about Xu Song-Zhu at work was that she didn’t breathe.

He’d met her a dozen times by then. At dinners, at Ren Hao’s flat, at the long table above the noodle shop on the night he’d married Isla, where she’d sat opposite him and timed her future husband’s toast on her phone. He knew her as a woman who laughed with her whole body and could make Ren Hao go quiet with one look. He’d never seen her with a case.

She came up the station stairs just before nine on a Wednesday in April with a grey waterproof evidence box under one arm and a folder under the other, and put both on his desk before he’d finished standing up.

“Inspector Song. Good, you’re here. Ren Hao said you’d be here, he said you’re always here at this time, he said something about ten minutes that I didn’t follow. I’m here as the lab, not as a guest, so I’ve been told to behave professionally, which I think is unreasonable given that he also told me you were impossible to impress. And no, before your squad asks, we’re not related. Song’s my given name. You can have the surname.”

“Thank you,” said Wei Long.

“He also says you don’t drink enough water. I think that’s an attempt to make me like you. It’s working. Can I show you a phone?” She snapped the catches on the box.

From the visitor’s chair beside his desk, where she’d been sitting since 8:59 with a coffee and her shoes off under the desk, Isla lowered her cup. He looked at her. She was already smiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Recovered from the harbour on Saturday. East side of the old quay. About thirty metres from where the car went in. Your divers sent it to us because your lab’s backed up into June and ours isn’t, and because it’s the kind of wreck I’m good at. I don’t think it belongs to the driver,” said Song-Zhu, lifting a sealed bag out of the box with gloved hands. Inside was a phone with no screen, its casing split along one edge and furred white with salt.

The car had gone off the quay on a Thursday night, one man dead at the wheel.

“Why?” said Wei Long.

“Because the driver’s phone was in his jacket, and this one was under the passenger floor mat, and the passenger seat was gone when they lifted the car, and nobody’s found a passenger. And because the position’s from the diver’s first report, not the recovery photographs, and the two don’t match, and I’m not prepared to let anyone write it up as the victim’s phone just because it came out of the same car. So I’ve brought the dive log, the support vessel’s log, the photographs, the chain of custody and a list of what I can’t tell you yet, which is longer than the list of what I can.” She put the bag down on his blotter.

“Good,” said Wei Long.

She stopped. “Good?”

“Good that you brought the documentation.”

“Oh.” She looked disappointed, as if she’d been braced for an argument and been handed a chair. Isla put her cup down.

“She’s been waiting all evening to tell somebody about that floor mat,” Isla said.

“Thank you. Finally. Someone who understands,” said Song-Zhu, pointing at her.

✦ ✦ ✦

For the next nineteen minutes she explained the phone.

She was precise, and technically flawless, and almost alarmingly enthusiastic. She talked about salt corrosion, about which parts of a storage chip survived four days in a harbour, about why the casing had split on the long edge and not the short one. She didn’t stop. She didn’t need to. Every sentence led into the next one like a corridor.

Wei Long listened. He asked questions. He wrote things down. By every outward sign he was keeping up.

Isla, from the visitor’s chair, watched something happen to him that she’d never seen.

His pauses were getting shorter. He always left a gap after a person finished speaking; she’d learned it in a stairwell in March three years ago, and squad rooms had learned it, and witnesses had broken in it. He left the gap now, out of habit, and every time, before it was a second long, Song-Zhu had already filled it with the next thing.

“...and the interesting part is that it doesn’t seem to have taken the same pressure as the driver’s phone, which suggests the floor assembly shielded it, though I can’t prove that without a structural look at the floor pan, and the damage pattern on the long edge is consistent with...”

“Have you got the dive photographs?” said Wei Long.

“Three sets. I’ve marked the frames.”

“Can I see them?”

“Yes. I’ve also got four minutes of video from the diver’s helmet camera. It isn’t exciting unless you enjoy watching a man fight a cable, but the last thirty seconds are useful.”

He considered. “Show me the last thirty seconds.”

Song-Zhu looked at him with frank approval. “You’re a practical man.”

Isla hid her face in her coffee. The last thirty seconds were useful. In the torchlight, under the passenger footwell of a car lying on its roof in the black, the phone was wedged under a buckled section of floor, face down, with the charging port uppermost.

“Can you enlarge that?” said Wei Long.

She did. “There. The upper edge is crushed, but the port’s nearly intact. That’s what made me think there’s a chance.”

“Was it on, when it came up?”

“Dead. Completely. And nobody’s to try charging it unless they want to destroy the only thing on it. I’ve put that in writing three times.”

“We’ll send it for specialist extraction.”

“I can do the extraction. That’s what I came to ask. One more thing. There’s a five-minute gap in the recovery time. The diver logs 09:42. The boat logs 09:47. It might be nothing. But if anyone’s going to build a timeline out of this, I want the gap written down, not tidied.” She was already packing the photographs back into the folder. Then she stopped.

He nodded once. “Agreed.”

“Excellent. I like you,” said Song-Zhu.

Isla made a small noise into her cup.

“Thank you,” said Wei Long.

“No, really. He said you’d be impossible. You’re the easiest person I’ve worked with this year. And you’re so much quieter than him.”

“Most people are.”

Song-Zhu laughed, the whole-body laugh, and Isla laughed with her, and Wei Long looked across at his wife, and recognised the face she was wearing. It was the one she wore when she’d found something funny and intended to keep it for later, possibly for years.

✦ ✦ ✦

Song-Zhu’s phone rang as she was snapping the box shut. She looked at the screen.

“Speak of the devil. I’m still at the station. No, I haven’t finished. Because I’m discussing a case, Hao. He’s being helpful. Hao, I’ve been here twenty-three minutes. You can’t possibly miss me that much. That’s not what I said. Yes. Yes. I ate. No, coffee isn’t lunch, I know coffee isn’t lunch, I’ll eat when I’m back. Stop asking. I’m hanging up. I love you. I’m hanging up.” She answered. A longer pause, and her eyes went to the ceiling. She glanced at the empty paper cup by her elbow.

She hung up.

“Protective?” said Isla.

“Obnoxiously.” Song-Zhu glanced down at her left hand, at the ring Hao had gone out and bought her the morning after she’d proposed to him on an airfield three Saturdays ago, because he couldn’t bear to be proposed to and not buy something. Then she looked at Wei Long. “Does he do that to you as well?”

“Sometimes.”

“Ring to ask if you’ve eaten?”

“Yes.”

“Ask what you’ve eaten?”

“Yes.”

“Ask why you didn’t have something else?”

He thought about it. “Occasionally.”

Song-Zhu nodded with immense seriousness. “That’s Ren Hao. That’s the whole family. It’s genetic.”

She turned to Isla.

“You do it too,” said Song.

“I do not.”

“You sent me a text this morning that said Have you eaten? Don’t lie.”

“That was a reasonable question,” said Isla, with dignity, and Wei Long looked from one to the other and said nothing at all, which both of them noticed.

She left at 9:21 with three copies of the recovery documents, two direct numbers, a written list of questions for the dive team, and an instruction to Sham, who’d come in for a stapler and been seized, that nobody was to touch the phone without gloves. She asked on her way out whether the station had decent coffee, was told no, said that explained a great deal about the police, and went.

The office was noticeably quieter.

✦ ✦ ✦

Isla stayed in the visitor’s chair. Wei Long opened the first document. She said nothing. He turned a page. She still said nothing. He looked up.

“What?”

“Nothing. You were so patient.” She swung her bare foot under the desk.

“I was working.”

“You were listening extremely hard.”

“She brought relevant evidence.”

“You didn’t get a gap in edgeways for nineteen minutes.”

“I answered the relevant questions.”

“She asked whether you’d had a difficult childhood because you didn’t smile when she told you about the charging port.”

He paused. “That wasn’t about the phone.”

“It was about you.”

“I noticed.”

She laughed, and stood up, and came round the desk in her stockinged feet, and sat on the corner of it, on the dive log, because it was twenty-one minutes past nine and the ten minutes were hers and Song-Zhu had had nineteen of them.

“You enjoyed that,” he said.

“So much. I’ve finally met somebody who talks faster than I do.”

He looked at her. “You don’t talk fast.”

“Excuse me?”

“You’re more selective.”

She stared at him. Then her face went warm all at once. “That’s a diplomatic way of calling me talkative.”

“It wasn’t an insult.”

“I know it wasn’t. You were impressed with her.” She straightened his collar.

“She was competent. She knew exactly what she’d brought and exactly what it couldn’t prove, and she said so before anybody asked. Most experts I see do the opposite. And she wrote down the five minutes.” He put his pen down.

“I knew it,” said Isla.

“Knew what?”

“You like competent women.”

He looked up at her on the corner of his desk with her shoes off and his collar in her fingers.

“I married one,” said Wei Long.

She went still. It was an unfair thing to say, in that voice, without warning, and he knew it. She leaned down and kissed him over the dive log, with her hand on the side of his face, and he kissed her back, and at the door Sham, coming back with the stapler, turned round and went out again without a sound.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 10:40, at home, Ren Hao rang him. Wei Long was at the kitchen table with the forensic submission form.

“Inspector. Where’s my fiancée?”

“Not here.”

“I know she was at the station.”

“She left at 9:21.”

“Did she talk too much?”

Wei Long looked across the room at Isla on the sofa, who was looking back at him. He thought about nineteen minutes, and a corridor of sentences, and the five-minute gap written down instead of tidied away.

“She was thorough,” he said.

“That’s a polite word for yes.”

“She brought useful evidence.”

“Of course she did. She’s the best there is. She said you hardly interrupted her once.”

“I didn’t need to.”

“She liked that, apparently. She said you’re restful. Nobody’s ever called me restful.” Ren Hao sounded personally aggrieved.

“No,” said Wei Long.

Isla took the phone out of his hand.

“Hao. She’s a grown woman. She’ll eat when she gets home. Stop ringing her every twenty minutes.”

“I don’t ring her every twenty minutes.”

Wei Long looked at the clock. Ren Hao had rung his fiancée, by Song-Zhu’s own count in a text that came through while Isla was still talking, four times since six.

“Good night, Hao. Come here, Inspector,” said Isla, and hung up, and handed the phone back, and patted the sofa beside her.

He went. She tucked herself against his shoulder.

“I think you have a type,” she said, after a while.

“What type?”

“Women who talk too much.”

He thought about it with his cheek against her hair.

“I don’t think that’s the part I like,” he said.

“Which part do you like?”

“The part where they know exactly what they’re doing.”

“And the talking?”

“I’ve got used to the talking. She’s much faster, though.” He waited exactly long enough for her to relax.

She sat up.

“Excuse me?”

He was already smiling.

“Good night, Isla,” said Wei Long, and she took hold of his shirt and kissed him to make him take it back, and he didn’t, and for once in his life he’d started an argument on purpose that he had no intention of being allowed to finish.

chapters.title: Vancouver at Christmas
chapters.desc: He meets the snow, her parents in person, and a moose-shaped biscuit. He overhears Song-Zhu ask the professors how to propose to their son, and tells no one. Her childhood bedroom: explicit and silent.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s only a matter of time.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Wei Long learned about Vancouver was that snow was beautiful from inside a warm car. The second was that it was less beautiful down the back of his collar.

“Don’t move,” said Isla.

“I’m not moving.”

“You’re making it worse.”

“I’m removing it.”

“You’re spreading it.” She came round the side of the taxi in her cream coat and her red scarf and reached up and brushed it out of his hair with her gloved hand. Some had caught on his eyelashes. He blinked, and she started to laugh.

“What?”

“You look so serious.”

“I’m cold.”

“That’s different.”

She brushed a flake off his cheekbone with her thumb and left her thumb there. Behind her the street went away under white: wooden houses with deep porches, bare trees holding the snow along every branch as if someone had piped it on, the pavement glittering under the streetlights in the four o’clock dark.

“You’ve never seen snow properly,” she said.

“I’ve seen snow.”

“Not like this.”

He looked down the street. “No. Not like this,” he admitted.

“Welcome to Vancouver,” said Isla, and took his hand, and led him up the steps of the house she’d grown up in.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father opened the door: tall, silver at the temples, a green cardigan with leather on the elbows, reading glasses pushed up into his hair and forgotten there. He pulled Isla into a hug on the doorstep, snow and all, and then held her at arm’s length.

“You’re thin.”

“I’m not thin, Dad.”

“You look thin.”

“You’re comparing me to when I was nineteen.”

“I remember exactly what you looked like at nineteen. Song Wei Long. We’ve spoken on a screen for two and a half years. It’s good to see the rest of you,” said her father, and turned to Wei Long, and held out his hand.

“Professor Ren. Thank you for having me.”

“Please don’t call me sir.”

“I didn’t.”

“You were about to,” said her father, delighted, exactly as he had on a laptop two and a half years ago, and Isla’s mother appeared behind him in the hall, small and quick, with Isla’s eyes and a voice made for lecture theatres, and said, “Let them in, it’s minus eight,” and kissed her daughter, and then looked up at Wei Long and put both her hands on his arms.

“Inspector.”

“Professor.”

“Not at the dinner table. Anywhere else, if you must,” said her mother.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was an education. Her father taught literature and her mother political science, and between them they could turn any remark into a conversation that needed a reading list. Wei Long had been ready for questions. He hadn’t been ready for her mother to ask him, over the soup, whether he thought justice was fundamentally an institution or a personal virtue.

He answered carefully. Her mother listened. Then her father asked a follow-up. Then her mother disagreed with her father. Under the table, Isla found his hand and gripped it, and mouthed sorry at the salt cellar.

“But surely you can’t separate the individual officer from the institution,” said her father.

“No. But the institution still has to answer for what it does to the individual. Even when the individual is right,” said Wei Long.

There was a short silence. Her mother smiled. Her father found his glasses in his hair and looked at Wei Long through them.

“Good,” he said.

Isla, under the table, squeezed his fingers. He knew what that meant. He’d survived the interrogation.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning she found him in the kitchen in his socks, contemplating a plate of biscuits on the counter: stars, trees, snowflakes, and one brown moose with white icing antlers and a crooked smile.

“What’s this?”

“A moose.”

“I know it’s a moose. Why is there a moose?”

“Because we’re in Canada.”

“Is the moose associated with Christmas?”

“Not traditionally.”

“Then...”

“Because it’s cute,” said Isla, and he looked at the moose and then broke off one of its antlers and ate it.

She stared at him. “You’ve injured it.”

“It’s a biscuit.”

“It’s a Christmas moose.”

“It’s still a biscuit,” he said, and she took the rest of it out of his hand and ate it herself, to spare it further suffering, and he kissed her with sugar on her mouth just as her mother came in with the coffee.

“Good morning. I’ve made another forty,” said her mother, looking at the empty space on the plate.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao and Song-Zhu arrived on Christmas Eve in a hire car, with two bags, a bottle of wine and enough noise to announce them from the end of the street.

“I’m here. I missed you,” shouted Ren Hao in the hall, and hugged his sister, lifting her off the floor.

“You saw me a week ago.”

“I missed you since then.”

Wei Long took the bag off the bottom stair before Ren Hao fell over it.

“Still carrying everyone’s things, Inspector? Good. You’re useful,” said Ren Hao, and went to find his father.

Song-Zhu kissed Isla’s cheek. “He’s been like this since the airport. I nearly left him at a petrol station.”

Within an hour Ren Hao was in the kitchen arguing with his father about a novel neither of them had finished, and Wei Long had been given a box of decorations to carry upstairs.

He was halfway along the upstairs hall when he heard Song-Zhu’s voice through the half-open door of the little study at the end.

“Professor? Both of you? Can I ask you something? It’s private.”

There was a pause. Then Isla’s mother, with great interest: “Oh?”

He kept walking. He had no intention of listening. The hall was narrow, and the house old, and the door open.

“I want to propose to Hao,” said Song-Zhu.

He stopped. Then he put the box down on the landing table and didn’t pick it up again.

“Oh, that’s lovely,” said Isla’s mother, and her voice had gone thick.

“I didn’t know if you’d think it was strange.”

“Why would it be strange?” said her father.

“Because we stopped. Last year. For four months. I couldn’t say it to him, and he couldn’t stop trying to fix it, and we stopped. We’re better now than we’ve ever been. I know I want my whole life with him. But I don’t want him to think I’m asking to make up for that. I don’t want it to be an apology. I want it to be the start of something.” Song-Zhu’s voice went lower.

“Then don’t make it an apology. Make it a question,” said Isla’s mother.

“I thought that’s what a proposal was.”

“You’d be amazed,” said her father, dryly, “how many people turn it into a lecture on their own history.”

Her mother said, “Ask him, because you want to begin something. Not because you want to prove you’d have chosen differently. He’ll hear the difference. He’s always heard everything.”

Wei Long looked at the box of ornaments on the landing table. He thought about a custody desk, and three folded pages, and seventeen paragraphs that had been mostly about the past, and a woman who’d said yes into his collar before he’d got to the end of any of it.

Downstairs, he heard Isla’s mother start to cry, and her husband say something gentle, and Song-Zhu laugh, wetly.

He picked the box up, and carried it to the end of the landing, and never told anyone he’d heard a word.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found Isla on the floor of her childhood bedroom with a shoebox of photographs. Isla at ten with a missing front tooth and a library card held up to the camera like a passport. Isla at fifteen next to a noticeboard of school prizes with an expression of profound fury.

“You look unhappy.”

“I came second.”

He considered this. “Understandable.”

She laughed and leaned against his shoulder and went through them one by one, and he listened to every story, the funny ones and the ones that made her stop before she finished. On the inside of the wardrobe door, in faded pencil, there was a ladder of lines with dates beside them, from a hand-high line at the bottom to one just under his chin.

“My mother measured me every Christmas,” said Isla, “until I left.”

“May I?”

She looked at him. Then she found a pencil on the desk. He stood with his back to the door while she tugged him down and ruled a line above his head, and wrote beside it, in her small round hand, W.L. 2027.

“That’s unfair. You’re much too tall,” she said, looking at the gap between her last line and his.

“Shall I bend?”

“No,” said Isla, and slid her arms round him, and the snow went on falling past the window.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was nearly midnight when they went to bed. Her parents had retired. Ren Hao and Song-Zhu were across the landing, and the old house ticked and settled round them, the heating clanking somewhere in the walls.

She came up behind him at the window in his shirt with the sleeves rolled twice.

“Still cold?”

“No.”

“Liar. What?” He turned round in her arms. She looked up at him.

“Nothing. I like looking at you. In this room. I didn’t know this room.” He touched her cheek.

“Now you do,” she said, and kissed him.

It began slowly. When she drew back he followed, and she smiled against his mouth.

“My parents are downstairs.”

“I know.”

“Hao is across the landing. Hao hears everything.”

“I know.”

“So. We’ll have to be quiet,” said Isla, under her breath.

They were. He undid the buttons of the shirt she was wearing, his shirt, one at a time, in the dark, and pushed it off her shoulders, and kissed every place he uncovered while she bit her lip. She pushed him down onto the narrow bed she’d slept in at sixteen and the springs complained, once, and they both froze, and she put her hand over her mouth to keep the laugh in. He took her wrist and drew her hand away and kissed the inside of it, and then put his own hand gently over her mouth instead, and looked at her above it until she nodded. Then he went down the bed with his mouth, slowly, and she arched under him in silence with her own fist pressed against her lips and her other hand in his hair, and when she came it was without a sound, shaking, her eyes wide open on the ceiling of the room she’d grown up in.

She pulled him up. She was the one who put her hand over his mouth then, smiling, as he came into her, and he closed his eyes and breathed against her palm. They moved together on the narrow bed as slowly as it allowed, with the snow ticking at the window and the heating clanking in the wall, and every time the springs began to speak they stopped, and waited, and laughed without any noise, and began again. When he came he did it with his face pressed into her neck and her palm still over his mouth and her other hand spread on his back, holding him there.

They lay together afterwards in the dark in a bed too small for one, and outside Vancouver went on snowing.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning there was a small box beside his watch on the bedside table. She found it before she’d opened her eyes properly.

“What’s that?”

“For you.”

“Why didn’t you give it to me last night?”

“You were occupied,” said Wei Long, and she covered her face with both hands.

Inside, on blue velvet, was a silver bookmark, long and thin, engraved along its length in his square capitals: FOR ALL THE BOOKS THAT MADE YOU. She ran her thumb along the words.

“You remembered. The library,” she said.

“You told me. Once, in the car.”

“That was two years ago.”

“I wrote it down,” he said, and she put the bookmark on the pillow and kissed him, and this time didn’t try to be quiet at all.

At breakfast her mother had made pancakes and her father was reading the paper and Ren Hao was stealing from Song-Zhu’s plate, which Song-Zhu allowed, watching Isla’s mother over her coffee with the look of someone turning a piece of advice over and over in her hands. A moose biscuit had been placed, without comment, on Wei Long’s plate.

“Your friend,” said Isla.

“It’s not my friend.”

“You ate its brother.”

He broke off an antler.

Her father looked over the top of the paper. “I hope you’re enjoying the biscuits, Inspector. Your future mother-in-law has made eighty.”

Isla choked on her coffee. Ren Hao looked up with his mouth full. Her mother didn’t look up at all.

“It’s only a matter of time,” she said serenely, and passed Wei Long the syrup.
